## Sources

<!-- Added 2026-05-23: Designing Machine Learning Systems (Chip Huyen; O'Reilly 2022) — full 11-chapter book ingest. Predecessor to [[ai-engineering-chip-huyen]] (2024); same author, broader scope (classical ML + DL production systems, pre-LLM era). -->
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 1: Overview of Machine Learning Systems](sources/dmls-ch01-overview.md) — [[ChipHuyen|Chip Huyen]] frames an ML system as algorithm + data + interface + infrastructure + ops; defines when (not) to use ML; surveys consumer vs. enterprise use cases; contrasts ML in research vs. production across stakeholders, computational priorities, data, fairness, and interpretability.
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 2: Introduction to Machine Learning Systems Design](sources/dmls-ch02-intro-design.md) — Business-to-ML objective translation, the four system requirements ([[Reliability]] / [[Scalability]] / [[Maintainability]] / [[Adaptability]]), the iterative six-step ML lifecycle, problem framing as inputs/outputs/objective, decoupling-vs-Pareto for multi-objective ranking, and the mind-vs-data debate.
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 3: Data Engineering Fundamentals](sources/dmls-ch03-data-engineering.md) — Data sources, serialization formats ([[JSON]] / [[CSVFormat|CSV]] / [[Parquet]] / [[Protobuf]] / [[Avro]] / [[Pickle]]), relational / [[DocumentModel|document]] / [[GraphModel|graph]] data models, [[OLTP]] vs. [[OLAP]] (and their convergence), [[ETL]] / [[ELT]], request-driven vs. event-driven dataflow, and batch vs. stream processing.
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 4: Training Data](sources/dmls-ch04-training-data.md) — Sampling (probability vs. non-probability families incl. [[ReservoirSampling|reservoir]] / [[importancesampling|importance]] / [[StratifiedSampling|stratified]]), labeling (hand-labels / [[NaturalLabel|natural]] / [[WeakSupervision|weak supervision]] via [[Snorkel]] / [[SemiSupervisedLearning|semi-supervised]] / [[TransferLearning|transfer]] / [[ActiveLearning|active learning]]), [[ClassImbalance|class imbalance]] (resampling, [[FocalLoss|focal]] / class-balanced loss), and [[DataAugmentation|data augmentation]] (label-preserving / [[Perturbation|perturbation]] / synthesis incl. [[Mixup]] / [[CycleGAN]]).
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 5: Feature Engineering](sources/dmls-ch05-feature-engineering.md) — Feature operations ([[Imputation|missing values]], [[FeatureScaling|scaling]], [[Discretization|discretization]], categorical encoding via the [[HashingTrick|hashing trick]], [[FeatureCrossing|feature crossing]], [[positionalencoding|positional embeddings]]), [[DataLeakage|data leakage]] (six causes incl. random-splitting time-correlated data, scaling before splitting, group leakage, COVID-imaging case), and what makes a "good" feature ([[FeatureImportance|importance]] + [[FeatureGeneralization|generalization]]).
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 6: Model Development and Offline Evaluation](sources/dmls-ch06-model-development.md) — Model-selection heuristics (avoid SOTA, start simple, beware human biases), [[ModelEnsemble|ensembling]] ([[Bagging|bagging]] / [[Boosting|boosting]] / [[Stacking|stacking]]; 20-of-22 Kaggle 2021 winners), [[ExperimentTracking|experiment tracking]] + [[Versioning|versioning]], [[DistributedTraining|distributed training]] (data / model / pipeline parallelism; gradient staleness), [[AutoML|AutoML]] (soft + hard incl. [[NeuralArchitectureSearch|NAS]] and [[LearnedOptimizer|learned optimizers]]), and offline evaluation ([[ZeroRuleBaseline|baselines]], [[PerturbationTest|perturbation]] / [[InvarianceTest|invariance]] / [[DirectionalExpectationTest|directional]] tests, [[ModelCalibration|calibration]], [[ConfidenceMeasurement|confidence]] measurement, [[DataSlicing|slice-based evaluation]] + [[SimpsonsParadox|Simpson's paradox]]).
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 7: Model Deployment and Prediction Service](sources/dmls-ch07-model-deployment.md) — Four [[MLDeploymentMyths|deployment myths]], [[BatchInference|batch]] vs. [[OnlineInference|online]] vs. [[StreamingPrediction|streaming]] prediction (Grubhub counterexample to "batch is cheaper"), cloud vs. [[EdgeComputing|edge]], [[ModelCompression|compression]] ([[Quantization|quantization]] / [[Pruning|pruning]] / [[KnowledgeDistillation|distillation]] / [[LowRankFactorization|low-rank factorization]] incl. Roblox BERT-on-CPU 7× latency / DistilBERT 40%-smaller-60%-faster-97%-capability), compilers + [[IntermediateRepresentation|IRs]] + lowering, [[AutoTVM|autoTVM]], and ML-in-the-browser via [[WebAssembly]].
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 8: Data Distribution Shifts and Monitoring](sources/dmls-ch08-distribution-shifts-monitoring.md) — Taxonomy of ML failure modes (software bugs vs. ML-specific: production-data discrepancy, [[EdgeCase|edge cases]], [[DegenerateFeedbackLoop|degenerate feedback loops]]), formal treatment of [[CovariateShift|covariate]] / [[LabelShift|label]] / [[ConceptShift|concept]] shift, drift-detection methods ([[KolmogorovSmirnovTest|KS]] / [[MaximumMeanDiscrepancy|MMD]] / [[LeastSquaresDensityDifference|LSDD]]), and the monitoring/[[observability|observability]] playbook (logs / dashboards / alerts, [[AlertFatigue|alert fatigue]], the four-artifact framing: raw inputs → features → predictions → accuracy).
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 9: Continual Learning and Test in Production](sources/dmls-ch09-continual-learning.md) — [[StatefulTraining|Stateful]] vs. [[StatelessRetraining|stateless]] retraining (Grubhub 45× compute reduction); the four-stage continual-learning maturity model; [[NaturalLabels|natural labels]] and [[FeedbackLoopLength|feedback-loop length]]; [[ContinuousColdStart|continuous cold start]]; [[FeatureReuseLogAndWait|log-and-wait]] feature reuse; and test-in-production ([[ShadowDeployment|shadow deployment]], [[ABTesting|A/B testing]], [[CanaryDeployment|canary release]], [[InterleavingExperiments|interleaving experiments]], [[MultiArmedBandits|bandits]] + [[ThompsonSampling|Thompson Sampling]] + [[ContextualBandits|contextual bandits]]).
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 10: Infrastructure and Tooling for MLOps](sources/dmls-ch10-infrastructure-mlops.md) — Huyen's four-layer infrastructure model (storage/[[ComputeLayer|compute]] → resource management → [[MLPlatform|ML platform]] → dev environment), [[Cron|schedulers]] vs. [[Orchestrator|orchestrators]], workflow managers ([[Airflow]] / [[Prefect]] / [[ArgoWorkflows]] / [[Kubeflow]] / [[Metaflow]]), [[ModelStore|model stores]] (the 8 artifacts) + [[ModelDeployment|deployment services]] + [[FeatureStore|feature stores]] ([[Feast]] / [[Tecton]] / [[Amundsen]] / [[DataHub]]), [[Jupyter|Jupyter]] + [[Papermill]] + [[Commuter]] dev environments, [[MultiCloud|multicloud]] + [[CloudRepatriation|cloud repatriation]] ([[Dropbox]] $75M case), and build-vs-buy.
- [Designing Machine Learning Systems — Ch 11: The Human Side of Machine Learning](sources/dmls-ch11-human-side.md) — UX trade-offs ([[ConsistencyAccuracyTradeoff|consistency vs. accuracy]], [[SpeedAccuracyTradeoff|speed vs. accuracy]] via [[SmoothFailing|smooth failing]] with a [[BackupModel|backup model]], [[MostlyCorrectPredictions|mostly-correct]] predictions presented as [[MultipleCandidatePredictions|multiple candidates]]); team structure ([[SubjectMatterExpert|SMEs]] as developers across the lifecycle; [[EndToEndDataScientist|end-to-end DS]] vs. [[FullCycleDeveloper|full-cycle developer]] debate); and [[ResponsibleAI|Responsible AI]] (the [[OfqualGradingAlgorithm|Ofqual A-level]] and [[StravaHeatmap|Strava heatmap]] case studies, six-step practitioner framework, [[ModelCard|model cards]], compactness-fairness ([[Pruning|pruning]] > [[Quantization|quantization]] on disparate impact) and privacy-accuracy trade-offs).

- [AI Engineering: Building Applications with Foundation Models](sources/ai-engineering-chip-huyen.md) — **[[ChipHuyen|Chip Huyen]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], December 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-16630-4).** The wiki's **first end-to-end AI-engineering textbook** — practical, framework-oriented guide that positions [[AIEngineering|AI engineering]] as a distinct discipline from traditional ML engineering: it works *with* readily available [[FoundationModel|foundation models]] rather than building models from scratch. Covers the full AI application development process across 10 chapters: foundation-model internals → evaluation methodology → prompt engineering → context construction ([[rag|RAG]] / [[Agent|agents]]) → [[FineTuning|finetuning]] → [[DatasetEngineering|dataset engineering]] → [[InferenceOptimization|inference optimization]] → architecture & user feedback. Anchors the **start-simple discipline** (prompt before RAG, RAG before agents, prompt before finetuning, finetuning before training-from-scratch) and frames **evaluation as the hardest part of AI engineering** (two full chapters out of ten). Per-chapter source pages mint **545 new concept pages** and **156 new entity pages** while updating ~250 existing pages in place; touches almost every concept the wiki already has individual paper-level entries for ([[rag]], [[Agent]], [[lora]], [[MIPROv2]], [[chainofthought]], [[react]], [[selfconsistency]], [[Hallucination]]). The 10 chapter source pages are listed individually below.
- [AI Engineering Ch 1 — Introduction to Building AI Applications with Foundation Models](sources/ai-engineering-ch01-intro.md) — Defines [[AIEngineering]] vs ML engineering, walks foundation-model use cases (coding, image/video, writing, education, conversational bots, info aggregation, data organization, workflow automation), the planning framework (use-case evaluation, critical-or-complementary, dynamic-or-static, reactive-or-proactive, build-vs-buy), and the [[AIEngineeringStack]]. Mints [[AIEngineering]], [[FoundationModel]], [[ModelAsAService]], [[PromptEngineering]], [[ModelAdaptation]], [[CrawlWalkRun]] + 30 more concepts and 28 entities.
- [AI Engineering Ch 2 — Understanding Foundation Models](sources/ai-engineering-ch02-foundation-models.md) — Training data ([[CommonCrawl]], [[MultilingualModel]], [[DomainSpecificModel]]), architecture ([[transformer]] alternatives — [[Mamba]] / [[Jamba]] / [[RWKV]] / [[StateSpaceModel]]), scale ([[ChinchillaScalingLaw]], [[ComputeOptimal]], [[EmergentAbilities]], [[InverseScaling]], [[ScalingBottlenecks]]), post-training ([[SupervisedFinetuning]], [[PreferenceFinetuning]], [[rlhf]], [[DirectPreferenceOptimization|DPO]], [[PPO]], [[RewardModel]]), sampling ([[Temperature]], [[Topk]], [[Topp]], [[MinP]], [[StructuredOutputs]], [[ConstrainedSampling]], [[TestTimeCompute]], [[Verifier]]), and probabilistic-output failure modes ([[Inconsistency]], [[Hallucination]] hypotheses, [[SnowballingHallucination]], [[InternalKnowledgeMismatch]]).
- [AI Engineering Ch 3 — Evaluation Methodology](sources/ai-engineering-ch03-evaluation-methodology.md) — Language-modeling metrics ([[Perplexity]], [[CrossEntropy]], [[BitsPerCharacter]], [[BitsPerByte]]), [[ExactEvaluation]] (functional correctness, [[NGramSimilarity]] — [[bleu]] / [[ROUGE]] / [[METEOR]] / [[CIDEr]] / [[TER]]; [[SemanticSimilarity]] — [[BERTScore]] / [[MoverScore]] / [[BLEURT]]; [[FuzzyMatching]], [[EditDistance]]), [[llmasjudge|AI-as-a-judge]] ([[PointwiseEvaluation]] / [[ReferenceBasedJudge]] / [[ReferenceFreeMetric]] / [[SelfEvaluation]] / [[SelfBiasJudge]] / [[VerbosityBias]] / [[RecencyBias]]), and [[ComparativeEvaluation]] ([[EloRating]] / [[BradleyTerry]] / [[TrueSkill]] / [[ChatbotArena]] / [[WinRate]] / [[TransitivityAssumption]]).
- [AI Engineering Ch 4 — Evaluate AI Systems](sources/ai-engineering-ch04-evaluate-ai-systems.md) — Evaluation criteria ([[DomainSpecificCapability]], [[GenerationCapability]], [[FactualConsistency]], [[safety]], [[InstructionFollowingCapability]], [[CostAndLatency]]), [[ModelSelection]] ([[ModelBuildVsBuy]], [[OpenWeight]] / [[OpenSourceModel]] / [[CommercialModel]], [[HardModelAttribute]] / [[SoftModelAttribute]], [[Leaderboard]] / [[OpenLLMLeaderboard]] / [[HELMLite]] / [[ChatbotArena]]), [[EvaluationPipeline]] design, [[DataSlicing]], [[SimpsonsParadox]], [[BootstrapEvaluation]], and [[DataContamination]] / [[BenchmarkDecontamination]]. Lifts [[safety]], [[factuality]], [[mmlu]], [[gpqa]], [[ifeval]] from stub to full pages.
- [AI Engineering Ch 5 — Prompt Engineering](sources/ai-engineering-ch05-prompt-engineering.md) — Foundations ([[InContextLearning]], [[SystemPrompt]] / [[UserPrompt]], [[InstructionHierarchy]], [[PromptTemplate]], [[ChatTemplate]], [[NeedleInAHaystack]], [[MiddleContextDegradation]], [[PromptStructure]], [[PromptRobustness]]), best practices ([[chainofthought]], [[selfconsistency]], [[PromptDecomposition]], [[Persona]], [[Roleplaying]], [[PromptIteration]]), [[DefensivePromptEngineering]] ([[PromptAttack]] taxonomy: [[PromptExtraction]] / [[ReversePromptEngineering]] / [[promptinjection]] / [[IndirectPromptInjection]] / [[Jailbreak]] / [[DANJailbreak]] / [[GrandmaExploit]] / [[PAIR]] / [[Obfuscation]] / [[OutputFormatManipulation]] / [[FactualProbing]] / [[TrainingDataExtraction]] / [[DivergenceAttack]] / [[CopyrightRegurgitation]]) + defenses ([[PromptSandwich]], [[InputGuardrail]] / [[OutputGuardrail]], [[Isolation]], [[HumanInTheLoopApproval]], [[UsagePatternMonitoring]], [[LLMRedTeaming]], [[AdvBench]], [[PromptRobustnessBenchmark]]).
- [AI Engineering Ch 6 — RAG and Agents](sources/ai-engineering-ch06-rag-agents.md) — [[rag|RAG]] mechanics ([[TermBasedRetrieval]] / [[BM25]] / [[TFIDF]] / [[InvertedIndex]] / [[SPLADE]]; [[EmbeddingBasedRetrieval]] + [[ApproximateNearestNeighbor|ANN]] — [[HNSW]] / [[LSH]] / [[ProductQuantization]] / [[IVF]] / [[Annoy]] / [[FAISS]] / [[ScaNN]] / [[Hnswlib]]; [[HybridSearch]] + [[ReciprocalRankFusion]]; [[ChunkingStrategy]] families; retrieval eval — [[ContextPrecision]] / [[ContextRecall]] / [[NDCG]] / [[MAP]] / [[MRR]] / [[BEIRBenchmark]] / [[ANNBenchmarks]]; [[QueryRewriting]], [[ContextualRetrieval]], [[MultimodalRAG]], [[RAGOverTabularData]], [[TextToSQL]]) + [[Agent]] discipline ([[ToolInventory]], [[FunctionCalling]], [[KnowledgeAugmentation]] / [[CapabilityExtension]] / [[WriteAction]], [[Planning]], [[CompoundErrorAccumulation]], [[PlanningGranularity]], [[IntentClassifier]], [[reflexion]], [[BerkeleyFunctionCallingLeaderboard]], [[TravelPlannerBenchmark]], [[Toolformer]] / [[Gorilla]] / [[Chameleon]] / [[SWEAgent]] / [[VoyagerAgent]]) + memory hierarchy ([[ShortTermMemory]] / [[LongTermMemory]] / [[InternalKnowledgeMemory]] / [[FIFOMemory]] / [[SummarizationMemory]] / [[ReflectionMemory]]).
- [AI Engineering Ch 7 — Finetuning](sources/ai-engineering-ch07-finetuning.md) — When to finetune vs RAG vs prompting; memory math (model / gradient / optimizer-state / [[ActivationMemory]]; [[BF16]] / [[FloatingPoint]] / [[AutomaticMixedPrecision]]; [[ActivationRecomputation]]; [[Quantization]] families); [[PEFT]] techniques ([[lora|LoRA]] / [[QLoRA]] / adapters / prefix tuning / prompt tuning / [[BitFit]]); [[ModelMerging]] ([[TaskVector]] / [[TIES]] / [[DARE]]); finetuning tactics (data curation, [[BatchSize]] / learning rate, [[knowledgedistillation]], [[CatastrophicForgetting]], [[AlignmentTax]], [[BiasMitigationFinetuning]], [[BehaviorBasedFailure]]).
- [AI Engineering Ch 8 — Dataset Engineering](sources/ai-engineering-ch08-dataset-engineering.md) — Data curation ([[DataQuality]] six-characteristics framework, [[DataQuantity]] / [[DataCoverage]] / [[DataDiversity]] / [[DataMix]] / [[DataAdditionDilemma]] / [[DataPruning]] / [[DataFlywheel]] / [[DataAcquisition]] / [[DataAnnotation]] / [[AnnotationGuidelines]]), [[DataAugmentation]] ([[Backtranslation]] / [[Perturbation]] / [[OnePixelAttack]] / [[CodeBackTranslation]]), [[DataSynthesis]] ([[AIPoweredDataSynthesis]], [[InstructionDataSynthesis]], [[ReverseInstruction]], [[RuleBasedDataSynthesis]], [[Simulation]] / [[Sim2Real]] / [[SelfPlay]], [[ProceduralGeneration]], canonical synthetic datasets — [[UltraChat]] / [[MetaMath]] / [[Cosmopedia]] / [[AlphaGeometry]] / [[StableToolBench]]), and [[DataDeduplication]] ([[BloomFilter]] / [[MinHashDeduplication]]). Names [[ModelCollapse]], [[SuperficialImitation]], [[Ossification]] as the AI-data-lineage risks.
- [AI Engineering Ch 9 — Inference Optimization](sources/ai-engineering-ch09-inference-optimization.md) — The book's most quantitative chapter. Fundamentals ([[ComputeBound]] vs [[MemoryBandwidthBound]], [[ArithmeticIntensity]], [[RooflineModel]], [[MFU]] / [[MBU]], [[Goodput]], [[TTFT]] / [[TPOT]] / [[TBT]] / [[TimeToPublish]], [[GPUUtilization]] critique); model-level ([[ModelCompression]] — [[Quantization]] / [[knowledgedistillation]] / [[Pruning]] / [[LowRankFactorization]], [[Sparsity]], attention optimizations — [[KVCache]] / [[multiqueryattention|MQA]] / [[GroupedQueryAttention|GQA]] / [[PagedAttention]] / [[CrossLayerAttention]] / [[LocalAttention]], [[SpeculativeDecoding]] / [[InferenceWithReference]] / [[ParallelDecoding]] / [[LookaheadDecoding]] / [[JacobiDecoding]] / [[MedusaDecoding]], [[PrefillDecodeDisaggregation]] / [[DistServe]]); service-level ([[Batching]] families — [[StaticBatching]] / [[DynamicBatching]] / [[ContinuousBatching]], [[PromptCaching]], [[MultiLoraServing]], [[ReplicaParallelism]] / [[ContextParallelism]] / [[SequenceParallelism]], [[Compiler]] stack — [[Triton]] / [[ROCm]] / [[TVM]] / [[MLIR]] / [[XLA]] / [[OperatorFusion]] / [[LoopTiling]]); accelerators ([[AIAccelerator]] taxonomy, [[GoogleTPU]] / [[Inferentia]] / [[MTIA]] / [[AppleNeuralEngine]], plus new entities [[AMD]] / [[Cerebras]] / [[Groq]] / [[Graphcore]]).
- [AI Engineering Ch 10 — AI Engineering Architecture and User Feedback](sources/ai-engineering-ch10-architecture-feedback.md) — Reference architecture (additive — [[ContextConstruction]] → [[Guardrail]] / [[InputGuardrail]] / [[OutputGuardrail]] → [[ModelGateway]] / [[ModelRouter]] → [[ExactCache]] / [[SemanticCache]] / [[PIIReverseDictionary]] → [[AIPipelineOrchestration]] → [[WriteAction]] → [[observability]] / [[Monitoring]] / [[RequestTrace]] / [[MTTD]] / [[MTTR]] / [[ChangeFailureRate]] / [[DriftDetection]] / [[SilentModelUpdate]]); [[ExplicitFeedback]] / [[ImplicitFeedback]] taxonomy ([[ConversationalFeedback]] / [[NaturalLanguageFeedback]] / [[ImplicitConversationalSignal]] / [[ErrorCorrection]] / [[RephraseAttempt]] / [[ActionCorrectingFeedback]] / [[UserEditFeedback]] / [[RegenerationSignal]] / [[InpaintingFeedback]] / [[FITSDataset]]); feedback failure modes ([[LeniencyBias]] / [[PositionBias]] / [[PreferenceBias]] / [[DegenerateFeedbackLoop]] / [[Sycophancy]]).

<!-- Added 2026-05-23 / extended 2026-05-24: Hands-On Large Language Models (Alammar & Grootendorst; O'Reilly 2024) — Chs 1-12 (full book). -->
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 12: Fine-Tuning Generation Models](sources/hands-on-llm-ch12-fine-tuning-generation-models.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** **Final chapter of the book; third chapter of Part III ("Training and Fine-Tuning Language Models")** — the generative-model counterpart to [[hands-on-llm-ch11-fine-tuning-representation-models|Ch 11]] (representation models), and the runnable-code resolution of [[hands-on-llm-ch01-introduction-to-llms|Ch 1]]'s *"forward-reference Ch 12 for fine-tuning generative models with RLHF / DPO"* promise. Walks the **two-stage fine-tuning pipeline for generative LLMs** end-to-end on [[TinyLlama|TinyLlama-1.1B]] using the Hugging Face stack ([[transformers]] + [[peft|PEFT]] + [[bitsandbytes]] + [[trl|TRL]]). **Stage 1 — [[SupervisedFinetuning|SFT]]** via [[QLoRA]]: 4-bit NF4 quantization ([[BitsAndBytesConfig|`BitsAndBytesConfig`]] — `load_in_4bit=True`, `bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4"`, `bnb_4bit_compute_dtype="float16"`, `bnb_4bit_use_double_quant=True`) + [[lora|LoRA]] adapter ([[LoraConfig|`LoraConfig`]] — `r=64`, `α=32`, `lora_dropout=0.1`, `bias="none"`, `task_type="CAUSAL_LM"`, `target_modules=["k_proj","gate_proj","v_proj","up_proj","q_proj","o_proj","down_proj"]` — all 7 Llama-family projection layers) + [[SFTTrainer|`trl.SFTTrainer`]] on 3,000 [[UltraChat|UltraChat 200k]] examples formatted in TinyLlama's `<|user|>...<|assistant|>` [[ChatTemplate|chat template]]; `optim="paged_adamw_32bit"`, `lr=2e-4`, `lr_scheduler_type="cosine"`, `num_train_epochs=1`, `fp16=True`, `gradient_checkpointing=True`, `per_device_train_batch_size=2`, `gradient_accumulation_steps=4`. Single-epoch SFT ≈ **1 hour on a free Google Colab Tesla T4**; loaded base uses ~1 GB VRAM (vs ~4 GB FP16). Merge via [[AutoPeftModelForCausalLM|`peft.AutoPeftModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(...).merge_and_unload()`]]. **Stage 2 — [[PreferenceFinetuning|Preference Tuning]]** via [[DPO]]: same QLoRA config applied via [[DPOTrainer|`trl.DPOTrainer`]] + [[DPOConfig|`trl.DPOConfig`]] on `argilla/distilabel-intel-orca-dpo-pairs` (~6,000 filtered `prompt + chosen + rejected` triples; filter: `status != "tie"`, `chosen_score >= 8`, `not in_gsm8k_train`); `beta=0.1`, `learning_rate=1e-5` (10× lower than SFT), `lr_scheduler_type="cosine"`, `max_steps=200`, `warmup_ratio=0.1`, `max_prompt_length=512`, `max_length=512`. Iterative adapter merging: merge SFT adapter into base → merge DPO adapter into SFT-merged model. **PEFT framing**: Houlsby et al. 2019 [[adapterlayers|adapters]] (fine-tuning 3.6% of BERT's parameters → within 0.4% of full FT on [[GLUE]]) + AdapterHub + LLaMA-Adapter as the adapter family; [[lora|LoRA]] (Hu et al. 2021, justified by [[IntrinsicDimension|intrinsic dimension]] — Aghajanyan, Zettlemoyer & Gupta 2020, arXiv:2012.13255) as the dominant alternative — *"two smaller matrices reconstruct one larger matrix"* — anchored in the GPT-3 175B 12,288×12,288 rank-8 → 197K-params-per-block example. **QLoRA innovations** (Dettmers et al. 2023, arXiv:2305.14314) walked operationally: [[BlockwiseQuantization|blockwise quantization]] (per-block quantization constants) + [[NormalFloat4|NF4]] (bin original weights by relative density to a normal distribution between –1 and 1) + [[DoubleQuantization|double quantization]] + [[PagedOptimizer|paged optimizers]] ([[PagedAdamW32bit|`paged_adamw_32bit`]]). **Reward-model + [[PPO]] baseline** explained as the algorithm DPO replaces: [[RewardModel|reward model]] = SFT-initialized model with language-modeling head replaced by a scalar quality head; `prompt + chosen + rejected` triples → train `score(chosen) > score(rejected)`; Llama 2's **two-reward-model design** (helpfulness + safety) surfaced as the canonical multi-objective receipt. **[[DPO]]** mechanism: no reward model, no RL loop — compare trainable model against a frozen **reference model**, compute the **token-level log-probability shift** between them on chosen vs rejected, optimize trainable to be more confident on chosen / less confident on rejected. Forward-looks at [[ORPO]] (Hong, Lee & Thorne 2024, arXiv:2403.07691) as the SFT + DPO collapse into a single training pass. **Generative-LLM evaluation primer**: word-level metrics ([[Perplexity]] / [[ROUGE]] / [[bleu|BLEU]] / [[BERTScore]] — limitations *"do not account for consistency, fluency, creativity, or even correctness"*); public benchmarks (Table 12-1: [[MMLU]] / [[GSM8K]] / [[HellaSwag]] / [[TruthfulQA]] / [[HumanEval]] / [[GLUE]]); leaderboards ([[OpenLLMLeaderboard|Open LLM Leaderboard]]); [[LLMAsAJudge|LLM-as-a-judge]] (Zheng et al. NeurIPS 2024 — MT-Bench / Chatbot Arena); human evaluation via [[ChatbotArena|Chatbot Arena]] (Chiang et al. 2024, arXiv:2403.04132) — crowdsourced pairwise preferences → [[EloRating|Elo]] over 800k+ votes; [[GoodhartsLaw|Goodhart's Law]] (Strathern 1997) as the evaluation-discipline parable; *"you are the best evaluator"* with Alammar (Arabic) + Grootendorst (Dutch) native-language-eval anecdote. **Mints 3 new pages**: entities — [[transformers]] (Hugging Face library) / [[HuggingFacePEFT]] / [[HuggingFaceTRL]]. **Completes the 12-chapter ingest of *Hands-On Large Language Models*** — the wiki's third fully-ingested LLM book after [[ai-engineering-chip-huyen|*AI Engineering* (Huyen, O'Reilly 2024)]] and [[LLMEngineersHandbook|*LLM Engineer's Handbook* (Iusztin, Labonne & Vesa, Packt 2024)]].
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 11: Fine-Tuning Representation Models for Classification](sources/hands-on-llm-ch11-fine-tuning-representation-models.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** **Second chapter of Part III** (after [[hands-on-llm-ch10-creating-text-embedding-models|Ch 10]]) — the runnable-code resolution of [[hands-on-llm-ch01-introduction-to-llms|Ch 1]]'s *"forward-reference Ch 11 for fine-tuning representation models"* promise. Walks **four fine-tuning regimes for BERT-class encoders** on the same [[RottenTomatoes|rotten_tomatoes]] / [[CoNLL2003]] datasets: **(1)** full supervised fine-tuning of `bert-base-cased` via [[HuggingFace|Hugging Face]] [[Trainer|`Trainer`]] + [[DataCollatorWithPadding]] → **F1 = 0.85** (beats [[hands-on-llm-ch04-text-classification|Ch 4]]'s frozen 0.80); **(2)** [[LayerFreezing|layer freezing]] variants — freeze-everything-but-head F1 = 0.63, freeze-blocks-0–9 F1 = 0.80; *"training only the first five encoder blocks is enough to almost reach the performance of training all encoder blocks"*; **(3)** **[[SetFit]]** (Tunstall et al. 2022, arXiv:2209.11055) for **few-shot classification** — three-step pipeline (in-class/out-class pair sampling → [[ContrastiveLearning|contrastive]] [[SentenceTransformers|SentenceTransformer]] fine-tuning → classifier head; default [[LogisticRegression]]); 32 labels → F1 = 0.85, matching the full-data baseline; **(4)** [[ContinuedPretraining|continued pretraining]] with [[MaskedLanguageModel|MLM]] via `AutoModelForMaskedLM` + [[DataCollatorForLanguageModeling]] (15% [[TokenMasking|token masking]]; [[WholeWordMasking|whole-word masking]] via `DataCollatorForWholeWordMask`) — *"What a horrible [MASK]!"* shifts from generic *idea/dream/day* to domain-specific *movie/film/mess*. Then pivots to **[[NamedEntityRecognition|NER]] / [[TokenClassification|token classification]]** on [[CoNLL2003|CoNLL-2003]] — `AutoModelForTokenClassification` + [[DataCollatorForTokenClassification]] + the **[[BIOTagging|BIO-tagging]] scheme** (`O / B-PER / I-PER / B-ORG / I-ORG / B-LOC / I-LOC / B-MISC / I-MISC`) + a subtoken [[LabelAlignment|label-alignment]] function (first subtoken inherits word's label with `B-`; continuation subtokens get `I-`; `[CLS] / [SEP] / pad` get `-100` to be ignored by `CrossEntropyLoss`) + [[seqeval|`seqeval`]] for span-level F1. Closes by forward-referencing **Ch 12** for fine-tuning **generative** models. Mints [[SetFit]] / [[NamedEntityRecognition]] / [[TokenClassification]] / [[BIOTagging]] / [[CoNLL2003]] / [[LayerFreezing]] / [[DataCollatorForLanguageModeling]] / [[DataCollatorForTokenClassification]] / [[DataCollatorWithPadding]] / [[WholeWordMasking]] / [[TokenMasking]] / [[LabelAlignment]] / [[SequenceClassificationHead]] / [[TokenClassificationHead]] / [[FillMaskPipeline]] / [[seqeval]] / [[WNUT17]]; updates [[bert]] / [[FineTuningBert]] / [[ContinuedPretraining]] / [[MaskedLanguageModel]] / [[FineTuning]] / [[PartialFinetuning]] / [[FullFinetuning]] / [[Trainer]] / [[HuggingFace]] / [[FewShotLearning]] / [[ContrastiveLearning]] / [[LewisTunstall]] / [[RottenTomatoes]] / [[F1Score]] / [[DomainAdaptation]].
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 10: Creating Text Embedding Models](sources/hands-on-llm-ch10-creating-text-embedding-models.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** Opens **Part III** of the book (*Training and Fine-Tuning Language Models*) — the first chapter that crosses from *using* pretrained models to *creating* them. The **runnable-code resolution** of every forward reference Chs 2/4/5/8/9 parked on Ch 10 (the *"we will go in depth into [contrastive learning's] inner workings in Chapter 10 where we will create our own embedding model"* promise from Ch 9, the *"language models need to be trained on question-answer pairs to become better at retrieval — explained in Chapter 10"* promise from Ch 8). Walks **six training/fine-tuning regimes** on the same [[MNLI]] subset (50k pairs from [[GLUE]]) with the same [[STSB|STS-B]] evaluator, producing a ladder of STS Pearson cosine scores that demonstrates **loss-function choice can move performance by 20+ points on the same data**: **(1)** train-from-scratch with [[SoftmaxLoss|softmax loss]] on `bert-base-uncased` → **0.59**; **(2)** train-from-scratch with [[CosineSimilarityLoss|cosine similarity loss]] → **0.72**; **(3)** train-from-scratch with [[MultipleNegativesRankingLoss|MNR loss]] (a.k.a. [[InfoNCE]] / [[NTXentLoss|NT-Xent]]) on entailment triplets → **0.80**; **(4)** fine-tune `all-MiniLM-L6-v2` with MNR loss → **0.85** (highest); **(5)** [[AugmentedSBERT]] (Thakur, Reimers et al. 2020, arXiv:2010.08240) with 10k gold + 40k silver labeled by a fine-tuned [[CrossEncoder|cross-encoder]] → **0.71** (vs 0.72 for the supervised baseline — *"using only 20% of that data"*); **(6)** unsupervised [[TSDAE]] (Wang, Reimers & Gurevych 2021, arXiv:2104.06979) with [[CLSPooling|[CLS]-pooling]] and `DenoisingAutoEncoderLoss(tie_encoder_decoder=True)` on 50k unlabeled sentences → **0.70**. Introduces the **[[SBERTArchitecture|SBERT architecture]]** (drop the classification head, [[MeanPooling|mean-pool]] the final layer, train [[SiameseNetwork|siamese]] / [[BiEncoder|bi-encoder]]) as the modern default and contrasts it with the [[CrossEncoder|cross-encoder]] — *"a cross-encoder allows two sentences to be passed to the Transformer network simultaneously to predict the extent to which the two sentences are similar"* (more accurate but **does not produce reusable embeddings**; scales as $n(n-1)/2$ = 49,995,000 calls for $n=10{,}000$). Codifies **[[NLI|natural language inference]]-as-contrastive-data**: entailment → positive, contradiction → negative — the chapter's data-construction discipline for the [[GLUE]]'s [[MNLI]] worked example (50,000 of 392,702 annotated sentence pairs). Codifies the **[[HardNegatives|hard-negatives]] taxonomy** as a wiki first: **[[EasyNegatives|easy negatives]]** (random documents — what [[InBatchNegatives|in-batch negatives]] from MNR loss actually produce); **[[SemiHardNegatives|semi-hard negatives]]** (cosine-similar but not the right answer — minable from a pretrained embedding model); **[[HardNegatives|hard negatives]]** (related-but-wrong, the kind production embedding models actually need; usually require manual labeling or generative-model labeling) — with the canonical example: question = *"How many people live in Amsterdam?"* → positive = *"Almost a million people live in Amsterdam"* → hard negative = *"More than a million people live in Utrecht, which is more than Amsterdam."* The **[[AugmentedSBERT]] four-step recipe**: train a cross-encoder on a small annotated **gold dataset** → use it to label a much larger unlabeled pool → **silver dataset** → train the bi-encoder on gold + silver. The **[[TSDAE]] denoising recipe**: delete some words from a sentence (noise injection), encode the damaged sentence with **[[CLSPooling|[CLS]-pooling]] (NOT [[MeanPooling|mean-pooling]])** — the **only place in the wiki where [CLS]-pooling is recommended over mean-pooling** — *"in the TSDAE paper, this was shown to be more effective since mean pooling loses the position information"*; decode to the original; encoder and decoder share weights (`tie_encoder_decoder=True`); only the encoder is used at inference. Other unsupervised techniques named but not walked: **[[SimCSE]]** (Gao, Yao & Chen 2021, arXiv:2104.08821), **[[ContrastiveTension|Contrastive Tension (CT)]]** (Carlsson et al. ICLR 2021), **[[GPL|Generative Pseudo-Labeling]]** (Wang et al. 2021, arXiv:2112.07577). Closes with **[[DomainAdaptation|domain adaptation]] via [[AdaptivePretraining|adaptive pretraining]]**: TSDAE (or [[MaskedLanguageModel|MLM]]) on target-domain unlabeled text → fine-tune on whatever labeled pairs are available — *"although data from the target domain is preferred, out-domain data also works since we started with unsupervised training on the target domain."* Forward-references **Ch 11** for the MLM half of the recipe. Evaluation is anchored to **[[STSB|STS-B]]** via `EmbeddingSimilarityEvaluator` on `glue/stsb/validation` rescaled to `[0,1]`, with the broader **[[MTEB]]** suite (Muennighoff et al. 2022, arXiv:2210.07316 — 8 tasks / 58 datasets / 112 languages) flagged as the production model-selection rubric. **New mints**: [[SBERT]] / [[SBERTArchitecture]] / [[SiameseNetwork]] / [[MeanPooling]] / [[CLSPooling]] / [[MultipleNegativesRankingLoss]] / [[CosineSimilarityLoss]] / [[SoftmaxLoss]] / [[DenoisingAutoEncoderLoss]] / [[InBatchNegatives]] / [[HardNegatives]] / [[SemiHardNegatives]] / [[EasyNegatives]] / [[AugmentedSBERT]] / [[TSDAE]] / [[SimCSE]] / [[ContrastiveTension]] / [[GPL]] / [[GoldDataset]] / [[SilverDataset]] / [[DomainAdaptation]] / [[AdaptivePretraining]] / [[InfoNCE]] / [[NTXentLoss]] / [[STSB]] / [[MNLI]] / [[GLUE]] / [[AllMiniLML6V2]] / [[NandanThakur]] / [[KexinWang]] / [[TianyuGao]]. **Updates in place**: [[ContrastiveLearning]] / [[SentenceTransformers]] / [[BiEncoder]] / [[CrossEncoder]] / [[SemanticTextualSimilarity]] / [[NaturalLanguageInference]] / [[SNLI]] / [[MTEB]] / [[EmbeddingModel]] / [[TextEmbedding]] / [[SentenceEmbedding]] / [[NoiseContrastiveEstimation]] / [[Word2Vec]] / [[MaskedLanguageModel]] / [[AllMPNetBaseV2]] / [[bert]] / [[Pooling]] / [[NilsReimers]] / [[IrynaGurevych]] / [[JayAlammar]] / [[MaartenGrootendorst]] / [[HandsOnLLM]]. **Position in the wiki**: closes Part II's *use-pretrained-models* arc and opens Part III's *create-and-finetune-models* arc; the wiki's **first runnable end-to-end embedding-model training pipeline**; the **first concrete code-level walk of contrastive learning** (Chs 1, 2, 9 framed it; Ch 10 implements it); the wiki's first record of **gold-dataset / silver-dataset** as a data-quality taxonomy. **Soft contradiction flagged**: Ch 10's main thesis recommends [[MeanPooling]] over [[CLSPooling]] for supervised contrastive embeddings — but the TSDAE section explicitly recommends [CLS]-pooling for that one unsupervised denoising regime; the two recommendations are regime-specific, not conflicting, but it is the only place in the wiki where [CLS]-pooling is preferred over mean-pooling.
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 9: Multimodal Large Language Models](sources/hands-on-llm-ch09-multimodal-llms.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** The book's **vision-language chapter** and **the only chapter that extends the wiki's text-only LLM coverage to multimodal models that accept images** (and, by extension, audio / video — though Ch 9 walks only images). Closes **Part II** of the book before opening **Part III** on training and fine-tuning. Three architecturally distinct moves walked intuition → mechanism → runnable code: **(1) [[VisionTransformer|Vision Transformer (ViT)]]** — adapting the [[transformer|Transformer]] encoder to images by tokenizing the image into [[PatchEmbedding|16×16 patches]] and treating patch embeddings the same way as text token embeddings (Dosovitskiy et al. 2020, *"An image is worth 16x16 words"*, arXiv:2010.11929); the chapter's central mechanical observation — *"the moment the embeddings are passed to the encoder, they are treated as if they were textual tokens. From that point forward, there is no difference in how a text or image trains"* — is the structural reason the Transformer generalizes from language to vision and what makes adapter-style multimodal LLMs work; **(2) [[CLIP|Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP)]]** — Radford et al. 2021's multimodal *embedding* model that projects images and texts into the **same 512-dim vector space** via [[ContrastiveLearning|contrastive learning]] on (image, caption) pairs; walked via [[OpenCLIP]] (`openai/clip-vit-base-patch32`) using three [[HuggingFace|Hugging Face]] classes (`CLIPTokenizerFast` / `CLIPProcessor` / `CLIPModel`) on an AI-generated puppy-in-the-snow image — `text_embedding.shape == image_embedding.shape == torch.Size([1, 512])`, L2-normalize then dot product → **0.33 similarity** (high in CLIP's distribution, even though it sounds low — the chapter resolves the apparent paradox by walking a 3×3 similarity matrix where 0.33 is the highest in its row); the chapter codifies the wiki-novel observation *"in CLIP, the [CLS] token is actually used to represent the image embedding"* — the inverse of [[bert|BERT]]'s convention; four named applications — **zero-shot classification** / **clustering** / **search** / **generation** ([[StableDiffusion|Stable Diffusion]] cited as the canonical downstream generative use, Rombach et al. 2022); the [[SentenceTransformers|sentence-transformers]] CLIP wrapper (`SentenceTransformer("clip-ViT-B-32")`) is named as the few-lines-of-code easy-mode access path; **(3) [[BLIP2|BLIP-2]]** — Li et al. 2023's multimodal *generative* model (`Salesforce/blip2-opt-2.7b` loaded via `transformers.Blip2ForConditionalGeneration` + `AutoProcessor`) that bridges a **frozen [[VisionTransformer|ViT]]** and a **frozen LLM** (OPT-2.7b from [[meta]]) via the trainable **[[QFormer|Querying Transformer (Q-Former)]]** + a linear projection. Architecture decomposed into **two training stages** — **Stage 1**: Q-Former representation learning on three joint objectives ([[ImageTextContrastive|image-text contrastive]] / [[ImageTextMatching|image-text matching]] / [[ImageGroundedTextGeneration|image-grounded text generation]]) injects textual information into the frozen ViT's embeddings; **Stage 2**: the Q-Former's learnable embeddings serve as **[[SoftVisualPrompt|soft visual prompts]]** that condition the LLM — *"the LLM will be given information about the image in a similar manner to the context you would provide an LLM when prompting"* — the wiki's first runnable instance of soft-prompting where the soft prompt is derived from a **non-text** encoder. The chapter generalizes to the [[MultimodalLLM|adapter-on-frozen-encoder family]] via the cleanest formulation in the wiki: *"Both visual LLMs, although having different architectures, connect pretrained CLIP-like visual encoders with textual LLMs. The goal of these architectures is to project visual features from the input images to language embeddings such that they can be used as the input for an LLM"* — explicitly naming [[LLaVA15|LLaVA]] (2-layer MLP projector + Vicuna-13B) and [[Idefics2|Idefics 2]] (Mistral 7B backbone) as siblings of BLIP-2. **Two BLIP-2 use cases demonstrated**: **(a) [[ImageCaptioning|Image captioning]]** — supercar image → *"an orange supercar driving on the road at sunset"*; Rorschach inkblot → *"a black and white ink drawing of a bat"* (the chapter's light-touch flag of the **training-data-distribution-as-model-personality** observation); domain-specific images (specific cartoon characters / imaginary creations) may fail because the model was trained on largely public data — the Ch 9 analog of Ch 8's dense-retrieval-domain-transfer caveat. **(b) [[VisualQuestionAnswering|Visual question answering]] / multimodal chat** — the interface trick is to prompt the BLIP-2 processor with both `image` *and* `text`; with a prompt + image, the model answers; without a prompt, it captions. Worked second-turn: supercar + *"What would it cost me to drive that car?"* → *"$1,000,000"* (highly specific). Multi-turn chat is implemented by **concatenating prior `Question: ... Answer: ...` turns into the prompt** — the chapter ends with an `ipywidgets`-based fixed-image chatbot demonstration: *"Using this chat-based approach, we essentially created a chatbot that can reason about images!"* The chapter forward-references **Ch 10** (training and fine-tuning embedding models — Ch 9's deferred *"as we will see in Chapter 10, to make sure the representations are as accurate as possible, negative examples ... should also be included in the training process"*). **Position in the wiki**: where prior multimodal coverage was discipline-level framing ([[ai-engineering-ch03-evaluation-methodology|Huyen Ch 3]] on multimodal embedding spaces — naming CLIP / [[ULIP]] / [[ImageBind]]), architectural-pattern recognition ([[2408.08849-ecg-chat|ECG-Chat]] / [[MultimodalLLM]] codifying the [[LLaVA15|LLaVA]] adapter-on-frozen-encoder pattern), or native-multimodality contrast ([[2312.11805-gemini|Gemini]]'s from-the-start joint pretraining), Ch 9 is the **pedagogical bridge** — the chapter that runs both a CLIP-style embedding model and a BLIP-2 generative model with concrete shapes (`torch.Size([1, 512])` text/image embeddings; `224 × 224` preprocessed pixel tensor; `0.33` puppy/caption similarity) on a consumer-GPU notebook. **First wiki coverage of**: the [[VisionTransformer|ViT]] tokenization-by-patching construction made explicit as the structural analog to text tokenization; the [[CLIP]] training algorithm walked in three figures (encode → compare via cosine similarity → optimize for maximize-paired / minimize-unpaired); the [[OpenCLIP]] worked-code recipe with the **CLIP `[CLS]` convention inversion** observation; the [[BLIP2|BLIP-2]] architecture decomposed into the **three Q-Former training objectives** + **two training stages** — the wiki's first concrete architectural recipe for an adapter-on-frozen-encoder multimodal LLM; the [[SoftVisualPrompt|soft-visual-prompt]] mechanism where the soft prompt is derived from a non-text encoder; [[VisualQuestionAnswering|visual question answering]] as chat-based prompting around an image with a `prompt = "Question: ... Answer:"` template; the `Ġ`-as-space byte-level BPE convention codified at code-point-arithmetic granularity (space code-point 32 → Ġ code-point 288). **Updates in place**: [[CLIP]] / [[VisionTransformer]] / [[PatchEmbedding]] / [[ContrastiveLearning]] / [[QFormer]] / [[ImageTextContrastive]] / [[ImageTextMatching]] / [[ImageGroundedTextGeneration]] / [[SoftVisualPrompt]] / [[ImageCaptioning]] / [[VisualQuestionAnswering]] / [[ImageEncoder]] / [[ClsToken]] / [[CosineSimilarity]] / [[BPE]] / [[ByteLevelTokenization]] / [[bert]] / [[FoundationModel]] / [[MultimodalLLM]] / [[MultimodalRAG]] / [[MultimodalEmbeddingSpace]] / [[NaturalLanguageSupervision]] / [[nativemultimodality]] / [[ImageBind]] / [[ULIP]] / [[ZeroShotClassification]] / [[LLaVA15]] / [[transformer]] (concepts) and [[BLIP2]] / [[OpenCLIP]] / [[Salesforce]] / [[Idefics2]] / [[HuggingFace]] / [[openai]] / [[meta]] / [[Mistral]] / [[SentenceTransformers]] / [[StableDiffusion]] / [[GPT2]] / [[JayAlammar]] / [[MaartenGrootendorst]] / [[HandsOnLLM]] / [[OReilly]] (entities). **No direct contradictions** with the existing wiki corpus; soft consistency notes on the source page flag: the CLIP `[CLS]` convention inversion is a CLIP-specific override, not a BERT contradiction; the adapter vs native multimodality pair is two architecturally-distinct regimes for the same problem (cohabiting on [[MultimodalLLM]] and [[nativemultimodality]]); the ViT-vs-CNN scalability story is consistent with [[VisionTransformer]]'s prior small-data caveat (ViT does not beat ResNet on ImageNet-1k without 300M-image pretraining); image preprocessing distortion warning consistent with the wiki's embedding-input-preprocessing-as-load-bearing-step framing.
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 8: Semantic Search and Retrieval-Augmented Generation](sources/hands-on-llm-ch08-semantic-search-and-rag.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** The book's headline [[rag|RAG]] chapter — picks up the retrieval thread [[hands-on-llm-ch07-advanced-text-generation|Ch 7]] explicitly deferred and resolves it via the **three-category taxonomy** the chapter organizes itself around: **[[DenseRetrieval|dense retrieval]]** (embed query + documents, find nearest neighbors), **[[ReRanking|reranking]]** (rescore an existing shortlist with a stronger model — typically a [[CrossEncoder|cross-encoder]] / [[MonoBERT|monoBERT]]-style), and **[[rag|RAG]]** (text generation grounded on retrieved documents — with citations). Each category is walked intuition → runnable code → caveats → evaluation, with the canonical worked example being **a 15-sentence Wikipedia article on the film *Interstellar*** searched via [[Cohere]]'s `co.embed(input_type="search_document")` → [[FAISS|`faiss.IndexFlatL2`]] → `co.embed(input_type="search_query")` → `co.rerank(top_n=3)` → `co.chat(documents=...)` (managed-LLM RAG with **automatic span-level citations** — `ChatCitation(start=21, end=36, text='worldwide gross', document_ids=['doc_0'])`), and then replicated locally with [[Phi3Mini|Phi-3]] + [[BGESmallEnV15|`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`]] + [[FAISS]] + [[LangChain|`langchain.RetrievalQA`]]. The chapter opens with the structural observation that **the first industrial-scale LLM adoption was not chat — it was search**: within months of the 2018 BERT paper, [[google|Google]] announced *"one of the biggest leaps forward in the history of Search"* and [[microsoft|Microsoft]] Bing announced *"the largest quality improvements to our Bing customers in the past year."* The capability is named — **[[SemanticSearch|semantic search]]** — *"searching by meaning, and not simply keyword matching."* On a parallel track, the fast adoption of generative LLMs produced **[[Hallucination|hallucinations]]** at scale; the leading industry mitigation is [[rag|RAG]] ([[PatrickLewis|Lewis]] et al. 2020, *"Retrieval-Augmented Generation for Knowledge-Intensive NLP Tasks"*, NeurIPS 33: 9459–9474). **The signature dense-vs-keyword demonstration**: on the *Interstellar* corpus, the query *"how precise was the science"* returns the correct *"praise from many astronomers for its scientific accuracy and portrayal of theoretical astrophysics"* via dense retrieval but the wrong *"Interstellar is a 2014 epic science fiction film co-written, directed, and produced by Christopher Nolan"* via [[BM25|BM25 keyword search]] (which overlaps on the literal word *"science"*) — *"this wouldn't have been possible if we were only doing keyword search because the top result did not include the same keywords in the query."* **Three dense-retrieval caveats** named: out-of-distribution queries still return nearest-but-irrelevant results (mitigated via [[SimilarityThreshold|similarity thresholds]]); exact-phrase matching is a [[BM25]] strength → [[HybridSearch|hybrid search]] is the production default; domain transfer is hard (Wikipedia → legal). **[[Chunking|Chunking]] design space**: one-vector-per-document (slice or average) vs multiple-vectors-per-document (sentence / paragraph / overlapping / LLM-driven) — Ch 8 adds the top-level **one-vector-vs-multiple-vectors** axis the wiki's prior [[ai-engineering-ch06-rag-agents|Huyen Ch 6]] and [[leh-ch04-rag-feature-pipeline|LEH Ch 4]] coverage didn't make explicit. **Library vs database**: [[ApproximateNearestNeighbor|ANN]] libraries ([[Annoy]] / [[FAISS]]) vs [[VectorDatabase|vector databases]] ([[Weaviate]] / [[Pinecone]]) on the **CRUD-and-no-rebuild** axis (same distinction Huyen Ch 6 + LEH Ch 4 make). **Reranking** is framed as the easiest LLM-add to an existing search system — *"this one step can vastly improve search results and it's in fact what Microsoft Bing added to achieve the improvements to search results using BERT-like models"* — with the **headline efficacy claim**: *"on a multilingual benchmark like [[MIRACL]], a reranker can boost performance from 36.5 to 62.8, measured as [[NDCG|nDCG@10]]"* (≈2× lift). Mechanism: [[CrossEncoder|cross-encoder]] (query + result presented together) → relevance score [0, 1] = **classification problem** — Ch 8 explicitly back-references Ch 4's classification framing. Reference architecture: [[MonoBERT|monoBERT]] (*"Multi-stage document ranking with BERT"*). **Retrieval evaluation** walked step-by-step: [[PrecisionAtK|precision-at-k]] → [[AveragePrecision|average precision]] → [[MAP|mean average precision]] (*"likely an aesthetic choice because MAP sounds better than average average precision"*); [[NDCG]] named as the graded-relevance alternative; recommended reading: *Introduction to Information Retrieval* (Manning / Raghavan / Schütze) and *"Pretrained transformers for text ranking: BERT and beyond"* (Lin / Nogueira / Yates 2021). **Three IR components required**: text archive + queries + [[RelevanceJudgment|relevance judgments]]. **RAG section**: structural extension from search by adding an LLM at the end; *"this generation step is called [[GroundedGeneration|grounded generation]] because the retrieved relevant information we provide the LLM establishes a certain context that grounds the LLM in the domain we're interested in."* Managed example: Cohere `co.chat(message=query, documents=docs_dict)` with **automatic span-level [[CitationGeneration|citations]]** (the wiki's first runnable demonstration). Local example: [[Phi3Mini|Phi-3]] + [[BGESmallEnV15|`BAAI/bge-small-en-v1.5`]] + [[FAISS]] + [[LangChain|`langchain.RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(chain_type='stuff', ...)`]] — the **wiki's first runnable RetrievalQA receipt**. **Generative-search examples** named: [[Perplexity]], Microsoft Bing AI, [[gemini|Google Gemini]]. **Advanced RAG techniques continuum** (delegation-increasing): [[QueryRewriting]] (penguins/dolphins essay → *"Where do dolphins live"*) → [[MultiQueryRAG]] (Nvidia 2020 vs 2023 → two parallel queries) → [[MultiHopRAG]] (largest car manufacturers 2023 → Toyota/Volkswagen/Hyundai → three EV-followups) → [[QueryRouting]] (HR → Notion, customer → Salesforce) → [[AgenticRAG]] (LLM-as-agent over multiple data sources, with read+write symmetry). **Capability ceiling caveat**: *"likely only the largest managed models may be able to attempt this behavior"* — same agent-capability-cliff observation as [[hands-on-llm-ch07-advanced-text-generation|Ch 7's]] *"Phi-3-mini is not sufficient"* for ReAct. **RAG evaluation** — **four-axis taxonomy** per [[NelsonFLiu|Liu]], Zhang & [[PercyLiang|Liang]] 2023 *"Evaluating verifiability in generative search engines"* (arXiv:2304.09848): [[Fluency]] / [[PerceivedUtility|Perceived Utility]] / [[CitationRecall|Citation Recall]] / [[CitationPrecision|Citation Precision]]; automated via [[llmasjudge|LLM-as-a-judge]] with [[RAGAS|Ragas]] adding [[Faithfulness]] + [[AnswerRelevance|Answer Relevance]]. **Mints 22 concept pages**: [[DenseRetrieval]], [[SparseRetrieval]], [[GroundedGeneration]], [[GenerativeSearch]], [[CitationGeneration]], [[CitationRecall]], [[CitationPrecision]], [[Faithfulness]], [[AnswerRelevance]], [[Fluency]], [[PerceivedUtility]], [[RAGEvaluation]], [[MultiQueryRAG]], [[MultiHopRAG]], [[QueryRouting]], [[AgenticRAG]], [[MonoBERT]], [[SimilarityThreshold]], [[AveragePrecision]], [[PrecisionAtK]], [[RelevanceJudgment]], [[InformationRetrieval]], [[StopWord]] + the source-stub [[Lewis2020RAG]]. **Mints 8 entity pages**: [[MIRACL]], [[BGESmallEnV15]], [[BAAI]], [[CohereRerank]], [[CohereChat]], [[CohereEmbed]], [[PatrickLewis]], [[NelsonFLiu]], [[PercyLiang]]. Updates [[rag]] / [[SemanticSearch]] / [[EmbeddingBasedRetrieval]] / [[TermBasedRetrieval]] / [[BM25]] / [[HybridSearch]] / [[FAISS]] / [[Annoy]] / [[ApproximateNearestNeighbor]] / [[VectorDatabase]] / [[Chunking]] / [[ChunkingStrategy]] / [[CrossEncoder]] / [[ReRanking]] / [[QueryRewriting]] / [[MAP]] / [[NDCG]] / [[Hallucination]] / [[llmasjudge]] / [[RAGAS]] (concepts) and [[Cohere]] / [[LangChain]] / [[HandsOnLLM]] / [[JayAlammar]] / [[MaartenGrootendorst]] / [[Perplexity]] / [[meta]] / [[google]] / [[microsoft]] / [[gemini]] / [[Pinecone]] / [[Weaviate]] / [[Phi3Mini]] / [[SentenceTransformers]] / [[MTEB]] (entities) in place. **Position in the wiki**: the **third book-chapter RAG treatment** after [[ai-engineering-ch06-rag-agents|Huyen Ch 6]] (engineering-discipline framing) and [[leh-ch04-rag-feature-pipeline|LEH Ch 4]] (production-pipeline-recipe framing); Ch 8 is the **pedagogical-introduction-with-runnable-code** treatment — the chapter that puts dense retrieval, BM25, reranking, and grounded generation on the same 15-sentence corpus side-by-side. **First wiki coverage of**: the three-category retrieval taxonomy (dense / rerank / RAG); [[MonoBERT|monoBERT]] as the named cross-encoder architecture; the [[MIRACL]] reranker-lift benchmark; **span-level citation generation** as a runnable RAG primitive; the multi-query / multi-hop / query-routing / agentic-RAG continuum as Ch 8's named taxonomy; the Liu et al. 2023 four-axis RAG-evaluation taxonomy; the `RetrievalQA.from_chain_type(chain_type='stuff', ...)` LangChain primitive; the reranker-as-classification framing (Ch 4 → Ch 8 continuity). **First wiki appearance of** [[BAAI]], [[BGESmallEnV15]], [[MIRACL]], [[PatrickLewis]] (RAG paper first author), [[NelsonFLiu]] / [[PercyLiang]] (verifiability paper authors), and [[MonoBERT]]. The four-source wiki RAG curriculum is now complete: Ch 8 (intuition + runnable code on a 15-sentence corpus) → Huyen Ch 6 (engineering discipline) → LEH Ch 4 (ZenML batch pipeline) → [[dspy-rag-tutorial|DSPy RAG tutorial]] (MIPROv2 optimization). No direct contradictions; soft consistency notes on the source page reconcile dense-vs-sparse vs term-vs-embedding vocabularies, the Cohere `co.chat` citation primitive as Liu et al.'s axes operationalized, and the bge-small/gte-small transcription inconsistency in the chapter's local-RAG worked example.
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 7: Advanced Text Generation Techniques and Tools](sources/hands-on-llm-ch07-advanced-text-generation.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** **Part III Ch 2** and the **wiki's first LangChain-centric source** — picks up where [[hands-on-llm-ch06-prompt-engineering|Ch 6]] left off (*"what can we do to further enhance the experience and output that we get from the LLM without needing to fine-tune the model itself?"*) and walks four advanced techniques that **extend an LLM without fine-tuning** through [[LangChain]] as the organizing substrate: (1) **Model I/O** — loading the LLM, here a [[GGUF]]-quantized [[Phi3Mini|Phi-3]] via [[LangChainLlamaCpp|`langchain.LlamaCpp`]] (wraps [[llamacpp|`llama-cpp-python`]]); the empty-output gotcha reveals that `LlamaCpp.invoke()` does NOT auto-apply Phi-3's [[ChatTemplate|chat template]] (unlike `transformers.pipeline`), motivating explicit [[PromptTemplate|`PromptTemplate`]] use; (2) **Chains** — the [[LCEL|LangChain Expression Language]] pipe-operator composition primitive (`basic_chain = prompt | llm`) and the [[LLMChain|`LLMChain`]] named-output primitive with a three-stage story-generation worked example (`title | character | story`) that decomposes a single creative task across three sequential LLM calls; (3) **Memory** — the three pros-and-cons memory types as a design surface: [[ConversationBufferMemory]] (full history, hits token limit), [[ConversationBufferWindowMemory]] (last-k turns only, the [[LangChain]] operationalization of [[FIFOMemory|FIFO eviction]]), [[ConversationSummaryMemory]] (LLM-summarized running history; two LM calls per turn; the operationalization of [[SummarizationMemory|summarization-based memory]]); all three demonstrated with the same *"Maarten is 33"* identity-retention probe; (4) **Agents** — the [[react|ReAct]] framework (Yao et al. 2022, [[ShunyuYao|Shunyu Yao]] first author) implemented via [[LangChainAgent|`langchain.agents.create_react_agent` + `AgentExecutor`]] running a [[DuckDuckGoSearchResults|DuckDuckGo search]] + [[LLMMathTool|llm-math]] calculator inventory over [[ChatGPT|GPT-3.5-turbo]] (Phi-3-mini insufficient — Ch 7's honest acknowledgment of the agent capability cliff); canonical worked benchmark: *"What is the current price of a MacBook Pro in USD? How much would it cost in EUR if the exchange rate is 0.85 EUR for 1 USD?"* → *"$2,249.00 ... approximately 1911.65 EUR"* via two ReAct cycles (search → calculate). The chapter ends with a load-bearing **safety caveat** — *"there is no [[humanintheloop|human in the loop]] to judge the quality of the output or reasoning process. This double-edged sword requires a careful system design to improve its reliability"* — consistent with [[ai-engineering-ch06-rag-agents|Huyen Ch 6]]'s [[CompoundErrorAccumulation|compound-error-accumulation]] warning. Retrieval-augmented generation is **explicitly deferred to Ch 8**. **First wiki coverage of LangChain at runnable-code granularity**: Model I/O / Chains / Memory / Agents — four core abstractions; first runnable LangChain-native ReAct receipt, complementing existing [[DSPy]]-native `dspy.ReAct` coverage ([[dspy-modules]], [[dspy-tools]], [[dspy-customer-service-agent]]). The chapter names **[[DSPy]] and Haystack** as *"newer frameworks of note"* alongside LangChain — *"LangChain is one of the earlier frameworks that simplify working with LLMs through useful abstractions"*. Complements [[ai-engineering-ch06-rag-agents|Huyen Ch 6]] (design discipline for agents + memory hierarchy) with the **runnable LangChain operationalization**.
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 6: Prompt Engineering](sources/hands-on-llm-ch06-prompt-engineering.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** **Part III Ch 1** — the book's **first chapter whose subject is squarely [[PromptEngineering|prompt engineering]]**, opening the generation-focused half of the book and complementing [[ai-engineering-ch05-prompt-engineering|Huyen's *AI Engineering* Ch 5]] (the wiki's other book-chapter prompt-engineering treatment). Four movements: (1) **using a text generation model** — proprietary vs open source; loading via `transformers.pipeline` with [[Phi3Mini|Phi-3-mini]]; the chat template `<s><|user|>...<|end|><|assistant|>` that `apply_chat_template` hides; controlling output via [[Temperature|temperature]] + [[Topp|top_p]] + [[Topk|top_k]] (with Ch 6's use-case quadrant table mapping brainstorming/email/creative-writing/translation to high/low combinations); (2) **intro to prompt engineering** — basic ingredients (instruction + data + output indicator); instruction-based prompting tips (**specificity** is the most important; **[[Hallucination|hallucination]] mitigation** via *"if you don't know, say 'I don't know'"*; **order** — primacy + recency effects, *"information in the middle is often forgotten"* citing [[lostinthemiddle|Liu et al. 2023]]); (3) **advanced prompt engineering** — the **seven-component modular prompt** ([[Persona|persona]] + [[InstructionPrompt|instruction]] + [[ContextPrompt|context]] + [[OutputFormat|format]] + [[AudiencePrompt|audience]] + [[TonePrompt|tone]] + data — *"think of prompts as pieces of a larger puzzle"*; iteratively add/remove/reorder Lego blocks; emotional-stimulus components like *"This is very important for my career"* per [[EmotionPrompt|Li et al. 2023]]); **[[InContextLearning|in-context learning]]** via zero / one / [[FewShotLearning|few-shot]] prompting (the canonical *Gigamuru / screeg* made-up-word demonstration, requiring alternating `{"role": "user"}` / `{"role": "assistant"}` chat messages); and **chain prompting** = [[PromptDecomposition|prompt decomposition]] across LLM calls (`name + slogan` → `sales pitch` worked example — MindMeld Messenger / *"Unleashing Intelligent Conversations, One Response at a Time"*; three use cases — **response validation** / **parallel prompts** / **writing stories**); (4) **reasoning with generative models** — [[System1And2|Kahneman's System 1 vs System 2]] frames generative models as System 1 (constant-time, no self-reflection) and the reasoning-prompting techniques as **constructive operationalizations of System 2** (sitting in soft tension with [[2402.01817-llm-modulo|Kambhampati et al.'s]] critique that this resemblance is empty without external verifiers); **[[chainofthought|chain-of-thought]]** with both few-shot examples (Wei et al. 2022 — the tennis-balls + cafeteria-apples worked example) and the zero-shot *"Let's think step-by-step"* trigger (Kojima et al. 2022; alternative triggers like *"Take a deep breath"* and *"Let's work through this"* per Yang et al. 2023); the **compute justification** *"each additional token in this reasoning process allows the LLM to stabilize its output"*; **[[selfconsistency|self-consistency]]** (Wang et al. 2022 — N-CoT + majority vote with temperature/top_p stochasticity; *"becomes n times slower where n is the number of output samples"*); **[[TreeOfThoughts|tree-of-thought]]** (Yao et al. 2023) both architecturally (multi-call search over thoughts) and as a **single-prompt three-experts-roleplay approximation** (*"Imagine three different experts are answering this question. All experts will write down 1 step of their thinking, then share it with the group..."*); (5) **output verification** — four motivations (**structured output** / **valid output** / **ethics** / **accuracy**) and three control methods (**examples** / **grammar** / **fine-tuning** — fine-tuning deferred to Ch 12); the worked RPG character-profile JSON example shows few-shot output examples produce structural compliance (Lysandra Shadowstep / Leather Cloak of the Night / Dagger of Whispers); **grammar = [[ConstrainedSampling|constrained sampling]]** — names **[[Guidance]] / [[Guardrails]] / [[LMQL]]** as the canonical Python packages; the **wiki's first runnable [[GrammarConstrainedDecoding|grammar-constrained decoding]] demonstration** via [[llamacpp|`llama-cpp-python`]] + [[GGUF]]-quantized [[Phi3Mini|Phi-3]] + `response_format={"type": "json_object"}` produces a valid JSON warrior `{"name": "Eldrin Stormbringer", "class": "Warrior", "level": 10, "attributes": {...}, "skills": {...}, "equipment": [...]}` that `json.loads()` validates. Forward-references **Ch 7** (memory + tool use beyond chaining LLMs) and **Ch 12** (fine-tuning as the third output-control lever). **Mints 11 concept pages**: [[InstructionPrompt]], [[ContextPrompt]], [[OutputFormat]], [[AudiencePrompt]], [[TonePrompt]], [[OutputVerification]], [[GrammarConstrainedDecoding]], [[PromptChaining]], [[OneShotPrompting]], [[PrimacyEffect]], [[ZeroShotCoT]], [[EmotionPrompt]]. **Mints 1 entity page**: [[Guardrails]] (Shreya Rajpal's grammar-constrained output library — the third name in Ch 6's Guidance/Guardrails/LMQL triad). Updates [[PromptEngineering]] / [[chainofthought]] / [[selfconsistency]] / [[TreeOfThoughts]] / [[Persona]] / [[InContextLearning]] / [[FewShotLearning]] / [[ZeroShotLearning]] / [[ConstrainedSampling]] / [[Temperature]] / [[Topp]] / [[Topk]] / [[Hallucination]] / [[lostinthemiddle]] / [[ChatTemplate]] / [[PromptDecomposition]] / [[System1And2]] (concept pages) + [[Phi3Mini]] / [[HandsOnLLM]] / [[JayAlammar]] / [[MaartenGrootendorst]] / [[OReilly]] / [[HuggingFace]] / [[llamacpp]] / [[Guidance]] / [[Outlines]] / [[microsoft]] (entity pages) in place. **Position in the wiki**: complements rather than replaces existing prompt-engineering coverage. Where [[ai-engineering-ch05-prompt-engineering|Huyen Ch 5]] is the **rigorous-discipline framing** (six best practices + defensive prompt engineering + [[PromptStructure|three-part anatomy]] + [[PromptEngineeringTools|tools taxonomy]] with hidden-cost warnings), Alammar & Grootendorst Ch 6 is the **modular-component framing** (seven Lego-block prompt parts + build-it-up-iteratively workflow). **First wiki coverage of the seven-component modular prompt** (persona / instruction / context / format / audience / tone / data) as an iterable design surface. **First wiki coverage of the single-prompt three-experts-roleplay approximation of tree-of-thought**. **First wiki coverage of grammar-constrained decoding in worked runnable code** (via `llama-cpp-python` + GGUF Phi-3); the [[ConstrainedSampling]] page was previously conceptual-only. **First wiki worked example using `llama-cpp-python`** in the [[HandsOnLLM]] book corpus (Chs 1–5 used `transformers` only). **First wiki worked example using GGUF-quantized inference at chapter-tutorial level**. No direct contradictions; soft consistency notes flagged on the source page ([[System1And2]] constructive-vs-critical stance with [[2402.01817-llm-modulo]], [[chainofthought]] variant catalog vs Huyen Ch 5, [[PromptEngineering|prompt anatomy]] seven-component vs Huyen's three-part, [[ConstrainedSampling]] toolchain set Guidance/Guardrails/LMQL vs Huyen's guidance/outlines/instructor/llama.cpp — all reconciled).
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 5: Text Clustering and Topic Modeling](sources/hands-on-llm-ch05-text-clustering-topic-modeling.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** The book's **unsupervised twin of [[hands-on-llm-ch04-text-classification|Ch 4]]** and the wiki's first end-to-end walkthrough of modern embedding-based text clustering and topic modeling. Codifies the three-step **embed → reduce → cluster** pipeline ([[SentenceTransformers|sentence-transformers]] [[GTESmall|`thenlper/gte-small`]] 384-dim → [[UMAP]] 384→5 dim (`min_dist=0.0`, `metric='cosine'`, `random_state=42`) → [[HDBSCAN]] `min_cluster_size=50`, `metric='euclidean'`, `cluster_selection_method='eom'`) and extends it via **[[BERTopic]]** — [[MaartenGrootendorst|Grootendorst's]] own modular topic-modeling framework ([[2203.05794-bertopic|Grootendorst 2022, arXiv:2203.05794]]) — where stage 2 represents each cluster via **class-based [[TFIDF|TF-IDF]] ([[ClassBasedTFIDF|c-TF-IDF]])**. Run end-to-end on **[[ArXivNLP|`maartengr/arxiv_nlp`]]** — 44,949 cs.CL abstracts (1991–2024) from [[HuggingFace|Hugging Face]] — producing **156 clusters** (155 topics + outlier topic `-1` with 14,520 abstracts). Selected topics include automatic speech recognition (topic 0, 2,290 docs), medical NLP (topic 1), sentiment / aspect-based analysis (topic 2), neural machine translation (topic 3), and topic modeling itself (topic 22 — *the topic the BERTopic paper's own abstract is assigned to*). The chapter's second pedagogical move is the **representation-model abstraction** — BERTopic's reranking blocks layered on c-TF-IDF, applied **once per topic** not per document (*"if we have millions of documents and a hundred topics, the representation block only needs to be applied once for every topic instead of for every document"*): (1) **[[KeyBERTInspired]]** — rerank candidate keywords by cosine similarity to the per-topic average document embedding; modeled after [[MaartenGrootendorst|Grootendorst's]] [[KeyBERT]] package; (2) **[[MaximalMarginalRelevance|MMR]]** — iteratively select diverse-yet-relevant keywords via a `diversity` parameter; (3) **[[GenerativeTopicLabeling|LLM-based topic labeling]]** — feed each topic's keywords + 4 most-representative documents into a `[DOCUMENTS]` / `[KEYWORDS]` prompt template and have either [[FLANT5|Flan-T5-small]] (local) or [[ChatGPT|GPT-3.5-turbo]] (via [[openai|OpenAI]] API) emit a short natural-language label. Closes with a [[Datamapplot|`datamapplot`]] visualization of the top-20 GPT-3.5-labeled topics over a 2D [[UMAP]] projection. The chapter explicitly **forward-references Ch 6** (prompt engineering — topic-labeling prompt is its first complex prompt template) and **Ch 8** (semantic search — *"this idea of reranking an initial set of results is a main staple in neural search"*). It fulfils Ch 1's promise that *"bag-of-words is by no means completely obsolete"* — c-TF-IDF preserves bag-of-words at the topic-representation step while replacing topic discovery with embedding-based clustering. Classical [[LatentDirichletAllocation|LDA]] (Blei, Ng & Jordan 2003) is named as the explicit baseline contrasted with BERTopic on context-sensitivity, automatic K, and outlier handling. **Mints 24 concept pages**: [[TextClustering]], [[TopicModeling]], [[BERTopic]], [[UMAP]], [[HDBSCAN]], [[DBSCAN]], [[DensityBasedClustering]], [[CentroidBasedClustering]], [[DimensionalityReduction]], [[ClassBasedTFIDF]], [[KeyBERTInspired]], [[MaximalMarginalRelevance]], [[GenerativeTopicLabeling]], [[LatentDirichletAllocation]], [[GuidedTopicModeling]], [[SeededTopicModeling]], [[DynamicTopicModeling]], [[HierarchicalTopicModeling]], [[SemiSupervisedTopicModeling]], [[ZeroShotTopicModeling]], [[OnlineTopicModeling]], [[MultimodalTopicModeling]], [[Outlier]], [[NeuralSearch]], [[Plotly]], [[Datamapplot]]. **Mints 14 entity pages**: [[ArXiv]], [[ArXivNLP]], [[KeyBERT]], [[GTESmall]], [[GPT35Turbo]], [[AlibabaDAMOAcademy]], [[LelandMcInnes]], [[HaroldHotelling]], [[MartinEster]], [[DavidBlei]], [[AndrewNg]], [[MichaelJordan]], [[UMAPLibrary]], [[HDBSCANLibrary]] + the [[2203.05794-bertopic|BERTopic paper stub]] under sources. Updates [[BagOfWords]] / [[TFIDF]] / [[CosineSimilarity]] / [[CurseOfDimensionality]] / [[PCA]] / [[Embedding]] / [[SentenceEmbedding]] / [[HierarchicalClustering]] / [[KMeansClustering]] / [[Dendrogram]] / [[MTEB]] / [[Reproducibility]] / [[ReRanking]] / [[RepresentationModel]] / [[UnsupervisedLearning]] / [[TopicClustering]] / [[matplotlib]] / [[NumPy]] / [[pandas]] (concept pages) + [[HandsOnLLM]] / [[JayAlammar]] / [[MaartenGrootendorst]] / [[OReilly]] / [[HuggingFace]] / [[SentenceTransformers]] / [[FLANT5]] / [[ChatGPT]] / [[openai]] / [[google]] / [[sklearn]] / [[Gensim]] / [[NomicAtlas]] (entity pages) in place. **Position in the wiki**: complements rather than replaces existing clustering coverage. Where [[TopicClustering|LEH Ch 5's TopicClustering page]] named the pipeline (sentence-transformers → UMAP → HDBSCAN → LLM auto-label) in a single paragraph alongside Hugging Face's `text-clustering`, [[NomicAtlas]], BunkaTopics, and Lilac as tooling, *Hands-On LLMs* Ch 5 is the **full pedagogical walkthrough** that names [[BERTopic]] (Grootendorst's own framework) and runs the pipeline on a real dataset. **First wiki coverage of BERTopic, KeyBERT, UMAP, HDBSCAN, c-TF-IDF, KeyBERTInspired, MMR, GenerativeTopicLabeling, DensityBasedClustering, outlier handling in clustering, the ArXiv NLP dataset, and the gte-small embedding model**. **Second wiki appearance of [[sklearn|scikit-learn]] as an LLM-stack dependency** (after Ch 4) — this time providing `CountVectorizer` for the c-TF-IDF bag-of-words step. No direct contradictions; soft consistency notes flagged on the source page ([[TopicClustering]] / [[BagOfWords]] / [[TFIDF]] / [[HierarchicalClustering]] / [[KMeansClustering]] / [[ReRanking]] all reconciled across sources).
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 4: Text Classification](sources/hands-on-llm-ch04-text-classification.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** The book's **first applications chapter** — runs a single binary [[SentimentAnalysis|sentiment-analysis]] task ([[RottenTomatoes|`rotten_tomatoes`]] from [[HuggingFace|Hugging Face]]; 5,331 positive + 5,331 negative reviews from Pang & Lee 2005) across **four progressively more permissive pretrained-LLM classification regimes** with side-by-side weighted-average [[F1Score|F1]] scores: (1) **[[TaskSpecificModel|task-specific representation model]]** — [[TwitterRoBERTa|`cardiffnlp/twitter-roberta-base-sentiment-latest`]] via `transformers.pipeline`, **F1 = 0.80**; (2) **[[EmbeddingModel|embedding model]] + [[LogisticRegression]]** — [[SentenceTransformers|sentence-transformers]] [[AllMPNetBaseV2|`all-mpnet-base-v2`]] (768-dim) + [[sklearn|scikit-learn]] `LogisticRegression`, **F1 = 0.85**; (3) **[[ZeroShotClassification|zero-shot classification]] via [[LabelEmbedding|label embeddings]] + [[CosineSimilarity]]** — embed `["A negative review", "A positive review"]`, `argmax(cosine_similarity(...))`, **F1 = 0.78** with no labeled training data; (4) **[[GenerativeClassification|generative classification]] via instruction prompts** — [[FLANT5|`google/flan-t5-small`]] (encoder-decoder, `text2text-generation` pipeline, **F1 = 0.84**) and [[ChatGPT|`gpt-3.5-turbo-0125`]] (decoder-only via [[openai|OpenAI]] API, `temperature=0`, **F1 = 0.91** — the chapter's best result). The chapter's central pedagogical move is to **decouple the embedding step from the classification step**: by keeping the embedding model frozen, per-task work collapses from full BERT fine-tuning (Ch 11) to training a logistic regression on CPU over a 768-dim feature vector. It then generalizes to the **no-labels** case via zero-shot label embeddings — describing labels as sentences (*"A negative review"*), embedding the descriptions, and assigning labels by cosine similarity. The generative-models half introduces **[[GenerativeClassification|generative classification]] via [[PromptEngineering|prompt engineering]] + label parsing** (prompt: *"Is the following sentence positive or negative? "* → parse `"negative"` → 0, `"positive"` → 1). [[FLANT5|Flan-T5]]'s training recipe is sketched ([[spancorruption|span-corruption pretraining]] → multi-task instruction-tuning with 1,800+ tasks per Chung et al. 2022, *"Scaling instruction-finetuned language models"*); [[ChatGPT|ChatGPT]]'s training is sketched in three steps (pretraining → instruction-tuning on manually-created prompt+output pairs → [[PreferenceFinetuning|preference tuning]] on manually-ranked outputs). Names **rate limits + [[ExponentialBackoff|exponential backoff]]** for API workflows and the **OpenAI API cost** (3 cents for the 1,066-row Rotten Tomatoes test sweep at time of writing). Closes with the **[[DataContamination|benchmark-contamination caveat]]** — *"since we do not know what data the model was trained on, we cannot easily use these kinds of metrics for evaluating the model. For all we know, it might have actually been trained on our dataset!"* — flagging closed-source-LLM evaluation as epistemologically limited. The chapter opens with a load-bearing endorsement of **classical baselines**: *"it is highly advised to compare these examples against classic, but strong baselines such as representing text with [[TFIDF|TF-IDF]] and training a logistic regression classifier on top of that."* Walks confusion matrix → [[Precision|precision]] / [[Recall|recall]] / [[Accuracy|accuracy]] / [[F1Score|F1]] for the metric vocabulary. The [[MTEB|MTEB leaderboard]] is named as the canonical embedding-model selection rubric. **Mints 14 concept pages**: [[TaskSpecificModel]], [[EmbeddingModel]], [[ZeroShotClassification]], [[LabelEmbedding]], [[GenerativeClassification]], [[ClassificationHead]], [[BinarySentimentClassification]], [[ClassificationReport]], [[ConfusionMatrix]], [[Precision]], [[Recall]], [[Accuracy]], [[ExponentialBackoff]], [[BenchmarkContamination]] (alias for [[DataContamination]]). **Mints 12 entity pages**: [[RottenTomatoes]], [[TwitterRoBERTa]], [[CardiffNLP]], [[RoBERTa]], [[DistilBERT]], [[ALBERT]], [[sklearn]], [[MTEB]], [[BoPang]], [[LillianLee]], [[ColinRaffel]], [[HyungWonChung]]. Updates [[TextClassification]] / [[SentimentAnalysis]] / [[ZeroShotLearning]] / [[LogisticRegression]] / [[CosineSimilarity]] / [[F1Score]] / [[NaturalLanguageInference]] / [[t5]] / [[bert]] / [[DataContamination]] (concept pages) + [[HandsOnLLM]] / [[JayAlammar]] / [[MaartenGrootendorst]] / [[OReilly]] / [[HuggingFace]] / [[SentenceTransformers]] / [[AllMPNetBaseV2]] / [[FLANT5]] / [[ChatGPT]] / [[openai]] / [[Cohere]] / [[google]] (entity pages) in place. **Position in the wiki**: complements rather than replaces existing classification coverage. Where [[d2l-nlp-applications|D2L's NLP-Applications]] treatment is the **architecture-survey** (RNN baseline / textCNN / BERT fine-tuning) and [[SentimentAnalysis|the existing SentimentAnalysis page]] focuses on D2L's [[IMDb]] worked examples, Ch 4 is the **practitioner-comparison-table tour** with side-by-side F1 scores across four pretrained-LLM regimes on a single smaller dataset. **First wiki coverage of zero-shot classification via label embeddings + cosine similarity** as a distinct technique from prompt-engineering zero-shot or NLI-based zero-shot. **First wiki coverage of generative classification via instruction prompts + label parsing** for using decoder-only and encoder-decoder LLMs as classifiers. **First wiki worked example using `transformers.pipeline` for `text-classification` and `text2text-generation`** and **first wiki worked example using the OpenAI Chat Completions API**. **First wiki appearance of the [[RottenTomatoes|rotten_tomatoes]] dataset**, [[TwitterRoBERTa|Twitter-RoBERTa]], the [[MTEB]] leaderboard, and [[sklearn|scikit-learn]] as an explicit LLM-stack dependency. No direct contradictions; minor consistency notes flagged on the source page (zero-shot definition — prompt-engineering sense vs classification-without-labels sense are reconciled on [[ZeroShotLearning]] / [[ZeroShotClassification]]; F1 macro-vs-weighted averaging is consistent across [[2507.03152-medval|MedVAL]] and Ch 4 because Ch 4's data is balanced; TF-IDF baseline endorsement is consistent with Huyen Ch 4's discipline).
- [Hands-On LLMs Ch 3: Looking Inside Large Language Models](sources/hands-on-llm-ch03-looking-inside-llms.md) — **[[JayAlammar|Jay Alammar]] & [[MaartenGrootendorst|Maarten Grootendorst]] ([[OReilly|O'Reilly Media]], 2024, ISBN 978-1-098-15096-9).** The book's **Transformer-internals deep-dive** — *"the main intuitions of how Transformer language models work"* with text-generation models as the focus. Opens with the **autoregressive token-by-token generation loop** (one [[forwardpass|forward pass]] per output token) and breaks the model into three components — **[[Tokenizer|tokenizer]] → stack of [[transformer|Transformer blocks]] → [[LMHead|LM head]]** — then dissects [[Phi3Mini|Phi-3-mini]] via `print(model)`: 32,064-token vocabulary, 3,072-dim embeddings, **32 `Phi3DecoderLayer` blocks**, each containing a `Phi3Attention` with `qkv_proj` (3072→9216 fused [[QueryProjection|Q]]/[[KeyProjection|K]]/[[ValueProjection|V]] projection) and `Phi3RotaryEmbedding`, a `Phi3MLP` (`gate_up_proj` → `SiLU` → `down_proj` — [[SwiGLU]]-style gated MLP), `Phi3RMSNorm` for pre-norm placement, and a `Linear(3072 → 32064)` `lm_head`. Demonstrates the LM head produces `Paris` for *"The capital of France is"* via `lm_head_output[0, -1].argmax(-1)`. Introduces **parallel [[TokenStream|token-stream]] processing** (each token has its own computation track; cross-stream interaction only in attention; the count of streams = [[ContextLength|context length]]) and **[[KVCache|KV cache]]** as the inference-time optimization that caches K/V projections across decode steps — **4.5 s vs 21.8 s** measurement on Colab T4 / 100 tokens with Phi-3-mini (~5× speedup). Walks **[[selfattention|self-attention]] in two pedagogical steps**: (1) **relevance scoring** via query × keys matrix + [[Softmax|softmax]], (2) **combining information** via value-vector weighted sum; emphasizes that **three projection matrices** ([[QueryProjection|Q]] / [[KeyProjection|K]] / [[ValueProjection|V]]) are the learned attention parameters. **[[multiheadattention|Multi-head attention]]** runs the calculation in parallel per [[AttentionHead|attention head]]; *"increases the model's capacity to model complex patterns."* **Decoder attention is causal** (only attends to previous tokens; contrast with bidirectional [[bert|BERT]]).
