- [LEH Ch 1: Understanding the LLM Twin Concept and Architecture](sources/leh-ch01-understanding-llm-twin-concept.md) — Frames the book's [[LLMTwin]] project and introduces the [[FTIArchitecture|FTI (Feature/Training/Inference) pipeline]] pattern as the architectural backbone.
- [LEH Ch 2: Tooling and Installation](sources/leh-ch02-tooling-and-installation.md) — Stack tour: [[Pyenv]] / [[PoetryPython]] / [[PoeThePoet]], [[ZenML]] orchestrator, [[CometML]] + [[Opik]], [[MongoDB]] + [[Qdrant]], [[AmazonSageMaker]] + [[AWSCLI]] + [[AWSIAM]].
- [LEH Ch 3: Data Engineering](sources/leh-ch03-data-engineering.md) — End-to-end [[ETL]] crawler pipeline (Medium / Substack / GitHub / LinkedIn → [[MongoDB]]) with [[Selenium]] + [[BeautifulSoup]] + [[LangChain]] + a custom [[ODM]].
- [LEH Ch 4: RAG Feature Pipeline](sources/leh-ch04-rag-feature-pipeline.md) — Comprehensive [[rag|RAG]] primer + batch ZenML feature pipeline (clean → [[Chunking|chunk]] → [[Embedding|embed]] → load to [[Qdrant]]); covers vanilla and advanced RAG techniques.
- [LEH Ch 5: Supervised Fine-Tuning](sources/leh-ch05-supervised-fine-tuning.md) — Instruction-dataset construction, [[lora|LoRA]] / [[QLoRA]] memory math, chat templates, and the [[TwinLlama|TwinLlama-3.1-8B]] fine-tune with [[Unsloth]] + [[TRL]].
- [LEH Ch 6: Fine-Tuning with Preference Alignment](sources/leh-ch06-preference-alignment.md) — Preference-dataset structure (instruction / chosen / rejected), [[rlhf|RLHF]]+[[PPO]] vs [[DirectPreferenceOptimization|DPO]] derivation, and the TwinLlama-3.1-8B-DPO fine-tune.
- [LEH Ch 7: Evaluating LLMs](sources/leh-ch07-evaluating-llms.md) — Model vs system evaluation, public benchmarks ([[mmlu]] / [[ifeval]] / [[gaia]] / Chatbot Arena), task-specific metrics, [[LLMAsAJudge]], and [[RAGAS]] / ARES for RAG eval.
- [LEH Ch 8: Inference Optimization](sources/leh-ch08-inference-optimization.md) — KV cache + `torch.compile`, [[ContinuousBatching]], speculative decoding / Medusa, [[flashattention|FlashAttention-2]] + PagedAttention, model parallelism, and quantization formats (GGUF / GPTQ / AWQ / EXL2); compares TGI / vLLM / TensorRT-LLM.
- [LEH Ch 9: RAG Inference Pipeline](sources/leh-ch09-rag-inference-pipeline.md) — Advanced-RAG inference: query expansion + self-querying + filtered vector search + cross-encoder reranking, orchestrated by `ContextRetriever`.
- [LEH Ch 10: Inference Pipeline Deployment](sources/leh-ch10-inference-pipeline-deployment.md) — [[MicroservicesArchitecture|Microservices]] split: [[FastAPI]] business service + [[AmazonSageMaker]] LLM endpoint with [[HuggingFaceDLC]] / [[TextGenerationInference|TGI]] + [[ApplicationAutoScaling]].
- [LEH Ch 11: MLOps and LLMOps](sources/leh-ch11-mlops-and-llmops.md) — [[MLOps]] → [[LLMOps]] hierarchy, [[CICD]] + CT pipelines via [[GitHubActions]] + [[ZenML]] on AWS, [[Opik]] prompt tracing, drift detection ([[DataDrift]] / [[TargetDrift]] / [[ConceptDrift]]), guardrails and alerting.

- [Programming Paradigms for Dummies: What Every Programmer Should Know](sources/vanroy-programming-paradigms-for-dummies.md) — **[[PeterVanRoy|Peter Van Roy]] ([[UCL]], during sabbatical at [[IRCAM]], 2009; chapter in *New Computational Paradigms for Computer Music*, Assayag & Gerzso eds., IRCAM/Delatour).** 39-page paradigm-taxonomy chapter — **27 useful [[ProgrammingParadigm|programming paradigms]]** organized by two axes ([[ObservableNondeterminism|observable nondeterminism]] + [[NamedState|named state]]). Names the **four most important [[ProgrammingConcept|programming concepts]]** — records, [[Closure|lexically scoped closures]], independence ([[Concurrency|concurrency]]), [[NamedState|named state]] — and the **four kinds of [[DataAbstraction|data abstraction]]** ([[AbstractDataType|ADT]] / [[OPMObject|object]] / declarative object / stateful ADT). Argues for two design strategies: **[[DualParadigmLanguage|dual-paradigm languages]]** and **[[DefinitiveLanguage|definitive languages]]** (four-layer architecture: functional core → [[DeclarativeConcurrency|declarative concurrency]] → [[MessagePassingConcurrency|message passing]] → [[NamedState|named state]] — converged on independently by [[Erlang]] / [[E_Language|E]] / [[DistributedOz]] / [[CTM|Didactic Oz]]). Presents **four [[ConcurrencyParadigm|concurrent paradigms]] with no race conditions** — [[DeclarativeConcurrency]] (eager + lazy [[DataflowVariable|dataflow]]), [[FunctionalReactiveProgramming|FRP]], [[DiscreteSynchronousProgramming|discrete synchronous]], [[ConcurrentConstraintProgramming|constraint programming]]. Closes with [[SelfSufficientSystem|self-sufficient-systems]] architecture (interacting [[FeedbackLoop|feedback loops]] via [[Stigmergy|stigmergy]] + management) as the large-scale alternative to monolithic software. Direct intellectual descendant of [[vol1000-oz-programming-model|Smolka's 1995 OPM paper]] — Van Roy ran the **PERDIO** distributed-Oz project at [[DFKI]] with [[GertSmolka|Smolka]] in 1995. The wiki's **first paradigm-taxonomy survey** and the **programmer-facing sibling** of the formal-model OPM exposition; positions [[Oz]] in a 27-paradigm taxonomy. **Mints 16 concept pages** ([[ProgrammingParadigm]], [[KernelLanguage]], [[ObservableNondeterminism]], [[NamedState]], [[DataflowVariable]], [[Closure]], [[CreativeExtensionPrinciple]], [[DeclarativeConcurrency]], [[MessagePassingConcurrency]], [[SharedStateConcurrency]], [[FunctionalReactiveProgramming]], [[DiscreteSynchronousProgramming]], [[DataAbstraction]], [[SubstitutionPrinciple]], [[DefinitiveLanguage]], [[DualParadigmLanguage]]) + **4 [[SelfSufficientSystem|self-sufficient-systems]] concept pages** ([[SelfSufficientSystem]], [[FeedbackLoop]], [[Stigmergy]], [[CTM]]) + **2 [[Oz]]-ecosystem concept pages** ([[MozartProgrammingSystem]], [[DistributedOz]]) + **1 language anchor** ([[Erlang]]) + **3 entity pages** ([[PeterVanRoy]], [[UCL]], [[IRCAM]]). Heavy reuse from the [[vol1000-oz-programming-model|prior Oz ingest]] ([[Oz]] / [[OPM]] / [[ConcurrentConstraintProgramming]] / [[ComputationSpace]] / [[ConstraintStore]] / [[FirstClassProcedures]] / [[EncapsulatedSearch]] / [[Cell]] / [[Port]] / [[Agent]] / [[OPMObject]] / [[Propagator]] / [[GertSmolka]] / [[DFKI]]).
- [DSPy Tutorial — Retrieval-Augmented Generation](sources/dspy-rag-tutorial.md) — **Fourth wiki-corpus [[DSPy]] tutorial** (after [[dspy-conversation-history]], [[dspy-customer-service-agent]], [[dspy-custom-module]]) — and the **first DSPy receipt to combine all four [[DSPyProgrammingModel|Programming-Model artifacts]]** ([[DSPySignatures|Signatures]] / [[DSPyModules|Modules]] / [[DSPyMetrics|Metrics]] / [[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizers]]) end-to-end on a single task with measurable per-stage gains. Walks a three-stage performance ladder on [[RAGQAArenaTech|RAG-QA Arena Tech]] (~1K technical QA pairs, 200/300/500 train/dev/test): baseline [[chainofthought|`dspy.ChainOfThought`]] (no retrieval) **42%** → [[rag|RAG]] module wrapping [[chainofthought|CoT]] over `k=5` embedding-retrieved docs **55.5%** → [[MIPROv2|`dspy.MIPROv2`]] `auto="medium"` over the RAG module **61.1%** [[SemanticF1]]. Three load-bearing details: (i) **the metric is [[SemanticF1]]** — a reference-based [[llmasjudge|LLM-as-judge]] DSPy program that decomposes both gold and predicted answers into atomic claims and grades coverage, instantiating the [[dspy-metrics|AI-feedback metric pattern]] from page 11 of the *Learn* corpus; (ii) **retrieval uses [[openai|OpenAI]] `text-embedding-3-small`** over a 28K-document downsampled technical corpus, each doc truncated to 6K characters — the first wiki-corpus DSPy RAG receipt to use dense embeddings (the [[dspy-custom-module|Custom Module tutorial]] used [[ColBERTv2]] late interaction); (iii) **`auto="medium"` costs ~$1.50 and runs in ~20–30 min** on this dataset — the first concrete instance of [[dspy-optimizers|the Optimizers page's]] *$2 typical / cents-to-tens-of-dollars range* operating envelope on a multi-stage RAG program. **Cross-receipt convergence**: this is the **second worked instance** of [[MIPROv2|MIPROv2 Receipt 2]] (the first was the [[dspy-optimizers|Optimizers page's]] StackExchange subset, 53→61%) — **two independent benchmarks now converge on ~61% [[SemanticF1]] as the post-optimization ceiling** for a single-hop CoT-based RAG on gpt-4o-mini with `auto="medium"`. The tutorial's *further-improvement menu* names five axes for going beyond 61.1%: [[hotpotqa|multi-hop]] retrieval, other optimizers ([[GEPA]] / [[BetterTogether]]), [[DSPyMajority|ensembling]], [[BootstrapFinetune|distillation]], and recursive metric refinement. **Mints 2 concept pages** ([[SemanticF1]], [[RAGQAArenaTech]]); updates [[DSPy]] / [[rag]] / [[MIPROv2]] / [[MLflow]] in place. No contradictions.
- [The Oz Programming Model](sources/vol1000-oz-programming-model.md) — **Gert Smolka ([[DFKI]] Programming Systems Lab, July 1995; LNCS Vol. 1000 pp. 324–343).** Informal exposition of the **[[OPM|Oz Programming Model]]** — a concurrent programming model subsuming higher-order functional and object-oriented programming as facets of a single general model. **OPM = [[ConcurrentConstraintProgramming|concurrent constraint kernel]] (OCC) + [[FirstClassProcedures|first-class procedures]] + stateful [[Cell|cells]]** + a conservative extension for [[EncapsulatedSearch|encapsulated search]] generalizing constraint logic programming. Computation in a **[[ComputationSpace|computation space]]** (tasks + three-compartment store: [[ConstraintStore|constraint store]] / procedure store / cell store); tasks **synchronize on logic entailment** of guards (monotonic, declarative). [[Propagator|Propagators]] accommodate nonbasic expressive constraints; **threads** are the reduction strategy *"as sequential as possible and as concurrent as necessary"*; [[Port|ports]] / [[Agent|agents]] / [[OPMObject|objects]] are derived stateful abstractions built from cells + first-class procedures + names. **Critical design move**: search is encapsulated into concurrent agents via the **search combinator**, getting constraint logic programming *"out of its problem solving ghetto"*. The wiki's **first programming-language-theory paper** and first source from the [[DFKI]] / Smolka / Saraswat / AKL concurrent-constraint research line; predates the wiki's ML / DL cluster by 25 years and grounds the **declarative-shared-store** alternative to the wiki's existing [[Pthreads]] / [[Mutex]] / [[MPI]] concurrency vocabulary. **Mints 7 primary concept pages** ([[OPM]], [[Oz]], [[ConcurrentConstraintProgramming]], [[ComputationSpace]], [[ConstraintStore]], [[FirstClassProcedures]], [[EncapsulatedSearch]]) + **5 ancillary concept pages** ([[Cell]], [[Port]], [[Agent]], [[OPMObject]], [[Propagator]]) + **2 entity pages** ([[GertSmolka]], [[DFKI]]).
- [DSPy Tutorial — Building AI Applications by Customizing DSPy Modules](sources/dspy-custom-module.md) — **Third wiki-corpus [[DSPy]] tutorial** (after [[dspy-conversation-history]] and [[dspy-customer-service-agent]]) and the **first** to anchor on the custom `class MyProgram(dspy.Module)` shape itself rather than on a downstream application. Four positions: (1) subclass `dspy.Module` and implement `__init__` + `forward` — the two-method PyTorch-shaped contract; (2) `forward()` is unconstrained Python — *"you are not limited to calling only other DSPy modules; you can also integrate any standard Python functions, such as those for interacting with Langchain/Agno agents, MCP tools, database handlers, and more"*; (3) call the module instance directly, not `forward()` explicitly — *"the `__call__` method handles necessary internal processing"*; (4) custom modules unlock framework features — [[DSPyOptimizers|DSPy Optimizer]] introspection + [[MLflow]] tracing both walk `self.*` sub-module attributes, so plain-function pipelines get **neither**. Worked receipt: a three-stage [[rag|RAG]] program — `dspy.Predict(QueryGenerator)` → `dspy.ColBERTv2(url='http://20.102.90.50:2017/wiki17_abstracts')(query, k=1)` → [[chainofthought|`dspy.ChainOfThought("question,context->answer")`]] — the wiki's first end-to-end RAG code listing inside a [[DSPyModules|`dspy.Module`]] subclass and the canonical anchor for the public Wikipedia 2017 abstracts [[ColBERTv2]] endpoint that the [[dspy-modules|Modules page]], [[react|ReAct]] / [[hotpotqa|HotPotQA]] examples, [[MIPROv2]] / [[2407.10930-better-together|BetterTogether]] / [[2507.19457-gepa|GEPA]] demos, and [[2312.13382-dspy-assertions|DSPy Assertions]] tasks all assume but never document. Template-level anchor for **rung 2** of the [[DSPy]] application stack — the canonical worked starting receipt every other rung composes from. First wiki-corpus DSPy-specific [[MLflow]] tracing recipe — four-step opt-in ending in `mlflow.dspy.autolog()`. **Mints 1 concept page** ([[ColBERTv2]] — promoted from long-standing forward reference); updates [[DSPy]] / [[DSPyModules]] / [[MLflow]] / [[rag]] in place.
- [When Prompt Optimization Becomes Jailbreaking — Adaptive Red-Teaming of LLMs](sources/2603.19247-prompt-optimization-jailbreaking.md) — **Shamsi, Chekuru, Guzman & Garg ([[AlgoverseAIResearch|Algoverse AI Research]], arXiv:2603.19247v1, 21 Feb 2026).** Repurposes [[DSPy]] black-box prompt optimizers — [[MIPROv2]] (medium config), [[GEPA]] (light config), and **[[SIMBA]]** (batch=16, ≤4 steps) — as **automated jailbreak generators** by inverting the reward: instead of maximizing benign task accuracy, the optimizer maximizes a continuous **[[DangerScore|danger score]] $r \in [0, 1]$** from a cross-family [[LLMAsAJudge|LLM judge]] ([[GPT51|GPT-5.1]]). Seeds: 150 prompts evenly drawn from [[HarmfulQA]] + [[JailbreakBench]]. **All optimizers lift mean danger on every target**; **SIMBA wins all four cells**: [[qwen|Qwen-3 8B]] **0.090 → 0.792** (8.8× rise, most degraded), [[LLaMA4Maverick|LLaMA-4 Maverick]] 0.215 → 0.623, [[ClaudeSonnet45|Claude 4.5 Sonnet]] 0.046 → 0.347 (7.5× rise — largest *multiplier*), [[gemini|Gemini 2.5 Pro]] 0.645 → 0.774. Optimizer ranking **SIMBA > GEPA > MIPROv2 > baseline** is consistent across model families — *"the effect is driven by the optimization process rather than model-specific idiosyncrasies."* Inference via [[OpenRouter]]; human spot-check on 25 traces confirmed danger-score / human-judgment alignment. **Methodological headline**: *"static benchmarks may underestimate residual risk, indicating that automated, adaptive red-teaming is a necessary component of robust safety evaluation."* First wiki-corpus paper to use [[DSPy]] **offensively** as the attack pipeline (companion to defensive [[dspy-guardrails]]); first to anchor [[SIMBA]] empirically; first to score Claude 4.5 / Gemini 2.5 Pro / LLaMA-4 Maverick on the same axis.
- [ECG-Chat — A Large ECG-Language Model for Cardiac Disease Diagnosis](sources/2408.08849-ecg-chat.md) — **Zhao, Kang, Zhang, Han & Chen (April 2025).** First [[MultimodalLLM|multimodal LLM]] for [[ECG]] cardiac-disease report generation; pairs a [[CoCa]]-style [[ECGEncoder|1d-ViT ECG encoder]] with [[Vicuna13B]] under [[LoRA]], mitigates hallucination via [[GraphRAG]] (over 7 cardiology textbooks) + [[DSPy]] automated prompt tuning + [[DiagnosisDrivenPrompt|DDP]] classifier-into-prompt + [[plasTeX]] LaTeX templates. **Headline empirical results**: [[WaveformDataEnhancement|WDE]] lifts zero-shot [[PTB-XL]] retrieval R@1 from **2.14 → 64.7** (30× over prior best [[CoCa]]); DDP doubles BLEU-1 and triples Rhythm F1; GraphRAG+DSPy lifts [[RAGAS]] Faithfulness from 39.87 → 82.12 on [[ECGExpertQA]]. Releases **[[ECGInstruct]]** (45,044 ECG samples / 19K diagnosis + 25K dialogue, GPT-4o-generated) — first open ECG instruction-tuning corpus. **Scalability is data-bound** (43M→128M params: F1 ~flat; 80K→805K data: F1 45→52, R@1 0.86→64.7). The wiki's first ECG-modality MLLM and first record of [[DSPy]] + [[GraphRAG]] co-deployed in a clinical specialty pipeline.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.16 System Information](sources/dis-app2-16-sysinfo.md) — **Sixteenth and final leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — codifies system-state inspection: the dynamic [[TopCommand|`top`]] / `htop` process viewers ([[ProcessID|PID]] / CPU / memory / state, refresh-per-second), the [[ProcFS|`/proc`]] + [[SysFS|`/sys`]] pseudo-filesystems that expose [[OperatingSystem|OS]] state as readable files (`/proc/cpuinfo`, `/proc/meminfo`, `/proc/<PID>/status`), and convenience utilities [[Lscpu|`lscpu`]] / `lsmem` / [[Lshw|`lshw`]] that format the same data. **167th ingested DIS chapter — CLOSES Appendix 2 (Ch 17) AND THE ENTIRE [[DiveIntoSystems]] TEXTBOOK.** Mints **5 new concept pages**: [[TopCommand]], [[ProcFS]], [[SysFS]], [[Lscpu]], [[Lshw]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.15 Shell Programming](sources/dis-app2-15-shell-programming.md) — **Fifteenth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — codifies [[ShellProgramming|shell programming]]: [[ShellScript|scripts]] begin with a [[Shebang|`#!/bin/bash`]] line and `chmod u+x`; variables (`var=value`, `$var`); command-line arguments (`$@`, `$#`, `$1`...); conditionals (`if [ $x -eq 5 ]; then ... fi` — *"the space chars between them and the condition are very important"*); loops in both C-style (`for ((i=0; i<10; i++))`) and element-iteration (`for f in *.txt`) forms. C-side cross-walk: [[CommandLineArguments|`argc`/`argv`]] from [[dis-2-9-2-cmd-line-args|Ch 2.9.2]]. **166th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **3 new concept pages**: [[ShellProgramming]], [[ShellScript]], [[Shebang]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.14 Dotfiles](sources/dis-app2-14-dotfiles.md) — **Fourteenth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — codifies [[DotFile|dotfiles]] (filenames starting with `.` — hidden by default, revealed by `ls -a`) as the Unix customization mechanism. Anchors on [[BashRC|`.bashrc`]] for shell config: [[EnvironmentVariable|environment variables]] (`export NAME=value`), [[PathVariable|`PATH`]] extension (`PATH=$PATH:/home/user/mybin`), [[BashAlias|aliases]] (`alias rm="rm -i"` for safety, `alias gt31="cd ~/classes/CS31"` for convenience). Sibling files: `.vimrc` ([[VimEditor]] config), `.xsession` (X11 config). Changes apply after `source .bashrc` or shell restart. **165th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **5 new concept pages**: [[DotFile]], [[BashRC]], [[EnvironmentVariable]], [[PathVariable]], [[BashAlias]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.13 Pipes](sources/dis-app2-13-pipes.md) — **Thirteenth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — codifies the [[ShellPipe|shell pipe `|`]]: `cmd1 | cmd2` wires `cmd1`'s [[Stdout|stdout]] into `cmd2`'s [[Stdin|stdin]] with **no intermediate file** — *the* canonical Unix composability primitive. Chains arbitrarily: `cat file | grep pattern | wc -l`. **Shell-level surface** of the [[Pipe]] [[InterprocessCommunication|IPC]] primitive from [[dis-13-4-2-message-passing|Ch 13.4.2]] (the shell calls `pipe(2)` + `fork(2)` + `dup2(2)` under the hood). [[Xargs|`xargs`]] differs: it executes the downstream command **per input value** rather than streaming. **164th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **2 new concept pages**: [[ShellPipe]], [[Xargs]]. **Extends [[Pipe]] in place** with the shell-level framing.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.12 I/O Redirection](sources/dis-app2-12-io-redirect.md) — **Twelfth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — codifies the [[IORedirection|I/O redirection]] operators (`>`, `>>`, `<`, `2>`, `&>`) that rewire a process's [[StandardStream|standard streams]] — [[Stdin]] ([[FileDescriptor|fd]] **0**), [[Stdout]] (fd **1**), [[Stderr]] (fd **2**) — to and from files. `cmd > file` overwrites, `cmd >> file` appends, `cmd < file` reads stdin, `cmd 2> err` redirects stderr separately, `cmd &> all` merges both. Operators are independently combinable. **163rd ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **6 new concept pages**: [[IORedirection]], [[StandardStream]], [[Stdin]], [[Stdout]], [[Stderr]], [[FileDescriptor]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.11 Shell History](sources/dis-app2-11-history.md) — **Eleventh leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — codifies the [[BashHistory|bash command history]] mechanism: the [[HistoryCommand|`history`]] built-in lists numbered recent commands; the [[BangBang|`!`-prefix]] syntax recalls them — `!n` re-runs entry `n`, `!!` re-runs the most recent command (*"particularly useful for easily re-running commands that have a long list of command line arguments"*). When `!n` expands, the **expanded** command (not the shorthand) is recorded. **162nd ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **3 new concept pages**: [[BashHistory]], [[HistoryCommand]], [[BangBang]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.10 Timing](sources/dis-app2-10-timing.md) — **Tenth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — introduces the [[TimeCommand|`time`]] command for measuring program execution: prints **real** (wall-clock elapsed), **user** ([[CPUTime|CPU time]] in [[UserMode|user mode]]), **sys** ([[CPUTime|CPU time]] in [[KernelMode|kernel mode]]). Key insight: *"user time plus the sys time do not add up to real time"* — the gap reveals I/O blocking and OS scheduling. CPU-bound: `user + sys ≈ real`; I/O-bound: `user + sys ≪ real`. `time -p` enables POSIX-standard output for automation. **161st ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **1 new concept page**: [[TimeCommand]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.9 Process Control](sources/dis-app2-9-process-control.md) — **Ninth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **opens Appendix 2 second half**. Codifies process control at the [[UnixShell|shell]] level: trailing `&` starts a [[BackgroundProcess|background process]], [[JobControl|job control]] vocabulary (`CTRL-Z` suspends → [[SIGTSTP]], `bg` resumes in background, `fg` brings to foreground, `jobs` lists), [[Ps|`ps`]] lists processes, [[Kill|`kill <pid>`]] sends [[Signal|`SIGTERM`]] (default 15) or `SIGKILL` (`kill -9`), `pkill <name>` matches by command name, `CTRL-C` sends [[SIGINT]]. **Extends [[Ps]] + [[Kill]] in place** with the day-to-day Unix-CLI usage (prior coverage was [[dis-3-4-gdb-advanced|Ch 3.4]] GDB-debugging context only). **160th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **4 new concept pages**: [[JobControl]], [[BackgroundProcess]], [[SIGINT]], [[SIGTSTP]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.8 tar Archives](sources/dis-app2-8-tar.md) — **Eighth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — codifies [[Tar|`tar`]] as the canonical Unix archive tool: `-c` create / `-x` extract / `-t` list / `-v` verbose / `-f` filename, plus `-z` (gzip) and `-j` (bzip2) compression pipelines (`.tar.gz`, `.tar.bz2`). Composes with [[SCP|`scp`]] from Appendix 2.3 — archive + compress before bulk transfer to cut wire time. **159th ingested DIS chapter — closes Appendix 2 first half (subchapters 2.1–2.8).** Mints **1 new concept page**: [[Tar]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.7 File Permissions and chmod](sources/dis-app2-7-permissions.md) — **Seventh leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — codifies the **Unix discretionary access control** model: 3 permission bits ([[FilePermissions|**r**/**w**/**x**]]) × 3 principal categories (**u**ser / **g**roup / **o**ther) visible via `ls -l` as `-rwxr-xr--`. [[Chmod|`chmod`]] mutates them in either **octal** (`chmod 755` = `4r+2w+1x` per digit) or **symbolic** (`chmod u+w`, `chmod o-r`) notation. Related: `chgrp` for group reassignment. **158th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **2 new concept pages**: [[FilePermissions]], [[Chmod]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.6 grep and find](sources/dis-app2-6-grep-find.md) — **Sixth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — codifies the **content-search vs filename-search** split. [[Grep|`grep <pattern> <files>`]] outputs every line matching the regex (flags `-n` line numbers / `-i` case-insensitive / `-r` recursive / `-H` show filename); [[Find|`find <path> -name "*.c"`]] recursively walks the [[UnixFileSystem|filesystem]] for files matching a name glob. Both accept regex; routinely composed via pipes (`find ... \| xargs grep ...`). **157th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **2 new concept pages**: [[Grep]], [[Find]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.5 Make and Makefiles](sources/dis-app2-5-make.md) — **Fifth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — promotes [[Make|`make`]] from forward-reference to first-class coverage. **Rule model**: target + dependencies + command; `make` uses modification times to rebuild *"just the object and executable files that depend on files that have been modified since the last time they were built."* Variables (`CC`, `CFLAGS`, `SRCS` via `$(NAME)`) make Makefiles reusable. Essential once a [[CLanguage|C]] project has multiple `.c` / `.h` files or non-standard include / library paths — replaces hand-typed [[GCC|`gcc`]] commands. Modern alternatives: CMake, GNU Autotools. **156th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **1 new concept page** ([[Make]] — promoted from forward-reference); extends [[Makefile]] in place with the C-build framing.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.4 Unix Editors](sources/dis-app2-4-editors.md) — **Fourth leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — surveys the three terminal editors: **[[VimEditor|Vim]]** (modal — *insert* mode entered via `i`, *command* mode entered via `ESC`; `h j k l` nav, `:wq` save+quit, `vimtutor` for the 20-min interactive tutorial), **[[EmacsEditor|Emacs]]** (modeless chord-based — `C-x C-s` save, `C-x C-c` exit, `C-k` kill line, `C-y` yank), **[[NanoEditor|Nano]]** (beginner-friendly single-mode with on-screen shortcut hints; `C-x` exit). Default editor set via `~/.bashrc`: `export EDITOR=vim` + `export VISUAL=vim`. **155th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **3 new concept pages**: [[VimEditor]], [[EmacsEditor]], [[NanoEditor]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.3 SSH and SCP](sources/dis-app2-3-remote-access.md) — **Third leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — introduces **remote access**: [[SSH|`ssh username@hostname`]] *"starts a unix shell on the remote machine through which the user can access files and run applications"*; [[SCP|`scp src dest`]] mirrors [[UnixCommandLine|`cp`]] with `user@host:path` remote endpoints. **Key-based authentication** via `ssh-keygen -t rsa` mints `~/.ssh/id_rsa` (private — keep secret) + `~/.ssh/id_rsa.pub` (public — copy to the remote's `~/.ssh/authorized_keys`) — the same mechanism that gates GitHub / GitLab Git access. Cross-platform: native on Unix / macOS; PowerShell or PuTTY on Windows. **154th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **2 new concept pages**: [[SSH]], [[SCP]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.2 Man Pages](sources/dis-app2-2-man.md) — **Second leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — promotes [[ManPages|`man`]] from the cross-chapter forward reference into a first-class subchapter: `man <name>` (or `man <section> <name>` to disambiguate) opens the page in the [[Less|`less`]] pager — `q` quit, *space* page-down, `/` search. Numbered sections (§1 commands, §2 syscalls, §3 library functions, ...); standard sub-headings (**NAME** / **SYNOPSIS** / **DESCRIPTION** / **RETURN VALUE** / **SEE ALSO**); `apropos <keyword>` does a keyword search across all installed man pages. **153rd ingested DIS chapter.** No new concept pages — extends [[ManPages]] in place with the Appendix 2.2 discovery / `apropos` framing.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 2.1 Command Line Basics](sources/dis-app2-1-cmdline-basics.md) — **Opening leaf of Appendix 2** *Using Unix* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — introduces the [[UnixShell|shell]] as a *read-eval-print loop* (typically `bash` / `zsh` with a `$` prompt) and the [[UnixFileSystem|file system]] tree rooted at `/` (every non-root directory has exactly one parent). Codifies the core navigation + file-manipulation command vocabulary (`pwd` / `cd` / `ls` / `mkdir` / `rmdir` / `cp` / `mv` / `rm` / `touch` / `cat` / `less` / `wc`) plus path shortcuts (`.` / `..` / `~`). **Discipline**: filenames are **case-sensitive**; `rm` is **permanent** (use `rm -i`). **152nd ingested DIS chapter — opens Appendix 2 *Using Unix*.** Mints **2 new concept pages**: [[UnixCommandLine]], [[UnixFileSystem]].
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 1.8 Exercises (for Java Programmers)](sources/dis-app1-8-exercises.md) — **Closing leaf of Appendix 1** *Chapter 1 for Java Programmers* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — single-link redirect: *"Appendix 1 exercises are the same as the Chapter 1 Exercises."* Drills the full Appendix 1.1–1.6 surface — [[CompilationProcess|compile-then-run]], [[VariableDeclaration|typed declarations]], [[CArithmeticOperators|arithmetic]], [[Printf|`printf`]] / [[Scanf|`scanf`]] + [[AddressOfOperator|`&`]], [[ControlFlow|control-flow]], [[Function|functions]] with [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]], [[CArray|arrays]] / [[CString|strings]] (no `.length`, no bounds checking), [[CStruct|structs]] with [[StructAssignment|whole-record copy]] vs Java reference copy. **151st ingested DIS chapter — closes Appendix 1 and the Java-perspective cross-walk arc.** Structural sibling of [[dis-1-8-exercises]]. No new concept pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 1.7 Summary (for Java Programmers)](sources/dis-app1-7-summary.md) — **Penultimate leaf of Appendix 1** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — closing recap of the Java-vs-C cross-walk. Headline: *"C is an imperative and procedural language and Java is an object-oriented language"*; C arrays/strings operate at lower level than Java's `ArrayList` / `List` / `String`; minimal C library ecosystem; *"C's simpler abstractions grant programmers direct memory access control."* Forward-references Ch 2 (pointers + dynamic memory). **150th ingested DIS chapter.** Sibling of [[dis-1-7-summary]]. No new concept pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 1.6 Structs (for Java Programmers)](sources/dis-app1-6-structs.md) — **Sixth leaf of Appendix 1** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the [[Java]]-perspective retelling of [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]]. [[CStruct|`struct`]] ≈ Java class minus methods/inheritance/constructor/GC. **Value-vs-reference semantics is the load-bearing delta**: in C, `s2 = s1` copies all fields; in Java, the same statement copies a reference. [[PassByValue|Pass-by-value]] copies the whole struct in C (modifications invisible to caller); Java method calls pass references (modifications *do* affect caller). [[SizeOf|`sizeof(struct studentT)`]] exposes byte layout — Java abstracts this. **149th ingested DIS chapter.** Sibling of [[dis-1-6-structs]]. No new concept pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 1.5 Arrays and Strings (for Java Programmers)](sources/dis-app1-5-arrays-strings.md) — **Fifth leaf of Appendix 1** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the [[Java]]-perspective retelling of [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]. **Largest deltas of Appendix 1**: Java arrays have `.length`, C arrays don't; Java throws [[BoundsChecking|`ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`]], C has *"no bounds checking by the compiler or at runtime"*; Java's `String` class is heap-allocated immutable with rich methods, C's [[CString|string]] is a `char` array + [[NullTerminator|`'\0'`]] sentinel + [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]] manual machinery. *"`strcpy` poses a security risk because it assumes that its destination is large enough."* One semantic alignment: **array pass-to-function is by-reference in both languages**. **148th ingested DIS chapter.** Sibling of [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]. No new concept pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 1.4 Functions (for Java Programmers)](sources/dis-app1-4-functions.md) — **Fourth leaf of Appendix 1** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the [[Java]]-perspective retelling of [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]. C standalone [[Function|functions]] vs. Java class methods; C requires [[FunctionPrototype|prototypes]] (Java doesn't); [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]] identical for primitives in both (*"any change to a parameter's value in the function is not visible to the caller"*); C exposes the [[ExecutionStack|execution stack]] of [[StackFrame|stack frames]] explicitly (Java abstracts it). The "Java objects-by-reference" exception doesn't apply — Ch 1.4 only covers primitive-typed functions. **147th ingested DIS chapter.** Sibling of [[dis-1-4-functions]]. No new concept pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 1.3 Conditionals and Loops (for Java Programmers)](sources/dis-app1-3-conditionals.md) — **Third leaf of Appendix 1** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the [[Java]]-perspective retelling of [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]]. **Almost a no-op cross-walk**: [[IfStatement|`if`]] / [[ElseStatement|`else`]] / [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] / [[WhileLoop|`while`]] / [[DoWhileLoop|`do`-`while`]] / [[ForLoop|`for`]] / [[BreakStatement|`break`]] / [[ContinueStatement|`continue`]] are syntactically identical between Java and C. Single load-bearing delta: **C has no boolean type** — *"any integer expression that is zero (0) evaluates to false; nonzero evaluates to true"* ([[CBooleanExpression]]). Java's enhanced for-each loop has no C analog. **146th ingested DIS chapter.** Sibling of [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]. No new concept pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 1.2 Input/Output (for Java Programmers)](sources/dis-app1-2-input-output.md) — **Second leaf of Appendix 1** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the [[Java]]-perspective retelling of [[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]]. Java's `Scanner.nextInt()` ↔ C's [[Scanf|`scanf("%d", &n)`]] — the syntactic shock for Java programmers is **the [[AddressOfOperator|`&` operator]]** (C has no implicit pass-by-reference, so the caller must pass the variable's address explicitly). Java's `System.out.printf` ↔ C's [[Printf|`printf`]] with identical [[FormatSpecifier|`%`-specifier]] vocabulary (`%d` / `%g` / `%s` / `%c`) and [[EscapeSequence|escape sequences]]. *"`scanf` is picky about exact input formatting"* — less forgiving than Java's `Scanner`. **145th ingested DIS chapter.** Sibling of [[dis-1-2-input-output]]. No new concept pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Appendix 1.1 Getting Started Programming in C (for Java Programmers)](sources/dis-app1-1-getting-started.md) — **Opening leaf of Appendix 1** *Chapter 1 for Java Programmers* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the [[Java]]-perspective retelling of [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]] (Ch 1 is the Python-perspective version; Appendix 1 is the Java-cross-walk variant — same C content, different starting language). Java `javac` → [[JVM]] bytecode vs. C [[GCC|`gcc`]] → [[BinaryExecutable|native binary]]; Java `public static void main(String[] args)` inside a class vs. C [[MainFunction|`int main(void)`]] at file scope; Java `import` vs. C [[PreprocessorDirective|`#include`]] (+ `-lm` linker flag); Java `System.out.println` vs. C [[Printf|`printf`]] (no auto-newline). [[CArithmeticOperators|Arithmetic]] and [[IncrementOperator|increment]] operators are essentially identical. **144th ingested DIS chapter — opens Appendix 1.** Mints **1 new concept page** ([[JavaVsC]] — consolidated cross-walk).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 15.3 To Exascale and Beyond](sources/dis-15-3-exascale.md) — **Third and final leaf of Ch 15** *Looking Ahead: Other Parallel Systems* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **closes Ch 15 and the entire textbook**. Pivots from [[dis-15-2-distributed-memory|Ch 15.2's]] [[MPI]] / [[Cluster|cluster]] introduction into the **largest-scale parallel systems**: **HPC** (scientific supercomputers, [[ExascaleComputing|exascale]] — Frontier / Aurora / El Capitan) vs **HDA** (cloud-scale data centers, [[MapReduce]] / [[HadoopStreaming|Hadoop]] / Spark). Both build on [[MulticoreProcessor|multicore]] + [[GPU|GPU]] [[Cluster|clusters]]; differ in software stacks. Headline: *"90% of all online data was produced in the past two years, and that society produces 30 terabytes of user data per second."* 1,000-node centers see **>99.99% probability** of node failure — fault tolerance is mandatory. Three forward themes: fault tolerance at scale, edge computing (first mile vs last mile), HPC ↔ HDA convergence. Energy as binding constraint: *"maintaining one megawatt of supercomputer power costs approximately $1 million annually."* **143rd and final ingested DIS chapter — closes Ch 15 and the entire [[DiveIntoSystems]] textbook.** Mints **1 new concept page** ([[ExascaleComputing]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 15.2 Distributed Memory Systems](sources/dis-15-2-distributed-memory.md) — **Second leaf of Ch 15** *Looking Ahead: Other Parallel Systems* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — pivots from [[dis-15-1-gpu|Ch 15.1's]] heterogeneous-CPU+GPU framing into the **[[Cluster|cluster]] / distributed-memory** parallelism arc. Codifies *"A collection of computers working together is known as a **distributed memory system**"* — scale **out** across multiple autonomous machines connected by a network rather than scale **up** within a shared-memory box. Each node has its own [[ProcessAddressSpace|address space]]; coordination requires **explicit [[MessagePassing|message passing]]**. [[MPI]] is the standardized library — each process gets a **rank** 0..N−1 within an [[MPICommunicator|communicator]]; point-to-point [[MPISend|`MPI_Send`]] / [[MPIRecv|`MPI_Recv`]] plus collectives [[MPIBcast]] / [[MPIScatter]] / [[MPIGather]] / [[MPIReduce]] / [[MPIAllreduce]] / [[MPIBarrier]] / [[MPIAllgather]]. **Boss/worker pattern** worked example; [[MPIRecv|`MPI_Recv`]] blocking creates implicit synchronization. **Fault independence** vs shared-memory and **network clock skew** as structural challenges. **142nd ingested DIS chapter.** **No new concept pages** — pure reuse of [[ParallelProcessorsAlgorithms|ParProc Ch 4]] MPI corpus.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 15.1 Hardware Acceleration and CUDA](sources/dis-15-1-gpu.md) — **Opening leaf of Ch 15** *Looking Ahead: Other Parallel Systems* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — pivots from Ch 14's shared-memory [[Pthreads]] / [[OpenMP]] CPU-thread world into the **heterogeneous-computing** chapter. *"Heterogeneous computing is computing using multiple, different processing units found in a computer ... support for parallel computing using the computer's CPU cores and one or more of its accelerator units such as graphics processing units (GPUs)."* The [[GPU]] is a massively-parallel co-processor of [[StreamingMultiprocessor|streaming multiprocessors]] (SMs); [[CUDA]] is the programming model: `__global__` kernels launched with `<<<grid, block>>>` syntax, **separate host/device memory** managed via [[CudaMalloc|`cudaMalloc`]] / [[CudaMemcpy|`cudaMemcpy`]] / [[CudaFree|`cudaFree`]]. [[SIMT]] execution: 32-thread [[Warp|warps]] in lockstep. Three-level thread hierarchy ([[Grid|grid]] → [[Block|blocks]] → threads/warps); intra-block sync via [[CudaThreadSynchronize|`__syncthreads()`]], no native inter-block barrier. GPGPU sweet spot: **embarrassingly parallel** workloads — struggles when CPU↔GPU transfer dominates. **141st ingested DIS chapter — opens Ch 15.** Mints **1 new concept page** ([[CudaThreadIndex]] — `threadIdx` / `blockIdx` / `blockDim` indexing scheme); reuses extensively from [[ParallelProcessorsAlgorithms|ParProc Ch 5]] CUDA corpus.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.9 Exercises](sources/dis-14-9-exercises.md) — **Closing leaf of Ch 14** *Leveraging Shared Memory in the Multicore Era* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — exercise-set page that **fully closes Ch 14 and the [[DiveIntoSystems]] parallel-programming arc**. Three thematic areas: **threading fundamentals** ([[Pthreads]]-based scalar multiplication speedup analysis — operationalizing [[dis-14-1-multicore|14.1's]] 1/c [[ParallelSpeedup|speedup]] approximation against measurements), **[[Synchronization|synchronization]]** (parallel CountSort with [[Mutex|mutexes]] + [[Barrier|barriers]] — drills [[dis-14-3-synchronization|14.3]]), and **[[OpenMP]]** (implicit-threading practical considerations — drills [[dis-14-7-openmp|14.7]]). Structural sibling of [[dis-1-8-exercises]] / [[dis-2-11-exercises]] / [[dis-4-10-exercises]] / [[dis-5-11-exercises]] / [[dis-7-11-x86-64-exercises]] / [[dis-8-11-ia32-exercises]] / [[dis-9-11-arm64-exercises]] / [[dis-11-8-exercises]] / [[dis-13-6-exercises]] — the *exercise-set closes chapter* pattern. **140th ingested DIS chapter — closes Ch 14.** No new concept pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.8 Summary](sources/dis-14-8-summary.md) — **Penultimate leaf** of Ch 14 *Leveraging Shared Memory in the Multicore Era* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — prose-close recapping the chapter's arc from [[dis-14-1-multicore|14.1's]] motivation through [[dis-14-7-openmp|14.7's]] implicit-threading payoff. Four structural commitments: (1) [[Thread|threads]] as the fundamental concurrency unit (lightweight, shared-address-space siblings of [[Process|processes]] with their own [[Stack|stack]] / registers), (2) [[Synchronization|synchronization]] as necessary-but-not-sufficient ([[RaceCondition|race conditions]] / [[DataRace|data races]] emerge without coordination; primitives — [[Mutex|mutexes]], [[Semaphore|semaphores]], [[Barrier|barriers]], [[ConditionVariable|condition variables]] — make [[CriticalSection|critical sections]] atomic), (3) synchronization creates [[ParallelSpeedup|performance]] trade-offs (oversized critical sections serialize execution; [[Deadlock|deadlock]] from misordered acquisitions), (4) parallelism has inherent limits ([[AmdahlsLaw|Amdahl]] caps speedup at $1/S$; [[CacheCoherency|cache coherence]] and [[FalseSharing|false sharing]] tax shared writes; [[ThreadSafety|library functions]] may not be safe). Headline quotes: *"Threads are the fundamental unit of concurrent programs"*, *"Synchronization constructs ensure that programs work correctly"*, *"Be mindful when using synchronization constructs"*, *"Not all components of a program are parallelizable"*. **139th ingested DIS chapter.** No new concept pages — pure recap.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.7 Implicit Threading with OpenMP](sources/dis-14-7-openmp.md) — **Seventh leaf** of Ch 14 *Leveraging Shared Memory in the Multicore Era* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — pivots from [[Pthreads]] (the explicit-threading API Ch 14.2–14.6 used throughout) to **[[OpenMP]]**, the **[[ImplicitThreading|implicit-threading]]** alternative. Codifies the **central design trade**: programmer annotates *existing sequential code* with **`#pragma omp`** compiler directives instead of manually spawning, joining, and synchronizing threads — *"all the low-level work of creating and joining threads is abstracted away from the programmer."* **Four core pragmas**: [[OpenMPParallelPragma|`#pragma omp parallel`]] (spawn thread team), [[OpenMPForPragma|`#pragma omp for`]] (distribute loop iterations — default **static chunking**), [[OpenMPParallelForPragma|`#pragma omp parallel for`]] (combined idiom — the most common form), [[OpenMPCriticalPragma|`#pragma omp critical`]] (mutual-exclusion block — OpenMP analog of [[Mutex|`pthread_mutex_lock` / `_unlock`]]). The **`reduction(op:var)`** clause is the safe per-thread-accumulator combine — each thread gets a private accumulator, all are combined via `op` (`+`, `*`, `min`, `max`, etc.) at the loop's end. Supported by [[GCC|GCC]] / [[LLVM]] / [[Clang]] across C / C++ / Fortran via `-fopenmp`. **Trade-off vs [[Pthreads]]**: OpenMP loses fine-grained control ([[ConditionVariable|condition variables]], [[ReadersWriterLock|readers-writer locks]], custom attributes) for dramatic ergonomic ease — production parallel libraries often mix both. **138th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **5 new concept pages** ([[OpenMP]] top-level anchor, [[OpenMPParallelPragma]], [[OpenMPForPragma]], [[OpenMPParallelForPragma]], [[OpenMPCriticalPragma]]); reuses [[ParallelPragma]] / [[ScheduleClause]] / [[FlushPragma]] / [[OpenMPLocks]] / [[OpenMPSingle]] / [[OpenMPTaskDirective]].
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.6 Thread Safety](sources/dis-14-6-thread-safety.md) — **Sixth leaf** of Ch 14 *Leveraging Shared Memory in the Multicore Era* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — turns the *library function* dimension Ch 14.1–14.5 sidestepped into a first-class hazard. Codifies **[[ThreadSafety|thread safety]]** as a per-function property: *"a thread-safe function guarantees that it can be executed by multiple threads simultaneously without producing unintended side effects or incorrect results."* The C standard library is **not uniformly thread-safe**; The Open Group maintains an explicit thread-unsafe-function catalog; the programmer's burden is to consult it. **Headline distinction** — [[ThreadSafety|thread-safe]] vs [[Reentrant|reentrant]]: *"all thread safe code is re-entrant; however, not all re-entrant code is thread safe."* Reentrancy is **necessary but not sufficient**: a reentrant function can be paused mid-execution and re-invoked (typical hazard: signal handlers); thread safety additionally requires correct concurrent execution from independent threads. **Canonical worked example**: [[Strtok|`strtok()`]] (thread-unsafe — hidden static saved-position pointer, concurrent callers stomp on each other — DIS's `countElemsStr` parallel tokenization produces inconsistent results) vs [[StrtokR|`strtok_r()`]] (thread-safe — explicit `char **saveptr` parameter the caller owns per-thread, on its private [[Stack|stack]]); the `_r` suffix is the [[POSIX]] **reentrant-variant** naming convention. Two cures for thread-unsafe libc: wrap in a [[Mutex|mutex]] (correctness at cost of serialization) or use the `_r` variant when available (no contention). **137th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **3 new concept pages** ([[ThreadSafety]], [[Reentrant]], [[StrtokR]]); **extends [[Strtok]] in place** with the Ch 14.6 thread-unsafety framing (prior coverage was [[dis-2-6-strings|Ch 2.6]] tokenizer-introduction only).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.5 Cache Coherence and False Sharing](sources/dis-14-5-cache-coherence.md) — **Fifth leaf** of Ch 14 *Leveraging Shared Memory in the Multicore Era* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — pivots from [[dis-14-4-performance|Ch 14.4]]'s performance metrics into the **hardware-level subtlety** that destroys parallel speedup even with correct synchronization: **[[CacheCoherency|cache coherence]]** and its pathological inverse, **[[FalseSharing|false sharing]]**. Codifies the **[[SnoopingProtocol|snooping]]** mechanism (per-core L1 caches monitor the [[MemoryBus|memory bus]] for writes and invalidate matching lines) and the **write-invalidate** protocol family ([[MSI|MSI]] / [[MESI|MESI]] / MESIF) — *"every write to counts invalidates the entire line in every other L1 cache."* **Headline failure mode** — false sharing: writes to *different* array elements that happen to share a [[CacheLine|cache line]] trigger the same invalidation cascade as true sharing — *"repeated conflicts in the cache cause a series of misses."* **Measured pathology**: per-thread counter array slows from **0.34 s (1 thread) → 0.80 s (2 threads) → 0.77 s (4 threads)** — the **opposite of [[ParallelSpeedup|speedup]]**. Two mitigations: thread-local accumulators (same pattern as [[dis-14-3-1-mutex|14.3.1's]] lock-coarsening lesson — eliminate per-iteration shared-line contact) and cache-line padding (architecturally explicit, less portable). **136th ingested DIS chapter — opens Ch 14.5.** No new concept pages — fully reuses [[CacheCoherency]] / [[FalseSharing]] / [[MESI]] / [[CacheLine]] / [[SnoopingProtocol]] from the [[ParallelProcessorsAlgorithms|ParProc]] corpus.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.4.2 Advanced Performance Considerations](sources/dis-14-4-2-performance-advanced.md) — **Second sub-leaf** of [[dis-14-4-performance|Ch 14.4]] of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — extends [[dis-14-4-1-performance-basics|14.4.1]]'s [[AmdahlsLaw|Amdahl]] pessimism with the **[[GustafsonsLaw|Gustafson-Barsis Law]]** problem-scaling alternative — *"the amount of work that can be done in parallel varies linearly with the number of processors"* — and codifies the two complementary scalability regimes: **[[StrongScaling|strong scaling]]** (fixed problem, grow cores — Amdahl-bounded; linear means $\text{Speedup}(c)=c$) and **[[WeakScaling|weak scaling]]** (grow problem and cores together — Gustafson-bounded; linear means flat runtime). Names **[[Hyperthreading|hyperthreaded]] cores** as producers of nonlinear scaling curves due to shared-execution-resource contention. Closes with a benchmarking-discipline checklist (multiple trials, measure relevant code only, account for HT, monitor system contention). **135th ingested DIS chapter — closes Ch 14.4.** Mints **2 new concept pages** ([[StrongScaling]], [[WeakScaling]]); also mints [[GustafsonsLaw]] via its sibling 14.4.1.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.4.1 Parallel Performance Basics](sources/dis-14-4-1-performance-basics.md) — **First sub-leaf** of [[dis-14-4-performance|Ch 14.4]] of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — formalizes the two foundational metrics — **[[ParallelSpeedup|speedup]]** ($\text{Speedup} = T_1/T_c$ — promotes the informal 1/c rule from [[dis-14-1-multicore|Ch 14.1.2]]'s [[Speedup]] into the precise ratio) and **[[ParallelEfficiency|efficiency]]** ($= \text{Speedup}/c$, per-core utilization) — then introduces **[[AmdahlsLaw|Amdahl's Law]]** as the **theoretical ceiling**: $\text{Speedup}(c) = 1/(S + P/c)$, asymptote $1/S$ as $c \to \infty$. Worked example — **90% parallelizable code caps at 10× speedup** regardless of core count. Names the **critical-path** dependency-chain concept as the structural cause; Fibonacci generation as the canonical no-parallel-fraction foil. Real-world efficiency degrades with cores due to [[Synchronization|synchronization]] overhead, contention, and load imbalance. **134th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **3 new concept pages** ([[ParallelSpeedup]], [[ParallelEfficiency]], [[AmdahlsLaw]]) — promotes [[AmdahlsLaw|Amdahl]] from the [[Speedup]] / [[dis-14-1-multicore|Ch 14.1]] forward reference.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.4 Measuring Parallel Performance](sources/dis-14-4-performance.md) — **Hub leaf** of Ch 14.4 *Measuring Parallel Performance* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **fourth leaf** of Ch 14 *Leveraging Shared Memory in the Multicore Era*; pivots from [[dis-14-3-synchronization|Ch 14.3]]'s synchronization primitives into the **performance-measurement** arc. Two-tier organization: **14.4.1 *Performance Basics*** ([[ParallelSpeedup|speedup]], [[ParallelEfficiency|efficiency]], [[AmdahlsLaw|Amdahl's Law]]) and **14.4.2 *Advanced Performance Considerations*** ([[GustafsonsLaw|Gustafson-Barsis Law]], [[StrongScaling|strong]] / [[WeakScaling|weak]] scaling, benchmarking discipline). Hub framing: *"having a good understanding of the following topics will round out a reader's understanding of performance"* — basics suffice for an intro course, advanced material rounds it out. **133rd ingested DIS chapter — opens Ch 14.4.** Mints no concept pages directly; its two sub-leaves mint **5 new concept pages** total ([[ParallelSpeedup]], [[ParallelEfficiency]], [[AmdahlsLaw]], [[GustafsonsLaw]], [[StrongScaling]], [[WeakScaling]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.3.3 Other Synchronization Constructs](sources/dis-14-3-3-other-syncs.md) — **Third and final sub-leaf** of [[dis-14-3-synchronization|Ch 14.3]] *Synchronizing Threads* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — surveys the synchronization primitives [[dis-14-3-1-mutex|14.3.1]] and [[dis-14-3-2-semaphores|14.3.2]] leave on the table: **[[Barrier|barriers]]** (*"forces all threads to reach a common execution point before proceeding concurrently"* — Pthreads three-function API [[PthreadBarrierInit|`pthread_barrier_init(&barr, NULL, N)`]] / [[PthreadBarrierWait|`pthread_barrier_wait(&barr)`]] / [[PthreadBarrierDestroy|`pthread_barrier_destroy(&barr)`]]; first `N-1` callers block, the `N`-th releases all — phase-separator use case) and **[[ConditionVariable|condition variables]]** (*"blocks threads until specific conditions are satisfied, eliminating wasteful CPU polling"* — the blocking-wait + signaling primitive that pairs with a mutex; five-function API [[PthreadCondInit|`pthread_cond_init`]] / [[PthreadCondWait|`pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex)`]] (atomically releases mutex while blocking, re-acquires before returning) / [[PthreadCondSignal|`pthread_cond_signal`]] (wake one) / [[PthreadCondBroadcast|`pthread_cond_broadcast`]] (wake all) / [[PthreadCondDestroy|`pthread_cond_destroy`]]; egg-laying worked example — farmers wait for chickens, the canonical [[ProducerConsumer|producer/consumer]] pattern). **Critical pattern — predicate-loop discipline**: *"use a predicate loop (while, not if) around `pthread_cond_wait()` to handle spurious wakeups and condition changes"* — the textbook `while (!predicate) pthread_cond_wait(&cond, &mutex);` idiom that defends against (a) spurious wakeups (the OS may wake the waiter without a corresponding signal) and (b) condition changes between signal and waiter resumption. Also surveys [[ReadersWriterLock|readers-writer locks]] at the catalogue level — Pthreads `pthread_rwlock_rdlock` / `pthread_rwlock_wrlock` for read-heavy workloads admitting many concurrent readers OR one exclusive writer. **132nd ingested DIS chapter — closes the Ch 14.3 *Synchronizing Threads* arc.** Mints **9 new concept pages** ([[ConditionVariable]], [[PthreadBarrierInit]], [[PthreadBarrierWait]], [[PthreadBarrierDestroy]], [[PthreadCondInit]], [[PthreadCondWait]], [[PthreadCondSignal]], [[PthreadCondBroadcast]], [[PthreadCondDestroy]]) and extends [[Barrier]] in place with DIS's Pthreads three-function barrier API; also creates [[ReadersWriterLock]].
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.3.2 Semaphores](sources/dis-14-3-2-semaphores.md) — **Second sub-leaf** of [[dis-14-3-synchronization|Ch 14.3]] *Synchronizing Threads* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — introduces **[[Semaphore|semaphores]]** as the resource-count synchronization primitive that complements the [[Mutex|mutex]]'s ownership model: *"semaphores manage concurrent access to resource pools by tracking availability count rather than ownership."* **Counting vs binary** distinction — counting semaphores range from 0 to *r* (decrement to acquire, increment to release; value 0 blocks acquirers), binary semaphores have only locked/unlocked states. **Critical distinction from mutex**: *"any thread can unlock the semaphore (in contrast to a mutex, where the calling thread must unlock it)"* — semaphores have no ownership concept, making them the natural primitive for [[ProducerConsumer|producer/consumer]] patterns where producer and consumer are different threads. **Core POSIX API**: [[SemInit|`sem_init(sem, pshared, value)`]] (three params — address, sharing scope `0` for threads / nonzero for inter-process, initial count), [[SemWait|`sem_wait(sem)`]] (decrement-and-block — returns immediately if count > 0, blocks if 0), [[SemPost|`sem_post(sem)`]] (increment-and-wake — returns immediately, wakes one waiter), [[SemDestroy|`sem_destroy(sem)`]] (deallocate). **macOS portability gotcha**: `sem_init` deprecated → use `sem_open` / `sem_close` / `sem_unlink` (named semaphores). Use-case framing: *"semaphores excel where the goal isn't *who* owns what, but *how many* resources are still available — particularly useful for managing resource pools more simply and efficiently than mutex-condition variable combinations."* **131st ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **5 new concept pages** ([[Semaphore]], [[SemInit]], [[SemWait]], [[SemPost]], [[SemDestroy]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.3.1 Mutex](sources/dis-14-3-1-mutex.md) — **First sub-leaf** of [[dis-14-3-synchronization|Ch 14.3]] *Synchronizing Threads* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — operationalizes the [[CriticalSection|critical-section]] concept from the parent hub into the canonical [[Pthreads]] primitive: the **[[Mutex|mutex]]** (**mut**ual **ex**clusion lock). Defines a mutex as *"a synchronization primitive that ensures only one thread executes code within a critical section at any given time, preventing data races on shared variables."* Codifies the **four-function API** — declaration `pthread_mutex_t mutex;` (typically global), initialization [[PthreadMutexInit|`pthread_mutex_init(&mutex, NULL)`]] (in `main` before thread creation), acquire/release pair [[PthreadMutexLock|`pthread_mutex_lock(&mutex)`]] / [[PthreadMutexUnlock|`pthread_mutex_unlock(&mutex)`]], teardown [[PthreadMutexDestroy|`pthread_mutex_destroy(&mutex)`]] (after [[PthreadJoin|`pthread_join`]]-ing all workers). **Blocking semantics**: any other thread attempting to acquire the same lock will block until the holding thread unlocks. **Lock-placement performance lesson** — the chapter's headline empirical claim: *"Simply wrapping entire loops with locks produces correct results but serializes execution, eliminating parallelism benefits. Conversely, locking on every iteration creates expensive overhead. Optimal strategy: use local thread-private variables to accumulate intermediate results without contention, then acquire the lock only once to update shared state."* DIS's measured payoff — **1.92 s (single thread) → 0.13 s (4 threads)** on the worked accumulator example, an effective speedup ~15× across the dual axis (parallelism + lock-coarsening). **[[Deadlock]] risk surfaced**: *"Multiple interdependent locks can cause mutual blocking"* — illustrated with a banking scenario where thread A holds lock X waiting for Y, thread B holds Y waiting for X. **130th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **4 new concept pages** ([[PthreadMutexInit]], [[PthreadMutexLock]], [[PthreadMutexUnlock]], [[PthreadMutexDestroy]]) and **extends [[Mutex]] in place** with the canonical Pthreads four-function API (prior wiki coverage was the Embedded Rust `cortex_m::interrupt::Mutex` variant only); **extends [[Deadlock]] in place** with DIS's CPU-side banking-scenario framing.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.3 Synchronizing Threads](sources/dis-14-3-synchronization.md) — **Hub leaf** of Ch 14.3 *Synchronizing Threads* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — third leaf of Ch 14 *Leveraging Shared Memory in the Multicore Era*. Pivots from [[dis-14-2-posix|Ch 14.2]]'s thread-creation mechanics into the **why and what** of [[Synchronization|thread synchronization]]: *"enforcing a particular execution order among threads to ensure program correctness, even though it may increase runtime."* Codifies the **CountSort motivating example** — a parallel-sort implementation where multiple threads update a shared array without protection produces nondeterministic / wrong results, demonstrating that parallelizing work across cores is **necessary but not sufficient**. Names the **core taxonomy** the three sub-leaves elaborate: [[CriticalSection|critical section]] (region of code that must execute atomically), [[DataRace|data race]] (two or more threads simultaneously write to the same memory location producing incorrect results), [[RaceCondition|race condition]] (broader — any situation where simultaneous execution yields incorrect outcomes), and [[AtomicOperation|atomic operation]] (an action that executes without interruption from a thread's perspective — *"all or nothing behavior"*). **Headline structural rule** — the **default-unsafe assumption**: *"all operations should be assumed to be nonatomic unless mutual exclusion is explicitly enforced"* — the [[ReadModifyWrite|read-modify-write]] pattern is the canonical danger. **Heisenbug property**: *"not all concurrent execution sequences cause errors — races occur only under specific timing conditions, making them difficult to detect and reproduce."* **129th ingested DIS chapter.** Hub leaf; three sub-leaves drill each primitive. Mints **3 new concept pages** ([[Synchronization]], [[RaceCondition]], [[AtomicOperation]]); **extends [[CriticalSection]] / [[DataRace]] in place** with DIS framings.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.2 POSIX Threads](sources/dis-14-2-posix.md) — **Second leaf of Ch 14** *Leveraging Shared Memory in the Multicore Era* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — pivots from [[dis-14-1-multicore|Ch 14.1]]'s **motivation** to the **API**: [[Pthreads]], the IEEE [[POSIX]] standardized C threading library. Codifies the **four-step thread lifecycle** (declare `pthread_t` storage → spawn via [[PthreadCreate|`pthread_create`]] → run [[ThreadFunction|thread function]] with private stack + registers → reclaim via [[PthreadJoin|`pthread_join`]]); the two anchor signatures `pthread_create(pthread_t *thread, const pthread_attr_t *attr, void *(*thread_function)(void *), void *thread_args)` and `pthread_join(pthread_t thread, void **return_val)`; the [[ThreadFunction|thread-function]] prototype `void *func(void *arg)` ([[VoidStar|`void *`]] argument **and** return — the generic-typing convention that makes the API type-agnostic); the **[[ThreadID|TID]]** convention (user-supplied per-thread identifier passed as `thread_args`); the **[[GccPthreadFlag|`-pthread`]]** compile flag. Headline quote: *"You should never make any assumptions about the order in which threads will execute"* — correctness-by-ordering requires explicit synchronization deferred to later sections. **Promotes [[Pthreads]]** from the [[dis-3-6-gdb-pthreads|Ch 3.6]] forward-referenced stub to full coverage. **128th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **5 new concept pages** ([[PthreadCreate]], [[PthreadJoin]], [[ThreadFunction]], [[ThreadID]], [[GccPthreadFlag]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 14.1 Programming Multicore Systems](sources/dis-14-1-multicore.md) — **Opening leaf of Ch 14** *Leveraging Shared Memory in the Multicore Era* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — motivates explicit parallel programming as the **mandatory** response to the post-[[PowerWall|power-wall]] [[MulticoreProcessor|multicore]] reality [[dis-5-9-modern|Ch 5.9]] foreshadowed. Splits across **14.1.1 *Impact on Process Execution*** (multicore raises [[Throughput|throughput]] of many concurrent processes but not the CPU time of any one process) and **14.1.2 *Expediting with Threads*** ([[Thread|threads]] as the lightweight shared-address-space sibling of processes that *can* split one program across cores). Codifies the [[ConcurrencyVsParallelism|concurrency vs parallelism]] distinction — *"the simultaneous execution of instructions from processes running on multiple cores is referred to as parallel execution"* — and supplies the **1/c [[Speedup|speedup]] approximation rule**: *"if the number of threads matches the number of cores (c) and the operating system schedules each thread to run on a separate core in parallel, then the multithreaded process should run in approximately 1/c of the time."* **Scope note**: [[AmdahlsLaw|Amdahl's Law]] is **not** covered in 14.1 — formal serial-fraction analysis deferred. **127th ingested DIS chapter — opens Ch 14.** Mints **3 new concept pages** ([[SharedMemoryParallelism]], [[ConcurrencyVsParallelism]], [[Speedup]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 13.6 Exercises](sources/dis-13-6-exercises.md) — **Closing leaf of Ch 13** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — exercise-set page that fully closes Ch 13 *The Operating System*. Drills [[dis-13-2-processes|Ch 13.2]] via an inline three-nested-[[Fork|`fork()`]] tree-trace problem (diagram parent-child hierarchy + enumerate per-process output sequences) and [[dis-13-3-virtual-memory|Ch 13.3]] via external interactive *Early Access Interactive Virtual Memory Questions*. **126th ingested DIS chapter — closes Ch 13.** Structural sibling of [[dis-1-8-exercises]] / [[dis-2-11-exercises]] / [[dis-4-10-exercises]] / [[dis-5-11-exercises]] / [[dis-7-11-x86-64-exercises]] / [[dis-8-11-ia32-exercises]] / [[dis-9-11-arm64-exercises]] / [[dis-11-8-exercises]] — the *exercise-set closes chapter* pattern. **No new concept pages.**
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 13.5 Summary and Other OS Functionality](sources/dis-13-5-summary-advanced.md) — **Second-to-last leaf of Ch 13** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — recaps the Ch 13 arc ([[Process|processes]] + [[Multiprogramming|multiprogramming]] + [[VirtualMemory|virtual memory]] + [[ContextSwitch|context switching]] + [[InterprocessCommunication|IPC]]) and **names the OS subsystems Ch 13 deliberately deferred**: [[FileSystem|filesystems]], protection / security, [[SchedulingPolicy|scheduling policies]], [[Networking]], [[Virtualization]] / [[Hypervisor|hypervisors]], [[LoadableKernelModule|loadable kernel modules]], and runtime tuning. Headline quotes: *"a [[Hypervisor|hypervisor]] virtualizes the system hardware and allows the host OS to run multiple virtual guest operating systems"* and *"a [[LoadableKernelModule|loadable kernel module]] is executable code that can be loaded into the kernel and run in kernel mode"*. Recommends [[OperatingSystemsThreeEasyPieces|*Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces*]] (Arpaci-Dusseau & Arpaci-Dusseau, 2018) as the canonical follow-on. **125th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **3 new concept pages** ([[Hypervisor]], [[Virtualization]], [[LoadableKernelModule]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 13.4.3 Shared Memory](sources/dis-13-4-3-shared-memory.md) — **Third sub-leaf of Ch 13.4** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — closes the IPC sub-arc with the **shared-memory** [[InterprocessCommunication|IPC]] family: *"the OS can support sharing pages of virtual address space by setting entries in the page tables of sharing processes to the same physical frame number"*. Reuses [[dis-13-3-virtual-memory|Ch 13.3]]'s [[PageTable|page-table]] machinery — distinct [[VirtualAddress|VAs]] in two different process tables alias to the same [[PhysicalAddress|physical frame]]; both sides then load/store directly — **no syscall per access**, the **fastest** IPC family. Names `shmget`; defers `shmat` / `shmdt` / `shmctl` / POSIX `shm_open`+[[Mmap|`mmap`]] / synchronization to Ch 14. Application owns synchronization ([[Mutex]] / [[Semaphore]] — also deferred). [[Thread|Threads]] briefly noted as in-process analog. **124th ingested DIS chapter — closes Ch 13.4.** Mints **1 new concept page** ([[SharedMemoryIPC]] — disambiguated from the existing CUDA-on-chip [[SharedMemory]] page).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 13.4.2 Message Passing](sources/dis-13-4-2-message-passing.md) — **Second sub-leaf of Ch 13.4** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — formalizes the **message-passing** [[InterprocessCommunication|IPC]] family as an OS-managed channel: *"processes with private virtual address spaces can communicate ... by sending and receiving messages to one another."* Two concrete channels: **[[Pipe|pipes]]** — *"a one-way communication channel for two processes running on the same machine"* (canonical example `cat foo.c | grep factorial` via the `pipe(2)` syscall + [[Fork]] + [[Dup2]] + [[Exec]]); and **[[Socket|sockets]]** — *"a two-way communication channel"* spanning same-machine *and* network ([[TCP]]/IP). Arbitrary byte-stream payload overcomes [[dis-13-4-1-signals|13.4.1]]'s fixed 32-signal namespace; per-message OS copy is the cost vs [[SharedMemoryIPC|shared memory]]. **123rd ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **3 new concept pages** ([[MessagePassing]], [[Pipe]], [[NamedPipe]] (FIFO forward reference)).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 13.4.1 Signals](sources/dis-13-4-1-signals.md) — **First sub-leaf of Ch 13.4** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — formalizes the **[[Signal|signal]]** [[InterprocessCommunication|IPC]] family as **asynchronous software interrupts** kernel-delivered between [[Process|processes]]. [[Kill|`kill(pid, sig)`]] is the universal send primitive — *"`kill` isn't limited to termination signals — it delivers any signal type."* Receiver flow: OS pauses execution → [[SignalHandler|signal handler]] runs → control returns. Two registration syscalls — *"Linux supports two different system calls that can be used to change the default behavior of a signal or to register a signal handler on a particular signal: `sigaction` and `signal`"* (`sigaction` POSIX-preferred). Four default actions; `SIGKILL` + `SIGSTOP` **uncatchable**. **`SIGCHLD` reaping idiom** — `waitpid(-1, &status, WNOHANG)` in a loop, because the OS records *occurrence not count*. **Headline limit**: *"Systems define a fixed number of signals (e.g., Linux defines 32 different signals)"* — predefined events only, not arbitrary data. **122nd ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **1 new concept page** ([[SignalHandler]]) and **extends [[Signal]] / [[Kill]] in place** from their [[dis-3-4-gdb-advanced|Ch 3.4]] GDB-context introduction into the OS-IPC context.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 13.4 Interprocess Communication](sources/dis-13-4-ipc.md) — **Fourth leaf of Ch 13 *The Operating System*** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **opening hub** of the IPC sub-arc (13.4.1 Signals + 13.4.2 Message Passing + 13.4.3 Shared Memory). Pivots from [[dis-13-3-virtual-memory|13.3]]'s per-process [[VirtualMemory|virtual-memory]] isolation into the *inverse* problem: applications that need to coordinate. Codifies [[InterprocessCommunication|IPC]] as *"mechanisms by which operating systems enable processes to exchange information or coordinate their execution"* and introduces the **three canonical families**: [[Signal|signals]] (event notification, no payload), [[MessagePassing|message passing]] (OS-managed byte-stream channel), [[SharedMemoryIPC|shared memory]] (overlap virtual address spaces directly). Each sub-leaf drills one family. **121st ingested DIS chapter — opens Ch 13.4.** Mints **1 new concept page** ([[InterprocessCommunication]]).
*342 entries.*

- [Dive into Systems — Ch 13.3 Virtual Memory](sources/dis-13-3-virtual-memory.md) — **Third leaf** of Ch 13 *The Operating System* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — supplies the **address-translation mechanism** under [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]]'s four-region [[ProcessMemory|program memory]] cartoon: every process sees its own private [[VirtualAddress|virtual address space]], the OS maps [[VirtualMemory|virtual]] to [[PhysicalAddress|physical]] addresses through a per-process [[PageTable|page table]], and the [[TLB|translation lookaside buffer]] caches recent translations to avoid two memory accesses per load. Fixed-size [[Page|pages]] (typically 4 KiB) replace contiguous-allocation; [[Paging]] decouples virtual contiguity from physical layout. **[[PageFault|Page fault]]** = the page-table entry says *"not resident"* — the OS reads the page from the [[SwapFile|swap file]] on disk (millions of cycles), evicts another page if needed, retries the access. **[[DemandPaging|Demand paging]]** loads pages on first reference rather than at process start — a process's virtual address space can exceed physical RAM. **120th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **10 new concept pages** ([[VirtualMemory]], [[VirtualAddress]], [[PhysicalAddress]], [[PageTable]], [[Page]], [[Paging]], [[PageFault]], [[TLB]] promoted from forward-ref, [[SwapFile]], [[DemandPaging]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 13.2 Processes](sources/dis-13-2-processes.md) — **Second leaf** of Ch 13 *The Operating System* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — turns the [[Process]] noun named in [[dis-13-1-booting-running|13.1]] into a full state machine + OS data structure + POSIX [[SystemCall|syscall]] API. **Four [[ProcessState|process states]]** (Ready / Running / Blocked / Exited); the **[[ProcessControlBlock|process control block]]** (PID + address space + register snapshot + open files + state); the **mechanism / policy split** ([[ContextSwitch|context switch]] = *how*, [[Scheduler|scheduling]] = *which*). [[Multiprogramming|Multiprogramming]] (switch on I/O block) + [[Timesharing]] (quantum-bounded preemption) keep the CPU busy. POSIX surface: [[Fork|`fork()`]] (returns twice — `0` to child, child [[ProcessID|PID]] to parent), [[Exec|`execvp`]] (overlays image, never returns on success), [[Wait|`wait` / `waitpid`]] (reaps [[Zombie|zombies]], unblocks parent on [[Signal|`SIGCHLD`]]). [[Init|`init` (PID 1)]] is the root of the process hierarchy. Closes with the [[WallTime|wall time]] vs [[CPUTime|CPU time]] distinction. **119th ingested DIS chapter.** Mints **11 new concept pages** ([[ProcessState]], [[ProcessControlBlock]], [[Exec]], [[Wait]], [[Scheduler]], [[ProcessScheduling]], [[Multiprogramming]], [[Zombie]], [[Init]], [[WallTime]], [[CPUTime]]) and extends [[Process]] / [[Fork]] in place.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 13.1 Booting and Running the OS](sources/dis-13-1-booting-running.md) — **Opening leaf** of Ch 13 *The Operating System* of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — pivots from Part IV performance-tuning into the **OS-implementation arc**. Codifies how the OS itself gets started ([[Booting]] via [[Firmware|firmware]] like [[BIOS]] / [[UEFI]] that loads the [[Bootloader|boot block]] from disk), how it launches user programs (allocate RAM → load binary → create [[Process|process]] state → initialize [[CPU]]), and the **interrupt-driven architecture** that lets the [[Kernel|kernel]] sleep until a hardware device or user program needs service. Codifies the **dual-mode CPU** ([[KernelMode]] vs [[UserMode]]) and the **[[SystemCall|system-call]] trap** as the controlled gateway between them — *"When an application wants to invoke a system call, it places the desired call's number in a known location and issues a trap instruction to interrupt the OS"*. **Two interrupt sources**: hardware ([[Interrupt|interrupt]] bus, devices) and software (traps from user-mode trap instructions). Kernel-in-every-address-space optimization makes [[ContextSwitch|context switching]] cheap — Meltdown vulnerability later forced stricter kernel-user separation. **118th ingested DIS chapter — opens Ch 13.** Mints **5 new concept pages** ([[Bootloader]], [[Kernel]], [[KernelMode]], [[UserMode]], [[SystemCall]]) and **extends [[Interrupt]] / [[ContextSwitch]] in place** with the OS-level treatment.

score = metric(x, pred)` with progress + tabular display)).
