Drills [[dis-5-3-gates|Ch 5.3]]–[[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]]: build a 1-bit [[XorGate|XOR]] from [[AndGate|AND]] / [[OrGate|OR]] / [[NotGate|NOT]] via the [[TruthTable|truth-table]] → Boolean → gate-network methodology; full 1-bit [[FullAdder|adder]] truth table; 4-bit [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation circuit; 4-way [[Multiplexer|MUX]] selection analysis + 16-way MUX select-bit count ($\log_2 16 = 4$); [[SRLatch|RS latch]] state tracing; gated [[DLatch|D latch]] [[WriteEnable|`WE`]] behaviour. **Structural sibling of [[dis-1-8-exercises|Ch 1.8]] / [[dis-2-11-exercises|Ch 2.11]] / [[dis-4-10-exercises|Ch 4.10]]** — drills foundational concepts via truth-table derivation, combinational-logic synthesis, sequential-storage elements, and control-signal timing. No new conceptual material. **61st ingested chapter — fully closes Ch 5 *Computer Architecture***.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.10 Summary](sources/dis-5-10-summary.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s short, no-new-material recap closing the **prose body** of Ch 5 *Computer Architecture* (Ch 5.11 exercises follow). Recaps the chapter arc as a top-down construction of the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|von Neumann architecture]]: [[LogicGate|logic gates]] → [[Circuit|circuits]] ([[ArithmeticLogicCircuit|arithmetic/logic]] / [[ControlCircuit|control]] / [[StorageCircuit|storage]]) → [[CPU]] ([[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] + [[RegisterFile|register file]] + [[ControlUnit|control unit]]) executing the [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute-WriteBack cycle]] dictated by the [[InstructionSetArchitecture|ISA]], with performance multipliers from [[InstructionPipelining|pipelining]] + [[InstructionLevelParallelism|ILP]] + [[MulticoreProcessor|multicore]] design. Closing quote: *"the general-purpose design of the von Neumann architecture allows it to execute any type of program"* — the Turing-complete reprogrammability that makes the model dominant after eight decades. **Structural sibling of [[dis-1-7-summary|Ch 1.7]] / [[dis-2-10-summary|Ch 2.10]] / [[dis-3-7-summary|Ch 3.7]] / [[dis-4-9-summary|Ch 4.9]]**. No new concept pages. **60th ingested chapter.**
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.9 Looking Ahead: CPUs Today](sources/dis-5-9-modern.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **closing section of Ch 5 *Computer Architecture***, fast-forwarding from the single-issue pipeline of [[dis-5-7-pipelining|Ch 5.7]] / [[dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced|Ch 5.8]] to the **modern multi-issue, multi-thread, multi-core reality**. Frames CPU evolution as a response to **[[MooresLaw|Moore's Law]]** (transistor density doubles ~2 yr; slowing from 2012; ending mid-2020s per Moore himself) — architects spent the budget on ever-more-complex single processors via **[[InstructionLevelParallelism|instruction-level parallelism (ILP)]]** (*"a set of design techniques used to support parallel execution of a single program's instructions on a single processor"*) until the early-2000s **[[PowerWall|power wall]]** capped single-core clock scaling. **Three ILP families** — **[[VectorProcessor|vector processors]]** ([[Cray1|Cray-1]] 1976; *"vector processors today primarily appear in GPU accelerators"* — i.e. **[[GPGPU]]**), **[[Superscalar|superscalar]]** (hardware out-of-order multi-issue; IPC up to issue width), **[[VLIW|VLIW (Very Long Instruction Word)]]** (compiler-scheduled multi-issue; simpler hardware but specialized compilers). Post-power-wall pivot: **[[HardwareMultithreading|hardware multithreading]]** in two variants — interleaved (Intel **[[HyperThreading|Hyper-Threading]]**, IPC ≤ 1; *"not true SMT"* per Ch 5.9) vs **[[SimultaneousMultithreading|simultaneous multithreading (SMT)]]** (pairs with superscalar to push IPC > 1) — and **[[MulticoreProcessor|multicore]]**: *"multicore microprocessor design is the primary way in which the performance of processor architectures can continue to keep pace with Moore's Law without increasing the processor clock rate."* Chip tables: AMD Zen / Intel Core / Xeon (2–8 cores × 2 threads), Oracle SPARC M7 (32 × 8 → IPC 64), IBM Power 9 (24 × 8-way SMT → IPC 192). **Programmer corollary**: explicit parallel programming is now mandatory for single-program speedup. **59th ingested chapter** — **closes Ch 5 *Computer Architecture***; **10 new concept pages** ([[InstructionLevelParallelism]], [[MooresLaw]], [[PowerWall]], [[VectorProcessor]], [[Cray1]], [[VLIW]], [[HardwareMultithreading]], [[SimultaneousMultithreading]], [[HyperThreading]], [[GPGPU]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **59 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.8 Advanced Pipelining Considerations](sources/dis-5-8-pipelining-advanced.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **realism-layer** follow-up to [[dis-5-7-pipelining|Ch 5.7]]'s idealized one-instruction-per-cycle pipeline. Confronts the failure modes — [[PipelineHazard|pipeline hazards]] — that break the ideal: **[[DataHazard|data hazards]]** (register-dependency interference, e.g. `MOV`→`ADD` on the same register before WriteBack lands) and **[[ControlHazard|control hazards]]** (branch direction unknown until Execute). Four mitigations catalogued: **[[PipelineStall|pipeline stalling]]** (inject [[NoOperation|NOP]] bubbles — simple but degrades CPI), **[[Forwarding|operand forwarding/bypassing]]** (*"rather than stalling, the pipeline reads the result from the previous operation"* — wires producer-stage output to consumer-stage input, eliminates the data-hazard stall), **[[BranchPrediction|branch prediction]]** via a [[BranchPredictor|branch predictor]] structure (*"the most common solution is to use a branch predictor, which will predict which way a branch will go, based on previous executions"* — names **[[Spectre]]** as a speculative-execution security side effect), and **eager execution** of both branch paths. Two performance layers on top: **[[Superscalar|superscalar]]** (replicate stage circuitry → multiple instructions per cycle) and **[[OutOfOrderExecution|out-of-order execution]]** (dynamically reorder ready instructions around stalled ones). Headline principle: *"compilers and processors do whatever they can to avoid pipeline stalls in order to maximize performance."* **Completes the scope-omission [[dis-5-7-pipelining|Ch 5.7]] explicitly flagged** (hazards / forwarding / branch prediction / out-of-order). **58th ingested chapter**; **9 new concept pages** ([[PipelineHazard]] / [[DataHazard]] / [[ControlHazard]] / [[BranchPrediction]] / [[BranchPredictor]] / [[Forwarding]] / [[PipelineStall]] / [[Superscalar]] / [[OutOfOrderExecution]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **58 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.7 Pipelining Instruction Execution](sources/dis-5-7-pipelining.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **throughput-optimization** follow-up to [[dis-5-6-instruction-execution|Ch 5.6]]'s sequential four-stage [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute]] baseline. Extends the cycle into an **overlapped [[InstructionPipelining|pipeline]]** in which a new instruction enters stage 1 every [[ClockCycle|cycle]] while older instructions advance through stages 2–4 simultaneously — exploiting the **stage-specific idleness** of the non-pipelined design (each stage's dedicated circuitry sits unused for three of every four cycles). Headline result: *"when the pipeline is full, the CPU completes the execution of one instruction every clock cycle"* — effective [[CyclesPerInstruction|CPI]] drops from 4 → 1 **without reducing individual-instruction latency** — *pipelining is a throughput, not latency, optimization*. For load/store instructions a **five-stage** Fetch-Decode-Execute-Memory-WriteBack pipeline is typical. Trade-off: additional storage and control circuitry between stages. Modern depth examples: **ARM 3+ stages**, **Intel Core i7 14 stages**. **Scope omission**: pipeline **hazards** (data / control / structural) are **not** introduced in Ch 5.7. **57th ingested chapter**; **3 new concept pages** ([[InstructionPipelining]] / [[PipelineStages]] / [[InstructionThroughput]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **57 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.5 Building a Processor](sources/dis-5-5-cpu.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **integration chapter** of Ch 5 *Computer Architecture* that assembles [[dis-5-4-circuits|Ch 5.4]]'s three circuit categories into a working [[CPU]]. Three subsections (5.5.1 The [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] / 5.5.2 The [[RegisterFile|Register File]] + *Special-Purpose Registers* / 5.5.3 The CPU) culminate in the **[[ProcessorDatapath|data path]]** umbrella: *"The data path consists of the parts of the CPU that perform arithmetic and logic operations (the ALU) and store data (registers), and the buses that connect these parts."* The [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] receives operands + an opcode (from bits of the current instruction) and emits a result + **condition-code bits** (negative / zero / carry-out — a `1` *"indicates that the condition holds"*); the internal op-select uses the [[Multiplexer|MUX]] from [[dis-5-4-2-control-circuits|Ch 5.4.2]] — closing **Ch 5.4.1's deferred MUX/op-select forward reference**. The [[RegisterFile|register file]] (8–32 [[CpuRegister|GP registers]]) gets full read/write wiring — `Sr0`/`Sr1` drive the read-port [[Multiplexer|MUXes]]; `Sw` drives a write-port [[Demultiplexer|DMUX]] routing the `WE` bit to exactly the destination register — **closing [[dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits|Ch 5.4.3]]'s deferred multi-register wiring forward reference**. Names the two special-purpose registers from [[dis-5-2-von-neumann|Ch 5.2]] ([[ProgramCounter|PC]] / [[InstructionRegister|IR]]) and the [[ClockSignal|clock]] that *"drives the circuitry of the CPU to execute program instructions."* **Forward-references**: the **control path** mechanism, [[ClockCycle|clock-cycle]] / [[ClockSpeed|clock-speed]] / [[CircuitDelay|circuit-delay]] quantitative treatment all deferred to the next section. **55th ingested chapter**; **4 new concept pages** ([[ProcessorDatapath]] — Ch 5.5's integration umbrella; [[ClockCycle]] / [[ClockSpeed]] / [[CircuitDelay]] — named-role-only forward-reference pages following the *"only what's covered"* rule).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.4.3 Storage Circuits](sources/dis-5-4-3-storage-circuits.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **third and closing subsection** of [[dis-5-4-circuits|Ch 5.4]] — delivers the **storage** category and **completes the three-category partition**. *"A storage circuit's value depends on its input values and also its currently stored value"* — feedback loop is the structural signature distinguishing sequential storage from the combinational siblings. Introduces the **[[SRAM]] (circuit-based) / [[DRAM]] (capacitor-based)** technology split that organizes the [[MemoryHierarchy|memory hierarchy]]. Three-layer build-up: [[SRLatch|RS latch]] (cross-coupled [[NandGate|NAND]] gates + feedback; hold when `S=R=1`, forbidden `S=R=0`) → [[DLatch|gated D latch]] (adds [[WriteEnable|`WE`]]; structurally eliminates the forbidden case) → 32-bit [[CpuRegister|register]] (32 D-latches sharing one `WE`). Names the [[RegisterFile|register file]] (registers + [[Decoder|decoder]] + [[Multiplexer|MUX]]) but defers full wiring. Uses *"flip-flop"* informally as a [[DLatch|D-latch]] synonym — no edge-triggered master-slave FF built; explicit [[ClockSignal|clock]] abstracted to `WE`. **Resolves the long-standing forward-reference** to [[StorageCircuit]] from the Ch 5.4 hub and both 5.4.1 / 5.4.2 siblings. **54th ingested chapter**; **8 new concept pages** ([[StorageCircuit]], [[Latch]], [[FlipFlop]], [[SRLatch]], [[DLatch]], [[WriteEnable]], [[ClockSignal]], [[RegisterFile]]) + [[DRAM]] (new) + [[CpuRegister]] updated in-place.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.4 Circuits](sources/dis-5-4-circuits.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **short hub** opening Ch 5.4 *Circuits* — turns [[dis-5-3-gates|Ch 5.3]]'s seven [[LogicGate|gates]] into the [[Circuit|digital circuits]] that *"implement the core functionality of the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|architecture]]."* Installs **hierarchical composition + [[Abstraction|black-box abstraction]]** as the design discipline (*"more complex circuits are constructed by combining simpler subcircuits and basic logic gates"*) and partitions processor circuitry into the **three categories** that map onto [[dis-5-2-von-neumann|Ch 5.2]]'s [[ProcessingUnit|processing]] / [[ControlUnit|control]] / storage decomposition: [[ArithmeticLogicCircuit|arithmetic & logic]] (Ch 5.4.1 — the [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]]'s inner mechanism), [[ControlCircuit|control]] (Ch 5.4.2 — drives the [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute cycle]]), and [[StorageCircuit|storage]] (Ch 5.4.3 — substrate beneath [[CpuRegister|registers]] / [[RAM|memory]]). **Hub page only** — no worked circuit at this level; subsections deliver the mechanisms. **51st ingested chapter**; **1 new umbrella concept page** ([[Circuit]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.3 Logic Gates](sources/dis-5-3-gates.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **gate-level zoom-in** below [[dis-5-2-von-neumann|Ch 5.2]]'s [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]]. *"Logic gates are the building blocks of the digital circuitry that implements arithmetic, control, and storage functionality in a digital computer."* Each [[LogicGate|gate]] implements one [[BooleanAlgebra|Boolean]] operation over 1-bit inputs, physically realized by [[Transistor|transistors]] as voltage-controlled switches. Two tiers: the **functionally-complete basis** [[AndGate|AND]] / [[OrGate|OR]] / [[NotGate|NOT]] (suffices to build any circuit, including the entire [[CPU]] — [[ClaudeShannon|Shannon]]'s 1937 thesis result), and the **derived gates** [[NandGate|NAND]] / [[NorGate|NOR]] / [[XorGate|XOR]] / [[XnorGate|XNOR]] (convenience extensions, each composable from the basis — e.g. *"(A NOR B) ≡ NOT(A OR B)"*). Every gate is specified by its [[TruthTable|truth table]]; **M-bit gates** are M copies of the 1-bit gate operating in parallel — the hardware mechanism beneath [[dis-4-6-bitwise|Ch 4.6]]'s [[BitwiseOperator|C bitwise operators]] (`&` / `|` / `^` / `~`). [[XorGate|XOR]] is the headline arithmetic gate — `Sum = A XOR B XOR CarryIn` in the [[FullAdder|full-adder]] of [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] and the mode-controlled invert in [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]]'s subtraction trick. **50th ingested chapter**; **10 new concept pages** ([[LogicGate]], [[AndGate]], [[OrGate]], [[NotGate]], [[NandGate]], [[NorGate]], [[XorGate]], [[XnorGate]], [[TruthTable]], [[Transistor]]); [[BooleanAlgebra]] / [[ClaudeShannon]] connected as forward references from [[dis-5-1-history|Ch 5.1]]. [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **50 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.2 The von Neumann Architecture](sources/dis-5-2-von-neumann.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **operational follow-up** to [[dis-5-1-history|Ch 5.1]]'s historical narrative — decomposes the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|von Neumann architecture]] into **five functional units** ([[ControlUnit|control unit]] + [[ProcessingUnit|processing unit]] = [[CPU]]; [[RAM|memory unit]]; [[InputDevice|input unit]]; [[OutputDevice|output unit]]) connected by three [[Bus|system buses]] ([[ControlBus|control]] / [[AddressBus|address]] / [[DataBus|data]]). [[ProcessingUnit|Processing unit]] = [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] + [[CpuRegister|register file]]; [[ControlUnit|control unit]] owns the [[ProgramCounter|PC]] and [[InstructionRegister|IR]]. Operational restatement of the [[StoredProgram|stored-program]] principle: *"there is no distinction between instructions and data in the von Neumann architecture"* — they share [[RAM|memory]] **and** [[CpuRegister|register]] storage. Architecture's *operational heart* is the **[[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle|fetch-decode-execute-store cycle]]**: fetch instruction at [[ProgramCounter|PC]] into [[InstructionRegister|IR]] → decode opcode + operand locations → [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] executes → store result via the buses → repeat. [[RAM|Memory]] is **[[ByteAddressable|byte-addressable]]** — a 32-bit [[AddressBus|address bus]] caps it at $2^{32}$ bytes (4 GiB). Touchscreens / storage drives / NICs are bidirectional [[IODevice|I/O devices]]. **15 new concept pages** ([[ControlUnit]], [[ArithmeticLogicUnit]], [[ProcessingUnit]], [[Bus]], [[ControlBus]], [[AddressBus]], [[DataBus]], [[IODevice]], [[InputDevice]], [[OutputDevice]], [[FetchDecodeExecuteCycle]], [[ProgramCounter]], [[InstructionRegister]], [[ByteAddressable]], [[DataWord]]) + 4 in-place expansions ([[VonNeumannArchitecture]] / [[CPU]] / [[CpuRegister]] / [[StoredProgram]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 5.1 The Origins of Modern Computing](sources/dis-5-1-history.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s opening section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 5 *Computer Architecture* — the corpus's first descent into **historical lineage** rather than a technical mechanism. Traces how the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|stored-program]] model emerged in the **1930s–1940s** as a **convergence** of independent threads: [[ClaudeShannon|Shannon]]'s [[BooleanAlgebra|Boolean]] circuit thesis (1937), [[AlanTuring|Turing]]'s [[TuringMachine|abstract machine]] (1937), [[KonradZuse|Zuse]]'s [[Z3]] (1941), [[TommyFlowers|Flowers]]'s [[Colossus]] (1943), [[HowardAiken|Aiken]]'s [[HarvardMarkI|Mark I]] (1944), [[JohnMauchly|Mauchly]] / [[PresperEckert|Eckert]]'s [[ENIAC]] (1945), and [[JohnVonNeumann|von Neumann]]'s [[EDVAC]] paper — **not a single linear progression**. Explicitly foregrounds the women whose contributions were historically underrecognized (the six [[ENIAC]] programmers; [[GraceHopper]]; the [[WomensRoyalNavalService|WRNS]] operators of [[Colossus]]). Closes by naming the [[VonNeumannArchitecture|von Neumann architecture]] — **instructions + data in the same internal memory** — as the unifying synthesis Ch 5.2+ operationalizes. **10 new entity pages** ([[AlanTuring]], [[JohnVonNeumann]], [[CharlesBabbage]], [[AdaLovelace]], [[KonradZuse]], [[TommyFlowers]], [[HowardAiken]], [[JohnMauchly]], [[PresperEckert]], [[GraceHopper]]); **9 new concept pages** ([[TuringMachine]], [[VonNeumannArchitecture]], [[Z3]], [[Colossus]], [[HarvardMarkI]], [[ENIAC]], [[EDVAC]], [[AnalyticalEngine]], [[StoredProgram]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 0 Introduction](sources/dis-0-introduction.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] ([[UnitedStatesMilitaryAcademy|West Point]]), [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] & [[KevinCWebb|Webb]] ([[SwarthmoreCollege]]) open *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* with the thesis that **understanding what a [[ComputerSystem|computer system]] is and how it runs your programs lets you write efficient code**. Defines a computer system as [[ComputerHardware|hardware]] ([[CPU]] / [[RAM]] / I/O / storage) **plus** an [[OperatingSystem|OS]] that delivers [[Abstraction|abstractions]], policies, and mechanisms — pointedly excluding calculators and bare [[Microcontroller|microcontrollers]] from the definition. Surveys modern form factors ([[SingleBoardComputer|SBCs]] like the [[RaspberryPi]], smartphone [[SystemOnAChip|SoCs]], universally [[MulticoreProcessor|multicore]]) and previews the book's C-centric, active-reading pedagogy across [[BinaryRepresentation|binary representation]], architecture, OS, [[MemoryHierarchy|memory hierarchy]], and [[ParallelComputing|multicore parallel programming]]. **Opens the *Dive into Systems* corpus**; complements the embedded-`no_std` world of [[TheEmbeddedRustBook]] from the **OS-yes** side of the [[HardwareAbstractionLayer|HAL]] split.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.1 Getting Started Programming in C](sources/dis-1-1-getting-started.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s first content section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1 *By the C, the Beautiful C*. Cross-walks [[Python]] vs. [[CLanguage|C]] on the canonical hello-world: `#include` ≠ `import`, `{ }` blocks ≠ indentation, `;`-terminated statements, [[Printf|`printf`]] without auto-`\n`. Introduces the [[CompilationProcess|compile-then-run]] model with [[GCC|`gcc hello.c`]] / `./a.out` / `-o` / `-Wall` / `-g` / `-lm`, the [[MainFunction|`int main(void)`]] entry point and its [[ExitStatus|`return 0`]] success convention, the [[VariableDeclaration|`type_name variable_name;`]] *declare-before-use* rule, the [[CPrimitiveType|byte-width table]] for `char`/`short`/`int`/`long`/`long long`/`float`/`double` plus `unsigned` variants, the [[SizeOf|`sizeof`]] operator, the `'h'`-char-vs-`"h"`-string distinction, and the [[CArithmeticOperators|arithmetic operator]] set — flagging the [[IntegerDivision|integer-division truncation]] (`11/2 == 5`, `11/2.0 == 5.5`) and pre/post-[[IncrementOperator|`++`]] traps. **Delivers the minimum C-toolchain surface area** that [[dis-0-introduction|Ch 0]]'s *active-reading-by-typing-the-code* promise requires.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.2 Input/Output (printf and scanf)](sources/dis-1-2-input-output.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s second content section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1. Formalizes hosted [[CLanguage|C]] I/O via the [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] pair [[Printf|`printf`]] / [[Scanf|`scanf`]]: the [[FormatSpecifier|`%`-specifier]] vocabulary (`%d` int, `%g` float/double, `%s` string, `%c` char), the matched-arity rule, [[EscapeSequence|`\n`-is-explicit]] (restated from [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]]), and the same-`char`-two-displays trick (`%d` → `65`, `%c` → `A`). Introduces the [[AddressOfOperator|address-of operator `&`]] as the *first sighting of a [[CMemoryAddress|memory address]] as a value* — needed because [[Scanf|`scanf`]] must be told **where** to deposit each parsed value, not just **what type**. Covers `scanf`'s whitespace-skipping between numeric reads and its [[Scanf|fragility]] under malformed input (Ctrl-C escape; Ch 2 has the robust recipe). The Python-vs-C input contrast: `input()` returns `str` requiring conversion, `scanf` parses typed values directly into typed memory locations.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.3 Conditionals and Loops](sources/dis-1-3-conditionals-loops.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s third content section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1. Adds the [[ControlFlow|control-flow]] layer on top of [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]]'s types/arithmetic: [[IfStatement|`if`]] / [[ElseStatement|`else` / `else if`]] branching with parenthesized tests and `{ }` blocks (not Python-style indentation), the [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] / [[CaseLabel|`case`]] integer-dispatch construct with its **fall-through-by-default** semantics requiring an explicit [[BreakStatement|`break`]], and the three loop forms [[WhileLoop|`while`]] (test-first, zero-or-more), [[DoWhileLoop|`do`–`while`]] (test-last, at-least-once, semicolon-terminated), and [[ForLoop|`for`]] (general three-clause `init; cond; step` loop, *not* sequence iteration as in [[Python]]). Codifies the **integer-as-boolean** rule ([[CBooleanExpression|`0` is false, any nonzero true]]), the [[RelationalOperator|`==` `!=` `<` `<=` `>` `>=`]] family (with the `=`-vs-`==` footgun), the [[LogicalOperator|`!` `&&` `||`]] family with [[ShortCircuitEvaluation|short-circuit evaluation]] making `if (p != NULL && *p == 0)` safe, the [[CommaOperator|comma operator]] for chaining init/step expressions, and the design rule **[[ForLoop|`for`]] for [[DefiniteIteration|definite]] iteration, [[WhileLoop|`while`]] for [[IndefiniteIteration|indefinite]] iteration** despite the two being capability-equivalent. [[BreakStatement|`break`]] exits the innermost loop or [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]]; [[ContinueStatement|`continue`]] skips to the next iteration (running [[ForLoop|`for`]]'s step first).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.7 Summary](sources/dis-1-7-summary.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s closing summary of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1 *By the C, the Beautiful C*. - [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.5 Overflow](sources/dis-4-5-overflow.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.5** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **detection-rules section** that formalizes the [[IntegerOverflow|integer-overflow]] phenomenon [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] and [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]] named-and-deferred. Defines overflow as *"a computation that lacks the storage to represent its result has **overflowed**"* and supplies the **two encoding-specific detection rules**: (1) **unsigned** — *"the carry out must match the carry in, otherwise the operation causes overflow"* (MSB [[CarryOut|carry-out]] in addition mode = overflow; absent expected carry-out in subtraction mode = overflow — resolving [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]]'s deferred caveat); (2) **[[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] signed** — same-sign operands producing a different-sign result indicates overflow (mixed-sign addition can never overflow). Worked 4-bit examples: $4 + 5 = -7$ (pos + pos → neg = overflow); $-3 + (-8) = 5$ (neg + neg → pos = overflow); $5 + (-4) = 1$ (mixed → no overflow possible). The **same N-bit [[FullAdder|adder]]** produces both `CF` (unsigned) and `OF` (signed) flag signals simultaneously; software / the [[CCompiler|C compiler]] chooses which to consult based on operand types — the operational pay-off of [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4]]'s interpretation-invariance thesis. Three canonical real-world consequences cited: **YouTube view counter (2014)** approaching $2^{32}-1$ on Gangnam Style (migrated to 64-bit pre-wrap); **Pac-Man (1980)** 8-bit unsigned level counter wrapping at level $256$ (the *"split-screen kill screen"*); **[[Therac25|Therac-25]] (1980s)** flag-variable overflow *"bypassed safety mechanisms"* contributing to patient radiation overdoses. Chapter stays at hardware-mechanics layer — does **not** discuss the [[CLanguage|C]]-language semantics (signed overflow is [[UndefinedBehavior|UB]]; unsigned is defined wrap), captured separately on [[UndefinedBehavior]]. **Closes the deferral chain** from [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] (*"the hardware simply drops or truncates"* the MSB carry-out — Ch 4.5 says what it *means*) and [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]] (*"doesn't necessarily indicate overflow"* — Ch 4.5 supplies the full rule). **2 new concept pages** ([[IntegerOverflow]] — promoted from forward-reference stub; [[UndefinedBehavior]] — new). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **42 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4.3 Multiplication and Division](sources/dis-4-4-3-mult-div.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.4.3** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **third and final subsection** of [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4 *Binary Integer Arithmetic*]]; **closes the [[BinaryArithmetic|binary integer arithmetic]] block**. Transfers the pencil-and-paper **long-multiplication** and **long-division** algorithms from decimal to base $2$, instantiating the [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4]] base-transfer thesis on the two remaining arithmetic operations. Opens with the explicit scope disclaimer *"these methods do not reflect the behavior of modern hardware and are not meant to be comprehensive"* — Ch 4.4.3 is deliberately a **manual-calculation** treatment, not a hardware-multiplier or hardware-divider treatment. **[[BinaryMultiplication|Multiplication]]**: per-multiplier-bit partial-product rows (each row is *the multiplicand itself or zero* — binary's digit alphabet $\{0,1\}$ eliminates decimal's $9\times 9$ multiplication table), each shifted left by its bit position, summed via [[BinaryAddition|Ch 4.4.1 binary addition]]; worked example $\mathtt{0b0101} \times \mathtt{0b0011}$ (5 × 3) → $\mathtt{0b0101} + \mathtt{0b1010} = \mathtt{0b1111}$ (15). **[[BinaryDivision|Division]]**: grade-school long division with the per-step "fits / doesn't fit" decision reducing to a single magnitude comparison $R \ge B$ (vs. decimal's $0$–$9$ digit guess); trial-subtraction uses [[BinarySubtraction|Ch 4.4.2 subtraction]]; worked example $\mathtt{1011}_2 \div \mathtt{11}_2$ (11 ÷ 3) → quotient $\mathtt{0011}_2 = 3$, remainder $\mathtt{10}_2 = 2$. Restates **integer-division truncation** explicitly — *"in most languages (for example, C, Python 2, and Java) the fractional portion of the result gets truncated"* — supplying the binary-level mechanism behind the [[IntegerDivision|integer-division]] trap [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]] introduced at the C-language level. The `%` modulus operator returns the integer remainder ($11 \% 3 = 2$), completing the [[CArithmeticOperators|C arithmetic-operator]] surface area for integer division. **Hardware-reuse theme continues**: addition (Ch 4.4.1) / subtraction (Ch 4.4.2) / multiplication (partial-product summation) / division (trial-subtraction) all share the same $N$-bit adder core. **Explicitly NOT covered** by Ch 4.4.3: hardware multipliers (Booth's algorithm / Wallace trees), hardware dividers (restoring / SRT), the [[BitShift|bit-shift]] power-of-two shortcut (multiply by $2^k$ = left-shift $k$; divide by $2^k$ = right-shift $k$), signed-multiplication sign handling, division-by-zero trap behaviour, multiplication overflow rules. **2 new concept pages** ([[BinaryMultiplication]], [[BinaryDivision]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **41 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4.2 Subtraction](sources/dis-4-4-2-subtraction.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.4.2** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **second subsection** of [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4 *Binary Integer Arithmetic*]]. Delivers the headline **hardware-reuse insight**: subtraction is implemented as **addition of the [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation** — *"subtracting $7 - 3$ is equivalent to expressing the operation as $7 + (-3)$"* — so the existing [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] [[BinaryAddition|adder]] serves subtraction with **no new arithmetic hardware**. The *flip-all-bits-and-add-one* [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation recipe ([[dis-4-3-signed|Ch 4.3]]) splits cleanly across the adder's existing inputs: the **bit-flip** is a row of [[XOR|XOR]] gates on operand B; the **add one** is delivered for free by setting [[CarryIn|`CarryIn`]] of the least-significant-bit adder to `1` — cashing in the architectural hook [[dis-4-4-1-addition|Ch 4.4.1]] flagged with *"this feature becomes critical for subtraction implementations."* Worked example 1 ($7 - 3$): flip $\mathtt{0b0011}$ to $\mathtt{0b1100}$, add to $\mathtt{0b0111}$ with `CarryIn = 1` → $\mathtt{0b10100}$ → truncate MSB → $\mathtt{0b0100} = 4$. Worked example 2 ($7 - (-3)$): flip $\mathtt{0b1101}$ to $\mathtt{0b0010}$, add to $\mathtt{0b0111}$ with `CarryIn = 1` → $\mathtt{0b1010} = 10$ — same mechanism handles **all four sign combinations** without special-casing. Caveat: in subtraction mode the MSB carry-out *"doesn't necessarily indicate overflow"* — its meaning differs from the addition case; full [[IntegerOverflow|overflow]] rule deferred. **1 new concept page** ([[BinarySubtraction]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **40 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4.1 Addition](sources/dis-4-4-1-addition.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.4.1** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **first subsection** of [[dis-4-4-arithmetic|Ch 4.4 *Binary Integer Arithmetic*]]. Instantiates the chapter-level interpretation-invariance thesis on the column-by-column [[BinaryAddition|binary addition]] algorithm — *decimal long-addition transfers directly to base 2, only the base changes from $10$ to $2$*. Headline observation: because the only multi-bit elementary sum is $1 + 1 = \mathtt{0b10}$, every column produces at most a **one-bit [[Carry|carry]]** into the next position — strictly simpler than decimal (where carries can be any digit $0$–$9$). Introduces the **eight-row [[FullAdder|full-adder]] truth table** (`DigitA` × `DigitB` × `CarryIn` → `Sum` + `CarryOut`; `Sum = XOR`, `CarryOut = majority`) as the per-bit primitive [[ComputerHardware|hardware]] implements. Worked example $\mathtt{0b0010} + \mathtt{0b1011} = \mathtt{0b1101}$ — position 1's $1+1$ carries into position 2; result reads as **13** ([[UnsignedInteger|unsigned]]) or **−3** ([[TwosComplement|two's complement]]) per [[dis-4-3-signed|Ch 4.3]]'s negative-weight MSB rule, making interpretation-invariance concrete on one bit pattern. Names the [[CarryOut|carry-out]] from the MSB as the bit *"the hardware simply drops or truncates"* — the silent-overflow root mechanism that subsequent Ch 4 sections will formalize as [[IntegerOverflow|integer overflow]]. [[CarryIn|Carry-in]] at the rightmost position is implicit `0` for standard addition but **exists architecturally** because [[BinarySubtraction|subtraction]] sets it to `1` to deliver the *add one* half of [[TwosComplement|two's complement]]'s *flip-and-add-one* negation recipe (preview of [[dis-4-4-2-subtraction|Ch 4.4.2]]). **2 new concept pages** ([[BinaryAddition]], [[Carry]]). - [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.4 Binary Integer Arithmetic](sources/dis-4-4-arithmetic.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.4** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **hub page** for the three-subsection [[BinaryArithmetic|binary integer arithmetic]] block (4.4.1 Addition / 4.4.2 Subtraction / 4.4.3 Multiplication & Division). Headline thesis: decimal place-value arithmetic algorithms transfer directly to [[BinaryNumber|binary]] (only the base changes from $10$ to $2$), and — crucially — *"it does not matter to the arithmetic procedures whether we choose to interpret the operands or result as signed or unsigned"* — the signed/unsigned **interpretation-invariance** that lets [[ComputerHardware|hardware]] designers build a single [[ArithmeticLogicUnit|ALU]] adder serving both [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned]] and [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] operands. Operational pay-off of [[dis-4-3-signed|Ch 4.3]]'s negative-weight MSB encoding: the bit-level steps are identical across encodings; only the post-hoc interpretation of the result bits differs. Worked algorithms (carry propagation, *"flip and add one"* subtraction, shift-and-add multiplication) delegated to the 4.4.1 / 4.4.2 / 4.4.3 subsection pages. No new concept pages at the hub level. - [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.3 Signed Binary Integers](sources/dis-4-3-signed.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.3** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **signed-encoding extension** of [[dis-4-1-bases|Ch 4.1]]'s unsigned-only treatment. Codifies the two historical [[SignedInteger|signed-integer]] encodings: [[SignMagnitude|sign-magnitude]] (presented as historical context only — *"no modern systems use signed magnitude"* — with the dual-zero pathology `0b0000 = +0`, `0b1000 = −0` as the disqualifier) and [[TwosComplement|two's complement]] (the universal modern standard — the [[MostSignificantBit|MSB]] becomes a place-value digit with **negative weight** $-2^{N-1}$, formula $-(d_{N-1} \cdot 2^{N-1}) + \sum_{i<N-1} d_i \cdot 2^i$, unique zero, asymmetric range $[-2^{N-1},\,2^{N-1}-1]$ with one more negative than positive). Headline negation recipe: *"flip all the bits and add one"* — worked example $13 = $ `0b00001101` → flip to `0b11110010` → add 1 → `0b11110011 = −13`. Adds the [[SignExtension|sign-extension]] rule for widening signed values across bit widths (replicate the high-order bit — non-negatives prepend zeros, negatives prepend ones — preserving both sign and magnitude). **[[OnesComplement|One's complement]] is not covered** — the chapter jumps directly from sign-magnitude to two's complement. **5 new concept pages** ([[SignedInteger]], [[TwosComplement]], [[SignBit]], [[SignMagnitude]], [[SignExtension]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **37 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.2 Converting Between Bases](sources/dis-4-2-conversion.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.2** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **mechanics companion** to [[dis-4-1-bases|Ch 4.1]]. Operationalizes the positional-notation framework $\sum d_i \cdot B^i$ as four concrete [[BaseConversion|base-conversion]] algorithms: (1) **base-$B$ → decimal** via direct evaluation of the place-value sum (`0b110100110 = 422`, `0x9F = 159`); (2) **decimal → base-$B$ via powers-of-target-base** subtraction ($9742 \to$ `0x260E` by walking $4096, 256, 16, 1$); (3) **decimal → base-$B$ via [[RepeatedDivisionMethod|repeated division]]** with bottom-up remainder collection — for $B = 2$ this simplifies to *"if the value is even, the next bit is 0; if odd, the next bit is 1"* ($422 \to$ `0b110100110`); (4) **[[BinaryHexConversion|binary ↔ hex]] per-nibble table lookup** exploiting $16 = 2^4$ — `0xB491 ↔ 1011 0100 1001 0001` with no arithmetic. Octal works the same way with 3-bit groupings ($8 = 2^3$), but hex dominates on modern 8/16/32/64-bit aligned hardware. Frames methods 2 and 3 as **interchangeable** — powers-of-$B$ wins when you've memorized $B^k$, repeated division wins for unfamiliar bases or programmatic implementation. **4 new concept pages** ([[BaseConversion]], [[BinaryHexConversion]], [[RepeatedDivisionMethod]], [[PositionalNotation]]). - [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.8 Real Numbers in Binary](sources/dis-4-8-floating-point.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.8** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — extends Ch 4's binary-representation arc from integers to **real numbers**, opening with the impossibility result *"for any binary encoding of real numbers, there exist values that cannot be represented exactly."* Surveys two encodings: **[[FixedPoint|fixed-point]]** (extends [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned-integer]] place-value to negative powers of 2 at a pinned binary point — `0b000101.10 = 5.5`) and **[[FloatingPoint|floating-point]]** under the **[[IEEE754|IEEE 754]] 32-bit standard** (1-bit [[SignBit|sign]] / 8-bit biased [[Exponent|exponent]] / 23-bit [[Mantissa|significand]] with implicit leading 1 — *"the significand gets multiplied by $2^{\text{exponent} - 127}$, where the 127 is a bias"* — worked example `0b11000001101101000000000000000000 = -22.5`). Headline shared pathology: **rounding makes arithmetic non-associative** — under truncation $(0.75 / 2) \cdot 3 = 0.75$ but $(0.75 \cdot 3) / 2 = 1.00$ where the exact answer is $1.125$. Two cited real-world catastrophes: the **1991 Patriot missile** failure in Dhahran (accumulated $0.1 \cdot$ time-counter rounding drift → Scud-interception miss → 28 dead U.S. soldiers) and the **1996 Ariane 5** explosion 39 seconds after launch (64-bit-float → 16-bit-signed-int [[IntegerOverflow|conversion overflow]] — the [[dis-4-5-overflow|Ch 4.5]] phenomenon striking at the float-to-int boundary). **Explicit scope omissions** (wiki-flagged): no 64-bit `binary64`, no denormals / [[NaN|NaN]] / $\pm\infty$, no rounding-mode enumeration, no machine-epsilon. **5 new concept pages** ([[FloatingPoint]], [[IEEE754]], [[Mantissa]], [[Exponent]], [[FixedPoint]], [[FloatingPointPrecision]] — 6 total). - [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.7 Integer Byte Order](sources/dis-4-7-byte-order.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.7** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **memory-layout section** that closes Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation* by codifying **[[ByteOrder|byte order]]** ([[Endianness|endianness]]): how the [[Byte|bytes]] of a multibyte integer are laid out across consecutive [[MemoryAddress|memory addresses]]. *"Byte order, sometimes referred to as endianness, describes the order in which the bytes of a multibyte value are ordered in memory."* Distinguishes **[[BigEndian|big-endian]]** (MSByte at lowest address — matches left-to-right written numerals; used by [[PowerPC]] / [[SPARC]] / [[Motorola68k]] / mainframes / network protocols) from **[[LittleEndian|little-endian]]** (LSByte at lowest address — appears reversed; used by [[X86]] / [[X86_64]] / [[ARM]] / [[RISCV|RISC-V]] — virtually all deployed modern CPUs as of 2025). Demonstrates with a [[CCast|`char *` cast]] over `int value = 0xAABBCCDD;` — on x86 the bytes walk out as `DD CC BB AA`, **proof of little-endian storage**. Three canonical scenarios where endianness leaks out of the [[Abstraction|abstraction]]: (1) **network transmission** — *"The IETF defines big-endian as the network byte order"*, the standardization that makes [[TCPIP|TCP/IP]] interoperable regardless of host endianness ([[POSIX]] supplies [[Htonl|`htonl` / `ntohl` / `htons` / `ntohs`]] in `<arpa/inet.h>`); (2) **file formats** — binary files written on one host and read on another with different endianness yield garbage unless the format pins endianness ([[JPEG]] big-endian, [[BMP]] / [[WAV]] little-endian, [[TIFF]] declares per-file); (3) **debugger / raw-memory inspection** — `gdb`'s [[GdbExamineMemory|`x/4xb`]] shows reversed bytes on little-endian hosts. Architecture map: [[X86]] always little-endian; [[ARM]] / [[MIPS]] / [[PowerPC]] are technically [[BiEndian|bi-endian]] but virtually always run little-endian in deployment ([[POWER8]]+ on Linux flipped to little-endian to ease x86 porting). Etymology: Jonathan Swift's *[[GulliversTravels|Gulliver's Travels]]* (1726) via [[DannyCohen|Danny Cohen]]'s 1980 [[IETF]] IEN-137 memo *On Holy Wars and a Plea for Peace*. **Closes Ch 4 *Binary and Data Representation***: Ch 4.1–4.6 treated multibyte integers as undifferentiated bit-strings; Ch 4.7 adds the address-level layout dimension that matters at cross-machine / cross-file / cross-wire boundaries. **4 new concept pages** ([[ByteOrder]] umbrella, [[Endianness]] alias, [[BigEndian]], [[LittleEndian]]). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **44 chapters**.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 4.6 Bitwise Operators](sources/dis-4-6-bitwise.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 4.6** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **operator-surface section** that exposes [[CLanguage|C]]'s six [[BitwiseOperator|bitwise operators]] (`&`, `|`, `^`, `~`, `<<`, `>>`) as the per-bit primitives that *"directly apply [[LogicGate|logic-gate]] behavior to bit sequences"*. Bridges from Ch 4.1–4.5's value-level [[BinaryRepresentation|binary representation]] and [[BinaryArithmetic|integer arithmetic]] into the **bit-manipulation idioms** systems code uses: **[[BitwiseAnd|AND `&`]]** (masking — `26 & 54 = 18`); **[[BitwiseOr|OR `|`]]** (setting bits — `26 | 54 = 62`); **[[BitwiseXor|XOR `^`]]** (toggling / difference detection — `26 ^ 54 = 44`); **[[BitwiseNot|NOT `~`]]** (inverting — `~26 = -27` because *"bitwise NOT only flips the bits and doesn't add one"* — one short of [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] negation, hence the `~x = -x - 1` identity); **left shift `<<`** (zero-fill from right, truncate at MSB — multiplication by $2^N$, `13 << 3 = 104`); **right shift `>>`** — **the [[LogicalRightShift|logical]] / [[ArithmeticRightShift|arithmetic]] split** dispatched by operand type: [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned]] → zero-fill ([[LogicalRightShift|logical]] — `0xFF000000 >> 12 = 0x000FF000`); signed → replicate [[SignBit|sign bit]] ([[ArithmeticRightShift|arithmetic] — `0xFF000000 >> 12 = 0xFFFFF000`), *"The C compiler automatically selects the appropriate shifting variant based on variable declaration."* Names the **canonical category error**: *"programmers often confuse the bitwise `&&` and `||` operators with `&` and `|` operators"* — the [[LogicalOperator|logical operators]] short-circuit on truth values; the bitwise operators act per bit on the operand width. Codifies the **bit-test / set / clear / toggle / mask** idioms (`x & (1<<i)` / `x |= (1<<i)` / `x &= ~(1<<i)` / `x ^= (1<<i)` / `(x >> shift) & ((1<<width) - 1)`). Hardware payoff: bitwise operators map **one-to-one onto [[LogicGate|logic gates]]** (AND / OR / XOR / NOT) and execute in **one clock cycle with no carry propagation** — the cheapest ops in the [[InstructionSetArchitecture|ISA]]; shifts implement as a **barrel-shifter** switch network. **Closes the [[dis-4-4-3-mult-div|Ch 4.4.3]]-deferred *"bit-shift power-of-two shortcut"*** for multiplication and division (`x * 16 = x << 4`; `x / 16 = x >> 4` unsigned), the **strength-reduction** pattern compilers apply automatically. **Scope notes**: rotation operators (`ROL` / `ROR`), [[CStruct|struct]] bit-fields, popcount / clz / ctz / bswap intrinsics, the XOR-swap idiom, and shift UB rules (shift-by-≥-width, signed-shift-overflow) are out of chapter scope; wiki page records the C-level UB pitfalls. **2 new concept pages** ([[BitwiseOperator]], [[BitShift]]). - [Dive into Systems — Ch 3.6 Debugging Multi-threaded Programs](sources/dis-3-6-gdb-pthreads.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 3.6** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — **closes Ch 3 *C Debugging Tools*** by extending the [[GDB]] block from single-threaded to multi-threaded programs. Frames concurrent debugging as fundamentally harder (multiple execution streams, thread interactions, non-determinism) with three practical mitigations: minimize active thread count during development, include the thread ID in debug output, scope verbose logging to one thread. Introduces the **[[GDB]] thread-debugging vocabulary** layered on [[Pthreads]]: (1) [[GdbInfoThreads|`info threads`]] — enumerate all active threads (`*` marks current); (2) [[GdbThreadSwitch|`thread <N>`]] — switch the inspection context to a specific thread's [[StackFrame|stack]] / [[LocalVariable|locals]] / [[CpuRegister|registers]] (multi-thread analog of [[GdbBacktrace|`frame N`]]); (3) **thread-qualified breakpoints** via `break <loc> thread <N>` — fire only for the named thread; (4) [[GdbThreadApply|`thread apply all <cmd>`]] — broadcast a [[GDB]] command across every thread, canonical use `thread apply all bt` for the **deadlock-diagnostic** multi-thread call-stack snapshot; (5) [[GdbSet|`set print thread-events`]] / [[GdbSet|`set scheduler-locking`]] for thread-lifecycle notifications and stop-the-world override. Names [[GDB]]'s **three thread identifiers** ([[Pthreads|`pthread_t`]] / kernel **LWP ID** / **GDB thread number**), each with typical 1:1 correspondence. Notes the default **stop-the-world breakpoint** behaviour (*"by default, reaching any breakpoint pauses all threads"*) and the scheduler-locking flip for observing real concurrency. Worked example: five threads racing on shared `count += i` with thread-qualified breakpoints surfaces the [[RaceCondition|race-condition]] symptom. **Promotes [[Pthreads]] from cross-corpus stub to first-class DIS concept** (DIS's first Pthreads sighting; full coverage deferred to Ch 14). **4 new concept pages** ([[GdbInfoThreads]], [[GdbThreadSwitch]], [[GdbThreadApply]]) + [[Pthreads]] entity in-place update. - [Dive into Systems — Ch 3.4 Advanced GDB Features](sources/dis-3-4-gdb-advanced.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 3.4** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **advanced-workflows extension** to the [[dis-3-1-gdb|Ch 3.1]] / [[dis-3-2-gdb-commands|Ch 3.2]] [[GDB]] block. Surfaces the workflows **beyond *"compile, run, set breakpoints, step, print"*** — the cross-process, signal-driven, and `fork()`-aware features that turn [[GDB]] from a single-program debugger into a tool for **already-running**, **signal-handling**, and **multi-process** programs. Five short sections, each a self-contained workflow: (1) **[[GDB]] ↔ `make` integration** — running `make` from inside the [[GDB]] session preserves the [[Breakpoint|breakpoint]] list across rebuilds (*"GDB accepts the `make` command to rebuild an executable during a debugging session"*); (2) **[[GdbAttach|attaching to a running process]]** via `gdb <executable> <pid>` (PID discovered with [[Ps|`ps -A | grep`]]) — the [[Ptrace]]-backed user-side primitive for debugging long-running services / daemons / heisenbugs, with the **self-pause idiom** `kill(getpid(), SIGSTOP)` as the corpus's first **debugger-aware program design** pattern; (3) **[[GdbFollowFork|`set follow-fork-mode child` / `parent`]]** — *"by default, GDB follows the parent after a call to `fork()`"* — chooses which side of a [[Fork|`fork()`]]ed program [[GDB]] follows, the headline primitive for **multi-process debugging** the corpus has been building toward; (4) **[[GdbSignalControl|signal control]]** — `signal SIGCONT` / `signal SIGUSR1` to **send** [[Signal|signals]] to the debuggee, `handle SIGBUS stop` to **intercept** [[Signal|signals]] in [[GDB]], `info signal` / `info SIGALRM` to inspect handling rules — names [[SIGBUS]] as the canonical alignment-fault scenario distinct from [[SegmentationFault|`SIGSEGV`]] (*"if a program tries to access memory with a misaligned memory address for the type it is accessing, it receives a `SIGBUS` signal"*); (5) **[[DataDisplayDebugger|DDD]] settings reset** — `rm -rf ~/.ddd` to fix the *"Waiting until GDB ready"* startup hang. **6 new concept pages** ([[GdbAttach]], [[GdbFollowFork]], [[GdbSignalControl]], [[Ps]], [[Fork]], [[Signal]], [[SIGBUS]], [[Kill]] — 8 total) + [[DataDisplayDebugger]] in-place update note. - [Dive into Systems — Ch 3.3 Debugging Memory with Valgrind](sources/dis-3-3-valgrind.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **Ch 3.3** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 3 *C Debugging Tools* — **the second of the two debugging tools** [[dis-2-10-summary|Ch 2.10]] forward-referenced (the first being [[GDB]] in [[dis-3-1-gdb|Ch 3.1]] / [[dis-3-2-gdb-commands|Ch 3.2]]). Introduces [[Valgrind]] and its default tool [[Memcheck]] as the **heap-memory-error detector** complementing [[GDB]]'s general-purpose [[Debugger|debugger]] role — *"Valgrind's Memcheck debugging tool highlights heap memory errors in programs."* Catalogues the **four heap-error classes** [[Memcheck]] catches: [[UninitializedReadError|uninitialized reads]] (e.g., `x = ptr[3]` before assignment), **invalid memory access** (*"reading or writing a value at an unallocated memory location, which often indicates an array out-of-bounds error"* — heap-side [[BufferOverflow|buffer overflow]]), [[UseAfterFree|use-after-free]] including *"freeing already freed memory"* ([[DoubleFree|double-free]]), and [[MemoryLeak|memory leaks]] (*"a chunk of allocated heap memory space that is not referred to by any pointer variable in the program, and thus it cannot be freed"*). Operationalizes the workflow: [[GccDashG|`gcc -g`]] then `valgrind -v ./a.out` (default tool = memcheck; redirect with `>& output.txt`; add `--leak-check=yes` for per-leak stack traces). Codifies the **three-part error-message anatomy** (error type/size + access stack trace + allocation-site stack trace, all `==PID==`-tagged) and the **explicit scope boundary**: *"Valgrind does not detect stack memory access errors at the same granularity as it does with heap memory, and it does not detect memory access errors with global data memory."* Recommends pairing with [[GDB]] — set a [[Breakpoint|breakpoint]] at Valgrind's flagged line, [[GdbBacktrace|`bt`]] / [[GdbPrint|`print`]] for root cause. **Promotes [[Valgrind]] from forward-ref stub to first-class tool**; introduces 3 new concept pages ([[Valgrind]], [[Memcheck]], [[UninitializedReadError]]) + 1 wiki-only treatment ([[AddressSanitizer]] — not in the chapter but the canonical modern alternative). [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **30 chapters** (Chs 1–2 complete; Ch 3 in progress — Ch 3.1 + 3.2 + 3.3 now form the **three-section debugging-tools block**, with both forward-referenced tools delivered).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 3.2 GDB Commands in Detail](sources/dis-3-2-gdb-commands.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **command-reference companion to [[dis-3-1-gdb|Ch 3.1]]** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 3 *C Debugging Tools*. Fans the [[GDB]] vocabulary out into a categorized reference: **CLI ergonomics** ([[GdbTabCompletion|TAB completion]] / short abbreviations / RETURN-repeats), **execution control** ([[GdbRun|`run [args]`]] / [[StepDebug|`step N` / `next N` / `cont` / `until N`]] / `quit`), **code listing** ([[GdbList|`list N M` / `list func` / `list file:N`]]), **call-stack walk** ([[GdbBacktrace|`where` / `bt` / `frame N`]]), **breakpoint management** ([[GdbBreakpointManagement|`enable` / `disable` / `delete` / `clear` / `ignore N M` / `condition N (expr)`]]), **state inspection** ([[GdbPrint|`print/x` / `print/t` / `print/c` / `print *(int *)addr`]] / [[GdbDisplay|`display`]] / [[GdbExamineMemory|`x/nfu addr`]] / [[GdbWhatis|`whatis`]] / [[GdbInfo|`info locals` / `info args` / `info break` / `info registers` / `info frame`]]), and **live mutation** ([[GdbSet|`set var x = expr`]]). Two headline additions over [[dis-3-1-gdb|Ch 3.1]]: (1) the **[[ConditionalBreakpoint|conditional-breakpoint]] workflow** — *"pause at a breakpoint inside a loop only after some number of iterations or pause the program at a breakpoint only when the value of a variable has an interesting value"* — and (2) the **[[GdbExamineMemory|`x/nfu`]] raw-memory inspection** primitive that escapes [[GdbPrint|`print`]]'s type awareness. Also introduces [[Watchpoint|watchpoints]] (write-triggered halt — the dual of [[Breakpoint|breakpoints]]) as the named-and-deferred sibling primitive. **Closes the GDB command surface** for the *Dive into Systems* corpus — every command [[dis-3-1-gdb|Ch 3.1]] named-and-deferred is detailed here. **11 new concept pages** ([[GdbPrint]], [[GdbDisplay]], [[GdbExamineMemory]], [[GdbInfo]], [[GdbBreakpointManagement]], [[ConditionalBreakpoint]], [[GdbSet]], [[GdbRun]], [[GdbList]], [[GdbWhatis]], [[Watchpoint]]); [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **29 chapters** (Chs 1–2 complete, Ch 3 in progress — Ch 3.1 narrative + Ch 3.2 reference for [[GDB]] done; [[Valgrind]] still pending).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 3.1 Debugging with GDB](sources/dis-3-1-gdb.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **opening section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 3 *C Debugging Tools***. Delivers the **first half** of [[dis-2-10-summary|Ch 2.10]]'s forward-referenced *"two debugging tools"* — [[GDB|GNU GDB]] as a general-purpose [[CLanguage|C]] [[Debugger|debugger]] ([[Valgrind]] deferred to Ch 3.2). Frames a [[Debugger|debugger]] as *"a program that controls the execution of another program… it allows programmers to see what their programs are doing as they run"*, then codifies the workflow: (1) compile with [[GccDashG|`gcc -g`]] + **no [[CompilerOptimization|`-O2`]]** — *"compiler-optimized code is often very difficult to debug because sequences of optimized machine code often do not clearly map back to C source code"*; (2) launch `gdb ./a.out`; (3) set [[Breakpoint|breakpoints]] with `break`; (4) [[GdbRun|`run`]] until halt; (5) inspect with [[GdbPrint|`print`]] / [[GdbList|`list`]]; (6) advance with [[StepDebug|`next` / `step` / `cont`]] (headline distinction: *"to inspect the function's behavior, use `step` instead of `next`"*); (7) walk the call stack with [[GdbBacktrace|`bt` / `where` / `frame N`]] — operationalizing [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s [[StackFrame|stack-of-frames]] model at runtime. Two bug taxonomies: **logic bugs** (run-to-completion, wrong output → breakpoint near suspected mis-step) vs **crashes** (typically [[SegmentationFault|segfaults]] → `bt` at halt site, or [[CoreFile|core-file]] post-mortem via `gdb ./a.out core`). Mentions [[DataDisplayDebugger|DDD]] as the GUI wrapper. **Promotes [[GDB]] from forward-ref entity stub** ([[rust-embedded-book-intro-tooling|Embedded Rust I.4]] toolchain inventory) to **fully treated debugger** with complete command vocabulary — the hosted-Unix-process angle complements the Embedded Rust remote-debug-over-OpenOCD angle. **Opens Ch 3** — [[DiveIntoSystems]] corpus now at **28 chapters** (Chs 1–2 complete, Ch 3 starting). **9 new concept pages** ([[Debugger]], [[Breakpoint]], [[StepDebug]], [[GdbBacktrace]], [[CoreFile]], [[DebugSymbol]], [[GccDashG]], [[CompilerOptimization]], [[DataDisplayDebugger]]); [[GDB]] entity expanded in-place.
