- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.7 Compiling C to Assembly](sources/dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **seventh and final subsection of [[dis-2-9-advanced|Ch 2.9]]** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — closes Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C* by exposing the `.c` → `.s` → `.o` → executable pipeline through three [[GCC|`gcc`]] invocations and one inspection tool. Promotes [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly language]] from named-and-deferred to first-class: [[GCC|`gcc -m32 -S simpleops.c`]] stops after [[CompilationStage|compile]] to emit human-readable [[IA32|IA32]] assembly, `gcc -m32 -c myfunc.s` re-feeds hand-written `.s` through the [[AssemblyStage|assemble stage]], and `gcc -m32 -o myprog myfunc.o main.c` links mixed assembly+C through the standard [[LinkingStage|link-edit]] path. Headline payoff — the [[CompilationProcess|five-stage pipeline]] is **not a black box**: *"a compiler can compile C code to assembly code, and it can compile assembly code into a binary form that links into a binary executable program."* Walks a `simpleops.c` worked example pairing C statements (`x = 1; x = x + 2; y = x * 100;`) with their IA32 translations (`movl $1, -8(%ebp); addl $2, -8(%ebp); movl -8(%ebp), %eax; imull $100, %eax, %eax; movl %eax, -4(%ebp)`) — surfaces the `%ebp`-relative [[StackFrame|stack-frame]] addressing convention and AT&T `mov src, dst` syntax. Introduces [[Objdump|`objdump -d`]] as the disassembly tool that inverts the [[AssemblyStage|assemble stage]] for inspecting `.o` machine-code-with-mnemonics mappings. Closing motivation: *"because C is a portable language and is much higher level than assembly languages, the vast majority of operating system code is written in C"* — the [[ISA|ISA]]-portability rationale that justifies C's OS dominance and opens onto Ch 3 (assembly / [[ComputerArchitecture|architecture]]). **4 new concept pages** ([[AssemblyLanguage]] — promoted from forward-ref stub, [[IA32]], [[ISA]], [[Objdump]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.6 Writing and Using Your Own C Libraries](sources/dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **sixth subsection of [[dis-2-9-advanced|Ch 2.9]]** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **author-side companion to [[dis-2-9-5-libraries|Ch 2.9.5]]**'s consumer-side library treatment. Walks the three-step recipe: (1) define the API in a [[HeaderFile|`.h`]] wrapped in a [[HeaderGuard|`#ifndef`/`#define`/`#endif` guard]] with [[FunctionPrototype|prototypes]] + types + `extern` globals; (2) implement in [[CSourceFile|`.c`]] files using [[StaticFunction|`static`]] for module-private helpers; (3) build either a [[StaticLibrary|`.a` archive]] via [[ArCommand|`ar -rcs libmylib.a mylib.o`]] or a [[DynamicLibrary|`.so` shared object]] via `gcc -fPIC -c` + `gcc -shared`. Codifies the [[PositionIndependentCode|`-fPIC`]] requirement for shared objects, the `extern` declaration-vs-definition split, the [[QuotedInclude|`#include "..."`]] vs [[AngleInclude|`<...>`]] search-path distinction, and the three consumption forms (`mylib.o` direct / `mylib.c` compile-and-link / `-L. -lmylib` standard). Closing payoff: *"this approach applies equally to structuring and compiling larger C programs composed of multiple C source and header files"* — the library recipe **is** the C modularization discipline. **7 new concept pages** ([[HeaderGuard]], [[IncludeGuard]], [[ArCommand]], [[PositionIndependentCode]], [[StaticFunction]], [[QuotedInclude]], [[AngleInclude]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.5 C Libraries: Using, Compiling and Linking](sources/dis-2-9-5-libraries.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **fifth subsection of [[dis-2-9-advanced|Ch 2.9]]** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — the **first corpus crossing from *C the language* to *C the build workflow***. Decomposes a [[CLibrary|C library]] into **two halves** — an **API** delivered as [[HeaderFile|`.h`]] files and a precompiled **implementation** delivered as either a [[StaticLibrary|static archive `lib<name>.a`]] or a [[DynamicLibrary|shared object `lib<name>.so`]]. Refines [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]]'s four-stage [[CompilationProcess|compile-then-run]] cartoon into a **five-stage pipeline**: [[PreprocessingStage|preprocess]] → [[CompilationStage|compile]] → [[AssemblyStage|assemble]] → [[LinkingStage|link-edit]] → [[RuntimeLinking|runtime link]] — exposed by [[GCC|`gcc`]] flags `-E` / `-S` / `-c` for stages 1/2/3 and **two linker flags `-l<name>` / `-L<path>`** for the search-and-bind protocol at stage 4. Codifies the **`-l`-name-vs-`lib`-filename abstraction** — `-lpthread` looks up `libpthread.so` *or* `libpthread.a` — *"the compiler can choose to dynamically link when both a shared object (`.so`) and an archive (`.a`) version of a library are available."* Separates the **diagnostic error modes by stage** — missing [[HeaderFile|header]] surfaces at preprocess (*"No such file or directory"*) or compile (*"implicit declaration"*); missing **library link** surfaces at link as [[UndefinedReferenceError|*"undefined reference"*]] from [[Linker|`ld`]]; missing `.so` at launch surfaces as *"cannot open shared object file"* from [[DynamicLinker|`ld.so`]] — the [[CompilerVsLinker|compiler-vs-linker]] taxonomy. Closes with [[LDLibraryPath|`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`]] for [[RuntimeLinking|runtime shared-object resolution]] outside default paths. The `-pthread` flag is the chapter's **one canonical gotcha** in an otherwise uniform `-l<name>` interface. **17 new concept pages** ([[CLibrary]], [[StaticLibrary]], [[DynamicLibrary]], [[Linker]], [[StaticLinking]], [[DynamicLinking]], [[ObjectFile]], [[PreprocessingStage]], [[CompilationStage]], [[AssemblyStage]], [[LinkingStage]], [[RuntimeLinking]], [[DynamicLinker]], [[LDLibraryPath]], [[UndefinedReferenceError]], [[CompilerVsLinker]], [[CSourceFile]]); **2 updated in-place** ([[CompilationProcess]] — four-stage → five-stage refinement; [[GCC]] — `-E` / `-S` / `-c` / `-l<name>` / `-L<path>` / `--static` / `-pthread` flag table).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.4 Pointer Arithmetic](sources/dis-2-9-4-pointer-arithmetic.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **fourth subsection of [[dis-2-9-advanced|Ch 2.9]]** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — finally delivers the [[PointerArithmetic|pointer-arithmetic]] mechanism [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] named-and-deferred, [[dis-2-5-arrays|Ch 2.5]] silently relied on for its `arr[i] == *(arr + i)` identity, and [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]] presupposed for the static-vs-dynamic indexing parity. Codifies (a) the **[[PointerIncrement|type-scaled-increment]] rule** — *"when incremented, a pointer points to the next storage location of the type it points to"* — `ptr++` advances by `sizeof(*ptr)` bytes (1 for `char *`, 4 for `int *`, 8 for `double *`); (b) the **general N-scaling identity** *"`ptr + N` makes the pointer point `N` storage locations beyond its current value (or makes it point to `N` elements beyond the current element)"* — which is what makes [[ArrayIndexing|`arr[i]` ≡ `*(arr + i)`]] type-correct across pointer types; (c) the **dynamic-2D divergence** — single-`malloc` of `N*M` ints permits continuous pointer-arithmetic traversal of all elements ([[RowMajorOrder|row-major]] contiguous), while [[ArrayOfArrays|array-of-arrays]] via N+1 mallocs requires resetting the pointer at each row (rows in separate heap chunks); (d) the **anti-recommendation** — *"in most cases, we recommend against using pointer arithmetic to access array elements: it's easy to make errors and more difficult to debug when you do."* Closes the [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] deferral list (`void *` resolved in [[dis-2-9-3-voidstar|Ch 2.9.3]], pointer arithmetic resolved here). **3 new concept pages** ([[PointerArithmetic]], [[PointerIncrement]], [[PointerDifference]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.3 The void* Type](sources/dis-2-9-3-voidstar.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **third subsection of [[dis-2-9-advanced|Ch 2.9]]** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — finally delivers the **[[VoidPointer|`void *`]] type-erased pointer** that [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] named-and-deferred and that [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]] silently relied on as [[Malloc|`malloc`]]'s return type. Codifies (a) the **size-uniformity rationale** — *"every pointer variable requires the same number of storage bytes, and because they're all the same size, the compiler can allocate space for a `void *` variable without knowing the type it points to"* — pointer width is platform-fixed (4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 on 64-bit), pointee size is irrelevant to the pointer-variable's storage; (b) the **mandatory [[TypeCast|recast]] before [[DereferenceOperator|dereference]]** rule — `void *` carries no pointee-type information, so `*vp` is a type error; the programmer must supply the target type via the `(type *)pointer` syntax, conventionally written `*((int *)args)` with double parens for clarity; (c) the **two canonical use cases** — [[Malloc|`malloc`]]'s [[GenericPointer|generic-return-type]] pattern that fits any caller-chosen [[PointerType|pointer type]] (`int *p = (int *)malloc(sizeof(int)*10);`), and [[Pthreads|pthread]] thread-main parameters that accept `void *args` for type-erased argument passing (`int num = *((int *)args);`). Resolves the [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] *"`void *` deferred to later Ch 2 sections"* promise. **3 new concept pages** ([[VoidPointer]], [[TypeCast]], [[GenericPointer]]) + 1 supporting page ([[Memcpy]] — named-and-deferred as a `void *`-bearing routine).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.2 Command Line Arguments](sources/dis-2-9-2-cmd-line-args.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **second subsection of [[dis-2-9-advanced|Ch 2.9]]** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — extends the [[MainFunction|`main`]] signature from `int main(void)` to the **full [[CommandLineArguments|`argc`/`argv`]] form** `int main(int argc, char *argv[])`, finally delivering the argument-passing-from-the-shell mechanism the prior 19 chapters elided. Codifies the **two-parameter protocol** — `argc` is the integer count of arguments (program name included), `argv` is a [[CArray|`char *` array]] of [[CString|C-string]] arguments terminated by a [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] sentinel at `argv[argc]` — and the **string-arrive-as-strings** rule that forces numeric arguments through a conversion function ([[Atoi|`atoi`]] for the simple case, [[Strtol|`strtol`]] for production code needing error detection). **3 new concept pages** ([[CommandLineArguments]], [[MainArgcArgv]], [[Strtol]]); **2 updated** ([[MainFunction]], [[Atoi]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.1 Constants, switch, enum, and typedef](sources/dis-2-9-1-advanced-switch.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **first subsection of [[dis-2-9-advanced|Ch 2.9]]** of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* — bundles **four small language features** ([[CConstant|`#define` constants]] / [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] / [[CEnum|`enum`]] / [[Typedef|`typedef`]]) into one section because they share a purpose: **giving meaningful names to values and types**. Resolves [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]]'s [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] deferral and [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]] / [[dis-2-7-structs|Ch 2.7]]'s [[Typedef|`typedef`]] deferral. Codifies (a) **`#define const_name (literal_value)`** — preprocessor textual substitution; *"constants are not lvalues and cannot be reassigned at runtime"*; the parenthesization convention prevents precedence surprises; (b) the **three [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] rules** — case values must be **literal values, not expressions**; without [[BreakStatement|`break`]] execution **falls through**; `default:` is optional and conventionally last — plus the compiler-jump-table optimization angle that motivates `switch` over [[IfStatement|`if`]] / [[ElseStatement|`else if`]] for dense dispatch; (c) **[[CEnum|enumerated types]]** grouping related integer constants — default sequential numbering from 0 (`enum days_of_week { MON, TUES, WED, THURS, FRI }`), custom value assignment (`SUN = 1, MON, // 2 ...`), **four advantages over [[CConstant|`#define`]]** (logical grouping / type safety / implicit sequential values / easy insertion-removal), and the runtime reality check that *"enumerated types print their integer values, not constant names"* (`printf("%d\n", TUES)` outputs `2`); (d) **[[Typedef|`typedef`]]** with three canonical aliasing patterns ([[CEnum|enum]] / [[CStruct|struct]] / primitive-width — `typedef enum class_year classYr;` / `typedef struct studentT studentT;` / `typedef unsigned long long ull;`) plus the **combined struct-typedef one-liner** `typedef struct studentT { ... } studentT;` as the idiomatic form. Headline pairing: **[[CEnum|`enum`]] + [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]]** — the chapter's worked example dispatches on an `enum days_of_week` value with stacked-labels-for-shared-body and intentional fall-through (FRI → MON/WED). Closing motivation: *"these features collectively enhance code clarity, maintainability, and organization by creating meaningful names for values and types, while also enabling the compiler to potentially optimize branching logic."* **4 new concept pages** ([[CConstant]], [[CEnum]], [[ConstQualifier]], [[TypedefExpansion]]); **3 updated** ([[SwitchStatement]], [[CaseLabel]], [[Typedef]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9 Advanced C Features](sources/dis-2-9-advanced.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s ninth section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C* — **short hub / intro page** that closes Ch 2 by forwarding to **seven advanced subsections** (2.9.1–2.9.7) covering both **language-feature cleanup** ([[CConstant|`const`]] / [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] / [[CEnum|`enum`]] / [[Typedef|`typedef`]] in 2.9.1; [[CommandLineArguments|`argc` / `argv`]] in 2.9.2; [[VoidPointer|`void *`]] in 2.9.3; [[PointerArithmetic|pointer arithmetic]] in 2.9.4) and **the [[CompilationProcess|compile-and-link]] toolchain** (using [[CLibrary|libraries]] in 2.9.5; writing your own libraries with [[HeaderFile|`.h`]] / [[CSourceFile|`.c`]] separation in 2.9.6; [[CLanguage|C]] → [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] in 2.9.7). Chapter intro: *"Almost all of the C programming language has been presented in previous sections. In this section, we cover a few remaining advanced C language features and some advanced C programming and compiling topics."* Resolves three Ch 1 / Ch 2 deferrals — [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] (deferred [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]]), [[Typedef|`typedef`]] (deferred [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]] / [[dis-2-7-structs|Ch 2.7]]), [[VoidPointer|`void *`]] + [[PointerArithmetic|pointer arithmetic]] (deferred [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]]) — and surfaces the **first bridge from *C the language* to *C the build workflow*** that Ch 3 (assembly / architecture) opens onto. **Hub page** — substance lives in 2.9.1–2.9.7 (ingest separately); no new concept pages.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.8 Input / Output](sources/dis-2-8-io.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s eighth section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C* — **returns to [[CLanguage|C]] I/O** with the depth [[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]] deferred. Three movements: (1) **standard I/O deepened** — the three default streams ([[StandardInput|`stdin`]] / [[StandardOutput|`stdout`]] / [[StandardError|`stderr`]] — `stderr` newly introduced) + shell [[StreamRedirection|stream redirection]] (`< > 2> &> 2>&1`) + an expanded [[FormatSpecifier|specifier table]] (`%u` / `%p` / `%ld` / `%lld` / `%x` / `%o` / `%e` + width / precision / justification `%5.3f` / `%-20s`); (2) **file I/O** on [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]] via a four-step protocol — [[Fopen|`fopen(path, mode)`]] → I/O → [[Fclose|`fclose`]] — with [[FileMode|`"r"` / `"w"` / `"a"` modes]], the four function families [[Fgetc|`fgetc`]]/[[Fputc|`fputc`]], [[Fgets|`fgets`]]/[[Fputs|`fputs`]], [[Fprintf|`fprintf`]]/[[Fscanf|`fscanf`]], and position primitives [[Fseek|`fseek`]] (`SEEK_SET`/`SEEK_CUR`/`SEEK_END`) / [[Rewind|`rewind`]]; (3) **the [[Fscanf|`fscanf`]] specifier deepening** — [[ScanfCharClass|`%[abc]` / `%[^abc]` / `%[^\n]` / `%20s`]] — the **robustness fix** for the [[Scanf|`scanf`]] fragility [[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]] flagged-and-deferred. Headline payoff: **standard-I/O ↔ file-I/O symmetry** — [[Printf|`printf`]]/[[Fprintf|`fprintf`]], [[Scanf|`scanf`]]/[[Fscanf|`fscanf`]], [[Getchar|`getchar`]]/[[Fgetc|`fgetc`]], [[Putchar|`putchar`]]/[[Fputc|`fputc`]] differ only in whether they take an explicit [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]]; [[StandardInput|`stdin`]] / [[StandardOutput|`stdout`]] / [[StandardError|`stderr`]] **are** [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]] values, making standard streams a special case of the file API. Codifies (a) the **[[CPrimitiveType|`int`]]-not-`char` rule** for character-I/O returns ([[EOF|`EOF`]] = 257th value); (b) the **[[NullPointer|`NULL`]]-check-on-[[Fopen|`fopen`]] discipline**; (c) the **trailing-`\n` footgun** in mixed numeric / `%c` reads; (d) the **[[Fgets|`fgets`]] + `sscanf` production-grade input recipe**. **13 new concept pages** ([[FilePointer]], [[Fopen]], [[Fclose]], [[FileMode]], [[Fgetc]], [[Fputc]], [[Fgets]], [[Fputs]], [[Fprintf]], [[Fscanf]], [[EOF]], [[Feof]], [[StandardError]]) + **7 supporting** ([[Getchar]], [[Putchar]], [[Ungetc]], [[Fseek]], [[Rewind]], [[StreamRedirection]], [[ScanfCharClass]]).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.7 Structs](sources/dis-2-7-structs.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s seventh section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C* — **returns to [[CStruct|structs]] with the full [[Pointer|pointer]] / [[Malloc|dynamic-memory]] toolkit Ch 2.2–2.6 supplied**, deepening [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]]'s three-step dot-operator treatment along **five axes**: (1) **review** — define-declare-access + [[StructAssignment|whole-struct copy]] + the *"complete copy of all field bytes is copied to the parameter"* [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]] rule re-stated; (2) **[[PointerToStruct|pointer-to-struct]]** with [[Malloc|`malloc(sizeof(struct studentT))`]] + the [[ArrowOperator|`->`]] shorthand — *"while technically correct, the syntax `(*sptr).field` is cumbersome. C provides the **arrow operator** as shorthand"* — finally delivering the [[ArrowOperator|`->`]] operator [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]] named-and-deferred; (3) **[[StructPointerField|pointer fields inside structs]]** requiring the **two-step `malloc` discipline** — one allocation for the struct + separate allocations for each pointer field (`p1.name = malloc(sizeof(char) * 8); strcpy(p1.name, "Zhichen");`) — with the chapter's headline **compositional field-access rule** *"start from the outermost variable type and use its type syntax to access individual parts"* generating the `p1.age` / `p2->age` / `p1.name[2]` / `p2->name[2]` access-pattern table; (4) **[[ArrayOfStructs|arrays of structs]]** in **three forms** — static `class1[40]` (`class1[i].field`), dynamic single-block `class2 = malloc(sizeof(struct studentT) * 15)` (`class2[i].field` — re-applying [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]]'s *"`arr[i]` syntax for static and dynamic"* unification to struct elements), array-of-pointers `class3[40]; class3[i] = malloc(...); class3[i]->field` (the [[ArrayOfArrays|Ch 2.5 array-of-arrays]] tradeoff pattern restated — N+1 [[HeapMetadata|heap headers]] in exchange for sparse/variable-size flexibility) — with the type-compatibility caveat that *"`classroom3` (array of pointers) cannot be passed to a function expecting `struct studentT` arrays"*; (5) **[[SelfReferentialStruct|self-referential structs]]** — `struct node { int data; struct node *next; }` — finally delivering the [[LinkedDataStructure|linked-data-structure]] use case [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] named-and-deferred, with the [[LinkedList|linked-list]] worked example using **prepend-to-head** O(1) insertion and the chapter's *"build linked data structures (linked lists, trees, graphs) without contiguous memory requirements"* contrast with [[CArray|arrays]]. **5 new concept pages** ([[PointerToStruct]], [[StructPointerField]], [[SelfReferentialStruct]], [[LinkedList]] + expanded [[LinkedDataStructure]]); **expanded** [[ArrowOperator]] / [[Typedef]] / [[ArrayOfStructs]] from stub-and-deferred to fully treated.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.6 Strings and the String Library](sources/dis-2-6-strings.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s sixth section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C* — **returns to [[CString|C strings]] with the full [[Pointer|pointer]] / [[Malloc|dynamic-memory]] toolkit Ch 2.2–2.5 supplied**, deepening [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]'s three-function introduction ([[Strlen|`strlen`]] / [[Strcpy|`strcpy`]] / [[Sprintf|`sprintf`]]) into the full [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]] surface area. Three subsections — (1) **statically allocated strings** restates the [[CArray|`char` array]] + [[NullTerminator|`'\0'`]] convention with *"failure to allocate enough memory will yield undefined results that range from program crashes to major security vulnerabilities"*; (2) **dynamically allocated strings** plugs [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]]'s [[Malloc|`malloc`]] machinery into [[CString|C-strings]] with the `strlen(s) + 1` byte-count discipline; (3) **the libraries** — comparison ([[Strcmp|`strcmp`]] / [[Strncmp|`strncmp`]]), bounded copy ([[Strncpy|`strncpy`]] / [[Strlcpy|`strlcpy`]]), concatenation ([[Strcat|`strcat`]] / [[Strncat|`strncat`]]), search ([[Strchr|`strchr`]] / [[Strstr|`strstr`]]), tokenization ([[Strtok|`strtok`]]), character classes ([[CtypeLibrary|`<ctype.h>`]]), and numeric conversion ([[Atoi|`atoi`]]). Codifies the **caller-owns-the-destination-size** contract that [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] flagged but deferred, the [[Strncpy|`strncpy`]] *non-termination footgun*, the [[Strlcpy|`strlcpy`]] (glibc 2.38, 2023) modern fix, and the [[ManPages|`man`]] system as the canonical reference. **12 new concept pages**; updated [[Strcpy]] with the Ch 2.6 safety deepening.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.5 Arrays in C](sources/dis-2-5-arrays.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s fifth section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C* — **returns to [[CArray|arrays]] with the full [[Pointer|pointer]] / [[DynamicMemoryAllocation|dynamic-memory]] toolkit Ch 2.2–2.4 supplied**, deepening the [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] 1D-static treatment along three axes: (1) **[[DynamicallyAllocatedArray|dynamic 1D arrays]]** at parity with static ones at `arr[i]` indexing and at function parameters (*"when passing an array to a function, C copies the value of the base address to the parameter. That is, both the parameter and the argument refer to the same memory locations"*); (2) **[[MultidimensionalArray|2D arrays]]** finally introduced — static `int matrix[N][M]` plus the two dynamic forms — with the **[[RowMajorOrder|row-major]] layout** rule and the *"sizes of other dimensions must be fully specified so that the compiler can generate the correct offsets into the array"* parameter-declaration rule (first dimension elidable, trailing dimensions mandatory because they feed `&m[i][j] = m_base + i*M + j`); (3) **two dynamic-2D allocation strategies, two tradeoffs** — single-`malloc` of `N*M` ints (`int *`, manual `arr[i*M+j]` offset, **best cache locality**, one heap header) vs. [[ArrayOfArrays|array-of-arrays]] via N+1 mallocs (`int **`, **double-indexing `arr[i][j]`** ergonomics, rows not contiguous, N+1 heap headers) — *"the double-indexing syntax (`[i][j]`) of statically declared 2D arrays cannot be used when allocating a 2D array using [the single-malloc] method"* — the syntactic restriction that motivates the memory-cost tradeoff. Codifies [[ArrayDecay|array decay]] (`int[N]` → `int *`; `int[N][M]` → `int (*)[M]`) as the unifying primitive behind [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]'s pass-by-reference exception, [[dis-2-3-pointers-functions|Ch 2.3]]'s pass-by-pointer recipe, and [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]]'s heap-array indexing. **4 new concept pages**: [[MultidimensionalArray]] / [[RowMajorOrder]] / [[ArrayDecay]] / [[ArrayOfArrays]]; **updated** [[CArray]] / [[ArrayIndexing]] / [[PassByReference]] with the Ch 2.5 deepening.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.4 Dynamic Memory Allocation](sources/dis-2-4-dynamic-memory.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s fourth section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C* — **finally delivers the [[DynamicMemoryAllocation|dynamic-memory-allocation]] mechanism** [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]] named and deferred and [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] forward-referenced as pointers' *second* use case. The two-call API — [[Malloc|`malloc(n)`]] (request `n` bytes; return [[Pointer|pointer]] or [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] on failure) and [[Free|`free(p)`]] (release back to the heap) — with [[SizeOf|`sizeof`]] for byte-count arithmetic, [[Exit|`exit(1)`]] for the canonical OOM escape, and the *"set the pointer to [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] after [[Free|`free`]]ing"* discipline as the load-bearing defense against [[UseAfterFree|use-after-free]] / [[DanglingPointer|dangling pointer]] / [[DoubleFree|double-free]] (`free(NULL)` is a defined no-op; `*NULL` reliably [[SegmentationFault|segfaults]]). Headline payoff: **unification with [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] static arrays** — [[DynamicallyAllocatedArray|heap-allocated arrays]] use identical `arr[i]` syntax (`int *arr = malloc(sizeof(int) * 20); arr[5] = 42;`); the [[dis-2-3-pointers-functions|Ch 2.3]] [[PassByPointer|pass-by-pointer]] calling convention accepts both static and dynamic arrays through *"the same parameter declarations"*. Brief implementation peek introduces the [[FreeList|free list]] of unused chunks and the [[HeapFragmentation|fragmentation]] mixed `malloc`/`free` traffic produces (per-chunk [[HeapMetadata|metadata]] is implicit — `free` takes only a pointer because size lives in the header). **9 new concept pages** + 3 supporting pages; expands the prior [[DynamicMemoryAllocation]] stub from Ch 2.1's nominal placeholder into the corpus's canonical reference.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.3 Pointers and Functions](sources/dis-2-3-pointers-functions.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s third section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C* — **operationalizes [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]]'s [[PassByPointer|pass-by-pointer]] idiom** as the entire subject of the section. Distills pass-by-pointer to a three-step recipe ([[PointerDeclaration|pointer-typed parameter]] → [[AddressOfOperator|`&`]]-of-variable at call site → [[DereferenceOperator|`*`]]-deref in body) and walks a complete `change_value` worked example whose printed output `x: 100 y: 30` makes the **two return channels** simultaneously visible — `y` receives the [[ReturnStatement|`return`]]'s original-value (30) while `x` is mutated through the pointer parameter (to 100). Supplies the **surgical re-statement** of the [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]] [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]] rule for pointer-parameter contexts: *"the parameter still gets the value of its argument, but it is passed the value of an address … by dereferencing a pointer parameter, the function can change the contents of memory that both the parameter and its argument refer to; through a pointer parameter, a function can modify a variable that is visible to the caller after the function returns."* The pass-by-pointer mechanism *upholds* pass-by-value — the pointer is what's copied — and caller-visible mutation is the *consequence* of dereferencing the copied [[CMemoryAddress|address]], not a violation of the rule. The [[StackFrame|stack-frame]] diagram (Figure 1) shows the cross-frame pointer that makes the mechanism work: `change_value`'s frame holds `input` storing the [[CMemoryAddress|address]] of `main`'s `x`. Folds [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]'s [[CArray|array]] [[PassByReference|pass-by-reference]] story under the same mechanism (*"we have already seen similar functionality with array parameters … In general, this same idea can be applied by passing pointer parameters"*) — array-by-reference and explicit pointer parameters are now revealed as **the same mechanism** (pass-by-value of a [[Pointer|pointer]]). The section also names the **single-return-slot restriction** of [[CLanguage|C]] [[Function|functions]] that pass-by-pointer routes around: pointer parameters give *additional* output channels alongside the [[ReturnStatement|`return`]] value. **One new concept page**: [[OutputParameter]] — the named [[CLanguage|C]] convention specialization, the *write-only-on-success* slice of the [[PassByPointer|pass-by-pointer]] space; updated: [[PassByPointer]] (worked-example section + Ch 2.3 source link) and [[PassByValue]] (the surgical re-statement for pointer-parameter contexts).
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.2 C Pointer Variables](sources/dis-2-2-pointers.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s second section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C* — **the chapter that finally explains [[Pointer|pointers]]**, the headline Ch 2 deferral [[dis-1-7-summary|Ch 1.7]] flagged. Defines a pointer as *"a level of indirection to accessing program memory"*: a variable storing another variable's [[CMemoryAddress|memory address]]. The three syntactic moves — [[PointerDeclaration|declaration]] `int *ptr;` (with the dual-role `*` — type-spelling in declarations, [[DereferenceOperator|dereference operator]] in expressions), [[AddressOfOperator|`&`]]-initialization `ptr = &x;` (finally promoted from [[Scanf|`scanf`]]-magic to a general-purpose move) or [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] assignment (*"indicates that it doesn't refer to any particular address"*), and [[DereferenceOperator|`*` dereference]] `*ptr = 8;` to write through. Enumerates the five capabilities pointers unlock: [[PassByPointer|pass-by-pointer]] output parameters (workaround for [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]] rule), [[DynamicMemoryAllocation|dynamic memory allocation]] (deferred to Ch 2.4), efficient large-[[CStruct|struct]] passing, [[LinkedDataStructure|linked dynamic data structures]], byte reinterpretation. Codifies two safety rules — *initialize before use* and *never dereference [[NullPointer|`NULL`]]* (`if (ptr != NULL) { *ptr = 6; }` — callback to [[ShortCircuitEvaluation|short-circuit]] from [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]]) — with [[SegmentationFault|segfault]] as the canonical failure mode. **Reconciles** the [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]] / [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]] vs [[PassByReference|pass-by-reference]] tension: *C is always pass-by-value; pass-by-reference is just pass-by-value of a pointer.* Pointer arithmetic, `void *`, and pointer-to-struct via [[ArrowOperator|`->`]] (named-and-deferred in [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]]) all deferred to later Ch 2 sections.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 2.1 Parts of Program Memory and Scope](sources/dis-2-1-scope-memory.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s **opening section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 2 *A Deeper Dive Into C***. Upgrades [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s [[ExecutionStack|stack-of-frames]] cartoon into the full **four-region [[ProcessMemory|program-memory]] model**: a running [[CLanguage|C]] program's [[AddressSpace|address space]] partitions into [[CodeSection|code section]] (instructions), [[DataSection|data section]] ([[GlobalVariable|globals]]), [[HeapSection|heap]] ([[DynamicMemoryAllocation|dynamic allocation]] — *named, mechanism deferred to Ch 2.4*), and [[StackSection|stack]] ([[LocalVariable|locals]] + [[FunctionParameter|parameters]] — [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s [[ExecutionStack|execution stack]] now placed inside the broader address space). Supplies the corpus's **first formal definition of [[VariableScope|scope]]** (*"a variable's scope defines when its name has meaning … the set of program code blocks in which a variable is bound to a program memory location"*); [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s [[FunctionScope|function scope]] was operational. Introduces **[[GlobalVariable|global variables]]** as a new variable class: declared outside any function body, in [[GlobalScope|global scope]] (any code can name them), living in the [[DataSection|data section]] (program-lifetime storage) — paired with the style rule *"avoid programming with global variables whenever possible"* and the rationale that local-variable-only code is *"more modular, more general-purpose, and easier to debug."* Worked `g_x` + three-distinct-`val` example makes the *same-name-different-scopes* rule concrete. **Does not yet discuss** `static`, block scope, or file scope — those deferred to later chapters. **Opens Ch 2 of the *Dive into Systems* corpus.**
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.6 Structs](sources/dis-1-6-structs.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s sixth content section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1. Introduces the second **aggregate** [[CLanguage|C]] type — the [[CStruct|`struct`]] — as the *heterogeneous* counterpart to [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]'s [[CArray|array]]: a bundle of named typed [[StructMember|fields]] (`char name[64]; int age; float gpa; int grad_yr;`) treated as a single coherent unit. Codifies the three-step usage discipline (define type outside any function, declare variables with the two-word `struct studentT` name, access fields via the [[MemberAccessOperator|dot operator `.`]]) and three load-bearing semantic rules: (1) structs are [[LValue|lvalues]] — `s2 = s1;` is legal whole-record copy including embedded [[CArray|array]] fields (the sharp contrast with array names, which are not lvalues); (2) structs pass to functions by [[PassByValue|value]] — *re-contradicting* [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]'s array-by-reference exception, mutations to a struct parameter (including its embedded `char name[64]`) do not persist in the caller; (3) [[SizeOf|`sizeof(struct studentT)`]] reports ≥ 76 bytes for the canonical four-field example, with padding-may-make-it-larger caveat foreshadowing the layout-and-alignment story of later chapters. Pointer-to-struct field access via the [[ArrowOperator|`->`]] operator, [[ArrayOfStructs|arrays of structs]], and [[Typedef|`typedef`]] are *referenced and deferred* to Section 2.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.5 Arrays and Strings](sources/dis-1-5-arrays-strings.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s fifth content section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1. Introduces the first **aggregate** types: the [[CArray|`int arr[N]`-style array]] (ordered, fixed-capacity, contiguous, same-type) and the [[CString|`char` array + `'\0'`]] convention that constitutes a [[CLanguage|C]] string. Codifies three load-bearing rules: (1) [[ArrayIndexing|indexing is zero-based and unchecked]] — [[BoundsChecking|no bounds checking]] at compile time or runtime, `arr[N]` is *undefined behavior* not an exception; (2) [[CArray|arrays]] pass to functions [[PassByReference|by reference]] (technically: their base address is what's copied) — **contradicting** [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s blanket [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]] rule, an apparent contradiction Ch 1.6 resolves via pointer decay; (3) [[CString|C strings]] are terminated by the [[NullTerminator|null byte `'\0'`]] (*not* the digit `'0'`), and buffers must size `strlen + 1` to fit it. Opens the [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]] library with three functions — [[Strlen|`strlen`]] / [[Strcpy|`strcpy`]] / [[Sprintf|`sprintf`]] — paired with the chapter's signature safety warning that [[Strcpy|`strcpy`]] *"poses a security risk because it assumes that its destination is large enough,"* foreshadowing the [[BufferOverflow|buffer-overflow]] discussion in Ch 2.6. Multidimensional arrays deferred to Ch 2.5.
- [Dive into Systems — Ch 1.4 Functions](sources/dis-1-4-functions.md) — [[SuzanneJMatthews|Matthews]] / [[TiaNewhall|Newhall]] / [[KevinCWebb|Webb]]'s fourth content section of *[[DiveIntoSystems]]* Ch 1. Promotes [[MainFunction|`main`]] from *the only [[Function|function]]* to *one [[Function|function]] among many*: introduces the [[FunctionDefinition|definition]]-vs-[[FunctionPrototype|prototype]] split (full header+body vs. header-only declaration, with the *prototypes-at-top-of-file, definitions-below* idiom that lets [[MainFunction|`main`]] call code defined later), the [[FunctionParameter|parameter]]-vs-[[FunctionArgument|argument]] vocabulary distinction (parameters are named placeholders, arguments are values at the call site), the [[ReturnStatement|`return`]] statement and its [[ReturnType|return-type]] header slot, and the [[VoidType|`void`]] return type for side-effect-only functions. **Headline rule: [[PassByValue|arguments are passed by value]]** — *"each function parameter is assigned the value of the corresponding argument … any change to a parameter's value in the function is not visible to the caller."* §1.4.1 opens up the runtime: every [[FunctionCall|call]] pushes a new [[StackFrame|stack frame]] (a.k.a. activation record) onto the [[ExecutionStack|execution stack]] holding that activation's [[LocalVariable|locals]] and [[FunctionParameter|parameters]]; only the *top* frame is in [[FunctionScope|scope]]; [[ReturnStatement|return]] pops the frame. Worked examples: `void print_table(int start, int stop)` and `int max(int n1, int n2)` called from [[MainFunction|`main`]].

- [IIR Ch. 2: The Term Vocabulary and Postings Lists](sources/iir-ch02-term-vocabulary-postings.md) — Document delineation, character decoding, [[Tokenization]], stop words, [[Stemming]]/[[Lemmatization]] (Porter), skip-pointer placement at √P, biword vs positional indexes, combination schemes for phrase queries.
- [IIR Ch. 3: Dictionaries and Tolerant Retrieval](sources/iir-ch03-dictionaries-tolerant-retrieval.md) — Dictionary search structures (hash vs B-tree), wildcard queries via permuterm & k-gram indexes, spelling correction with [[EditDistance]] (Levenshtein DP), context-sensitive correction, Soundex phonetic matching.
- [IIR Ch. 4: Index Construction](sources/iir-ch04-index-construction.md) — Hardware-motivated indexing — Reuters-RCV1 stats, BSBI external-merge algorithm, SPIMI single-pass in-memory indexing, [[MapReduce]] distributed indexing (parser/inverter), dynamic indexing with logarithmic merging.
- [IIR Ch. 5: Index Compression](sources/iir-ch05-index-compression.md) — Heaps' law M = k·T^b and [[ZipfsLaw]] cf_i ∝ 1/i; dictionary-as-string with front coding & blocked storage; postings compression via variable byte codes and gamma codes (unary + binary offset); RCV1 compression ratios.
- [IIR Ch. 6: Scoring, Term Weighting and the Vector Space Model](sources/iir-ch06-vector-space-model.md) — Parametric/zone indexes, weighted zone scoring with learned g; tf, idf = log(N/df_t), tf-idf; cosine similarity on length-normalized vectors; COSINESCORE algorithm; SMART notation (ddd.qqq); pivoted length normalization.
- [IIR Ch. 7: Computing Scores in a Complete Search System](sources/iir-ch07-complete-search-system.md) — Efficient top-K via heap selection O(J log K); inexact top-K shortcuts (index elimination, champion lists, static quality score g(d), impact ordering, cluster pruning with √N leaders); tiered indexes; query-term proximity; putting an end-to-end IR system together.
- [IIR Ch. 8: Evaluation in Information Retrieval](sources/iir-ch08-ir-evaluation.md) — Test-collection paradigm (Cranfield, TREC), precision/recall/F_β; ranked-retrieval evaluation with precision-recall curves, 11-point interpolated AP, MAP, R-precision, NDCG with log_2(i+1) discount; kappa for inter-annotator agreement; A/B testing & snippet generation.
- [IIR Ch. 9: Relevance Feedback and Query Expansion](sources/iir-ch09-relevance-feedback-query-expansion.md) — [[RocchioAlgorithm]] update q_m = αq_0 + β·centroid(D_r) − γ·centroid(D_nr); Ide dec-hi; probabilistic feedback; pseudo-relevance feedback; indirect feedback from clickthrough; global query expansion via thesauri / WordNet / automatic co-occurrence thesaurus.
- [IIR Ch. 10: XML Retrieval](sources/iir-ch10-xml-retrieval.md) — Structured retrieval beyond flat documents — XML data model & XPath, structural-term / lexicalized-subtree index, context-resemblance similarity, schema diversity challenge, INEX benchmark & NEXI query language, text-centric vs data-centric distinction.
- [IIR Ch. 11: Probabilistic Information Retrieval](sources/iir-ch11-probabilistic-ir.md) — Probability Ranking Principle (Robertson 1977), Binary Independence Model, Retrieval Status Value RSV_d = Σ log[p_t(1−u_t)/(u_t(1−p_t))]; tree-structured term dependencies; Okapi [[BM25]] with k_1, b parameters; Bayesian network IR.
- [IIR Ch. 12: Language Models for Information Retrieval](sources/iir-ch12-language-models-ir.md) — Query likelihood model P(q|M_d) with multinomial unigram LMs; Jelinek-Mercer linear-interpolation smoothing λ; Dirichlet smoothing with μ; Ponte & Croft 1998 experiments; contrast with vector-space and probabilistic IR. (NB: 2008-era statistical LMs — predecessors to modern neural [[LanguageModel]]s.)
- [IIR Ch. 13: Text Classification and Naive Bayes](sources/iir-ch13-text-classification-naive-bayes.md) — Multinomial vs Bernoulli [[NaiveBayes]] for text; MAP with [[LaplaceSmoothing]]; feature selection via [[MutualInformation]] I(U;C) and chi-square X²(t,c); micro vs macro F1; Reuters-21578 evaluation; properties of NB (high bias, low variance).
- [IIR Ch. 14: Vector Space Classification](sources/iir-ch14-vector-space-classification.md) — Rocchio classification with class centroids; k-nearest-neighbor with Voronoi tessellation, kNN test-time O(|D|M_a); linear vs nonlinear classifiers, one-vs-rest for multiclass; bias-variance decomposition E[(γ̂−γ)²] = bias² + variance for classifier selection.
- [IIR Ch. 15: Support Vector Machines and Machine Learning on Documents](sources/iir-ch15-svm-ml-on-documents.md) — Max-margin SVM (maximize 2/||w||) for linearly separable case; soft margin with slack ξ_i; kernel trick K(x_i, x_j) (polynomial, RBF); multiclass via one-vs-rest / structural SVMs; learning-to-rank with pairwise loss (RankingSVM); features & zones for text.
- [IIR Ch. 16: Flat Clustering](sources/iir-ch16-flat-clustering.md) — Cluster hypothesis; partitional vs hierarchical, hard vs soft; K-means (Lloyd's algorithm) minimizing RSS; choosing K via elbow / AIC / BIC; EM model-based clustering; external evaluation with purity, NMI, Rand Index, F-measure for clustering.
- [IIR Ch. 17: Hierarchical Clustering](sources/iir-ch17-hierarchical-clustering.md) — Hierarchical agglomerative clustering with priority queue O(N² log N); single-link (chaining) vs complete-link vs group-average vs centroid linkage; monotonicity & inversions; divisive top-down clustering with bisecting K-means; cluster labeling via differential test.
- [IIR Ch. 18: Matrix Decompositions and Latent Semantic Indexing](sources/iir-ch18-lsi-matrix-decompositions.md) — Eigendecomposition review; singular value decomposition C = UΣV^T; truncated SVD as best low-rank approximation (Eckart-Young theorem in Frobenius norm); latent semantic indexing C_k = U_k Σ_k V_k^T with query folding; handling synonymy & polysemy.
- [IIR Ch. 19: Web Search Basics](sources/iir-ch19-web-search-basics.md) — Pre-Google search history; bow-tie web graph (SCC/IN/OUT/tendrils); web spam & cloaking; advertising economics (CPC/CPM/CPA); Broder's query intent taxonomy (informational/navigational/transactional); capture-recapture index size estimation; near-duplicate detection via shingling + min-hash on Jaccard similarity.
- [IIR Ch. 20: Web Crawling and Indexes](sources/iir-ch20-web-crawling-indexes.md) — Crawler must/should-haves (politeness, robots.txt, freshness, scalability, distributed); Mercator-style URL frontier with front (priority) + back (per-host) queues; DNS as bottleneck; duplicate-elimination hash; sitemaps; term-partitioned vs document-partitioned distributed indexes; connectivity servers with gap encoding.
- [IIR Ch. 21: Link Analysis](sources/iir-ch21-link-analysis.md) — Web-as-graph + anchor-text propagation; [[PageRank]] as stationary distribution of teleporting Markov chain π = πP with P = (1−α)A + αE/N solved by power iteration; topic-sensitive PageRank; Kleinberg's HITS with mutually reinforcing hubs h(v)=Σa(u) and authorities a(v)=Σh(u) as eigenvectors of A^TA and AA^T.

- [Into the Unknown Unknowns: Engaged Human Learning through Participation in LM Agent Conversations (Jiang, Shao, Ma, Semnani & Lam 2024)](sources/2408.15232-co-storm.md) — [[YuchengJiang|Jiang]] / [[YijiaShao|Shao]] / [[DekunMa|Ma]] / [[SinaSemnani|Semnani]] / [[MonicaLam|Lam]] ([[stanforduniversity|Stanford]] + [[YaleUniversity|Yale]]; arXiv 2408.15232v2, Oct 2024) introduce **[[CoSTORM|Collaborative STORM (Co-STORM)]]** — successor to the [[STORM]] writing system that turns one-shot Wikipedia-style report generation into a *mixed-initiative collaborative discourse* between a user and multiple LM agents. Architecture: $N=3$ [[PerspectiveGuidedExpert|perspective-guided experts]] + a [[ModeratorAgent|moderator]] that reranks **uncited** sources via $\cos(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{t})^\alpha (1-\cos(\mathbf{i},\mathbf{q}))^{1-\alpha}$ (on-topic but unexplored) to surface [[UnknownUnknowns|unknown unknowns]]; a dynamic hierarchical **[[CoSTORMMindMap|mind map]]** $\mathcal{M}=(\mathcal{C},\mathcal{E})$ with `insert` + `reorganize` operations as shared knowledge substrate and report outline; a [[TurnManagement|turn-management protocol]] that invokes the moderator after $L=2$ consecutive non-question turns. Implementation: [[gpt-4o|gpt-4o-2024-05-13]] over [[DSPy]] (zero-shot — no [[MIPROv2]]/[[2507.19457-gepa|GEPA]] optimization), [[YouCom|You.com]] search filtered to [[Wikipedia]] *Reliable sources*. Introduces the **[[WildSeek]] dataset** — 100 (topic, goal) pairs across 24 domains from publicly-deployed STORM logs; the **first dataset in this wiki to capture user *goals*** (not just queries). Automatic eval: Co-STORM beats [[RAGChatbot|RAG Chatbot]] and STORM+QA on every report-quality dim (Relevance 3.78 / Breadth 3.79 / Depth 3.77 / Novelty 3.05 vs 3.57/3.50/3.26/2.44 RAG and 3.61/3.61/3.43/2.50 STORM+QA — Depth/Novelty $p<0.05$) graded by **[[Prometheus2|Prometheus 2]]**; **+[[InformationDiversity]]** 0.602 vs 0.59 baselines; **2× unique URLs / turn** (6.04 vs 2.94). Human eval ($n=20$): **70% prefer Co-STORM over [[GoogleSearch|Google Search]]**, **78% over [[RAGChatbot|RAG Chatbot]]**, less-effort 80%/67%, serendipity wins $p=0.030$/$p=0.009$. **Ablations**: removing the moderator drops scores more than removing multi-experts (Novelty 3.05→2.89, Depth 3.77→3.41) — *"having just one expert and one moderator can already provide most of the benefits"*; the **moderator is load-bearing**, perspective multiplicity is auxiliary. **First Yale-affiliated paper** in this wiki (via [[DekunMa]]). **Mints 14 concept pages** ([[CoSTORM]], [[STORM]], [[WildSeek]], [[UnknownUnknowns]], [[CollaborativeDiscourse]], [[CoSTORMMindMap]], [[ModeratorAgent]], [[PerspectiveGuidedExpert]], [[UtteranceIntent]], [[TurnManagement]], [[MixedInitiativeDiscourse]], [[InformationDiversity]], [[Prometheus2]], [[RAGChatbot]], [[InformationSeeking]]) + **8 entity pages** ([[YuchengJiang]], [[YijiaShao]], [[DekunMa]], [[SinaSemnani]], [[MonicaLam]], [[YaleUniversity]], [[StanfordOVAL]], [[YouCom]]); updates [[stanforduniversity]] in place. Resolves the long-standing [[Shao2024]] dangling reference invoked by the [[2406.11695-mipro|MIPRO]] / [[2407.10930-better-together|BetterTogether]] / [[2507.19457-gepa|GEPA]] [[DSPy]]-optimizer line.

- [Made With ML — Attention](sources/madewithml-foundations-attention.md) — Learned softmax-weighted pooling over RNN hidden states; interpretability via per-token weights; taxonomy of attention variants.
- [Made With ML — CI/CD for Machine Learning](sources/madewithml-mlops-cicd.md) — GitHub Actions workflows around Anyscale Jobs/Services that retrain on PR, comment results, and roll out on merge — enabling continual learning.
- [Made With ML — Command-Line Interface (CLI)](sources/madewithml-mlops-cli.md) — Replacing argparse/`__main__` with Typer-based CLIs using `Annotated` typed options; one decorated function per subcommand.
- [Made With ML — Convolutional Neural Networks](sources/madewithml-foundations-convolutional-neural-networks.md) — 1-D CNN text classifier with multi-width filters, max-pooling, batch normalization, and filter-activation interpretability.
- [Made With ML — Data Engineering for Machine Learning](sources/madewithml-mlops-data-engineering.md) — Modern data stack walkthrough — lake/database/warehouse archetypes, Airbyte ELT into BigQuery, dbt transforms with tests.
- [Made With ML — Data Preparation](sources/madewithml-mlops-preparation.md) — CSV ingestion into pandas + stratified train/val splits via sklearn, separate holdout test for stable model comparison.
- [Made With ML — Data Preprocessing](sources/madewithml-mlops-preprocessing.md) — Preparing (missing/outliers/cleaning) + transforming (scaling/encoding/extraction); scibert tokenization for the text task.
- [Made With ML — Data Quality](sources/madewithml-foundations-data-quality.md) — Empirically demonstrates "garbage in, garbage out" by training the same MLP on full vs reduced datasets.
- [Made With ML — Distributed Data Processing](sources/madewithml-mlops-distributed-data.md) — Scaling preprocessing via Ray Data `map_batches` with the same pandas function, plus stratified distributed splitting.
- [Made With ML — Distributed Training](sources/madewithml-mlops-training.md) — Fine-tunes SciBERT with Ray Train; benchmarks GPT-3.5/GPT-4 zero/few-shot before fine-tuning yields comparable results.
- [Made With ML — Documenting Code](sources/madewithml-mlops-documentation.md) — Comments/typing/docstrings/docs as four distinct artifacts; auto-generated docs site with MkDocs + mkdocstrings; published to GitHub Pages.
- [Made With ML — Embeddings](sources/madewithml-foundations-embeddings.md) — Dense embeddings over one-hot via Word2Vec (CBOW/skip-gram), FastText, and GloVe; random-init vs frozen-GloVe vs fine-tuned-GloVe on a CNN classifier.
- [Made With ML — Evaluating Machine Learning Models](sources/madewithml-mlops-evaluation.md) — Fine-grained eval beyond accuracy: per-class metrics, confusion-matrix sample analysis, confident learning, slicing, SHAP/LIME, behavioral tests, AB/canary/shadow online eval.
- [Made With ML — Experiment Tracking](sources/madewithml-mlops-experiment-tracking.md) — MLflow tracking wired into Ray Train via `MLflowLoggerCallback`; runs sorted by val_loss, best checkpoint loaded via `Result.from_path`.
- [Made With ML — Exploratory Data Analysis (EDA)](sources/madewithml-mlops-exploratory-data-analysis.md) — Goal-driven, cyclical EDA — tag distribution + per-class wordclouds to validate feature signal for the tagging task.
- [Made With ML — Hyperparameter Tuning](sources/madewithml-mlops-tuning.md) — Ray Tune + HyperOpt + ASHA scheduler tunes dropout_p / lr / lr_factor / lr_patience; best trial reaches F1=0.947.
- [Made With ML — Jobs and Services](sources/madewithml-mlops-jobs-and-services.md) — Productionize ML workloads using Anyscale Jobs (batch dev pipelines) and Services (canary-rolloutable endpoints) backed by shared S3 artifacts.
- [Made With ML — Linear Regression](sources/madewithml-foundations-linear-regression.md) — From-scratch NumPy then PyTorch implementation establishing the forward/loss/backward/update training loop and L2 regularization template reused everywhere later.
- [Made With ML — Logging for ML Systems](sources/madewithml-mlops-logging.md) — Python `logging` module mechanics (Logger/Handler/Formatter), dict-based config with rotating file handlers, placement guidance — log inside orchestration, not helpers.
- [Made With ML — Logistic Regression](sources/madewithml-foundations-logistic-regression.md) — Extends linear regression to multinomial classification via softmax + cross-entropy; logistic regression as the standard final layer of every later neural network.
- [Made With ML — Machine Learning Product Design](sources/madewithml-mlops-product-design.md) — ML Canvas product-design template (Background/Value/Objectives/Solution/Feasibility) applied to a content-tagging service.
- [Made With ML — Machine Learning Systems Design](sources/madewithml-mlops-systems-design.md) — How to engineer the ML system — data, metrics (F1), offline/online eval, batch vs online inference, and feedback loops.
- [Made With ML — Model Serving](sources/madewithml-mlops-serving.md) — Batch vs online inference with Ray Serve + FastAPI; framework selection criteria; threshold-based custom logic to route low-confidence predictions.
- [Made With ML — Monitoring Machine Learning Systems](sources/madewithml-mlops-monitoring.md) — Layered monitoring (system health → sliding performance → delayed outcomes → importance weighting → drift detection) with KS, chi-squared, MMD tests.
- [Made With ML — Moving from Notebooks to Scripts](sources/madewithml-mlops-scripting.md) — Why notebooks fail in production (stateful, non-linear, hard to test); canonical script layout (config/data/train/tune/evaluate/predict/serve/utils).
- [Made With ML — Neural Networks](sources/madewithml-foundations-neural-networks.md) — Introduces MLPs with ReLU, backprop via autograd, weight initialization, and dropout — the reusable feed-forward unit inside every later architecture.
- [Made With ML — NumPy](sources/madewithml-foundations-numpy.md) — NumPy fundamentals — array creation, indexing, arithmetic, dot product, axis-aware reductions, broadcasting, reshape, joining, dim expansion.
- [Made With ML — Pandas](sources/madewithml-foundations-pandas.md) — End-to-end tabular pipeline — load, EDA, filter/sort/group, loc/iloc indexing, NaN handling, one-hot encoding, feature engineering, save.
- [Made With ML — Pre-commit Hooks](sources/madewithml-mlops-pre-commit.md) — Pre-commit framework config (`.pre-commit-config.yaml`), three hook flavors (built-in/custom/local), and discipline against `--no-verify`.
- [Made With ML — Python for Machine Learning](sources/madewithml-foundations-python.md) — Python language primer covering variables, collection types, control flow, comprehensions, functions, classes, magic methods, inheritance, decorators.
- [Made With ML — PyTorch Fundamentals](sources/madewithml-foundations-pytorch.md) — Bridge from NumPy to PyTorch — tensor API, device placement (CUDA), autograd graph and .backward() mechanics, reproducible seeding.
- [Made With ML — Recurrent Neural Networks](sources/madewithml-foundations-recurrent-neural-networks.md) — Vanilla RNN then gated variants (LSTM, GRU) and bidirectional GRU; exposes vanishing-gradient and non-parallelizability issues that motivate attention.
- [Made With ML — Setup](sources/madewithml-mlops-setup.md) — Local + Anyscale cluster setup with Python 3.10, Ray initialization, and Workspace/JupyterLab tooling.
- [Made With ML — Styling and Formatting Code](sources/madewithml-mlops-styling.md) — Black + isort + flake8 trio configured in pyproject.toml, with a Makefile wrapping the three commands; foundation for pre-commit and CI enforcement.
- [Made With ML — Testing ML Systems: Code, Data and Models](sources/madewithml-mlops-testing.md) — Pytest mechanics (parametrize/fixtures/markers/coverage), great_expectations data validation, CheckList behavioral tests, testing-vs-monitoring boundary.
- [Made With ML — Transformers](sources/madewithml-foundations-transformers.md) — Scaled dot-product attention, multi-head attention, and positional encoding from *Attention Is All You Need*; HuggingFace pretrained SciBERT as feature extractor.
- [Made With ML — Utilities](sources/madewithml-foundations-utilities.md) — Refactors ad-hoc training code into reusable PyTorch utilities (set_seeds, Dataset/DataLoader, Trainer with early stopping, save/load).
- [Made With ML — Versioning Code, Data and Models](sources/madewithml-mlops-versioning.md) — Three-artifact versioning (code via Git, data via DVC/GitLFS/Dolt/Pachyderm, models via MLflow + S3 + Postgres); "version pointers, not artifacts".
- [Made With ML — Working in Notebooks](sources/madewithml-foundations-notebooks.md) — Setup primer for interactive notebooks via Google Colab or local JupyterLab, covering cells, execution, and basic editing.

- [ParProcBook Ch1: Introduction to Parallel Processing](sources/parproc-ch01-intro-parallel-processing.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s opening chapter (pp. 1–30) of *Programming on Parallel Machines* — motivates parallel processing along speed/memory/locality axes; surveys the three hardware paradigms ([[SharedMemoryArchitecture|shared-memory]] / [[MessagePassingArchitecture|message-passing]] / [[SIMD]]) and the matching software worldviews ([[Pthreads]] / [[OpenMP]] / [[MPI]] / [[Snow]] / [[Rdsm]]) via worked sieve, matrix-vector multiply, and [[SamplingBucketSort|sampling bucket sort]] examples.
- [ParProcBook Ch2: Recurring Performance Issues](sources/parproc-ch02-recurring-performance-issues.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s short Ch2 (pp. 31–42) installs the vocabulary the rest of the book uses to explain *why parallel code is slow*: [[CommunicationBottleneck|communication bottlenecks]], [[LoadBalancing|load balancing]], [[EmbarrassinglyParallel|embarrassingly parallel]] (old vs new meaning), the headline thesis that **[[StaticTaskAssignment|static (but randomized) task assignment] typically beats [[DynamicTaskAssignment|dynamic]]** (via an $O(1/\sqrt{m})$ chunk-time concentration argument and a Mandelbrot timing table where `random` 15.7s beats `dynamic` 21.4s and `static` 47.8s), [[WorkStealing]] / [[Cilk]], [[Latency]] vs [[Bandwidth]], and a [[SharedMemoryArchitecture|shared-memory]]-vs-[[MessagePassingArchitecture|message-passing]] revisit now scrambled by [[GPU]] scalability.
- [ParProcBook Ch3: Shared Memory Parallelism](sources/parproc-ch03-shared-memory-parallelism.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch3 (pp. 43–80) descends from Ch2's vocabulary into the **hardware substrate** of shared memory: [[MemoryInterleaving|interleaving]] (high-order vs low-order) and [[BankConflict|bank conflicts]] with the `gcd(s,b)=1` stride theorem; the bus / [[Crossbar|crossbar]] ($n^2$, Sun Enterprise 10000 16×16) / [[OmegaNetwork|omega-delta]] ($O(\log n)$) interconnect scaling table; [[NUMA]] PE structure delivered in full; synchronization hardware [[TestAndSet|TAS]] / Intel `LOCK` prefix / [[FetchAndAdd|F&A]] with §3.7 packet-combining; [[CacheCoherency|cache coherency]] (snoopy invalidate vs update, directory-based, [[MESI]] state machine in full transition tables) plus [[FalseSharing]]; [[MemoryConsistency]] (sequential / release / scope, SPARC `MEMBAR`) distinguished from coherency; [[Multicore]] flattened to "just SMPs"; [[ProcessorAffinity]]; [[SoftwareDSM|software DSM]] with [[JIAJIA]] (page-based / scope-consistent / home-based / multi-writer) as the case study; and three [[Barrier|barrier]] iterations (use-once → race-buggy reusable → two-counter alternating-parity) plus parallel [[TreeBarrier|tree]] / [[ButterflyBarrier|butterfly]] barriers.
- [ParProcBook Ch4: Introduction to OpenMP](sources/parproc-ch04-introduction-to-openmp.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch4 (pp. 81–118) installs [[OpenMP]] as *"the de facto standard for shared-memory programming"* via a recurring [[DijkstraAlgorithm|Dijkstra shortest-path]] worked example progressively annotated with each pragma: [[ParallelPragma|parallel]] / [[OpenMPSingle|single]] / [[Barrier|barrier]] / [[CriticalSection|critical]] / [[ParallelFor|for]] (with `collapse(N)`) / [[ScheduleClause|schedule(static/dynamic/guided/runtime)]] / [[ReductionClause|reduction(op:var)]] (with the eight-row identity-element table) / [[OpenMPTaskDirective|task]] (worked on recursive [[Quicksort]]) / [[AtomicClause|atomic]] (with GCC's `lock addl` lowering) / [[FlushPragma|flush]] (under [[RelaxedConsistency|relaxed consistency]] with seven auto-flushing synchronization points) / [[WorkSharing|combined `parallel for`]] / [[OpenMPLocks|`omp_lock_t`]]; plus an in-place matrix transpose, the [[MandelbrotSet]] timing case under `#ifdef` schedule switches, a root-finding bracketing example, mutual outlinks via randomized [[StaticTaskAssignment|static assignment]] + `omp atomic`, adjacency-matrix transformation via two-phase prefix-sum, and maximal-burst time-series via `omp for` + per-thread bests + `omp critical`; closes with a compiler section (Omni / Ompi / GCC `-fopenmp`) and a performance section showing Dijkstra timings on quad-core (1000-vertex parallelization *hurts*, 25000-vertex helps ~2×, fine-tuning replaces `critical` with a `mymins[2*nth]` array + post-barrier `single` reducer for ~15% gain).
- [ParProcBook Ch6: Introduction to Thrust Programming](sources/parproc-ch06-thrust-programming.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch6 (pp. 157–180) cashes Ch5 §5.18.2's deferral and gives [[Thrust]] its dedicated treatment: a C++ STL-modeled template library whose **same source compiles to either CUDA, OpenMP or Intel TBB back ends** via a `-DTHRUST_DEVICE_BACKEND=` macro. Walks the API surface — `host_vector` / `device_vector`, `sort` / `transform` / `reduce` / `copy_if` / `unique` / `scatter` / `gather` / `inclusive_scan` / `sequence` / `for_each` / `generate` — through eight worked examples (counting distinct values, a plain-C `extern "C"` wrapper around `thrust::sort`, percentile filtering with `copy_if`, doubling every k-th element via raw-pointer-functor interop, scatter/gather permutation, matrix transpose twice (once with [[ScatterOperation|`scatter()`]] + a [[Functor|functor]] over [[CountingIterator|`thrust::sequence`]], once with [[FancyIterator|fancy iterators]] and `make_transform_iterator` fusion), an adjacency-matrix transform using counting iterators + `thrust::identity` + a [[DiscardIterator|discard iterator]] + side-effecting functor, and a one-line [[PrefixScan|`inclusive_scan`]]). Establishes the **[[Functor|functor]] = stateful callable** idiom (*"what distinguishes functors from function pointers — we can save state"*), the **[[FancyIterator|fancy-iterator]] family** ([[CountingIterator|counting]] / [[TransformIterator|transform]] / [[ZipIterator|zip]] / [[DiscardIterator|discard]] / [[PermutationIterator|permutation]] iterators) with their **fusion** rationale (eliminate intermediate arrays + their kernel calls), the **Thrust↔CUDA interop** casts (`raw_pointer_cast` / `device_ptr`), the **synchronicity rule** (all Thrust calls synchronous *except* `transform()`-family — inverted from raw CUDA), and Thrust's surprising **absence of a parallel loop primitive** (compensated by `sequence` + `transform` or `for_each` over a counting iterator). The §6.9 timing comparison delivers the counterintuitive headline: a hand-rolled `for_each` + raw-pointer-functor matrix transpose **beats** the Thrust-distribution-example fancy-iterator implementation by ~2× on OpenMP and slightly on CUDA — **fancy iterators are not unconditionally faster**.
- [ParProcBook Ch10: The Parallel Prefix Problem](sources/parproc-ch10-parallel-prefix-problem.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch10 (pp. 223–234) centralises the [[PrefixScan]] primitive: [[HillisSteeleScan|Hillis-Steele]] $\log_2 n$-round data-parallel algorithm, blocked n > p strategy, platform support (MPI / TBB / [[Thrust]]), and three applications — parallel prefix summing in [[OpenMP]], [[RunLengthEncoding|run-length decompression]] (OpenMP + Thrust), and [[MovingAverage|moving average]] via `exclusive_scan` + `transform`; closes with C++11 [[LambdaFunction]] syntax as a functor alternative.
- [ParProcBook Ch11: Introduction to Parallel Matrix Operations](sources/parproc-ch11-parallel-matrix-operations.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch11 (pp. 235–256) covers parallel matrix operations end-to-end: [[PartitionedMatrix|partitioned matrices]] as the algebraic foundation, [[FoxAlgorithm|Fox's algorithm]] for MPI-based [[MatrixMultiplication|matrix multiplication]], OpenMP / CUDA (Edgar tiling: 500× speedup) / R Snow / gputools implementations, matrix powers for [[GraphConnectedness|graph connectedness]] / [[FibonacciNumbers|Fibonacci]] / [[MatrixInversion|matrix inversion]], [[GaussianElimination|Gaussian elimination]] and [[JacobiAlgorithm|Jacobi iteration]] for solving linear systems, [[PowerMethod|power method]] and CULA SVD for [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]], [[SparseMatrix|sparse matrices]] with CSR format, and a library survey (CUBLAS, CUSP, CULA, ScalaPACK, OpenBLAS).
- [ParProcBook Ch12: Introduction to Parallel Sorting](sources/parproc-ch12-parallel-sorting.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch12 (pp. 257–272) surveys parallel sorting across all three paradigms: [[Quicksort]] (separation process, OpenMP fork, [[Hyperquicksort]] on hypercubes), [[MergeSort]] (sequential, shared-memory, binary-tree message-passing, [[CompareExchange]], [[BitonicMergesort]]), [[BubbleSort]] (serial structure, [[OddEvenTransposition]] variant, [[CUDA]] implementation), [[Shearsort]] (2D mesh, snakelike output), [[SamplingBucketSort]] with sampling (MPI implementation), [[RadixSort]] (CUDPP segmented scan), and [[EnumerationSort]] (rank-count sort, trivially parallelizable outer loop).
- [ParProcBook Ch13: Parallel Computation for Audio and Image Processing](sources/parproc-ch13-audio-image-processing.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch13 (pp. 273–290) develops [[FourierSeries]] / [[DiscreteFourierTransform]] / [[FastFourierTransform]] mathematics, derives the FFT as a divide-and-conquer recursion (O(n²) → O(n log n)), presents two parallel strategies (FFT recursion analogous to Quicksort; matrix approach via Ch11 methods), exploits 2-D DFT separability for parallel image transforms, surveys FFT software ([[CUFFT]], [[FFTW]], R `fft()`), and applies frequency-domain filtering to [[ImageSmoothing]] (low-pass) and [[EdgeDetection]] (high-pass). Optional sections cover vector-space foundations (§13.9) and bandwidth (§13.10).
- [ParProcBook Ch14: Parallel Computation in Statistics/Data Mining](sources/parproc-ch14-statistics-data-mining.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch14 (pp. 291–304) surveys five statistical/data-mining workloads: [[ItemsetAnalysis]] + [[AprioriAlgorithm]] (breadth-first frequent-itemset search with support-based pruning; embarrassingly parallel inner loops), [[KernelDensityEstimation]] (smooth nonparametric density via kernel-weighted sums; parallelized by distributing t-values or reducing to parallel [[FastFourierTransform|FFT]]), [[Histogram]] computation for images in CUDA (Podlozhnyuk histogram64/256 subhistogram-merge algorithm with bank-conflict elimination), [[KMeansClustering]] (full [[Snow]] parallel implementation: `clusterCall` + `Reduce`), [[PrincipalComponentAnalysis]] (dimension reduction via leading eigenvectors; reuses Ch11 parallel eigenvector methods), and [[MonteCarloSimulation]] (embarrassingly parallel simulation requiring independent parallel RNG streams: CURAND, RngStream, SPRNG, OpenMP Mersenne Twister).
- [ParProcBook Appendix B: Review of Matrix Algebra](sources/parproc-appB-matrix-algebra.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Appendix B (pp. 313–320) is a compact math primer covering notation, [[MatrixMultiplication|matrix multiplication]], [[MatrixTranspose|transpose]], [[LinearIndependence|linear independence]], [[Determinant|determinants]], [[MatrixInversion|matrix inverse]] (including QR route), [[Eigenvalue|eigenvalues]] and [[Eigenvector|eigenvectors]], [[Rank|rank]], and R syntax (`%*%` / `t()` / `solve()` / `eigen()` / `qr()`).
- [ParProcBook Appendix A: Miscellaneous Systems Issues](sources/parproc-appA-systems-issues.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Appendix A (pp. 305–312) is a systems primer covering three topics that recur throughout the book: §A.1 [[Timesharing]] (OS quantum/timeslice scheduling enforced by hardware timer interrupts + [[ContextSwitch]] mechanics); §A.2 [[MemoryHierarchy]] (§A.2.1 [[CacheMemory]] hit/miss/eviction; §A.2.2 [[VirtualMemory]] page-table mechanism, page faults, goals of VM; §A.2.3 [[LocalityOfReference]] explaining >90% hit rates, [[TranslationLookasideBuffer]] eliminating double-access overhead); §A.3 array issues (§A.3.1 [[RowMajorOrder]] storage — the i*c+j formula central to parallel code; §A.3.2 subarray pointer arithmetic; §A.3.3 [[MemoryAllocation]] — `malloc()`/`new` expensive in parallel programs, prefer global arrays, use `gcc -mcmodel=medium` for large arrays).
- [ParProcBook Appendix C: R Quick Start](sources/parproc-appC-r-quick-start.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Appendix C (pp. 321–338) is a self-contained R primer for C/C++ programmers covering [[Rlanguage|R]]'s data model (vectors, column-major matrices, lists, [[DataFrame|data frames]]), [[RVectorization|R vectorization]] as the primary performance technique (~476× loop vs built-in), recycling, [[S3Classes|S3 OO classes]], workhorse functions (`apply`/`lapply`/`sapply`/`Reduce`), graphics (`lattice`/`ggplot2`), the [[Snow|`parallel`]] package, debugging tools, and complex numbers. Final appendix; closes the *Programming on Parallel Machines* corpus (Ch1–Ch14 + App A–C).
- [ParProcBook Ch9: MapReduce Computation](sources/parproc-ch09-mapreduce-computation.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch9 (pp. 213–222) covers the [[MapReduce]] paradigm (map/shuffle/reduce phases; scatter/gather-plus-sort) via [[Hadoop]] streaming (R word-count example, [[HDFS]] disk architecture, combiner optimization) and introduces [[Snowdoop]] — a lightweight pure-R alternative using [[Snow]]'s `clusterCall` + `Reduce` that avoids Java/configuration overhead and keeps worker data in RAM across iterations for iterative algorithms like [[KMeansClustering]].
- [ParProcBook Ch8: Introduction to MPI](sources/parproc-ch08-introduction-to-mpi.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch8 (pp. 187–212) is the dedicated [[MPI]] chapter: *"MPI is the de facto standard for message-passing software."* Walks the API surface (`MPI_Init` / `MPI_Finalize` / `MPI_Comm_size` / `MPI_Comm_rank` / [[MPISend|`MPI_Send`]] / [[MPIRecv|`MPI_Recv`]]) via a parallel [[DijkstraAlgorithm|Dijkstra]] worked example, then refactors it with [[CollectiveCommunication|collective communications]] ([[MPIBcast|`MPI_Bcast`]] / [[MPIReduce|`MPI_Reduce`]] / [[MPIAllreduce|`MPI_Allreduce`]] / [[MPIGather|`MPI_Gather`]] / [[MPIAllgather|`MPI_Allgather`]] / [[MPIScatter|`MPI_Scatter`]] / [[MPIBarrier|`MPI_Barrier`]]) — three hand-written functions disappear into three collective calls; documents the 12-op reduce table (`MPI_MAX` / `MPI_MIN` / `MPI_SUM` / `MPI_PROD` / `MPI_LAND` / `MPI_LOR` / `MPI_LXOR` / `MPI_BAND` / `MPI_BOR` / `MPI_BXOR` / `MPI_MAXLOC` / `MPI_MINLOC`); installs the [[SPMD|Single Program Multiple Data]] execution model (*"though the nodes are all running the same program, they will likely be working on different parts of the program's data"*); the implementation taxonomy (MPICH + LAM + the LAM→Open-MPI succession + the *"not to be confused with [[OpenMP]]"* warning); the typed-message endianness/word-width broker story; a 0-removal stream-compaction example with variable-length receive via `MPI_Get_count`; an attach-GDB-with-`while (dbg) ;` debugging workflow; the four-call sub-[[MPICommunicator|communicator]] recipe (`MPI_Comm_group` → `MPI_Group_incl` → `MPI_Comm_create` → `MPI_Group_rank`); the §8.7 [[BufferingMPI|buffering/synchrony/safety]] deep-dive (TCP/IP stream coalescing + the exact MPI-standard send semantic — *"`MPI_Send(x,...)` will return only when it is safe for the application program to write over the array which it is using to store its message"* — + the OS-buffer→app-buffer copy that [[Infiniband]] RDMA eliminates + the classic synchronous-tag-mismatch [[Deadlock|deadlock]] pattern + the *"asynchronous communication is considered unsafe"* terminology); §8.7.3 [[NonblockingComm|"living dangerously"]] with `MPI_Isend` / `MPI_Irecv` / `MPI_Wait` / `MPI_Probe`; and §8.7.4's `MPI_Sendrecv_replace` as the safe-exchange alternative.
- [ParProcBook Ch7: Message Passing Systems](sources/parproc-ch07-message-passing-systems.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s short Ch7 (pp. 181–186) backfills the **hardware substrate** of the [[MessagePassingArchitecture|message-passing paradigm]] [[parproc-ch01-intro-parallel-processing|Ch1]] surveyed: a historical detour through 1980s–90s **[[Hypercube|hypercubes]]** (Intel + nCube/Oracle; d-cube of $D = 2^d$ PEs with bit-flip neighbor rule, inductive duplicate-and-prefix construction, sub-cube / root / partner formalism, dedicated point-to-point links vs the [[NetworkOfWorkstations|NOW]]'s shared medium); the modern **NOW / [[Beowulf]] / [[Cluster]]** continuum (Ch7 explicitly retires *NOW* in favor of *cluster*); the *"network is literally the weakest link"* motto with **[[Infiniband]]** as the prescribed answer (switch-based fabric similar to [[OmegaNetwork|Ω-net]], **RDMA** to bypass the app↔OS-space copy, hardware-supported collectives + true multicast, 1–3 μs [[Latency]] + 1–2 GB/s [[Bandwidth]] + 5–10% CPU usage); the **MPI_Bcast-is-not-magic** gotcha (without IB-style multicast hardware + a matching MPI build, `MPI_Bcast` is O(P) sequential sends); the modern hybrid-NOW programming choice (pure MPI vs MPI+OpenMP per-node); and a §7.4 reframing of [[ScatterGather|scatter/gather]] as the *higher-level paradigm bridging [[MPI]] / [[Snow]] / [[MapReduce]]* (motivated by *"writing message-passing code is a lot of work, as the programmer must explicitly arrange for transfer of data"*). Reframes Ch1's three-paradigms-of-equal-stature posture into a *"message-passing currently dominates"* claim grounded in cloud computing + Top500 — the single biggest contemporary-status update in the parproc corpus.
- [ParProcBook Ch5: Introduction to GPU Programming with CUDA](sources/parproc-ch05-cuda-gpu-programming.md) — [[NormMatloff]]'s Ch5 (pp. 119–156) pivots from CPU to GPU, framing [[CUDA]] on [[NVIDIA]] hardware as a third paradigm beyond Ch3's shared memory and Ch4's OpenMP — *"GPUs can run hundreds or thousands of threads at once"*. The chapter walks the hardware model (streaming multiprocessors hosting [[Block|blocks]] of threads scheduled in 32-thread [[Warp|warps]] under [[SIMT]] lockstep, with [[ThreadDivergence|thread divergence]] as the "performance killer" within a warp and the SM as an "OS in hardware" doing latency hiding by warp-swap on memory stall), the memory hierarchy (programmer-managed on-chip [[SharedMemory|shared]] vs off-chip [[GlobalMemory|global]], plus host-writable cached [[ConstantMemory]], 2D-cached [[TextureMemory]], abundant per-thread registers, and global-in-disguise local memory — with [[MemoryCoalescing|coalescing]] of half-warp consecutive-word accesses and bank-conflict avoidance as the two big global/shared optimizations), the [[Grid|grid]] / block / thread / warp four-level [[KernelLaunch|launch hierarchy]] (`kernel<<<grid,block,shmem>>>(...)`), intra-block `__syncthreads()` vs inter-block atomic ops or host-roundtrip synchronization, the 128–256 threads/block design rule, and worked examples — row sums (with a 62s→4.5s CPU-vs-GPU column-sum showdown), mutual outlinks via `atomicAdd`, Sieve of Eratosthenes in shared memory (with divergence-aware multiple-of-prime partitioning across threads), cumulative sums, and a two-kernel adjacency-matrix transformation. Closes with [[LoopUnrolling|`#pragma unroll`]] for register allocation, [[ShortVectors|short vectors]] (`int4`/`char2`) for 4× bandwidth, [[TrueCaching|true caching]] (split on-chip between shared and L1), [[UnifiedMemory|`managed` unified memory]] (hardware-assisted from [[NVIDIAPascal|Pascal]]), and the [[CUBLAS]] / [[Thrust]] / [[CUFFT]] wrapper-library tour.

- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.1: Preliminaries](sources/pydata-preliminaries.md) — Scope (structured-data manipulation), survey of the essential Python data ecosystem ([[NumPy]], [[pandas]], [[matplotlib]], [[IPython]]/[[Jupyter]], [[SciPy]], [[scikitlearn]], [[statsmodels]]), Miniconda installation, import conventions, and the GIL caveat.
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.10: Data Aggregation and Group Operations](sources/pydata-data-aggregation.md) — [[SplitApplyCombine|split-apply-combine]] (term coined by [[HadleyWickham]]) implemented as `DataFrame.groupby`. Group keys (column / dict / Series / function / index level), aggregation (built-ins, multi-function, dict-per-column), `apply` (general split-apply-combine), `transform` (group-preserving), `pivot_table`, `crosstab`.
