[[Patsy]] formula syntax (`y ~ x0 + x1`, `C(category)`, transforms) for design matrices.
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.13: Data Analysis Examples](sources/pydata-data-analysis-examples.md) — Capstone — five worked exploratory analyses on real datasets (1.USA.gov / Bitly, MovieLens 1M, US Baby Names 1880–2010, USDA Food Database, 2012 FEC donations) exercising the full pipeline (load → clean → wrangle → group → plot).
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.2: Python Language Basics, IPython, and Jupyter Notebooks](sources/pydata-python-basics.md) — Self-contained primer on Python language features (indentation, everything-is-an-object, dynamic + duck typing, scalar types, control flow) and the [[IPython]] shell + [[Jupyter]] notebook (tab completion, introspection, `%run`/`%pdb`/`%timeit`).
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.3: Built-In Data Structures, Functions, and Files](sources/pydata-python-builtin.md) — Workhorse Python primitives: tuple / list / dict / set, comprehensions, functions (scope, multi-return, first-class, [[LambdaFunctions|lambda]], [[Generators|generators]], `itertools`), exception handling, file I/O (with bytes/unicode semantics).
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.4: NumPy Basics: Arrays and Vectorized Computation](sources/pydata-numpy-basics.md) — Introduces the [[NDArray|ndarray]] and array-oriented computing: construction, dtypes, vectorized arithmetic, indexing (basic / slicing / boolean / fancy), transposition, [[UniversalFunctions|ufuncs]], `np.where`, descriptive stats, sorting / unique / set logic, file IO, `numpy.linalg`, PRNG, random-walks example.
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.5: Getting Started with pandas](sources/pydata-pandas-basics.md) — Primer on the [[Series]] / [[DataFrame]] / [[pandasIndex|Index]] trio. Reindex, drop, label/positional selection (`.loc`/`.iloc`), arithmetic with data alignment, function application (`apply`/`map`/`transform`), sorting / ranking, descriptive stats, correlation/covariance, `unique`/`value_counts`/`isin`.
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.6: Data Loading, Storage, and File Formats](sources/pydata-accessing-data.md) — pandas IO surface — text (CSV/TSV/JSON/HTML/XML), binary (Excel/[[HDF5]]/Feather/ORC/[[Parquet]]/Pickle), web APIs (`requests` + `pd.json_normalize`), and SQL databases via [[SQLAlchemy]]. `pandas.read_csv`'s ~50 options plus chunked iteration.
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.7: Data Cleaning and Preparation](sources/pydata-data-cleaning.md) — Missing data (`isna`/`dropna`/`fillna`), dedup, value mapping / replace / rename, discretization (`pd.cut`/`qcut`), outliers, sampling, dummy variables, [[ExtensionDataTypes]] (`Int64`/`boolean`/`string` + `pd.NA`), string methods (Python `str` + `re` + `Series.str` vectorized), [[CategoricalData|Categorical]] extension type.
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.8: Data Wrangling: Join, Combine, and Reshape](sources/pydata-data-wrangling.md) — [[HierarchicalIndexing|MultiIndex]], database-style joins (`pd.merge`), `concat`, `combine_first`, and reshape between long/wide formats (`stack`/`unstack`/`pivot`/`pivot_table`/`melt`).
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Ch.9: Plotting and Visualization](sources/pydata-plotting-and-visualization.md) — [[matplotlib]] primer (Figure / Axes / Subplots; styles; ticks/labels/legends; annotations; saving; rc config) and the higher-level interfaces — pandas `.plot` accessor and [[seaborn]] (line / bar / hist / scatter / facet-grid / categorical).
- [Python for Data Analysis 3E — Preface](sources/pydata-preface.md) — Front matter and acknowledgments for [[WesMcKinney]]'s 3rd edition (2022); open-access web edition via [[Quarto]]; in-memoriam dedication to [[JohnHunter]] (1968–2012, creator of [[matplotlib]]); pandas origin story at [[AQRCapitalManagement]] (2008).

- [The Embedded Rust Book — Collections](sources/rust-embedded-book-collections-index.md) — File 29/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — single-file *Collections* chapter. **Delivers** the opt-in heap recipe forecast in [[rust-embedded-book-intro-no-std]] and contrasts [[AllocCrate|`alloc`]] (heap-backed, familiar `std` API) head-to-head with [[HeaplessCrate|`heapless`]] (fixed-capacity, stack-allocated, no allocator). Two-piece activation contract for `alloc`: a [[GlobalAllocator|`#[global_allocator]`]] `static` implementing [[GlobalAlloc|`GlobalAlloc`]] (chapter implements an illustrative [[BumpPointerAllocator|bump-pointer allocator]] wrapping `cortex_m::interrupt::free` for single-core interrupt safety; null `*mut u8` = OOM; recommends a battle-tested crates.io allocator like [[AllocCortexMCrate|`alloc-cortex-m`]] in production) **plus** an [[AllocErrorHandlerAttribute|`#[alloc_error_handler]`]] `fn(Layout) -> !` for [[OutOfMemory|OOM]] (unstable `alloc_error_handler` feature). [[HeaplessCrate|`heapless`]] needs no setup — capacity baked into the type signature via [[Typenum|`typenum`]] (`Vec<_, U8>`), all insertion methods return `Result`, collections never reallocate, **`push` is constant time**. Four-axis trade-off: (1) **OOM** — implicit + non-local in `alloc` (via [[MemoryFragmentation|fragmentation]] and leaks; *"memory leaks are possible in safe Rust"*); impossible in pure-`heapless` programs; (2) **memory** — heap accounting is hard (`shrink_to_fit` allocator-discretionary, fragmentation inflates apparent usage); `heapless` lets the linker statically detect RAM overcommit and is visible to `-Z emit-stack-sizes` / `stack-sizes` tooling, at the cost of a lower load factor (can't shrink); (3) **[[WorstCaseExecutionTime|WCET]]** — `alloc::Vec::push` includes a realloc tail dependent on runtime capacity; `heapless::Vec::push` is *"constant time"* — decisive for hard real-time; (4) **ease of use** — `alloc` = global-allocator setup + familiar API; `heapless` = no setup + per-instance capacity choice + pervasive `Result` (some find this *"excessive or too cumbersome"*).
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Concurrency](sources/rust-embedded-book-concurrency-index.md) — File 28/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — single-file *Concurrency* chapter. Frames embedded concurrency as the union of three sources ([[Interrupt|interrupt handlers]], multithreading, multi-core) and walks one running 1 Hz frequency-counter example through six escalating fixes for the same [[DataRace|data race]]: (1) no concurrency, (2) `static mut` + `unsafe` (broken — exhibits load-increment-store race), (3) [[CriticalSection|critical sections]] via `cortex_m::interrupt::free`, (4) [[Atomic|atomic instructions]] (`AtomicUsize::fetch_add` — multi-core safe; `thumbv6` load/store-only vs `thumbv7` full CAS), (5) safe abstraction over [[UnsafeCell]] with a `&CriticalSection` token parameter ([[ZeroCostAbstraction|zero-cost compile-time proof]] of being inside a critical section), (6) the **`cortex_m::interrupt::Mutex<Cell<u32>>`** and **`Mutex<RefCell<Option<T>>>`** generalizations — the canonical embedded peripheral-sharing pattern. Names [[Send]] / [[Sync]] explicitly, defines [[InteriorMutability]]'s three layers ([[UnsafeCell]] → [[CellRust|`Cell`]] → [[RefCell]]), introduces [[Deadlock]] as a non-`unsafe` failure mode that critical-section-gated mutexes sidestep by construction, and names three higher-level alternatives: [[RTIC]] (static-priority + compile-time resource tracking, deadlock-free), [[Embassy]] (`async`/`await` ecosystem), and RTOSs (FreeRTOS / ChibiOS).
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Getting Started](sources/rust-embedded-book-start-index.md) — Chapter intro (file 10/44) of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — opens Part 2 (*Getting Started*) after the intro chapter closed at file 9. Six-line preface scoping the chapter's "write → build → flash → debug" loop and announcing the pedagogical contract: **most examples run without hardware** via [[QEMU]] (the [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M]] emulator); only the Hardware sub-section requires the physical [[STM32F3DISCOVERY]] board flashed via [[OpenOCD]]. Promotes [[QEMU]] from the toolchain inventory ([[rust-embedded-book-intro-tooling]]) to the default execution substrate for the chapter's exercises.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Installation](sources/rust-embedded-book-intro-install.md) — Chapter 5 (file 5/44) of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — short pointer chapter laying down the **OS-agnostic** install manifest before branching into per-OS sub-pages. Three moves: install [[Rustup]] (verify [[Rustc|`rustc`]] ≥ 1.31), `rustup target add` the right [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M]] [[RustTarget|target triple]] (F3 board → `thumbv7em-none-eabihf`; seven Cortex-M triples enumerated M0/M0+/M1 → M33F/M35PF), then `cargo install` [[CargoBinutils|`cargo-binutils`]] (+ `rustup component add llvm-tools`) and [[CargoGenerate|`cargo-generate`]]. Caveats: Windows needs VS 2019 C++ Build Tools; some Linuxes need `libssl-dev` + `pkg-config`. Operationalizes [[CrossCompilation|cross-compilation]] from the prior [[rust-embedded-book-intro-tooling|tooling chapter]] into shell commands.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Installation (Linux)](sources/rust-embedded-book-intro-install-linux.md) — File 6/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the **Linux-specific** install branch off [[rust-embedded-book-intro-install]]. Two halves: (1) distro-specific package install for [[GDB]] / [[OpenOCD]] / [[QEMU|`qemu-system-arm`]] on Ubuntu / Debian / Fedora / Arch — note `gdb-multiarch` (modern Debian/Ubuntu) vs `arm-none-eabi-gdb` (older Ubuntu, Arch) vs plain `gdb` (Fedora); (2) a [[UdevRules|udev rule]] (`/etc/udev/rules.d/70-st-link.rules`) matching the F3 board's [[STLink|ST-LINK]] USB IDs (`0483:3748` V2, `0483:374b` V2-1) with `TAG+="uaccess"` so [[OpenOCD]] drives the probe without `sudo`. Closes with `udevadm control --reload-rules` + `lsusb` / `getfacl` verification.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Installation (macOS)](sources/rust-embedded-book-intro-install-macos.md) — File 7/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the **macOS-specific** install branch off [[rust-embedded-book-intro-install]], sibling to [[rust-embedded-book-intro-install-linux|the Linux branch]]. Shortest of the three OS branches: install [[GDB|`arm-none-eabi-gdb`]] + [[OpenOCD]] + [[QEMU]] through either [[Homebrew|Homebrew]] (`brew install …`) or [[MacPorts]] (`sudo port install …`; note the `arm-none-eabi-gcc` port carries `gdb`). No udev / driver / signing step — macOS grants the seat user USB access by default. Side-note: `brew install --HEAD openocd` as a crash workaround for the released [[OpenOCD]] formula.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Installation (Windows)](sources/rust-embedded-book-intro-install-windows.md) — File 8/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the **Windows-specific** install branch off [[rust-embedded-book-intro-install]], closing the three-OS trio with [[rust-embedded-book-intro-install-linux|Linux]] and [[rust-embedded-book-intro-install-macos|macOS]]. No package manager (no Chocolatey / scoop); each tool ships as a vendor binary: [[GDB|`arm-none-eabi-gdb`]] from ARM's official `.exe` installer (tick "Add path to environment variable"), [[OpenOCD]] from the third-party [[xPackProject|xPack project]] (no official Windows release; manually extend `%PATH%`), [[QEMU]] from the QEMU project's own Windows builds. Mandatory [[STMicroelectronics]] `stsw-link009` USB driver for the [[STLink|ST-LINK]] — without it [[OpenOCD]] won't see the probe. Picks 32-bit vs 64-bit driver to match OS bitness. No Zadig / WinUSB substitution involved.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Interrupts](sources/rust-embedded-book-start-interrupts.md) — File 17/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the *Getting Started* chapter's **Interrupts** sub-section and **closes the Getting Started chapter**, immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-start-exceptions|Exceptions]]. Deliberately brief — defers detailed mechanics to the [[rust-embedded-book-start-exceptions|exceptions chapter]]. Three substantive contributions: (1) the **exception-vs-interrupt distinction** — both flow through the same [[NVIC|controller]] and [[VectorTable|vector table]], but exceptions are Cortex-M architectural (fixed names) while interrupts are **vendor- and chip-specific** (names auto-generated from the [[SVDFile|SVD]] by [[Svd2Rust|`svd2rust`]]); (2) the [[InterruptAttribute|`#[interrupt]`]] attribute — **must** be used via the device-crate re-export (`use lm3s6965::interrupt;`), not directly from `cortex-m-rt-macros`, so the compiler can verify the named interrupt exists on the target chip; (3) the three NVIC-level advanced-use properties — [[InterruptPriority|programmable priorities]], **nesting/preemption** by higher-priority handlers, and the **clear-reason requirement** (the handler must clear the peripheral flag, or the [[NVIC]] re-pends endlessly). Same `static mut`-is-safe story as `#[exception]` — software-uncallable handler ⇒ no reentrancy on a single core ⇒ `&mut` is unique.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Memory-mapped Registers](sources/rust-embedded-book-start-registers.md) — File 13/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the *Getting Started* chapter on **peripheral access**, immediately after the hardware sub-section ([[rust-embedded-book-start-hardware]]). Pedagogical hinge from runtime / linker / debug plumbing into actual register-twiddling. Builds the **four-layer crate stack** ([[MicroArchitectureCrate|micro-arch]] → [[PeripheralAccessCrate|PAC]] → [[HALCrate|HAL]] → [[BoardCrate|board]]) and walks each: [[CortexMCrate|`cortex-m`]] exposes the core-standardized [[SysTick]] peripheral via `Peripherals::take()`; [[Tm4c123xCrate|`tm4c123x`]] (TI Tiva-C, generated by [[Svd2Rust|`svd2rust`]] from the chip's [[SVDFile|CMSIS-SVD]]) introduces the closure idiom `reg.read()` / `reg.write(|w| …)` / `reg.modify(|r, w| …)` that replaces the C read-modify-write footgun; `tm4c123x_hal` shows the [[HALCrate|HAL]] layer wrapping the [[PeripheralAccessCrate|PAC]] with `constrain()` / `split()`, [[TypeStateProgramming|type-state]] GPIO pin modes (`into_af_push_pull::<AF1>()`), and a `Clock` borrow that makes constructing a `Serial` without first configuring the PLLs a **compile error** — "all with no run-time cost." Defers [[EmbeddedHalCrate|`embedded-hal`]] portability to the forward-referenced *Portability* chapter; defers `stm32f3-discovery` and other board crates as out-of-scope (book stays hardware-agnostic).
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Exceptions](sources/rust-embedded-book-start-exceptions.md) — File 16/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the *Getting Started* chapter's **Exceptions** sub-section, immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-start-panicking|Panicking]]. Introduces the [[CortexMRTCrate|`cortex-m-rt`]] [[ExceptionAttribute|`#[exception]`]] attribute as the declarative surface for [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M]] exception handlers ([[SysTick]], [[HardFault]], `NMI`, …, plus the catch-all [[DefaultHandler]]). Two non-obvious guarantees: handlers are **software-uncallable** (`SysTick();` is a compile error) and `static mut` inside the body is therefore **safe** (hardware-only invocation precludes reentrancy on a single core; multicore breaks this and needs explicit sync). Three worked examples: a [[SysTick]] counter over [[ARMSemihosting|semihosting]] on [[QEMU]]; a `DefaultHandler(irqn: i16)` override (negative ⇒ architectural exception, ≥ 0 ⇒ device [[Interrupt|IRQ]]); a [[HardFault]] post-mortem with the mandatory `fn(&ExceptionFrame) -> !` signature, dumping the [[ExceptionFrame|`ExceptionFrame`]] (r0…r12, lr, pc, xpsr) and cross-referencing `pc` against `cargo objdump` to find the faulting `ldr r0, [r0]` instruction. QEMU caveat: `qemu-system-arm -machine lm3s6965evb` does not check memory loads, so the `HardFault` example only fires on real hardware.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Panicking](sources/rust-embedded-book-start-panicking.md) — File 15/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the *Getting Started* chapter's **Panicking** sub-section, immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-start-semihosting|Semihosting]]. Names panicking as a **core language primitive** (runtime-checked ops like out-of-bounds indexing emit panics) and makes the [[NoStd|`no_std`]]-specific point that the program must **explicitly declare its panic behavior** via the [[PanicHandlerAttribute|`#[panic_handler]`]] attribute on a `fn(&PanicInfo) -> !` (the [[PanicInfo|`core::panic::PanicInfo`]] struct carries the location + payload). Surveys the four pre-packaged crates ([[PanicAbortCrate|`panic-abort`]] / [[PanicHaltCrate|`panic-halt`]] / [[PanicItmCrate|`panic-itm`]] / [[PanicSemihostingCrate|`panic-semihosting`]]) and the **profile-conditional swap** pattern (`panic-halt` for `dev` to breakpoint `rust_begin_unwind`, `panic-abort` for `release` to minimize binary size). Documents the `use panic_X as _;` linker-idiom and points readers at the `panic-handler` crates.io keyword (covering the modern [[Knurling]] alternative [[PanicProbeCrate|`panic-probe`]]). Worked example: out-of-bounds `xs[xs.len()]` under `panic-semihosting` on [[QEMU]] → `panicked at 'index out of bounds: ...', src/main.rs:12:13`.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Portability](sources/rust-embedded-book-portability-index.md) — File 27/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **opens** (and is the sole content file of) the *Portability* chapter, **resolving** the long-standing forward reference from [[rust-embedded-book-start-registers]] and [[EmbeddedHalCrate]]. Single-file chapter. Names [[Portability]] as the *"very important topic"* of embedded development (vendor + family + peripheral fragmentation), pins the standard solution as a [[HardwareAbstractionLayer|HAL]] (quoting Wikipedia), and explains why the OS-syscall flavor of HALs is the wrong fit for embedded (*"firmware images compiled as a whole … no operating systems"*). Introduces [[EmbeddedHalCrate|`embedded-hal`]] as *"a set of traits which define implementation contracts between HAL implementations, drivers and applications."* The chapter's central architectural payoff is the **M·N → M+N complexity collapse**: *"if M is the number of peripheral HAL implementations and N the number of drivers … the API provided by the embedded-hal traits will make the implementation complexity approach M+N."* Enumerates the six named trait families ([[GPIO]] input/output, serial, [[I2C]], [[SPI]], timers/countdowns, ADC) and the three-role user taxonomy: (1) **HAL implementation** — chip-specific types + factory functions + trait impls, in four flavors (low-level registers, OS-syscall like Linux sysfs, mock-for-testing, adapter-as-HAL like an I2C multiplexer); (2) **[[DriverCrate|Driver]]** — chip-agnostic, trait-bounded generic, with three component categories (sensors, displays, actuators); (3) **Application** — the layer where porting effort concentrates (*"the part which requires the most adaptation efforts"*) — pin reassignment, peripheral-conflict resolution, bus-config differences. Introduces [[Portability]], [[DriverCrate]], and [[HardwareAbstractionLayer]] as new concepts.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Zero Cost Abstractions](sources/rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-zero-cost-abstractions.md) — File 26/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **fourth and final** named sub-section of the *Static Guarantees* chapter, immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-design-contracts]]. **Closes the chapter** by naming the cost model behind every prior typestate / static-guarantee claim in the corpus. Defines [[ZeroCostAbstraction|Zero Cost Abstraction]] as *"the ability to move certain behaviors to compile time execution or analysis"* and substantiates it with five lines of `core::mem::size_of` evidence on the file-25 [[GPIO]] API: `size_of::<Enabled>() == 0`, `size_of::<Input>() == 0`, `size_of::<PulledHigh>() == 0`, and (most importantly) `size_of::<GpioConfig<Enabled, Input, PulledHigh>>() == 0` — the fully parameterized three-axis typestate handle is **zero bytes wide**. Names [[ZeroSizedType|Zero Sized Types (ZSTs)]] as the mechanism: unit-struct state markers *"contain no actual data … act 'real' at compile time … however the optimizer will completely strip them away."* The worked transition `into_input_high_z(self) -> GpioConfig<Enabled, Input, HighZ>` compiles to **a single store of a constant register value** — *"renders to the same machine code as a direct register access."* Three resources zeroed: *"no more CPU, RAM, or code space tracking the state of `GpioConfig`."* Closes with the compositional property (*"as long as all components used are zero sized types, the whole structure will not exist at runtime"*) and the **macro escape hatch** for combinatorial state taxonomies — the forward-pointer to `embedded-hal`-style production HAL implementations.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — HAL GPIO](sources/rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-gpio.md) — File 36/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **fourth and final leaf-section** of the *HAL Design Patterns* sub-chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-index]]) and the **GPIO Interfaces** group of the [[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-checklist|HAL Checklist]]; **by far the most substantive** of the four leaves. Three named patterns — **`C-ZST-PIN`** (each pin is a dedicated [[ZeroSizedType|ZST]], returned from a `split()` method on the port — *"a zero-cost GPIO abstraction when all pin assignments are statically known"*, operationalizes [[ZeroSizedType]] / [[ZeroCostAbstraction]] from [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-zero-cost-abstractions]] for [[GPIO]] pins); **`C-ERASED-PIN`** (two-stage type erasure — `PA0::erase_pin(self) -> PA { pin: u8 }` collapses 16 distinct types into a 1-byte handle, then `PA::erase_port(self) -> Pin { port: Port, pin: u8 }` collapses 4 ports into a 2-byte handle; trades compile-time-pin-distinctness for heterogeneous-collection-ability — `[Pin; N]` / `Vec<Pin>` / `&dyn` — *"these fields can be packed to reduce the memory footprint"*); **`C-PIN-STATE`** (two-axis typestate — `Input<Floating|PullUp|PullDown>` and `Output<PushPull|OpenDrain>` parameterized via `PhantomData<S>`, with `into_input<N: InputState>(self, input: N) -> Pin<Input<N>>` / `into_output<N: OutputState>(self, output: N) -> Pin<Output<N>>` **consuming-`self` transitions** **plus** `with_input_state<N, R>(&mut self, input: N, f: impl FnOnce(&mut PA1<N>) -> R) -> R` / `with_output_state` **scoped-reconfiguration variants** for *"temporarily reconfigur[ing] a pin in a different state without moving it"*, all bounded by **sealed traits** `PinState: sealed::Sealed` / `OutputState: sealed::Sealed` / `InputState: sealed::Sealed` so users cannot add their own states — applies the [[TypeStateProgramming|typestate]] pattern from [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-design-contracts]] to pin configuration). The three patterns **stack**: a fully-static `PA1<Output<PushPull>>` is a zero-sized handle whose state is compile-time-verified; `.erase_pin()` produces `PA<Output<PushPull>>` (1 byte) **still in the same typestate**; `.erase_port()` reduces to `Pin<Output<PushPull>>` (≤2 bytes), again unchanged in typestate — *"both erased and non-erased pin types should provide the same API."* **GPIO dominates the HAL Checklist**: 3 of 8 items (37.5%) are GPIO-specific. Introduces [[ErasedPin]] and [[PinTypeState]] as new concepts.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — HAL Interoperability](sources/rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-interoperability.md) — File 34/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **second leaf-section** of the *HAL Design Patterns* sub-chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-index]]) and the **Interoperability** group of the [[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-checklist|HAL Checklist]]. Three short-form named patterns: **`C-FREE`** — wrapper types provide a `free(self)` destructor method that consumes the wrapper and returns the raw [[Peripheral|peripheral]] (and any other non-`Copy` objects it was constructed from; tuple return for multi-resource wrappers), shutting down / resetting the peripheral so a subsequent `new(peripheral)` round-trips cleanly — the **only legal reclaim path** out of the [[Singleton|singleton]] discipline from [[rust-embedded-book-peripherals-singletons]]; **`C-REEXPORT-PAC`** — [[HALCrate|HAL]] crates **reexport** their [[PeripheralAccessCrate|PAC]] at the crate root under the **fixed alias `pac`** (regardless of the underlying [[Svd2Rust|svd2rust]]-generated crate name), so the lower-level register-access escape hatch is reachable as `stm32f4xx_hal::pac::*` without adding a second dependency; **`C-HAL-TRAITS`** — HAL types implement **all applicable** [[EmbeddedHalCrate|`embedded-hal`]] traits (multiple traits per type allowed, e.g. a `Serial` implementing both `Read` and `Write`, or a [[TypeStateProgramming|typestate]]-parameterized GPIO pin implementing different trait sets in different states) — the authoring-side discipline that triggers the M·N → M+N complexity collapse argued in [[rust-embedded-book-portability-index]]. Sole 8-line code example: `pub struct Timer(TIMER0); impl Timer { pub fn new(periph: TIMER0) -> Self; pub fn free(self) -> TIMER0 }` — the by-value `self` on `free` makes the [[BorrowChecker|borrow checker]] guarantee no `Timer` reference outlives the reclaim. No new pages.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — HAL Checklist](sources/rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-checklist.md) — File 32/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the **top-level Checklist** of the *HAL Design Patterns* sub-chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-index]], file 31/44). Pure aggregator (~25 lines, no prose, no code): a single GitHub-flavored-Markdown checkbox list of **eight named patterns** across **four groups**, each labeled by a short-code with a hyperlink to the leaf file anchor — mirroring the [Rust API Guidelines Checklist](https://rust-lang.github.io/api-guidelines/checklist.html) convention. Groups: **Naming** *(crate aligns with Rust naming conventions)* — `C-CRATE-NAME`; **Interoperability** *(crate interacts nicely with other library functionality)* — `C-FREE` (wrapper types provide a destructor method), `C-REEXPORT-PAC` (HALs reexport their [[PeripheralAccessCrate|register access crate]]), `C-HAL-TRAITS` (types implement the [[EmbeddedHalCrate|`embedded-hal`]] traits — the M·N → M+N complexity-collapse mechanism from [[rust-embedded-book-portability-index]]); **Predictability** *(crate enables legible code that acts how it looks)* — `C-CTOR` (constructors are used instead of extension traits); **GPIO Interfaces** *(GPIO Interfaces follow a common pattern)* — `C-ZST-PIN` (pin types are zero-sized by default — operationalizes [[ZeroSizedType|ZSTs]] / [[ZeroCostAbstraction]] from [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-zero-cost-abstractions]] for [[GPIO]] pins), `C-ERASED-PIN` (pin types provide methods to erase pin and port — for runtime dispatch / heterogeneous collections), `C-PIN-STATE` (pin state should be encoded as type parameters — the [[TypeStateProgramming|typestate]] pattern from [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-design-contracts]] applied to pin configuration). **GPIO dominates**: 3 of 8 items (37.5%) are GPIO-specific. Short-codes are designed to be **cite-able in code review** (*"this violates C-ZST-PIN"*). No new vocabulary; the patterns themselves are defined in the leaf files. No new pages.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — HAL Naming](sources/rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-naming.md) — File 33/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **first leaf-section** of the *HAL Design Patterns* sub-chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-index]]) and the **Naming** group of the [[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-checklist|HAL Checklist]]. Single named pattern: **`C-CRATE-NAME`** — HAL crates should be named after the chip or family of chips they support; the name **must end with `-hal`** to distinguish from [[PeripheralAccessCrate|register access (PAC)]] crates; **dashes, not underscores** (e.g. `stm32f4xx-hal`). Cite-able in code review as *"this violates `C-CRATE-NAME`."* No new pages.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — HAL Predictability](sources/rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-predictability.md) — File 35/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **third leaf-section** of the *HAL Design Patterns* sub-chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-index]]) and the **Predictability** group of the [[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-checklist|HAL Checklist]] (Naming → Interoperability → **Predictability** → GPIO). Two short-form named patterns: **`C-CTOR`** — *"All [[Peripheral|peripherals]] to which the [[HALCrate|HAL]] adds functionality should be wrapped in a new type, even if no additional fields are required for that functionality. Extension traits implemented for the raw peripheral should be avoided."* — the wrapper-new-type-over-extension-trait discipline that is the **structural prerequisite** for [[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-interoperability|`C-FREE`]]'s consuming-`self` reclaim (extension traits cannot consume the raw [[Peripheral|peripheral]] by value; new-type wrappers can) **and** for the [[TypeStateProgramming|typestate]] parameterization from [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-design-contracts]] (type parameters attach to a wrapper, not to the raw peripheral); **`C-INLINE`** — *"All 'small' functions should be marked `#[inline]`. […] Functions that are very likely to take constant values as parameters should be marked as `#[inline]`. This enables the compiler to compute even complicated initialization logic at compile time, provided the function inputs are known."* — the explicit cross-crate inlining hint, motivated by the **default-off cross-crate inlining policy** of [[Rustc|rustc]] for non-generic functions and embedded's code-size sensitivity; this is the boundary-spanning mechanism that recovers the [[ZeroCostAbstraction|zero-cost-abstraction]] property from [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-zero-cost-abstractions]] across the HAL/application crate boundary (without `#[inline]`, a `set_high()` that compiles to a single store **in** the HAL crate degrades to a non-inlined function call **from** the application). Flags a minor inconsistency: `C-INLINE` is introduced here but is **not** listed in the file-32 [[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-checklist|HAL Checklist]] (which enumerates only `C-CTOR` under *Predictability*) — either deliberate curation (Rust-general hygiene rather than HAL-specific) or an omission. Cite-able in code review as *"this violates `C-CTOR`."* / *"this violates `C-INLINE`."* No new pages.

- [The Embedded Rust Book — Design Contracts](sources/rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-design-contracts.md) — File 25/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **third named sub-section** of the *Static Guarantees* chapter, immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-state-machines]]. **Closes the loop** opened in file 24: presents two API designs for the same imaginary [[GPIO]] register block under the explicit [[DesignByContract|Design by Contract]] framing. Design A is **runtime-checked** — every `set_direction` / `set_input_mode` / `set_output_status` / `get_input_status` method returns `Result<(), ()>` and begins with `if self.periph.read().enable().bit_is_clear() { return Err(()); }` guard chains (*"wast[ing] time and resources"*, *"much less pleasant for the developer to use"*). Design B is the same API recast as **[[TypeStateProgramming|typestate]]** — `GpioConfig<ENABLED, DIRECTION, MODE>` parameterized over eight zero-sized type markers (`Disabled` / `Enabled` / `Input` / `Output` / `HighZ` / `PulledLow` / `PulledHigh` / `DontCare`), consuming-`self` transition methods (`into_disabled`, `into_enabled_input`, `into_enabled_output`, `into_input_high_z`, `into_input_pull_down`, `into_input_pull_up`), and state-restricted `impl` blocks (`impl GpioConfig<Enabled, Output, DontCare> { fn set_bit }`; `impl<IN_MODE> GpioConfig<Enabled, Input, IN_MODE> { fn bit_is_set }`). **First fully worked multi-axis typestate example in the book** (vs. file 23's abstract `FooBuilder` → `Foo`). Worked example uses commented-out lines (*"Can't do this, pin isn't enabled! […] input pins don't have this interface! […] output pins don't have this interface!"*) to mark the four compile-error sites. Closes with the *Compile Time Functional Safety* statement: *"this incurs no runtime cost. It is impossible to set an output mode when you have a pin in an input mode. […] If they try to perform an illegal state transition, the code will not compile!"*
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Peripherals as State Machines](sources/rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-state-machines.md) — File 24/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — second named sub-section of the *Static Guarantees* chapter, immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-typestate-programming]]. **Grounds typestate in real hardware** by recasting a [[GPIO]] pin as a hierarchical [[FiniteStateMachine|finite state machine]]: seven leaf states (*Output: High / Low*, *Input: High Resistance / Pulled Low / Pulled High*) under three intermediate states (*Disabled*, *Configured as Output*, *Configured as Input*), with explicit walked-out transition paths (e.g. *Input: Pulled Low → Output: High* requires four steps, no diagonal jumps). Backs the state tree with an imaginary register-bit table (`enable`, `direction`, `input_mode` with `11` flagged **"Invalid state. Do not set"**, `output_mode`, `input_status`) — the valid-state set is **seven** leaf states, not the 32-combination Cartesian product. Then **sets up the negative example** the next sub-section will resolve: a naive `GpioConfig` struct wrapping an [[Svd2Rust|svd2rust]]-generated `GPIO_CONFIG` with independently-writable `set_enable` / `set_direction` / `set_input_mode` / `set_output_mode` / `get_input_status` methods — convenient but **not state-machine-safe**: nothing stops *"an output that is pulled low, or an input that is set high"*, and *"for some hardware [...] it could cause unexpected or undefined behavior."* *"Although this interface is convenient to write, it doesn't enforce the design contracts set out by our hardware implementation."* The bridge between abstract typestate ([[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-typestate-programming]]) and the concrete GPIO refactor the rest of the chapter will mechanize.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Typestate Programming](sources/rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-typestate-programming.md) — File 23/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the **first named sub-section** of the *Static Guarantees* chapter, immediately after the chapter opener at file 22 ([[rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-index]]). Defines [[TypeStateProgramming|typestate programming]] explicitly (linking [Wikipedia: typestate analysis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Typestate_analysis)) as "the encoding of information about the current state of an object into the type of that object." Names the [[BuilderPattern|builder pattern]] as the canonical Rust illustration — *"if you have used the Builder Pattern in Rust, you have already started using Typestate Programming!"* Walks one minimal worked example: a `FooBuilder` struct (un-configured state) whose `into_foo(self) -> Foo` method **consumes** the builder by value and returns a `Foo` struct (configured state); configuration methods like `.double_a()` likewise take `self` by value and return `Self`. Anchors the pattern on two specific Rust features — the **strong type system** (no implicit conversion between `FooBuilder` and `Foo`) and **move semantics by default** (`into_foo` consumes the builder, so it cannot be reused). Closes by framing the example as a **state machine**: two states encoded as types, one transition encoded as the `into_foo` method. The chapter that *names* what was operationally introduced for [[GPIO]] pin modes / clock configuration in [[rust-embedded-book-start-registers]].
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Static Guarantees](sources/rust-embedded-book-static-guarantees-index.md) — File 22/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **opens the Static Guarantees chapter** after the Peripherals chapter closed at file 21 ([[rust-embedded-book-peripherals-singletons]]). Very compact (~20 lines, no code) — generalizes the prior chapter's specific singleton/[[BorrowChecker]] result into the **framing concept** the wiki now records as [[StaticGuarantee]]: Rust's type system can check properties at compile time, reducing the need for runtime checks. Three concrete embedded examples preview the rest of the chapter: (1) data-race prevention via the standard `Send` / `Sync` marker traits, (2) **initialization ordering** — a serial interface can only be initialized after its pins are configured, (3) **configuration-dependent operations** — `set_low` on a floating-input [[GPIO]] pin is a **compile error**. Closes by re-summarizing the singleton/[[BorrowChecker]] resolution from [[rust-embedded-book-peripherals-singletons]] as the *access-control* instance of the same framing — peripherals as ownership-controlled values vs. global mutable state.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Singletons](sources/rust-embedded-book-peripherals-singletons.md) — File 21/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **closes the Peripherals chapter** (sub-sections: index → a-first-attempt → borrowck → **singletons**), immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-peripherals-borrowck]] (file 20/44) restated the "exactly one Rust value per physical [[Peripheral|peripheral]]" precondition the [[BorrowChecker|borrow checker]] needs. Resolves the precondition via the [[Singleton|singleton]] pattern: a runtime gate (`static mut PERIPHERALS = Some(...)` + `take_serial()` that `replace`s the inner with `None`) that hands out a peripheral handle **at most once** and panics on any subsequent call. Closes the [[rust-embedded-book-peripherals-a-first-attempt]] `SystemTimer::new()`-callable-twice gap. Three implementation tiers: (1) hand-rolled `Option<T>` + `replace`, (2) [[CortexMCrate|`cortex-m`]]'s `singleton!()` macro, (3) [[CortexMRTIC|`cortex-m-rtic`]]'s `#[rtic::app]` which hands `init` non-`Option` `cx.core` / `cx.device` handles. The **one-time `unsafe` bargain** — pay one `Option` + `replace` at startup, get whole-program [[BorrowChecker]] safety. Closes with the **"treat your hardware like data"** payoff: `&T` vs `&mut T` in function signatures (`fn read_button(gpio: &GpioPin)` vs `fn setup_spi_port(spi: &mut SpiPort)`) encode mutation intent, enforced **at compile time**.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — The Borrow Checker](sources/rust-embedded-book-peripherals-borrowck.md) — File 20/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the **Peripherals chapter's third sub-section**, immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-peripherals-a-first-attempt]] (which closed on the unresolved singleton gap). Pivot chapter: states the **three rules** for safe peripheral access — (1) every access through [[VolatileMemoryAccess|`volatile`]] methods, (2) read-only access may be **shared** by any number of holders, (3) read-write access requires the holder to have the **only** reference — and observes that rules (2) and (3) are **exactly** Rust's [[BorrowChecker|borrow checker]] discipline (`&T` shared, `&mut T` exclusive). If every [[Peripheral|peripheral]] is represented by **exactly one** Rust value, the [[BorrowChecker|borrow checker]] gives safe hardware sharing *for free*. Hardware is naturally unique (one [[SysTick]] per [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M]] core) but the code must **expose** that uniqueness — the singleton problem, deferred to the next sub-section (file 21/44).
- [The Embedded Rust Book — A first attempt in Rust](sources/rust-embedded-book-peripherals-a-first-attempt.md) — File 19/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the **Peripherals chapter's first code sub-section**, immediately after the chapter opener at file 18 ([[rust-embedded-book-peripherals-index]]). Walks the naive C-style translation of an MMIO register block in Rust (a [[ReprC|`#[repr(C)]`]] struct + integer-to-[[RawPointer|raw-pointer]] cast at `0xE000_E010` for [[SysTick]]: `SYST_CSR` / `SYST_RVR` / `SYST_CVR` / `SYST_CALIB`) and exposes its **four defects**: viral `unsafe`, no R/W discrimination, no aliasing control, **and it doesn't actually work** because the compiler will elide repeated stores absent [[VolatileMemoryAccess|volatile access]]. Patches each defect in turn — `core::ptr::read_volatile` / `write_volatile` for volatility; the [[VolatileRegisterCrate|`volatile_register`]] crate's `RW<T>` / `RO<T>` typed wrappers to encode read-only-ness in the type and lift the per-access `unsafe`; a "Rusty wrapper" struct (`SystemTimer` holding an `&'static mut RegisterBlock`) for a safe public API. Ends on the **singleton gap** — `SystemTimer::new()` is callable arbitrarily many times, so two threads can manufacture independent handles to the same physical registers; `&mut self` cannot stop this. Motivates the next sub-section on `Peripherals::take()` and the singleton pattern. Productionized version of this whole arc is what the [[CortexMCrate|`cortex-m`]] crate + [[PeripheralAccessCrate|PAC]] layer already provide.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Peripherals](sources/rust-embedded-book-peripherals-index.md) — File 18/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **opens the Peripherals chapter** after *Getting Started* closed at file 17 ([[rust-embedded-book-start-interrupts]]). Compact conceptual intro (three sub-sections, no code) defining [[Peripheral|peripherals]] as the silicon blocks on a [[Microcontroller|microcontroller]] for outside-world interaction (sensors / motors / displays / keyboards) and analogizing them to a desktop GPU offload. Explains why the embedded address space is **linear and real** ([[Microcontroller|MCUs]] lack an MMU — software uses physical addresses directly; writing `0x4000_0000` "may also be a completely valid action"); peripherals occupy the address-space gap between [[FlashMemory|Flash ROM]] near `0x0000_0000` and [[SRAM]] near `0x2000_0000` on [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M]]. Frames the [[MemoryMappedIO|memory-mapped peripheral]] model as the universal hardware-interface convention "no matter what language is used, whether that language is Assembly, C, or Rust" — a hardware API, not a software API (contrasted with Vulkan / Metal / OpenGL on GPUs). Worked example: [[SPI]] frequency register on the Nordic nRF52832 (`0x8000_0000` → 8 Mbps, `0x0200_0000` → 125 Kbps). Backstops the chapter's later sub-sections (singletons, ownership, RAII) with the underlying address-space mental model.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Introduction](sources/rust-embedded-book-intro-index.md) — Introduction chapter (file 1/44) of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook|The Embedded Rust Book]]*: scopes audience (Rust desktop developers *or* C/C++/Ada embedded developers), prerequisites ([[CrossCompilation|cross compilation]], [[MemoryMappedIO|memory-mapped peripherals]], [[Interrupt|interrupts]], [[I2C]] / [[SPI]] / serial), and conventions (all examples target [[ARMCortexM|ARM Cortex-M]] on the [[STM32F3DISCOVERY]] dev board from [[STMicroelectronics]]). Coordinated by the [[RustEmbeddedWorkingGroup]]'s resources team; dual MIT / Apache 2.0 (code) + CC-BY-SA 4.0 (prose) license. Opens the **Embedded Rust** corpus as a new domain in the wiki.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Hardware](sources/rust-embedded-book-intro-hardware.md) — Chapter 2 (file 2/44) of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]*: hardware tour of the [[STM32F3DISCOVERY]] dev board. Enumerates the application MCU ([[STM32F303VCT6]], a [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M4F]] at 72 MHz with 256 KiB [[FlashMemory|Flash]] / 48 KiB [[SRAM]] and integrated [[GPIO]] / [[I2C]] / [[SPI]] / [[USART]] / timers), the 9-axis [[IMU]] ([[LSM303DLHC]] accel+mag over [[I2C]] + [[L3GD20]] gyro over [[SPI]]), 8 user LEDs in a compass-rose, the on-board [[STM32F103]]-based [[STLink|ST-LINK]] debugger over the "USB ST-LINK" port (distinct from "USB USER" → application MCU), and the **3.3 V** absolute-maximum signaling contract.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Hardware (Getting Started)](sources/rust-embedded-book-start-hardware.md) — File 12/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the *Getting Started* chapter's **hardware sub-section** (distinct from the intro hardware tour at file 2/44, [[rust-embedded-book-intro-hardware]]). Adapts the [[QEMU]] walkthrough from [[rust-embedded-book-start-qemu]] to the real [[STM32F3DISCOVERY]] board: flip [[RustTarget|target triple]] to `thumbv7em-none-eabihf` ([[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M4F]] + FPU); rewrite `memory.x` with the [[STM32F303VCT6]]'s map (256 KiB [[FlashMemory|Flash]] @ `0x0800_0000` + 40 KiB [[SRAM]] @ `0x2000_0000`); remove the `debug::exit()` QEMU-only call from `hello.rs`; configure [[OpenOCD]] via an `openocd.cfg` pairing an interface cfg ([[STLink|ST-LINK]] variant per board revision) with a target cfg (`target/stm32f3x.cfg`); flash via [[GDB]]'s `load` command over [[OpenOCD]] on TCP 3333; enable semihosting with `monitor arm semihosting enable`; automate the whole sequence via the template's `openocd.gdb` script + a Cargo runner (`gdb -x openocd.gdb`) so `cargo run` drives a real-hardware debug session. Introduces [[OpenOCDConfig]] and [[GDBLoad]] as new concepts.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Interoperability](sources/rust-embedded-book-interoperability-index.md) — File 38/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **opens the *Interoperability* chapter** (Part 6's second chapter), the natural successor to file 37 ([[rust-embedded-book-c-tips-index]]) which forward-referenced *"A little C with your Rust / A little Rust with your C"*. Short three-section framing page: (1) the **`std::ffi` family** — C primitive type aliases (`c_uint` ≡ `unsigned int`, `c_void` ≡ `void`, etc.) + string conversions (`CString` for `String` → `char *`; `CStr` for `&str` → `const char *`), mirrored in `core::ffi` ([[NoStd|`no_std`]]) and `alloc::ffi` (alloc-required) since Rust 1.30, with [`cty`] / [`cstr_core`] as community crate equivalents for older toolchains; (2) **Build-system interop** — combining [[Cargo]] with Make / CMake is open work (tracked in [rust-embedded/book#61](https://github.com/rust-embedded/book/issues/61)); (3) **RTOS interop** — calling FreeRTOS / ChibiOS from Rust is *"still a work in progress"*, with only the [Zephyr Project](https://docs.zephyrproject.org/latest/develop/languages/rust/index.html) named as publicly-supported (tracked in [#62](https://github.com/rust-embedded/book/issues/62)). Reuses [[ReprC]] / [[RawPointer]] / [[Cargo]] / [[Rustc]] / [[NoStd]] / [[RustCoreLibrary]] / [[RustStandardLibrary]] from prior files; **no new pages** — pure pointer-and-promise framing.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — A little Rust with your C](sources/rust-embedded-book-interoperability-rust-with-c.md) — File 40/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **second leaf** of the *Interoperability* chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-interoperability-index]]) and the **deliberate mirror** of file 39 ([[rust-embedded-book-interoperability-c-with-rust]]). Operationalizes exposing **Rust to C/C++** as two halves: (1) **build a C-friendly Rust API** — declare the crate's output as a systems library via `[lib] crate-type = ["cdylib"]` (dynamic — emits `lib<name>.so` / `<name>.dll` / `lib<name>.dylib`) or `["staticlib"]` (static — emits `lib<name>.a` / `<name>.lib`) ([[CrateType]]); mark each exported function with [[NoMangle|`#[no_mangle]`]] (so the linker sees the literal source identifier instead of `_ZN8my_crate13rust_function17h...E`) and [[ExternC|`pub extern "C" fn`]] (so the calling convention matches the platform C ABI); references can't cross, so [[RawPointer|raw pointers]] stand in. The canonical exported shape is `#[no_mangle] pub extern "C" fn rust_function() {}`. (2) **Embed the produced library in an external build system** — *"This very much depends on your project and/or build system"*; Cargo emits the `.so` / `.dll` / `.a` artifact, the host project's `make` / `CMake` / IDE links it like any other system library; the C side needs a matching header — hand-written (`void rust_function();`) or auto-generated by [[Cbindgen|`cbindgen`]] (`github.com/eqrion/cbindgen`), the **inverse direction** of file 39's [[Bindgen|`bindgen`]]. **Same C-ABI-as-lingua-franca rule** as file 39: *"Because C++ has no stable ABI for the Rust compiler to target, we use `C` for any interoperability between different languages."* Introduces **3 new pages** — 2 concepts ([[NoMangle]], [[CrateType]]) and 1 entity ([[Cbindgen]]); [[ExternC]] updated **in-place** to cover the **exported** function-definition form (form 2) complementing the **imported** declaration-block form (form 1); [[Bindgen]] updated **in-place** to point at its symmetric counterpart.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — A little C with your Rust](sources/rust-embedded-book-interoperability-c-with-rust.md) — File 39/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **first leaf** of the *Interoperability* chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-interoperability-index]]). Operationalizes calling **C/C++ from Rust** as two orthogonal tasks: (1) **define the Rust-side interface** — for every C `typedef struct CoolStruct { int x; int y; }` + `void cool_function(int i, char c, CoolStruct* cs);`, emit `#[repr(C)] pub struct CoolStruct { pub x: cty::c_int, pub y: cty::c_int }` ([[ReprC]]) plus an `extern "C" { pub fn cool_function(i: cty::c_int, c: cty::c_char, cs: *mut CoolStruct); }` block ([[ExternC]]), with [[RawPointer|raw pointers]] (`*mut T` / `*const T`) standing in for Rust references (which C cannot represent) and `cty::c_int` / `cty::c_char` aliases standing in for platform-variable C primitives; auto-generate the whole interface from C headers via [[Bindgen|`bindgen`]] using `--ctypes-prefix=cty` + `--use-core` for [[NoStd|`no_std`]] compatibility. (2) **Build the C/C++ to a static archive** — three branches: already-prebuilt `lib*.a` (just link); complex `make`/`CMake` project (shell out via `std::process::Command` from [[BuildRs|`build.rs`]] and copy the archive into `target/`); small C source set (compile directly with the [[CcCrate|`cc` crate]] — `fn main() { cc::Build::new().file("src/foo.c").compile("foo"); }`). Two design rules: **C++ has no stable ABI for [[Rustc|rustc]]** → use the `C` ABI as the lingua franca even when wrapping C++ (typically via a thin C wrapper layer); **the package may be `thumbv7m-none-eabi` / [[NoStd|`no_std`]] but `build.rs` itself runs on the *host*** — *"This means you may use any Rust crates which will run on your compilation host."* Static archive (`cool-library.a`) is the embedded delivery format because [[BareMetalProgramming|bare-metal]] firmware has no dynamic loader. Introduces **4 new pages** — 2 concepts ([[BuildRs]] (Cargo's host-side pre-build hook) and [[ExternC]] (the calling-convention companion to [[ReprC]])) and 2 entities ([[Bindgen]] (auto-binding generator over C headers) and [[CcCrate]] (idiomatic-Rust host C compiler wrapper for `build.rs`)); [[ReprC]] and [[RawPointer]] are updated **in-place** to add the FFI-companion connections rather than duplicated.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — `no_std`](sources/rust-embedded-book-intro-no-std.md) — Chapter 3 (file 3/44) of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the conceptual hinge of the intro. Partitions embedded into [[HostedEnvironment|hosted]] (POSIX-class; [[RustStandardLibrary|`libstd`]] available) vs [[BareMetalProgramming|bare-metal]] (no OS, no pre-loaded code) regimes, then introduces [[NoStd|`#![no_std]`]] as the crate-level switch that links [[RustCoreLibrary|`libcore`]] instead of [[RustStandardLibrary|`libstd`]] — losing the [[HeapAllocation|heap]] / stack-overflow protection / pre-`main` [[RustRuntime|runtime]] / `Vec` / `HashMap`, but gaining the ability to write [[Bootloader|bootloaders]], firmware, and kernels. Lays out the opt-in heap recipe (`alloc` crate + global allocator, e.g. `alloc-cortex-m`).
- [The Embedded Rust Book — QEMU](sources/rust-embedded-book-start-qemu.md) — File 11/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the **first real code chapter** of *Getting Started* (after [[rust-embedded-book-start-index|the chapter opener at file 10]]). End-to-end walkthrough on the [[LM3S6965|LM3S6965]] [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M3]] emulated by [[QEMU]]: scaffold from the [[CortexMQuickstartTemplate|`cortex-m-quickstart`]] template (via [[CargoGenerate|`cargo-generate`]] / `git` / zip), write the canonical [[NoStd|`no_std`]] + `no_main` skeleton ([[PanicHaltCrate|`panic-halt`]] + [[CortexMRTCrate|`cortex-m-rt`]]'s `#[entry]` on a divergent `fn main() -> !`), pin the memory map in a `memory.x` [[LinkerScript|linker script]], [[CrossCompilation|cross-compile]] to `thumbv7m-none-eabi`, inspect with [[CargoBinutils|`cargo readobj` / `cargo size` / `cargo objdump`]] (exposes the [[VectorTable|`.vector_table`]] @ `0x0`, `.text` @ `0x400`), run on `qemu-system-arm -machine lm3s6965evb` via a Cargo `runner`, and [[GDB|remote-debug]] over `-gdb tcp::3333`. Modern `hello` uses [[Defmt|`defmt`]] over [[ARMSemihosting|semihosting]] decoded by [[QemuRun|`qemu-run`]] ([[Knurling]] / [[FerrousSystems]]); classic uses [[CortexMSemihostingCrate|`cortex-m-semihosting`]]'s `hprintln!`. Materializes every abstract construct from chapters 3–4 into one shell session.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Semihosting](sources/rust-embedded-book-start-semihosting.md) — File 14/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — the *Getting Started* chapter's **Semihosting** sub-section, immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-start-registers|Memory-mapped Registers]]. Compact operational chapter consolidating the `hprintln!` / `debug::exit` / `monitor arm semihosting enable` fragments scattered across [[rust-embedded-book-start-qemu]] and [[rust-embedded-book-start-hardware]] into one canonical write-up. Re-emphasizes the **"no extra wires, but super slow"** tradeoff (each write op = several ms over [[STLink|ST-Link]]); re-issues the **never-`debug::exit`-on-hardware** warning ("can corrupt your OpenOCD session"); shows [[QEMU]]'s native `-semihosting-config` support; closes with [[PanicSemihostingCrate|`panic-semihosting`]]'s `"exit"` feature as the recipe for `no_std` run-pass tests on QEMU — `assert_eq!` failure → host stderr log → `exit(EXIT_FAILURE)` → `$? = 1`. Introduces [[PanicSemihostingCrate]] as a new entity.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Tips for embedded C developers](sources/rust-embedded-book-c-tips-index.md) — File 37/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **opens Part 6, the *Tips for embedded C developers* chapter**, immediately after the *Design Patterns* chapter closed at file 36 ([[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-hal-gpio]]). Audience-flip chapter: prior chapters assumed Rust fluency or generic embedded background; this one assumes **embedded C fluency** and walks through the C→Rust idiom translation table the book deferred until now. Six sections — *Preprocessor* (no preprocessor in Rust → [[CargoFeatures|Cargo features]] + `#[cfg(...)]` for `#ifdef`, `const fn` for compile-time sizes, the [[RustMacro|macro system]] for function-style `#define`); *Build System* ([[Cargo]] + `build.rs` for custom build steps such as **linker-script generation**; **no post-build hooks**; [[CrossCompilation|cross-compiling]] as one `--target` flag; [[Xargo]] / `-Z build-std=core` for non-Tier-1 targets); *Iterators vs Array Access* (*"indexed access is an anti-pattern"* — bounds-checked, optimization-hostile; `arr.iter()` is the idiom); *References vs Pointers* (`&T` / `&mut T` governed by the [[BorrowChecker|borrow checker]]; *"where in C the default is mutable and you must be explicit about `const`, in Rust the opposite is true"*; [[RawPointer|raw pointers]] reserved for DMA / [[MemoryMappedIO|MMIO]]); *Volatile Access* (*"the access is the volatile primitive, not the type"* — `core::ptr::read_volatile` / `write_volatile`; forward-references [[Atomic]] and the [[rust-embedded-book-concurrency-index|Concurrency chapter]] for higher-level primitives — see [[VolatileMemoryAccess]]); *Packed and Aligned Types* (default repr makes **no layout guarantees**; **`#[repr(C)]`** for FFI/hardware ([[ReprC]]); **`#[repr(packed)]`** for protocol headers (alignment = 1; addresses via `addr_of!`); **`#[repr(align(n))]`** for explicit over-alignment; `repr(C)` + `repr(align(n))` is legal but `repr(packed)` + `repr(align(n))` is **not**). Pure cross-walk chapter; introduces **2 new concepts** — [[CargoFeatures]] and [[RustMacro]] — the language-level mechanisms prior files referenced obliquely but never made standalone.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Tooling](sources/rust-embedded-book-intro-tooling.md) — Chapter 4 (file 4/44) of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]*: the toolchain inventory. Build side — [[RustLanguage|Rust]] 1.31+ with [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M]] target ([[Cargo]] / [[Rustc]] / [[Rustup]]), [[CargoBinutils|`cargo-binutils`]] for LLVM `objdump`/`nm`/`size`, [[QEMU|`qemu-system-arm`]] for host emulation, [[CargoGenerate|`cargo-generate`]] for the project template. Debug side — three-layer [[OnChipDebugging|on-chip-debugging]] stack: probe-server ([[OpenOCD]] / [[ProbeRs|Probe-rs]]) ↔ debugger ([[GDB]] / [[ProbeRsVSCodeExtension|Probe-rs VS Code ext]] / [[TRACE32]]) ↔ hardware probe ([[STLink|ST-Link]] / [[JLink|J-Link]] / [[MCULink|MCU-Link]] / [[RustyProbe|Rusty-probe]]) over [[JTAG]] / [[SWD]]. Anchors the operational stack every later chapter assumes.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Unsorted topics](sources/rust-embedded-book-unsorted-index.md) — File 41/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **opens the *Unsorted topics* chapter** immediately after the *Interoperability* chapter closed at file 40 ([[rust-embedded-book-interoperability-rust-with-c]]). **Trivial placeholder**: two lines on disk — the heading `# Unsorted topics` and a blank line. No prose, no code, no claims — even shorter than the [[rust-embedded-book-design-patterns-index|Design Patterns]] opener (file 30/44, which at least had a one-sentence scope statement). Chapter title is the only editorial signal — a catch-all bin for content that didn't slot cleanly into any of the preceding ten chapters. **Zero new pages**.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Optimizations: the speed size tradeoff](sources/rust-embedded-book-unsorted-speed-vs-size.md) — File 42/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **first substantive leaf** of the *Unsorted topics* chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-unsorted-index]]). Tactical [[Cargo]]/[[Rustc|`rustc`]] reference on the **five [[OptLevel|`opt-level`]] values** across three regimes — `0` (no optimization, `dev` default, debugger-friendly but Flash-overflowing), `1`/`2`/`3` (speed; `release` default is `3`; `2` and `3` unconditionally unroll loops, `3` adds vectorization + more inlining), `"s"`/`"z"` (size; inherited from clang/LLVM, `"z"` is smaller). The chapter's signature trick is the **`profile-overrides` Cargo feature** that decouples top-crate optimization from dependencies — `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = "z"` keeps the application at `opt-level = 0` debug-friendly while shrinking all deps (worked example: `.text` 9060 → 3490 bytes, **6 KiB Flash saved**; granular form `[profile.dev.package.cortex-m-rt] opt-level = 0` opts a single dep back out). Also recommends **`[profile.release] debug = true`** because *"debuginfo is zero cost in the sense that it won't occupy space in Flash / ROM"* on [[BareMetalProgramming|bare-metal]]. Closes with the **inline-threshold table** (`3`→275, `2`→225, `"s"`→75, `"z"`→25 as of `rustc` 1.29.0) and the recommended workaround for the [[ZeroCostAbstraction|zero-cost-abstraction]] hit at `"s"`/`"z"` — `rustflags = ["-C", "inline-threshold=225"]` in `.cargo/config.toml`. Caveat: **generic code is monomorphized in the *instantiating* crate**, so `profile-overrides` on the *defining* dependency may have no effect. Introduces **1 new concept** — [[OptLevel]] — the dial itself with the regime table, Flash-budget tradeoff, `profile-overrides` recipe, and generic-instantiation caveat. [[FlashMemory]] updated **in-place** to point at [[OptLevel]] as the canonical source of the `opt-level = "z"` recommendation it already cited.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Performing Math Functionality](sources/rust-embedded-book-unsorted-math.md) — File 43/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **second substantive leaf** of the *Unsorted topics* chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-unsorted-index]]), immediately after [[rust-embedded-book-unsorted-speed-vs-size]] (file 42). Short single-recipe chapter: with [[RustStandardLibrary|`std`]] the math methods `f32::sqrt` / `f32::sin` / `f32::exp` / `f32::floor` come for free as inherent methods, but under [[NoStd|`#![no_std]`]] **these methods are not available** — [[RustCoreLibrary|`core`]] exposes `f32` / `f64` but not their transcendental / rounding operations (the canonical implementations live in C's `libm`, which `core` cannot depend on). The drop-in fix is the **[[LibmCrate|`libm`]] crate** — a pure-Rust port of C's `libm` exposing the same operations as **free functions** (`libm::sqrtf(x)` replaces `x.sqrt()`) callable from any `no_std` crate without a global allocator. Worked example rewrites the same four-operation program twice — once for hosted [[RustStandardLibrary|`std`]] with `println!`, once for [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M]] `no_std` ([[CortexMRTCrate|`cortex-m-rt`]] + [[CortexMSemihostingCrate|`cortex-m-semihosting`]] + [[PanicHaltCrate|`panic-halt`]] + [[ARMSemihosting|`hprintln!`]]) — the only syntactic delta is **method-call vs free-function**. Precision suffix follows C: `sqrtf` / `floorf` are `f32`, `sin` / `exp` are `f64` (the example calls `.into()` to widen). Closes with a five-crate **further-reading list** for when scalar `libm` is not enough — `cmsis-dsp-sys` (CMSIS DSP bindings, SIMD-accelerated on [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M4F]]+), `constgebra` (`const fn` linalg), `micromath` (compact `no_std` math), `microfft` (in-place FFT), `nalgebra` (general-purpose linalg with optional `no_std`). Introduces **1 new entity** — [[LibmCrate]] (the chapter's protagonist). No new concepts.
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Verify Installation](sources/rust-embedded-book-intro-verify.md) — File 9/44 of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — closes the intro chapter with an end-to-end smoke test. Procedure: Mini-USB into the "USB ST-LINK" connector on the [[STM32F3DISCOVERY]], then run `openocd -f interface/stlink.cfg -f target/stm32f3x.cfg`. Pass signal is the line `stm32f3x.cpu: hardware has 6 breakpoints, 4 watchpoints` — proves [[OpenOCD]] enumerated the [[STLink|ST-LINK]] probe over `hla_swd` and read [[STM32F303VCT6]] debug registers. Fallback cfgs (`stlink-v2.cfg`, `stlink-v2-1.cfg`) for old hardware revisions; `sudo` working but normal-user failing → fix [[UdevRules|udev rules]] from [[rust-embedded-book-intro-install-linux]].
- [The Embedded Rust Book — Appendix A: Glossary](sources/rust-embedded-book-appendix-glossary.md) — File **44/44** of *[[TheEmbeddedRustBook]]* — **closing file of the corpus**. Appendix A defines the vendor-acronym alphabet the preceding 43 chapters use freely: **[[BSP]]** (Board Support Crate, depends on a [[HALCrate|HAL]]), **[[FPU]]** (Floating-Point Unit, the `hf` suffix on `thumbv7em-none-eabihf`), **[[HALCrate|HAL]]** (Hardware Abstraction Layer, sits on top of a [[PeripheralAccessCrate|PAC]], may impl [[EmbeddedHalCrate|`embedded-hal`]] traits), **[[I2C]]** (Inter-IC, multi-drop addressed), **[[PeripheralAccessCrate|PAC]]** (Peripheral Access Crate, generated from an [[SVDFile|SVD]] via [[Svd2Rust|`svd2rust`]]), **[[SPI]]** (Serial Peripheral Interface), **[[SVDFile|SVD]]** (System View Description XML), **[[UART]]** (Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter), and **[[USART]]** (Universal Synchronous/Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter, UART superset). Each entry is two-to-four sentences plus pointers — pure cross-walk, no code, no claims beyond definitions. Introduces **3 new concepts** — [[BSP]] (the acronym-disambiguator that redirects to [[BoardCrate]]), [[FPU]] (with the M0/M3-vs-M4F target-triple table + soft-float fallback note), and [[UART]] (with the explicit UART-vs-USART comparison table) — every other glossary term already had a wiki page from prior chapters. **Closes the Embedded Rust corpus at 44/44 chapters.**

<!-- Added 2026-05-23: HuggingFace LLM Course (huggingface.co/learn/llm-course) — Chs 1–12 full ingest. 12 parallel opus subagents, one per chapter, on the live HTML rendered via WebFetch. Source pages live at `wiki/sources/hf-llm-course-ch01-*.md` through `wiki/sources/hf-llm-course-ch12-*.md`; raw concatenated markdown lives at `raw/hf-llm-course/ch01-*.md` through `raw/hf-llm-course/ch12-*.md`. Skipped: in-page quizzes/exams (no answers exposed). The modern LLM-centric re-framing of the original HF NLP course; new chapters cover production inference deployment (Ch 2 §8 — [[TGI]] / [[vLLM]] / [[LlamaCpp]] / [[FlashAttention]] / [[PagedAttention]]), SFT+LoRA (Ch 11 — [[TRL]] / [[PEFT]] / [[lighteval]]), and reasoning-RL (Ch 12 — [[GRPO]] / [[DeepSeekR1]] / [[Unsloth]]). -->
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 1: Transformer models](sources/hf-llm-course-ch01-transformer-models.md) — Introduces [[NLP]] and [[LanguageModel]]s, surveys the [[Transformer]] architecture and its three variants ([[BERT]]-like encoder-only / [[GPT]]-like decoder-only / [[T5]]-like encoder-decoder), teaches the `pipeline()` API across sentiment / zero-shot classification / generation / mask filling / [[NER]] / QA / summarization / translation / image classification / ASR, and closes with LLM inference internals ([[KVCache]], prefill vs decode, sampling — [[Temperature]] / [[Topp]] / [[Topk]] / [[BeamSearch]] / [[NucleusSampling]]) plus [[Bias]] / [[Hallucination]] limitations.
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 2: Using 🤗 Transformers](sources/hf-llm-course-ch02-using-transformers.md) — Unpacks `pipeline()` into tokenizer → model → postprocess, the `Auto*` factory family ([[AutoTokenizer]] / [[AutoModel]] / [[AutoModelForSequenceClassification]]), subword tokenization ([[BPE]] / [[WordPiece]] / [[SentencePiece]] / [[Unigram]]), batching mechanics ([[Padding]] / [[Truncation]] / [[AttentionMask]]), and a production-deployment §8 contrasting three serving stacks ([[TGI]] / [[vLLM]] / [[LlamaCpp]]) on memory architecture ([[FlashAttention]] 2 / [[PagedAttention]] / [[Quantization]] / [[GGUF]] / [[ContinuousBatching]] / [[KVCache]] paging).
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 3: Fine-tuning a pretrained model](sources/hf-llm-course-ch03-fine-tuning.md) — End-to-end [[FineTuning]] of `bert-base-uncased` on the [[MRPC]] paraphrase task from [[GLUE]]: dataset loading + `Dataset.map()` preprocessing, dynamic padding via [[DataCollatorWithPadding]], the [[Trainer]] / [[TrainingArguments]] / `compute_metrics` API, the manual [[PyTorch]] equivalent ([[AdamW]] + linear [[LearningRateScheduler]] + eval loop with the [[Evaluate]] library), 🤗 [[Accelerate]] for distributed training, and [[LearningCurves]] interpretation to diagnose [[Overfitting]] / [[Underfitting]] / erratic training.
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 4: Sharing models and tokenizers](sources/hf-llm-course-ch04-sharing-models.md) — Treats the [[HuggingFaceHub]] as the canonical model exchange: loading checkpoints via `pipeline()` / `Auto*` / `TFAuto*` classes; three publish paths — high-level `push_to_hub` (Trainer / Keras `PushToHubCallback` / model + tokenizer objects), the [[HuggingFaceHubLibrary]] (`create_repo` / `upload_file` / `Repository`), and raw [[Git]] + [[GitLFS]] — and a deep treatment of [[ModelCard]]s (README.md + YAML metadata: language / license / datasets / tags / metrics) grounded in Mitchell et al. "Model Cards for Model Reporting." Marks the end of Part 1 of the course.
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 5: The 🤗 Datasets library](sources/hf-llm-course-ch05-datasets-library.md) — Deep dive into 🤗 [[Datasets]] beyond the basic Hub-load flow: loading from local/remote CSV/TSV/JSON/JSONL/text/pandas via `load_dataset()`, `Dataset.map()` / `filter()` / `shuffle()` / `select()` / `sort()` / `unique()` / `rename_column()` slicing, format switching to/from Pandas, big-data handling via [[MemoryMapping]] backed by [[ApacheArrow]], [[DatasetStreaming]] (`streaming=True` → [[IterableDataset]]) for corpora bigger than disk, building a brand-new dataset from the GitHub REST API + `push_to_hub()`, and a [[SemanticSearch]] worked example using `sentence-transformers/multi-qa-mpnet-base-dot-v1` + [[FAISS]] via `Dataset.add_faiss_index()` / `Dataset.get_nearest_examples()`.
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 6: The 🤗 Tokenizers library](sources/hf-llm-course-ch06-tokenizers-library.md) — Deep dive into the [[Tokenization]] pipeline as implemented by the Rust 🤗 [[Tokenizers]] library (the "fast" tokenizers backing 🤗 Transformers): `AutoTokenizer.train_new_from_iterator()` for retraining on a new corpus, fast-tokenizer special powers ([[OffsetMapping]] / `word_ids()` for reproducing `token-classification` and `question-answering` pipelines by hand with overflow/stride), pedagogical implementations of the three dominant subword algorithms ([[BPE]] / [[WordPiece]] (BERT) / [[Unigram]] with [[SentencePiece]] (T5/XLNet/ALBERT)), and assembling a tokenizer block-by-block from `normalizers` ([[UnicodeNormalization]] — NFC/NFKC/NFD/NFKD) + `pre_tokenizers` + `models` + `trainers` + `post_processors` + `decoders`, wrapped in `PreTrainedTokenizerFast`.
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 7: Classical NLP tasks](sources/hf-llm-course-ch07-classical-nlp-tasks.md) — The "everything comes together" chapter: six end-to-end task recipes — **[[TokenClassification|token classification (NER)]]**, **[[MaskedLanguageModel|masked language modeling]]**, **translation**, **summarization**, **training a [[CausalLanguageModel|causal LM]] from scratch**, and **extractive [[QuestionAnswering|question answering]]** — each with both a `Trainer`/`Seq2SeqTrainer` path and a manual [[Accelerate]] training loop, plus a model pushed to [[HuggingFaceHub]] with an inference widget. Introduces task-specific data collators ([[DataCollatorForTokenClassification]] / [[DataCollatorForLanguageModeling]] / [[DataCollatorForSeq2Seq]]) handling `-100` label padding, random masking, and seq2seq label shifting; right-metric-per-task ([[seqeval]] for NER, [[Perplexity]] for MLM, [[SacreBLEU]] for translation, [[ROUGE]] for summarization, exact-match + F1 for QA); and canonical processing tricks (subword [[LabelAlignment]] via `word_ids()`, concat-then-chunk for MLM, `text_target` for seq2seq, sliding-window with `return_overflowing_tokens` for long-context QA, span-extraction post-processing). Datasets: [[CoNLL2003]], [[KDE4]], [[XSum]] / CNN-DailyMail, [[SQuAD]], [[CodeParrot]] / [[CodeSearchNet]].
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 8: How to ask for help](sources/hf-llm-course-ch08-asking-for-help.md) — The meta chapter: read tracebacks bottom-up; debug a broken Hub repo (typo in model id, missing `config.json` recovered via `AutoConfig.from_pretrained(base).push_to_hub(target)`); write a forum topic that actually gets answered (descriptive title, fenced code blocks, full traceback, runnable reproducer); bisect `trainer.train()` failures through the seven-stage [[DebuggingPipeline]] (data → dataloader → collator → forward → backward → optimizer → eval) with the canonical MNLI / `num_labels=3` walkthrough; CUDA errors are reported asynchronously, so always reproduce on CPU; the overfit-one-batch test is the universal sanity check; file a quality GitHub issue with a [[MinimalReproducibleExample]] and `transformers-cli env`.
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 9: Building and sharing demos with Gradio](sources/hf-llm-course-ch09-gradio-demos.md) — Teaches interactive web demos with [[Gradio]]: the high-level `gr.Interface(fn, inputs, outputs)` API, component palette (Textbox / Audio / Image / Label / Sketchpad / Slider / Dropdown / Radio / Button / Chatbot / Markdown), shareable links (`launch(share=True)`) → permanent hosting on [[HuggingFaceSpaces]] via `app.py`, one-line loading of Hub models via `Interface.load("huggingface/...")` (backed by the [[HuggingFaceInferenceAPI]]), advanced features (session state for chatbots, interpretation via default/[[SHAP]]), and the low-level [[GradioBlocks]] API for custom layouts (rows / columns / tabs), multi-step pipelines, and event-driven UIs.
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 10: Curate high-quality datasets with Argilla](sources/hf-llm-course-ch10-curating-datasets-argilla.md) — Hands-on introduction to [[Argilla]] (open-source data annotation platform, stewarded by Hugging Face) and the thesis that **quality of training data — not just quantity — is the lever that determines model quality**. Walks the end-to-end workflow on `SetFit/ag_news`: deploy an Argilla instance on [[HuggingFaceSpaces]], connect via the Python SDK, declare an annotation schema with `rg.Settings` (fields + questions + vectors + metadata), upload records with field mappings for [[PreAnnotation]], configure minimum-response thresholds to enable [[InterAnnotatorAgreement]], write [[AnnotationGuidelines]], and export the annotated dataset back to the Hub (filtered records or fully round-trippable Argilla dataset). Modern Argilla 2.x API; the legacy `FeedbackDataset` abstraction is now generalized by `rg.Settings`.
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 11: Fine-tune LLMs with SFT and LoRA](sources/hf-llm-course-ch11-sft-and-lora.md) — Practical guide to instruction-tuning open LLMs end-to-end: structuring conversations with [[ChatTemplate]]s (`apply_chat_template`, [[ChatML]] / Llama-3 / Mistral / Qwen formats), [[SupervisedFineTuning|Supervised Fine-Tuning]] with the [[TRL]] `SFTTrainer` (packing, `formatting_func`, [[SFTConfig]]), memory-efficient [[lora|LoRA]] via the [[PEFT]] library (`LoraConfig`: rank / alpha / target_modules; `PeftModel`; `merge_and_unload` for zero-latency inference; [[QLoRA]] for 4-bit base via [[bitsandbytes]]), and evaluation against [[MMLU]] / [[BBH]] / [[GSM8K]] / [[MATH]] / [[HumanEval]] / [[AlpacaEval]] / [[ChatbotArena]] plus the [[lighteval]] harness, with [[LLMAsJudge]] and domain-specific custom evals positioned as the production-quality rubric beyond benchmarks. Argues SFT is the lever that converts a base next-token model into an assistant-like instruct model — but only when prompting an existing instruct model is genuinely insufficient. Target model in the walkthrough: [[DeepSeekR1DistillQwen1.5B]]; dataset: smoltalk; base: [[SmolLM2]].
- [HuggingFace LLM Course — Ch 12: Build Reasoning Models like DeepSeek R1](sources/hf-llm-course-ch12-reasoning-models.md) — *"Open R1 for Students"* — teaches reasoning-via-RL centered on the [[DeepSeekR1]] paper and the [[GRPO|Group Relative Policy Optimization]] algorithm. Progresses from RL fundamentals (agent / environment / action / reward / policy) and [[rlhf|RLHF]], through a detailed walkthrough of the DeepSeek R1 training pipeline (Cold Start → Reasoning RL → [[RejectionSampling]] → Diverse RL) and the emergent **[[AhaMoment|"Aha Moment"]]** phenomenon observed in [[DeepSeekR1Zero|R1-Zero]] (the model spontaneously discovers chain-of-thought-like rethinking), then a mathematical deep-dive (§3b by Shirin Yamani) on GRPO's three-step objective (group sampling → [[GroupRelativeAdvantage|advantage standardization]] → [[ClippedSurrogateObjective|clipped policy update]] + [[KLPenalty|KL penalty]]) as the [[PPO]]-without-critic variant, and finally two practical exercises fine-tuning [[SmolLM2]]-135M and [[Gemma3]]-1B with [[GRPO]] via the [[TRL]] `GRPOTrainer` — the second using [[Unsloth]] + [[vLLM]] on [[GSM8K]] with XML-formatted chain-of-thought + [[VerifiableReward|verifiable rewards]] (format + correctness regex). Also names [[OpenR1]] (HF community project) and [[DeepSeekMath]] (the GRPO origin paper).
- [Pipelines & Prompt Optimization with DSPy](sources/dbreunig-pipelines-prompt-optimization-dspy.md) — **[[DrewBreunig|Drew Breunig]] (dbreunig.com, 2024-12-12).** The **first wiki-corpus third-party [[DSPy]] tutorial** (prior DSPy sources are Stanford's *Learn* docs and academic papers) and the **first DSPy receipt in the wiki to run an end-to-end [[MIPROv2|`dspy.MIPROv2`]] optimization loop entirely against local [[Ollama]]-hosted models** — no managed-API calls. Walks a single-stage Wikipedia-historic-event classifier built from a `typing.Literal[...]` class-based [[DSPySignatures|Signature]] + [[DSPyPredict|`dspy.Predict`]] over [[Llama|Llama 3.2 1b]] (task LM via `ollama_chat/llama3.2:1b`) and lifts it from **51.9% → 63.0%** with `auto="light"` in **0-shot mode** (`max_labeled_demos=0, max_bootstrapped_demos=0` — the [[dspy-optimizers|Optimizers page's]] instruction-only carve-out exercised in the wild). Adds a **two-model variant** — `prompt_model=Llama 3.3, task_model=Llama 3.2 1b` — that scores slightly lower numerically (62%) but produces qualitatively better, less overfit instructions; surfaces the `prompt_model=` / `task_model=` kwarg split that the wiki's prior [[MIPROv2|MIPROv2]] pages did not document. Trainset is **300 synthetic examples generated by [[Llama|Llama 3.3 70b]]** over Wikipedia event descriptions — a concrete instance of the [[dspy-optimization-overview|Optimization Overview's]] *"aim for at least 300 examples"* target met via synthetic-data bootstrap. Confirms three load-bearing wiki claims: [[DSPyPredict|`Predict`-generates-the-system-prompt]] (Breunig dumps the auto-generated prompt for the reader), [[dspy-optimizers|plain-text-JSON save/load inspectability]] (`optimized_classify.save("optimized_event_classifier.json")`), and the closing pitch — *"there's something really clean and freeing about ceding the details and nuance of the prompt back to an LLM"* — as the most accessible third-party restatement of [[DSPyProgrammingModel|the Programming Model's]] *"writing code instead of strings"* thesis the corpus has. Mints 1 entity ([[DrewBreunig]]).

- [DSPy](entities/DSPy.md) — Open-source [[StanfordUniversity|Stanford NLP]]-originated framework for **programming — not just prompting — LM systems** ([dspy.ai](https://dspy.ai/)). Small learnable API: declarative [[DSPySignatures|Signatures]] (typed input → output), composable [[DSPyModules|Modules]], and [[DSPyOptimizers|Optimizers]] that automatically tune prompts and/or weights against a metric and dev set. Documentation's three-stage model: **Programming → Evaluation → Optimization** ([[dspy-learn-index]]). Framework-level thesis (from [[dspy-programming-overview]]): *"DSPy is a bet on writing code instead of strings"*, with the [[DSPyProgrammingModel|separation-of-concerns decomposition]] factoring a conventional prompt into four named, swappable artifacts — Signatures / [[DSPyAdapters|Adapters]] / Modules / Optimizers. LM-agnostic via the [[DSPyLM|`dspy.LM`]] universal client routed through [[LiteLLM]] ([[dspy-language-models]]) — spans managed APIs ([[openai|OpenAI]] / [[anthropic|Anthropic]] / [[gemini|Gemini]] / [[Databricks]] / [[Anyscale]] / [[TogetherAI|Together AI]] / [[microsoft|Azure]]), self-hosted GPU ([[SGLang]]), and local laptop ([[Ollama]]) behind the same two-line API. The wiki's first dedicated LLM-programming-framework entity.

Three-line scaffolding (`mcp = FastMCP("Name")` + `@mcp.tool()` per function + `mcp.run()`) auto-derives JSON Schema from type hints (including [[Pydantic]] models). Python client `fal_client` exposes a submit-then-poll API; returned image URLs are CDN-hosted on `fal.media` (bytes not delivered inline). First wiki receipt: [[dspy-image-generation-prompting-tutorial]] uses `fal-ai/flux-pro/v1.1-ultra` as the image generator inside a [[DSPy]] critic-then-revise loop; returned URLs wrap into [[DSPyImage|`dspy.Image.from_url(url)`]] for the next iteration's `current_image` input.

- [Ross Girshick](entities/RossGirshick.md) — Computer-vision researcher (UC Berkeley → MSR → [[FAIR]]); architect of the **R-CNN family** ([[RCNN]] 2014, [[FastRCNN]] 2015, [[FasterRCNN]] 2015, [[MaskRCNN]] 2017) — the canonical two-stage detector lineage in [[d2l-computer-vision]] §`rcnn`.

- [Kavosh Asadi](entities/KavoshAsadi.md) — [[Amazon]] research scientist; co-author of [[d2l-reinforcement-learning]].
