Inherited from clang/LLVM; **five values across three regimes** — `0` (no optimization; `dev` profile default; statement-by-statement debugging but Flash-overflowing), `1`/`2`/`3` (speed; `release` profile default is `3`; `2` and `3` **unconditionally unroll loops** — no opt-out — and use inline-threshold 225/275; `3` adds vectorization), `"s"`/`"z"` (size; inline-threshold 75/25; `"z"` is the smaller of the two). The embedded **Flash-budget tension**: unoptimized binaries *"may not fit in your device"* (the [[STM32F303VCT6]]'s 256 KiB ceiling per [[FlashMemory]]), but `"s"`/`"z"`'s aggressive inline-threshold cuts can leave Rust's many small [[ZeroCostAbstraction|zero-cost-abstraction]] functions un-inlined — workaround is `rustflags = ["-C", "inline-threshold=225"]` in `.cargo/config.toml`. **Debuginfo is zero-cost on [[BareMetalProgramming|bare-metal]]** — symbols stay host-side in the ELF, never reaching the device — so `[profile.release] debug = true` is a free win for breakpoint-friendly release builds (variables still print as `$0 = <value optimized out>` in [[GDB]] once optimized). The chapter's signature trick — Cargo's **`profile-overrides`** feature decouples top-crate optimization from dependencies: `[profile.dev.package."*"] opt-level = "z"` keeps the application at `opt-level = 0` debugger-friendly while shrinking all deps (worked example: `.text` 9060 → 3490 bytes, **6 KiB Flash saved**); granular `[profile.dev.package.cortex-m-rt] opt-level = 0` opts a single dep back out. Caveat: **generic code is monomorphized in the *instantiating* crate**, so a `profile-overrides` bump on the *defining* dep may have no effect. ([[rust-embedded-book-unsorted-speed-vs-size]]).

### Added with [[rust-embedded-book-appendix-glossary]] (The Embedded Rust Book — Appendix A: Glossary) — closes the corpus at 44/44

- [BSP](concepts/BSP.md) — **B**oard **S**upport **C**rate (or, in the wider embedded world, **B**oard **S**upport **P**ackage); the acronym-disambiguator that redirects to [[BoardCrate]] for the long treatment. The glossary's one-line definition: *"provides a high level interface configured for a specific board, usually depends on a [[HALCrate|HAL]] crate."* Fourth and topmost layer of the embedded-Rust crate stack (above [[HALCrate]] / [[PeripheralAccessCrate]] / [[MicroArchitectureCrate]]). ([[rust-embedded-book-appendix-glossary]]).
- [FPU](concepts/FPU.md) — Floating-Point Unit; dedicated hardware block executing IEEE 754 arithmetic in hardware rather than via soft-float emulation. Encoded in the [[RustTarget|target triple]] as the `hf` suffix (`thumbv7em-none-eabihf` for [[ARMCortexM|Cortex-M4F]] / M7F vs `thumbv7em-none-eabi` for soft-float); ABI-incompatible across the boundary. The book's first hardware chapter ([[rust-embedded-book-start-hardware]]) flips to `hf` precisely because the [[STM32F303VCT6]] is a Cortex-M4F. Even with an FPU, `core` exposes float primitives but not their transcendental / rounding ops — see [[rust-embedded-book-unsorted-math]] and [[LibmCrate]]. ([[rust-embedded-book-appendix-glossary]]).
- [UART](concepts/UART.md) — Universal Asynchronous Receiver-Transmitter; the asynchronous-only subset of [[USART]] — two wires (TX + RX), no shared clock, start-bit + 8 data bits + optional parity + stop-bit at a configured baud rate. The [[rust-embedded-book-intro-index|Introduction chapter]] lists UART alongside [[I2C]] and [[SPI]] as a prerequisite "common interface" the embedded-experienced reader should already know. Most MCU vendors (including [[STM32F303VCT6|ST]]) expose USART peripherals that are simply configured into UART mode. ([[rust-embedded-book-appendix-glossary]]).

### Added with [[dis-1-1-getting-started]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 1.1 Getting Started in C)

- [C Language](concepts/CLanguage.md) — [[StaticallyTyped|Statically typed]], compiled, general-purpose systems language; the lingua franca of [[DiveIntoSystems]]. Defining traits: compiled (via [[CCompiler]] / [[GCC]] → [[BinaryExecutable]]), [[VariableDeclaration|declare-before-use]] with [[CPrimitiveType|primitive types]], `{ }` blocks, `;`-terminated statements, [[MainFunction|`int main(void)`]] entry, standard library via [[PreprocessorDirective|`#include`]] of [[HeaderFile|headers]], hosted I/O via [[Printf|`printf`]]. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [C Compiler](concepts/CCompiler.md) — The role of translating [[CLanguage|C]] source into a [[BinaryExecutable|binary executable]] the [[ComputerHardware|hardware]] can run directly; [[GCC]] is the canonical instance used throughout [[DiveIntoSystems]]. Necessitates the compile-then-run cycle that distinguishes C from interpreted [[Python]]. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [GCC (GNU Compiler Collection)](concepts/GCC.md) — Canonical [[CCompiler|C compiler]] used by [[DiveIntoSystems]]. Ch 1.1 introduces `gcc hello.c` / `./a.out`, plus the key flags `-o <name>` (rename output), `-Wall` (warnings), `-g` (debug symbols), and `-lm` (link `libm` for `<math.h>`). Parallel to [[Rustc]] on the Rust side of the wiki. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [Compilation Process](concepts/CompilationProcess.md) — Four-stage source-to-binary pipeline ([[PreprocessorDirective|preprocess]] → compile → assemble → link) [[GCC]] runs by default. The single most important difference between [[CLanguage|C]] and [[Python]]: C cannot just be run — it must first be compiled. What lets the rest of [[DiveIntoSystems]] (assembly, architecture, OS, caches, parallelism) assume essentially nothing sits between source and metal. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [Binary Executable](concepts/BinaryExecutable.md) — Machine-code-bearing file the [[ComputerHardware|hardware]] can directly execute; output of the [[CompilationProcess|compile process]]. Default name `a.out` from [[GCC]]; `-o <name>` overrides. Container is platform-specific (ELF / Mach-O / PE); the [[OperatingSystem|OS]] loader maps it and jumps to runtime startup which then calls [[MainFunction|`main`]]. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [main Function](concepts/MainFunction.md) — [[CLanguage|C]] program entry point with signature `int main(void) { ... return 0; }`. The `int` carries the [[ExitStatus|exit status]] (`0` = success); the `void` declares no command-line arguments at this introductory stage. The runtime startup in the [[BinaryExecutable|binary]] calls `main` after process initialization. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [Preprocessor Directive](concepts/PreprocessorDirective.md) — `#`-prefixed line the C preprocessor (stage 1 of the [[CompilationProcess]]) interprets *before* the actual compile. Ch 1.1 introduces `#include <stdio.h>` — splice a [[HeaderFile|header file]] into the translation unit; the C analog of [[Python]]'s `import`, with the constraint that it must appear at the top of the file outside any function body. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [Header File](concepts/HeaderFile.md) — `.h` file declaring the functions/types/macros an implementation file can use after a [[PreprocessorDirective|`#include`]]. Standard-library examples: `<stdio.h>` ([[Printf|`printf`]]), `<math.h>` (`sqrt` / `sin`, needs `-lm`), `<stdlib.h>` (`malloc` / `exit`), `<string.h>` (`strlen` / `strcpy`). ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [printf](concepts/Printf.md) — [[CLanguage|C]] stdlib formatted-output function declared in [[HeaderFile|`<stdio.h>`]]. **Does not auto-append a newline**, unlike [[Python]]'s `print` — explicit `\n` required in the format string. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [Variable Declaration (C)](concepts/VariableDeclaration.md) — `type_name variable_name;` (optionally `= value`). In [[CLanguage|C]], **all variables must be declared before they can be used** ([[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]]) — the rule that makes C [[StaticallyTyped|statically typed]] and gives the compiler the byte-layout info it needs. Ch 1.1 recommends declaring at the beginning of a block as style. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [C Primitive Types](concepts/CPrimitiveType.md) — Byte-width table: `char` 1, `short` 2, `int` 4, `long` 4-or-8 (platform-dependent), `long long` 8, `float` 4, `double` 8; each integer type has an `unsigned` variant. [[SizeOf|`sizeof`]] returns these widths. Load-bearing distinction: `'h'` is a 1-byte `char` (numeric 104, ASCII for *h*); `"h"` is a 2-byte string literal (`'h'` + `'\0'`). ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [sizeof](concepts/SizeOf.md) — Compile-time [[CLanguage|C]] operator returning the byte size of a type or expression (`sizeof(int)` → `4`). Evaluates at compile time — operand expressions are not actually executed, so `sizeof(x++)` does not increment. Underlies portable code (avoids hard-coding widths) and dynamic-allocation idioms (`malloc(n * sizeof(int))`). ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [C Arithmetic Operators](concepts/CArithmeticOperators.md) — `+` `-` `*` `/` `%` plus compound-assignment (`+=` etc.) and [[IncrementOperator|`++` / `--`]]. Ch 1.1 flags two traps explicitly — [[IntegerDivision|`/` truncates when both operands are integer]] (`11/2 == 5`, `11/2.0 == 5.5`) and the [[IncrementOperator|pre-vs-post-`++`]] semantic split. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [Integer Division](concepts/IntegerDivision.md) — In [[CLanguage|C]], division truncates when both operands are integer types — `11 / 2` evaluates to `5`, not `5.5`. Promote one operand to floating-point (`11 / 2.0`) for real division. A one-character source change silently flips the semantics; a frequent off-by-many source for averages, ratios, and normalization. The companion `%` operator returns the integer remainder. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [Increment / Decrement Operators](concepts/IncrementOperator.md) — `++x` / `x++` (and `--x` / `x--`) add or subtract `1` in place. **Pre-form** increments first then yields the new value; **post-form** yields the old value then increments. Standalone they are interchangeable; inside larger expressions they diverge. Ch 1.1 recommends *not* mixing them inside larger expressions — separate statements are clearer. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [Exit Status](concepts/ExitStatus.md) — The integer a process returns to its parent on termination; in [[CLanguage|C]], the value returned from [[MainFunction|`main`]] (or passed to `exit()`). Convention: `0` = success, non-zero = error. Shell exposes the last command's status as `$?`. `EXIT_SUCCESS` / `EXIT_FAILURE` macros in [[HeaderFile|`<stdlib.h>`]] make the intent explicit. ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).
- [Statically Typed](concepts/StaticallyTyped.md) — Type discipline where each variable / expression / signature is assigned a fixed type checked **at compile time**. [[CLanguage|C]] is the canonical wiki example — [[VariableDeclaration|declare-before-use]] with explicit [[CPrimitiveType|types]]; operator semantics (e.g., [[IntegerDivision|`/`]]) are picked from static operand types; zero runtime type overhead. Contrast with [[Python]] (dynamic — runtime type tags, errors at attempted operation). ([[dis-1-1-getting-started]]).

### Added with [[dis-1-2-input-output]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 1.2 Input/Output)

- [scanf](concepts/Scanf.md) — [[CLanguage|C]] stdlib formatted-**input** function declared in [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]]. Reads from [[StandardInput|stdin]] under a [[FormatSpecifier|format string]]; **every receiver argument must be prefixed with [[AddressOfOperator|`&`]]** because the function deposits parsed values into the caller's memory. Skips whitespace between numeric reads. **Fragile under malformed input** — Ch 1.2 explicitly recommends Ctrl-C and forward-references Ch 2 for robust input. ([[dis-1-2-input-output]]).
- [Format Specifier (C)](concepts/FormatSpecifier.md) — `%`-prefixed conversion token inside a [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] format string. Ch 1.2 introduces four: `%d` (int / promoted `char`-as-number), `%g` (float / double), `%s` (C string), `%c` (char-as-glyph). Matched-arity rule: count and types of arguments must equal count and types of specifiers. The two-faced display of a `char` — `%d` prints `65`, `%c` prints `A` — is the chapter's signature pedagogical move. ([[dis-1-2-input-output]]).
- [Address-of Operator (C `&`)](concepts/AddressOfOperator.md) — Unary `&x` yields the [[CMemoryAddress|memory address]] of `x`. **The chapter's first sighting of an address as a value** — Ch 1.2 uses it *only* inside [[Scanf|`scanf`]] calls (not yet as a pointer-typed declaration) so the *value-of-a-location* intuition lands before pointer-type syntax. Disambiguated from binary bitwise-AND `a & b` by position. ([[dis-1-2-input-output]]).
- [Memory Address (C)](concepts/CMemoryAddress.md) — The byte-indexed *location* of a variable in the process's address space; the abstract referent the [[AddressOfOperator|`&` operator]] names. Ch 1.2 introduces the concept *operationally* — `scanf` needs a *where* to store the parsed value — without yet introducing the pointer **type**. Foundation the later DIS pointer chapter will graft onto. ([[dis-1-2-input-output]]).
- [Escape Sequence (C)](concepts/EscapeSequence.md) — Backslash-prefixed in-literal token (`\n`, `\t`, `\\`, `\"`, `\'`, `\0`, `\r`) standing in for a single character. **Resolved at compile time** (vs [[FormatSpecifier|`%`-specifiers]] which are resolved at run time by [[Printf|`printf`]]/[[Scanf|`scanf`]]). [[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]] foregrounds `\n` since `printf` does not auto-append a newline. ([[dis-1-2-input-output]]).
- [Standard I/O Library (`<stdio.h>`)](concepts/StandardIOLibrary.md) — The C standard library [[HeaderFile|header]] declaring [[Printf|`printf`]] / [[Scanf|`scanf`]] / `fprintf` / `getchar` / `fopen` etc., plus the three default streams [[StandardInput|`stdin`]] / [[StandardOutput|`stdout`]] / `stderr`. The part of libc that *assumes a host [[OperatingSystem|OS]]* — present on hosted platforms, absent in [[BareMetalProgramming|bare-metal]] / freestanding builds. The load-bearing distinction between the [[DiveIntoSystems]] world (hosted) and the [[TheEmbeddedRustBook|embedded Rust]] world ([[NoStd|`no_std`]] + [[ARMSemihosting|semihosting]]). ([[dis-1-2-input-output]]).
- [Standard Input (stdin)](concepts/StandardInput.md) — Default input stream of a Unix-style process (file descriptor 0); the source [[Scanf|`scanf`]] reads from. Redirectable (`< input.txt`) and pipeable (`producer | ./prog`). Set up by the [[OperatingSystem|OS]] on process start and inherited from the parent shell. ([[dis-1-2-input-output]]).
- [Standard Output (stdout)](concepts/StandardOutput.md) — Default output stream of a Unix-style process (file descriptor 1); the sink [[Printf|`printf`]] writes to. **Line-buffered** on a terminal, **fully buffered** on a pipe / file — origin of the *"my prompt didn't show before the read"* surprise; workarounds are trailing [[EscapeSequence|`\n`]] or explicit `fflush(stdout)`. ([[dis-1-2-input-output]]).

### Added with [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 1.3 Conditionals and Loops)

- [Boolean Expression (C)](concepts/CBooleanExpression.md) — Integer-valued expression used as a truth value in a [[CLanguage|C]] control-flow test. **C has no dedicated boolean type**; per [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]] **`0` is false, any nonzero value (positive or negative) is true** — so `if (x)` is valid C and tests `x != 0`. Built from [[RelationalOperator|relational]] + [[LogicalOperator|logical]] operator families. The `=`-vs-`==` footgun lives here. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [break Statement (C)](concepts/BreakStatement.md) — Terminates the **innermost enclosing** loop ([[WhileLoop|`while`]] / [[DoWhileLoop|`do`–`while`]] / [[ForLoop|`for`]]) or [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] immediately. No labeled `break` in C — nested-loop exit requires a flag or `goto`. Standard terminator for each [[CaseLabel|`case`]] arm to suppress fall-through. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [case Label (C)](concepts/CaseLabel.md) — Target within a [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]] naming a specific value of the dispatch expression. **Must be a compile-time integer constant** — literals, `enum` values, `#define`d constants — no ranges, no variables, no runtime expressions. Multiple labels may stack onto one body for intentional fall-through. `default:` is the catch-all. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [Comma Operator (C)](concepts/CommaOperator.md) — Binary operator `a, b` that evaluates `a`, **discards** the result, then evaluates and yields `b`. Per [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]] its primary idiomatic use is chaining multiple init/step expressions inside a [[ForLoop|`for` loop]] header (`for (i=0, j=0; i<10; i+=1, j+=10)`). [[DiveIntoSystems]] cautions against overuse. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [continue Statement (C)](concepts/ContinueStatement.md) — Skips the rest of the current loop iteration and jumps to the next condition test. In a [[ForLoop|`for`]] it runs the **step** clause first, then re-tests — the subtle reason a `while`-translation of a `for` with `continue` must place step before the test. Targets only the **innermost** enclosing loop. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [Control Flow](concepts/ControlFlow.md) — The order in which a program's statements execute, beyond pure top-to-bottom sequencing. [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]] introduces the [[CLanguage|C]] vocabulary: branching ([[IfStatement|`if`]] / [[ElseStatement|`else`]] / [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]]), iteration ([[WhileLoop|`while`]] / [[DoWhileLoop|`do`–`while`]] / [[ForLoop|`for`]]), and structured jumps ([[BreakStatement|`break`]] / [[ContinueStatement|`continue`]]). ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [Definite Iteration](concepts/DefiniteIteration.md) — Loop family whose iteration count is **known at loop start** — counting from `0` to `n`, walking a fixed-size array. Per [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]] [[DiveIntoSystems]] recommends the [[ForLoop|`for` loop]] for definite iteration because its three-clause header surfaces the iteration count at a glance — even though [[ForLoop|`for`]] and [[WhileLoop|`while`]] are capability-equivalent. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [do–while Loop (C)](concepts/DoWhileLoop.md) — Test-last loop form `do { body } while (cond);` (note trailing `;`). **Always executes the body at least once** — distinguishes it from [[WhileLoop|`while`]]. Idiomatic for input prompts and menu loops where the loop body must run before the termination condition can be evaluated. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [else / else if Clause (C)](concepts/ElseStatement.md) — Optional companion to an [[IfStatement|`if`]] in [[CLanguage|C]]; runs when the preceding test was `0`. Chains as `if/else if/.../else` for multi-way branches; the trailing `else` is always optional. The *dangling-else* binds to the nearest unmatched `if` — [[DiveIntoSystems]] recommends `{ }` to make the binding explicit. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [for Loop (C)](concepts/ForLoop.md) — General three-clause iteration construct `for (init; cond; step) { body }` — **equivalent in expressive power to [[WhileLoop|`while`]]**, unlike [[Python]]'s sequence-iteration `for`. Any clause may be empty; `for (;;)` is the idiomatic infinite loop. [[DiveIntoSystems]] recommends it for [[DefiniteIteration|definite iteration]]. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [if Statement (C)](concepts/IfStatement.md) — [[CLanguage|C]]'s primary branching construct. Three shapes: one-way `if`, two-way `if`/[[ElseStatement|`else`]], multi-way `if`/`else if`/.../`else`. **Parentheses around the test are required**; the body is a `{ }` block (or a single statement). The `=`-vs-`==` footgun (`if (x = 0)` assigns then tests) lives here. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [Indefinite Iteration](concepts/IndefiniteIteration.md) — Loop family that runs **until a condition emerges** — read input until EOF, retry until success, wait for an event. Per [[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops|Ch 1.3]] [[DiveIntoSystems]] recommends [[WhileLoop|`while`]] (or [[DoWhileLoop|`do`–`while`]] when the loop must run at least once) for indefinite iteration. The contrasting family for [[DefiniteIteration|definite iteration]]. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [Logical Operator (C)](concepts/LogicalOperator.md) — Unary `!` (NOT) and binary `&&` (AND) / `||` (OR), combining [[CBooleanExpression|boolean expressions]] into compound tests. Treat any nonzero operand as true; return `0` or `1`. Apply [[ShortCircuitEvaluation|short-circuit evaluation]] — `B` skipped when the result is already known from `A`. **Not** to be confused with bitwise siblings `&` `|` `~`. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [Relational Operator (C)](concepts/RelationalOperator.md) — The six comparison operators `==` `!=` `<` `<=` `>` `>=`. Return `int` value `0` (false) or `1` (true) — the [[CBooleanExpression|integer-valued boolean]] convention. **`==` vs `=` is the signature [[CLanguage|C]] footgun**: `if (x = 0)` is legal — it assigns then tests the resulting `0` (always false). String comparison is *not* `==` — use `strcmp`. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [Short-Circuit Evaluation](concepts/ShortCircuitEvaluation.md) — Evaluation strategy in which a [[LogicalOperator|logical operator]] stops evaluating its operands as soon as the result is known. `A && B` skips `B` when `A` is false; `A || B` skips `B` when `A` is true. Makes guard idioms safe: `if (p != NULL && *p == 0)` cannot dereference a null pointer. Inherited by most C-family languages. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [switch Statement (C)](concepts/SwitchStatement.md) — Multi-way branch dispatching an integer-typed expression to one of several [[CaseLabel|`case` labels]] (which must be compile-time integer constants). **Fall-through is the default** — without an explicit [[BreakStatement|`break`]], execution continues into the next case. `default:` matches unhandled values. Equivalent to an `if`/`else if` chain only when every arm is equality against a constant. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).
- [while Loop (C)](concepts/WhileLoop.md) — Test-first loop form `while (cond) { body }` — body may run **zero times** if the test starts false. Equivalent in power to [[ForLoop|`for`]] in [[CLanguage|C]]; preferred for [[IndefiniteIteration|indefinite iteration]] per [[DiveIntoSystems]]' design rule. Pairs with [[DoWhileLoop|`do`–`while`]] (the test-last sibling) for the at-least-once case. ([[dis-1-3-conditionals-loops]]).

### Added with [[dis-1-4-functions]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 1.4 Functions)

- [Execution Stack](concepts/ExecutionStack.md) — The LIFO call stack a running [[CLanguage|C]] program uses to track active [[FunctionCall|function calls]]. Per [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]] §1.4.1, each [[FunctionCall|call]] pushes a [[StackFrame|stack frame]] onto the top; each [[ReturnStatement|return]] pops it. At any instant only the top frame is in [[FunctionScope|scope]]. Foundation the rest of [[DiveIntoSystems]] (assembly, calling conventions, [[MemoryHierarchy|memory hierarchy]]) will graft onto. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Function (C)](concepts/Function.md) — [[CLanguage|C]]'s primary unit of modularity and reuse: a named, typed, parameterized block of code with at most one return value. Header `<return type> <name>(<parameter list>)`; body is a `{ }` block. Per [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]] every function exists as a [[FunctionDefinition|definition]] (full body) and optionally as a [[FunctionPrototype|prototype]] (header-only declaration that lets [[MainFunction|`main`]] call code defined later). ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Function Argument (C)](concepts/FunctionArgument.md) — The concrete value supplied at a [[FunctionCall|call site]] to initialize a [[FunctionParameter|parameter]]. Matched **positionally** and **by type**, then copied into the parameter slot per [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]]. Contrast with [[FunctionParameter|parameter]] (the placeholder in the header). ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Function Call (C)](concepts/FunctionCall.md) — Syntactic and runtime act of invoking a [[Function|function]]: `<name>(<arguments>)`. At runtime: evaluate arguments, push a [[StackFrame|stack frame]] onto the [[ExecutionStack|execution stack]], initialize [[FunctionParameter|parameters]] [[PassByValue|by value]], transfer control into the body; on [[ReturnStatement|return]] pop the frame and resume the caller. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Function Definition (C)](concepts/FunctionDefinition.md) — Full header *plus* `{ ... }` body of a [[Function|function]] — the artifact the [[CCompiler|compiler]] turns into executable code. Per [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]] the idiomatic placement is *below* [[MainFunction|`main`]] with a [[FunctionPrototype|prototype]] at the top of the file. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Function Parameter (C)](concepts/FunctionParameter.md) — A named, typed placeholder declared in a [[Function|function]] header. Per [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]] each parameter is **initialized [[PassByValue|by value]]** from the corresponding [[FunctionArgument|argument]] at the [[FunctionCall|call site]]; inside the body it behaves as a [[LocalVariable|local variable]] in that activation's [[StackFrame|stack frame]]. Empty parameter list is spelled `void` (see [[MainFunction]]). ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Function Prototype (C)](concepts/FunctionPrototype.md) — Header-only declaration of a [[Function|function]] (`int max(int n1, int n2);`), with a `;` instead of a body. Lets [[CLanguage|C]]'s single-pass [[CCompiler|compiler]] type-check [[FunctionCall|calls]] before the [[FunctionDefinition|definition]] appears. The *prototypes-at-top, definitions-below* idiom is what makes [[HeaderFile|header files]] work at file scale. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Function Scope (C)](concepts/FunctionScope.md) — Lexical-scope rule for [[FunctionParameter|parameters]] and [[LocalVariable|local variables]] in a [[Function|function]] body: visible *only* within that function. Enforced at runtime by the [[StackFrame|stack frame]] discipline — only the top frame on the [[ExecutionStack|execution stack]] is in scope. Two functions can declare the same local name without conflict; they refer to different bindings. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Local Variable (C)](concepts/LocalVariable.md) — Variable [[VariableDeclaration|declared]] inside a [[Function|function]] body. Lives in that call's [[StackFrame|stack frame]]; in [[FunctionScope|scope]] only within the function; vanishes when the function [[ReturnStatement|returns]]. Each fresh [[FunctionCall|call]] gets fresh storage — the structural reason recursion works. A [[FunctionParameter|parameter]] is effectively a local initialized from the [[FunctionArgument|argument]]. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Pass-by-Value](concepts/PassByValue.md) — [[CLanguage|C]]'s parameter-passing discipline: each [[FunctionParameter|parameter]] is *initialized to the value of* the corresponding [[FunctionArgument|argument]]. The chapter's headline consequence: **mutations to a parameter inside the function are not visible to the caller**. Motivates the pointer chapter that follows (explicit address passing as the workaround for output parameters). Contrast with reference-passing in higher-level languages. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [return Statement (C)](concepts/ReturnStatement.md) — Ends the current [[Function|function]] and yields a value of its [[ReturnType|declared return type]] back to the caller (`return expr;`) or — in a [[VoidType|`void`]] function — ends it with no value (`return;` or simply falling off `}`). Pops the [[StackFrame|stack frame]] from the [[ExecutionStack|execution stack]]. In [[MainFunction|`main`]], `return 0;` becomes the process's [[ExitStatus|exit status]]. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Return Type (C)](concepts/ReturnType.md) — Typed slot at the front of a [[Function|function]] header naming the type of the value yielded by [[ReturnStatement|`return`]]. [[CLanguage|C]] functions return **at most one** value; functions that return nothing declare [[VoidType|`void`]]. [[CCompiler|Compiler]] uses this at every [[FunctionCall|call site]] to type-check the call expression's type. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [Stack Frame](concepts/StackFrame.md) — Per-call runtime record (a.k.a. **activation frame** / **activation record**) holding one active [[FunctionCall|call]]'s [[FunctionParameter|parameter]] values and [[LocalVariable|local variable]] values on the [[ExecutionStack|execution stack]]. Pushed on call, popped on [[ReturnStatement|return]]; only the *top* frame is in [[FunctionScope|scope]]. The structural reason recursion works (one activation = one frame, distinct storage). The substrate later [[DiveIntoSystems]] chapters open up at the assembly / calling-convention level. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).
- [void Type (C)](concepts/VoidType.md) — The *no-value* type in [[CLanguage|C]]. Per [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]] used as a [[ReturnType|return type]] for [[Function|functions]] that produce no value (e.g., `void print_table(int start, int stop)`) and in an empty [[FunctionParameter|parameter list]] (`int main(void)` declares no parameters — see [[MainFunction]]). Also serves as the type-erased pointer type `void *` in later chapters. ([[dis-1-4-functions]]).

### Added with [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 1.5 Arrays and Strings)

- [Array (C)](concepts/CArray.md) — [[CLanguage|C]]'s first **aggregate** type: an ordered, fixed-capacity, contiguous run of same-type elements. Capacity is part of the type (`int arr[10]` ≠ `int arr[20]`); used length is *not* tracked by the language. Per [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] *"C dictates the array layout in program memory"* — consecutive memory locations, the substrate for Ch 1.6 pointer arithmetic. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [Array Indexing (C)](concepts/ArrayIndexing.md) — Zero-based, **unchecked** `arr[i]` subscripting. Valid indices `0..N-1`; `arr[N]` is undefined behavior, *not* a thrown exception. Per [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] *"in C, it's up to the programmer to ensure that their code uses only valid index values when indexing into arrays."* The off-by-one footgun. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [Bounds Checking (and its absence in C)](concepts/BoundsChecking.md) — The runtime/compile-time verification that an [[ArrayIndexing|array index]] is in range — *absent* from [[CLanguage|C]] by design. Consequence: out-of-range access is **undefined behavior**, not an `IndexError`. Source of [[BufferOverflow|buffer overflows]], heisenbugs, and a substantial fraction of remote-code-execution CVEs. Bounds-checked alternatives: [[Python]], Java, Go, Rust. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [C String](concepts/CString.md) — Not a distinct type — a *convention* on top of a [[CArray|`char` array]]: a sequence of `char`s whose end is marked by the [[NullTerminator|null character `'\0'`]]. The lowest-level honest string representation: exactly what's in memory, no metadata header. The [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]] library and the [[FormatSpecifier|`%s`]] specifier both depend on the convention. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [Null Terminator](concepts/NullTerminator.md) — The byte with value `0x00` (written `'\0'` in source) that marks the end of a [[CString|C string]]. Emphatically **not** the digit `'0'` (`0x30 = 48`). [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]] functions find the end of a string by scanning forward until they see one. Per [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] *"failing to properly account for null characters is a common source of errors for novice C programmers."* ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [String Library (string.h)](concepts/StringLibrary.md) — The standard-library [[HeaderFile|header]] `<string.h>` supplying the canonical [[CString|C string]] manipulation functions. [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] opens with three: [[Strlen|`strlen`]], [[Strcpy|`strcpy`]], [[Sprintf|`sprintf`]]. Safer bounded variants (`strncpy`, `snprintf`) and the comparison family (`strcmp`, `strncmp`, `strchr`, `strstr`) deferred to Ch 2.6. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [strlen](concepts/Strlen.md) — Returns the number of characters in a [[CString|C string]] **excluding** the [[NullTerminator|null terminator]]. `O(n)` scan from the base address — there is no length field. The structural reason buffers must size `strlen(s) + 1` to fit the trailing `'\0'`. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [strcpy](concepts/Strcpy.md) — Copies a source [[CString|C string]] (including its `'\0'`) into a destination buffer. **The canonical unsafe function in the C standard library**: per [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] *"poses a security risk because it assumes that its destination is large enough."* The textbook [[BufferOverflow|buffer-overflow]] enabler. Safer alternatives `strncpy` / `snprintf` deferred to Ch 2.6. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [sprintf](concepts/Sprintf.md) — The [[Printf|`printf`]] family member that writes formatted output into a [[CString|C string]] buffer instead of [[StandardOutput|stdout]]. Same unbounded-write hazard as [[Strcpy|`strcpy`]]; `snprintf` is the safer variant. Declared in `<stdio.h>` (not [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]]) but conceptually a string-construction tool. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [Buffer Overflow](concepts/BufferOverflow.md) — The security failure mode where a program writes past the end of a fixed-capacity [[CArray|buffer]] into adjacent memory. [[CLanguage|C]]'s lack of [[BoundsChecking|bounds checking]] makes it possible; unbounded functions like [[Strcpy|`strcpy`]] and [[Sprintf|`sprintf`]] make it easy. Historical root of stack-smashing remote-code-execution exploits. Defenses: bounded library functions, stack canaries, NX bit, ASLR — or memory-safe languages. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).
- [Pass-by-Reference](concepts/PassByReference.md) — Parameter-passing convention where the function receives the storage location of the caller's argument, so mutations persist. In [[CLanguage|C]] this is achieved by passing [[CArray|arrays]] (or, Ch 1.6, pointers) — what's actually copied at the call is the **base address**, giving pass-by-reference semantics for the elements while the parameter slot itself still follows [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]]. The chapter's explicit contradiction-then-reconciliation with [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s blanket pass-by-value rule. ([[dis-1-5-arrays-strings]]).

### Added with [[dis-1-6-structs]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 1.6 Structs)

- [Struct (C)](concepts/CStruct.md) — [[CLanguage|C]]'s second **aggregate** type after the [[CArray|array]]: a *heterogeneous* bundle of named, typed [[StructMember|fields]] treated as one coherent unit. Per [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]] *"a `struct` is a type used to represent a heterogeneous collection of data; it's a mechanism for treating a set of different types as a single, coherent unit."* ([[dis-1-6-structs]]).
- [Struct Member (C)](concepts/StructMember.md) — A named, typed slot inside a [[CStruct|struct]] definition (a.k.a. *field*). Member types may be [[CPrimitiveType|primitives]], [[CArray|arrays]], or other structs; the compiler may insert alignment padding between members. ([[dis-1-6-structs]]).
- [Struct Definition (C)](concepts/StructDefinition.md) — The `struct <name> { <fields> };` syntax that introduces a new struct *type* (no storage allocated). [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]] places these outside any function, near the top of the file — parallel to the [[FunctionPrototype|function-prototype]] convention from [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]. ([[dis-1-6-structs]]).
- [Member Access Operator (C `.`)](concepts/MemberAccessOperator.md) — The dot operator `s.field` for reading/writing a [[StructMember|struct field]] given a [[CStruct|struct]] *value* or *variable*. Inherits the [[LValue|lvalue]]-ness of the underlying field type — so `s.age = 21;` works but `s.name = other.name;` does not (the field type `char []` is itself not an lvalue). ([[dis-1-6-structs]]).
- [LValue (C)](concepts/LValue.md) — An expression that designates an addressable storage location and may appear on the **left** of `=`. Per [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]] *"an lvalue represents a memory storage location appearing on the left side of assignment statements."* The asymmetry that explains why `s1 = s2;` (struct assignment) is legal but `arr1 = arr2;` (array assignment) is not. ([[dis-1-6-structs]]).
- [Struct Assignment (C)](concepts/StructAssignment.md) — Whole-record copy `s2 = s1;` enabled by structs being [[LValue|lvalues]]. Copies every byte including any embedded [[CArray|array]] fields (`char name[64]`), even though the same operation on a bare array would not compile. Implemented as a byte-wise `sizeof(struct ...)` memory copy. ([[dis-1-6-structs]]).
- [Arrow Operator (C `->`)](concepts/ArrowOperator.md) — Shorthand for *dereference-then-dot*: `p->field` ≡ `(*p).field`, where `p` is a pointer to [[CStruct|struct]]. Introduced to avoid the [[MemberAccessOperator|`*p.field`]] precedence trap. *Referenced and deferred* to Ch 2 of [[DiveIntoSystems]]. ([[dis-1-6-structs]]).
- [typedef (C)](concepts/Typedef.md) — Keyword introducing a single-word type alias for an existing (often multi-word) type. Idiomatic with [[CStruct|structs]]: `typedef struct studentT StudentT;` lets the programmer drop the `struct` keyword from declarations. *Referenced and deferred* to Ch 2 of [[DiveIntoSystems]]. ([[dis-1-6-structs]]).
- [Array of Structs (C)](concepts/ArrayOfStructs.md) — `struct studentT class[30];` — a contiguous run of `N` struct instances. Accessed `class[i].field`; per-element [[StructAssignment|struct assignment]] `class[1] = class[0];` is legal; the array as a whole inherits [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]'s [[PassByReference|pass-by-reference]] calling convention. *Referenced and deferred* to Ch 2 of [[DiveIntoSystems]]. ([[dis-1-6-structs]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-1-scope-memory]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.1 Parts of Program Memory and Scope)

- [Program Memory (Process Memory)](concepts/ProcessMemory.md) — The four-region partition of a running [[CLanguage|C]] program's [[AddressSpace|address space]]: [[CodeSection|code section]] (instructions), [[DataSection|data section]] ([[GlobalVariable|globals]]), [[HeapSection|heap]] ([[DynamicMemoryAllocation|dynamic allocations]]), [[StackSection|stack]] ([[LocalVariable|locals]] + [[FunctionParameter|parameters]]). Per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]] the variable class → region mapping determines lifetime and scope. The *headline picture* of Ch 2.1 — upgrades [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s [[ExecutionStack|stack-of-frames]] cartoon to full address-space geography. ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).
- [Address Space](concepts/AddressSpace.md) — The byte-indexed virtual range a [[CLanguage|C]] process can access; *"storage locations for everything it needs in its execution, namely storage for its instructions and data"* per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]]. The container the four [[ProcessMemory|program-memory]] regions partition. Virtual (not physical RAM); not portable across runs (ASLR randomizes layout). ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).
- [Code Section (C Program Memory)](concepts/CodeSection.md) — The region of a [[CLanguage|C]] program's [[AddressSpace|address space]] holding the [[CompilationProcess|compiled]] instructions; per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]] *"the program's instructions are stored in the code section of the memory."* Read-only + executable on modern OSes (W^X); program-lifetime; populated by the OS loader from the [[BinaryExecutable|binary]]'s `.text` segment. First of the four [[ProcessMemory|program-memory]] regions. ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).
- [Data Section (C Program Memory)](concepts/DataSection.md) — The region of a [[CLanguage|C]] program's [[AddressSpace|address space]] holding [[GlobalVariable|global variables]]; per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]] *"global variables are stored in the data section."* Program-lifetime; writable; bounded at link time; split under the hood into `.data` (initialized globals) + `.bss` (zero-initialized) — Ch 2.1 elides the split. Second of the four [[ProcessMemory|program-memory]] regions. ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).
- [Heap Section (C Program Memory)](concepts/HeapSection.md) — The region of a [[CLanguage|C]] program's [[AddressSpace|address space]] for [[DynamicMemoryAllocation|dynamically allocated]] storage; per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]] *"the heap portion of memory is the part of a program's address space associated with dynamic memory allocation."* Programmer-controlled lifetime ([[Malloc|`malloc`]] / [[Free|`free`]]); dynamic size. *Named here; mechanism deferred to Ch 2.4.* Third of the four [[ProcessMemory|program-memory]] regions. ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).
- [Stack Section (C Program Memory)](concepts/StackSection.md) — The region of a [[CLanguage|C]] program's [[AddressSpace|address space]] holding [[LocalVariable|locals]] + [[FunctionParameter|parameters]] — one [[StackFrame|frame]] per active [[FunctionCall|call]]. Per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]] *"local variables and parameters reside in the portion of memory for the stack."* The *same stack* as [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s [[ExecutionStack|execution stack]], now placed inside the four-region picture. LIFO; per-call lifetime; bounded (stack overflow); conventionally grows downward. Fourth of the four [[ProcessMemory|program-memory]] regions. ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).
- [Variable Scope (C)](concepts/VariableScope.md) — Per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]] *"a variable's scope defines when its name has meaning … the set of program code blocks in which a variable is bound to a program memory location."* The corpus's **first formal definition of scope** ([[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s [[FunctionScope]] was operational). Ch 2.1 introduces *two* scope classes — [[GlobalScope|global]] and [[FunctionScope|function]] — and defers [[BlockScope|block]] / [[FileScope|file]] / function-prototype scope to later chapters. ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).
- [Global Scope (C)](concepts/GlobalScope.md) — The [[VariableScope|scope]] class for [[GlobalVariable|globals]] declared *outside* any function. Per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]] *"global variables remain permanently in scope and can be used by any code in the program."* Backed by [[DataSection|data-section]] storage at a single compile-time address; program-lifetime; contrasted with [[FunctionScope|function scope]] across reachability, lifetime, and recursion-friendliness. ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).
- [Global Variable (C)](concepts/GlobalVariable.md) — A variable [[VariableDeclaration|declared]] *outside* any function body; per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]] *"declaring a variable outside of any function body creates a global variable. Global variables remain permanently in scope and can be used by any code in the program."* Lives in [[DataSection|data section]]; [[GlobalScope|global scope]]; program lifetime; zero-initialized by default (BSS); paired with the style rule *"avoid programming with global variables whenever possible"* — code using only [[LocalVariable|locals]] is *"more modular, more general-purpose, and easier to debug."* The Ch 2 alternatives: [[FunctionParameter|parameters]] / [[ReturnStatement|return values]] / [[Pointer|pointers]]. ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).
- [Dynamic Memory Allocation (C)](concepts/DynamicMemoryAllocation.md) — The runtime mechanism for requesting [[HeapSection|heap]] storage in [[CLanguage|C]] — *"the part of a program's address space associated with"* the heap per [[dis-2-1-scope-memory|Ch 2.1]]. Solves three cases [[GlobalVariable|globals]] / [[LocalVariable|locals]] cannot: size unknown at compile time, lifetime outliving the callee, lifetime shorter than the program. **Named in Ch 2.1; API ([[Malloc|`malloc`]] / [[Calloc|`calloc`]] / [[Realloc|`realloc`]] / [[Free|`free`]]) deferred to Ch 2.4.** ([[dis-2-1-scope-memory]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-2-pointers]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.2 C Pointer Variables)

- [Pointer (C)](concepts/Pointer.md) — A variable that stores the [[CMemoryAddress|memory address]] of another variable rather than a value directly; per [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] *"C's pointer variables provide a level of indirection to accessing program memory."* The pointer *points to* the variable whose address it holds; access requires the [[DereferenceOperator|`*` operator]]. The page [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]] / [[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]] / [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] / [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]] / [[dis-1-7-summary|Ch 1.7]] forward-referenced — held as a *placeholder* until Ch 2.2 supplied the definition. Five-use-case enumeration ([[PassByPointer|output params]], [[DynamicMemoryAllocation|dynamic alloc]], efficient [[CStruct|struct]] passing, [[LinkedDataStructure|linked structures]], byte reinterpretation) + the two-rule safety contract (*initialize before use*, *never deref [[NullPointer|`NULL`]]*). ([[dis-2-2-pointers]]).
- [Pointer Declaration (C)](concepts/PointerDeclaration.md) — The `type_name *var_name;` form that introduces a [[Pointer|pointer]] variable — `int *ptr;` ("`ptr` stores the memory address of an `int`") and `char *cptr;` per [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]]. **The `*` here is part of the type spelling**, not the [[DereferenceOperator|dereference operator]] — same lexeme, different syntactic role. Right-to-left reading rule, multi-variable-declaration trap (`int *p, q;` — only `p` is `int *`), and the safe-default initialization idiom `int *p = NULL;`. ([[dis-2-2-pointers]]).
- [Dereference Operator (C `*`)](concepts/DereferenceOperator.md) — Unary `*` operator that **accesses the value at the address a [[Pointer|pointer]] holds**. Canonical [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] example: `ptr = &x; *ptr = 8;` *"the memory location `ptr` points to is assigned 8."* The dual-role disambiguation with the declaration-`*` is the chapter's central learning objective. `*` and [[AddressOfOperator|`&`]] are conceptual inverses on lvalues: `*(&x) == x`. Three undefined-behavior failure modes — uninitialized pointer, [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] dereference, fabricated address — all produce [[SegmentationFault|segfaults]]. ([[dis-2-2-pointers]]).
- [Null Pointer (C `NULL`)](concepts/NullPointer.md) — The special [[Pointer|pointer]] value that *does not refer to any address*; per [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] *"any pointer can be given the special value `NULL`, which indicates that it doesn't refer to any particular address."* Macro from `<stddef.h>` (typically `((void *)0)`), assignable to any [[PointerType|pointer type]]. **Must never be [[DereferenceOperator|dereferenced]]** — `*NULL` is undefined behavior, typically a [[SegmentationFault|segfault]]. Three idiomatic uses: safe initialization, *no-result* sentinel from allocators / lookups, end-marker in [[LinkedDataStructure|linked structures]]. **Not** the same as `'\0'` ([[NullTerminator]]) or `0`. ([[dis-2-2-pointers]]).
- [Pointer Type (C)](concepts/PointerType.md) — The static type `T *` spelled in [[PointerDeclaration|pointer declarations]]: `int *`, `char *`, `struct studentT *`, etc. Even though every pointer is platform-width regardless of pointee, the pointee type is load-bearing — it determines [[DereferenceOperator|dereference]] yield type, pointer-arithmetic stride (`p + 1` advances `sizeof(T)` bytes), and assignment compatibility. Per [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] cross-type assignment like `char *cptr = &intvar;` is a type error with *"unpredictable behavior"* at runtime. [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] is the one universal value. `void *` deferred to Ch 2.4. ([[dis-2-2-pointers]]).
- [Pass-by-Pointer (C)](concepts/PassByPointer.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] idiom for letting a [[Function|function]] mutate caller storage: caller passes `&x`, callee writes via `*p`. Per [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] the first of the five [[Pointer|pointer]] use cases — *"implement functions whose parameters can modify values in the caller's stack frame."* **Reconciles** [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]]'s [[PassByValue|pass-by-value]] rule with [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]'s [[PassByReference|pass-by-reference]] exception: *C is always pass-by-value; pass-by-reference is just pass-by-value of a pointer.* Idiomatic uses: output parameters, multiple-return, in-place mutation, efficient large-[[CStruct|struct]] passing (avoid [[StructAssignment|whole-record copy]]). ([[dis-2-2-pointers]]).
- [Segmentation Fault](concepts/SegmentationFault.md) — The runtime error a hosted [[OperatingSystem|OS]] reports when a process accesses memory it shouldn't (signal `SIGSEGV` on POSIX). The canonical visible consequence of [[Pointer|pointer]] misuse in [[CLanguage|C]] — uninitialized pointer, [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] deref, fabricated invalid address per [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]]. **Not** a [[CLanguage|C]] exception — the default handler prints `Segmentation fault` and terminates. [[NullPointer|`NULL`]]-deref reliably segfaults because OSes leave the lowest page unmapped; *uninitialized* pointers are worse because they may silently corrupt rather than crash. Debugging discipline: `-g` symbols + `gdb` + `bt`; AddressSanitizer for sub-segfault corruptions. ([[dis-2-2-pointers]]).
- [Linked Data Structure (C)](concepts/LinkedDataStructure.md) — Collection of dynamically allocated [[CStruct|struct]] nodes connected via [[Pointer|pointer]] fields — linked lists, trees, graphs. Per [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] the fourth of the five [[Pointer|pointer]] use cases. Sits at the intersection of **two** Ch 2 features: pointers (the *link* mechanism, Ch 2.2) and [[DynamicMemoryAllocation|dynamic allocation]] (the *create-a-node-at-runtime* mechanism, Ch 2.4 deferred). [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] serves as the end-of-chain sentinel; the canonical traversal `while (cur != NULL) { ...; cur = cur->next; }` combines [[NullPointer]] / [[DereferenceOperator]] / [[ShortCircuitEvaluation]] / [[ArrowOperator]] into one idiom. ([[dis-2-2-pointers]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-3-pointers-functions]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.3 Pointers and Functions)

- [Output Parameter (C)](concepts/OutputParameter.md) — The named [[CLanguage|C]] convention for a [[FunctionParameter|function parameter]] whose purpose is to deliver a value *out* of the function back to the caller — implemented as a [[Pointer|pointer]] parameter ([[PointerDeclaration|`type *out`]] declaration → caller passes [[AddressOfOperator|`&dest`]] → callee writes via [[DereferenceOperator|`*out = value;`]]). Per [[dis-2-3-pointers-functions|Ch 2.3]] *"pointer parameters provide a mechanism through which functions can modify argument values."* The [[CLanguage|C]] workaround for the language's single-[[ReturnStatement|`return`]] restriction: multiple values out via multiple pointer parameters (`void divmod(int a, int b, int *q, int *r)`); idiomatic *error-code-in-return, value-through-output-parameter* pattern (used by [[Scanf|`scanf`]] / `strtol` / POSIX I/O). The *write-only-on-success* slice of the [[PassByPointer|pass-by-pointer]] space — distinct from *in-place mutation* (read-then-write) and *efficient struct passing* (read-only via [[PassByPointer|`const T *`]]). ([[dis-2-3-pointers-functions]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.4 Dynamic Memory Allocation)

- [malloc (C)](concepts/Malloc.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] standard-library function that requests a contiguous run of bytes on the [[HeapSection|heap]] at runtime. Per [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]] *"to call `malloc`, a program passes in the total number of bytes of contiguous heap memory to allocate."* Signature `void *malloc(size_t size);` declared in `<stdlib.h>`; argument computed with [[SizeOf|`sizeof`]]; returns a [[Pointer|pointer]] to the [[CMemoryAddress|base address]] or [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] on failure. The chapter's headline safety rule: *"Be sure to always test the return value of `malloc` for `NULL`. Dereferencing a `NULL` pointer will cause your program to crash!"* Pairs strictly with [[Free|`free`]]. ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [free (C)](concepts/Free.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] standard-library function that releases a heap allocation previously returned by [[Malloc|`malloc`]]. Signature `void free(void *ptr);` declared in `<stdlib.h>`. Per [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]] *"when a program no longer needs the heap memory it dynamically allocated with `malloc`, it should explicitly deallocate the memory by calling the `free` function."* Headline discipline: **set the [[Pointer|pointer]] to [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] after [[Free|`free`]]** — `free(NULL)` is a defined no-op (defuses [[DoubleFree|double-free]]), `*NULL` reliably [[SegmentationFault|segfaults]] (converts [[UseAfterFree|use-after-free]] to a visible failure). ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [Dynamically Allocated Array (C)](concepts/DynamicallyAllocatedArray.md) — An [[CArray|array]]-shaped buffer obtained at runtime via a single [[Malloc|`malloc(sizeof(T) * N)`]] call. The chapter's headline payoff: **same `arr[i]` indexing syntax as [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] static arrays** despite the different underlying type (`int *` vs `int[N]`) — and the same function-parameter signature (`void f(int *arr, int size)`) accepts both, via the [[dis-2-3-pointers-functions|Ch 2.3]] [[PassByPointer|pass-by-pointer]] mechanism. The compile-time-vs-runtime split is the headline reason dynamic arrays exist — `N` can come from input. ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [Memory Leak](concepts/MemoryLeak.md) — The failure mode where heap memory allocated via [[Malloc|`malloc`]] is never released via [[Free|`free`]] before the program ends or the last [[Pointer|pointer]] to it is lost. The bytes accumulate over the program's lifetime; long-running programs eventually hit [[Malloc|`malloc`]] returning [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] from out-of-memory. Defense: pair every `malloc` with exactly one `free`, document ownership, use [[Valgrind|Valgrind]] / AddressSanitizer. ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [Use-After-Free](concepts/UseAfterFree.md) — The failure mode where a [[Pointer|pointer]] is [[DereferenceOperator|dereferenced]] *after* the heap chunk it pointed to has been released via [[Free|`free`]]. Undefined behavior; one of the most-exploited bug classes in [[CLanguage|C]] code in the wild (browser / kernel CVEs). [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]]'s defense — set the pointer to [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] after `free` — converts silent UAF into a visible [[SegmentationFault|segfault]]. ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [Double-Free](concepts/DoubleFree.md) — The failure mode where the same heap chunk is passed to [[Free|`free`]] twice without an intervening [[Malloc|`malloc`]] re-allocating it. Corrupts the [[FreeList|free list]]; classic security-exploitation surface (unlink / fastbin / tcache poisoning). Defense: the same [[NullPointer|`NULL`]]-after-`free` discipline, since `free(NULL)` is a defined no-op. ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [Dangling Pointer (C)](concepts/DanglingPointer.md) — A [[Pointer|pointer]] that still holds a [[CMemoryAddress|memory address]] but the storage at that address is no longer valid (either [[Free|`free`]]d or scope-exited [[LocalVariable|local]]). The pointer *looks* usable but [[DereferenceOperator|dereferencing]] is undefined behavior. The *state* that enables [[UseAfterFree|use-after-free]] (the *operation*); defused by the [[NullPointer|`NULL`]]-after-`free` discipline. ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [Free List (Heap Manager)](concepts/FreeList.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] runtime's bookkeeping data structure for tracking unused [[HeapSection|heap]] chunks. Per [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]] *"a list of unused chunks of heap memory available for allocation."* The substrate [[Malloc|`malloc`]] walks and [[Free|`free`]] writes back to; corrupted by [[DoubleFree|double-free]] and adjacent [[BufferOverflow|buffer overflows]]; the source of [[HeapFragmentation|fragmentation]]. ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [Heap Fragmentation](concepts/HeapFragmentation.md) — The state where the [[HeapSection|heap]]'s free memory is scattered into many small non-contiguous chunks rather than a few large ones — *"chunks of free heap space interspersed with chunks of allocated heap space"* per [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]]. Emergent from mixed [[Malloc|`malloc`]] / [[Free|`free`]] traffic; can make `malloc(N)` fail even when total free bytes ≥ N. Defended by size-class arenas, coalescing on `free`, lifetime-grouped pool allocation. ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [Heap Metadata (Allocation Header)](concepts/HeapMetadata.md) — The per-chunk bookkeeping the heap manager stores immediately preceding each user-visible allocation. Records chunk size + allocated/free flag (+ [[FreeList|free-list]] prev/next when free). What makes [[Free|`free`]] callable with only a pointer — the size lives in the header. The classic [[BufferOverflow|buffer-overflow]] exploitation surface (corrupt the next chunk's header → controlled heap-write primitive). ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [exit (C)](concepts/Exit.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] standard-library function that terminates the process immediately with a status code (`void exit(int status);` from `<stdlib.h>`). Per [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]] the canonical OOM escape hatch — when [[Malloc|`malloc`]] returns [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] and the program has no recovery, `printf("Bad malloc\n"); exit(1);`. Equivalent to `return n;` from [[MainFunction|`main`]] but works anywhere; runs [[Stdio|`<stdio.h>`]] flushes + `atexit` handlers (vs `abort` which does not). ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).
- [size_t (C)](concepts/SizeT.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] standard library's unsigned integer type for sizes — the type returned by [[SizeOf|`sizeof`]] and the parameter type of [[Malloc|`malloc`]] / `memcpy` / `strlen` / `fread` / etc. Defined in `<stddef.h>`; platform-width (32-bit on 32-bit, 64-bit on 64-bit); large enough to represent the size of any object. Printf format `%zu` (C99+). The chapter doesn't dwell on it explicitly but every `malloc(sizeof(...))` call uses it. ([[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-5-arrays]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.5 Arrays in C)

- [Multidimensional Array (C)](concepts/MultidimensionalArray.md) — A [[CArray|C array]] of two or more dimensions (`int matrix[N][M]`); a grid of `N` rows × `M` columns of same-type elements stored in [[RowMajorOrder|row-major order]]. Per [[dis-2-5-arrays|Ch 2.5]] *"sizes of other dimensions must be fully specified so that the compiler can generate the correct offsets into the array"* — function parameters keep the first dimension optional and the rest mandatory because `&m[i][j] = m_base + i*M + j` needs `M`. Two dynamic 2D forms: single-`malloc` `int *` (memory-efficient, manual `arr[i*M+j]` indexing) and [[ArrayOfArrays|`int **` array-of-arrays]] (N+1 mallocs, double-indexing `arr[i][j]`). Deferred from [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]] and finally delivered here. ([[dis-2-5-arrays]]).
- [Row-Major Order](concepts/RowMajorOrder.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] memory-layout convention for [[MultidimensionalArray|multidimensional arrays]]: row 0 stored contiguously, then row 1, ..., with element `(i, j)` at byte offset `(i*M + j) * sizeof(elem)`. Per [[dis-2-5-arrays|Ch 2.5]] a static `int matrix[N][M]` is *"allocated to contiguous memory addresses"* this way; the same formula is what the single-`malloc` dynamic-2D form (`arr[i*M+j]`) writes by hand. The reason the trailing dimension of a 2D parameter is mandatory: the compiler needs `M` to compute offsets. **Cache-locality consequence**: the innermost loop should walk the rightmost index to traverse memory sequentially. Contrast with [[Fortran]] / [[MATLAB]] / [[CUBLAS]] column-major. ([[dis-2-5-arrays]]).
- [Array Decay (C)](concepts/ArrayDecay.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] language rule that an [[CArray|array]] expression is implicitly converted to a [[Pointer|pointer]] to its first element in most contexts. Per [[dis-2-5-arrays|Ch 2.5]] *"when passing an array to a function, C copies the value of the base address to the parameter. That is, both the parameter and the argument refer to the same memory locations"* — what's being copied *is* the decayed pointer. **The unifying primitive** underneath [[dis-1-5-arrays-strings|Ch 1.5]]'s pass-by-reference exception, [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]]'s pass-by-value reconciliation, [[dis-2-3-pointers-functions|Ch 2.3]]'s pass-by-pointer recipe, and [[dis-2-4-dynamic-memory|Ch 2.4]]'s static-vs-dynamic syntactic unification. Three contexts preserve the array type ([[SizeOf|`sizeof`]], [[AddressOfOperator|`&`]], string-literal initialization); everywhere else decays. The **lost-bound property** — the decayed pointer carries no length — is the substrate of every [[BufferOverflow|buffer-overflow]] CVE. For 2D: `int[N][M]` decays to `int (*)[M]` (pointer-to-row-of-`M`), *not* to `int **` — explains why the trailing-dimension parameter rule is non-negotiable and why static-2D and [[ArrayOfArrays|array-of-arrays]] parameter types are not interchangeable. ([[dis-2-5-arrays]]).
- [Array of Arrays (C — Dynamic 2D)](concepts/ArrayOfArrays.md) — The second of [[dis-2-5-arrays|Ch 2.5]]'s two dynamic-2D strategies: instead of one big [[Malloc|`malloc(N*M)`]], allocate **N+1 separate heap blocks** (one outer `int **` of `N` row pointers + one `int *` of `M` ints per row). **Preserves double-indexing `arr[i][j]`** at the cost of N+1 heap headers, non-contiguous rows, and worse cache locality. Function parameter type is `int **` — *not* interchangeable with the `int (*)[M]` that a static `int m[N][M]` decays to. Cleanup must free each row first, then the outer array — reverse-order or partial cleanup leaks. Also the only form that supports **ragged 2D** (rows of different lengths) and O(1) row-swap by pointer assignment. ([[dis-2-5-arrays]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-6-strings]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.6 Strings and the String Library)

- [strncpy (C)](concepts/Strncpy.md) — The bounded [[CString|C-string]] copy from [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]] — copies at most `size` bytes from `src` to `dst`. Per [[dis-2-6-strings|Ch 2.6]] **the chapter's most-emphasized footgun**: when `strlen(src) >= size`, `strncpy` *"copies the first size characters from src to dst and does not add a null character to the end of the dst"* — the programmer must explicitly write `dst[size-1] = '\0';` after the call. Bounded but **not safe by default**. Superseded by [[Strlcpy|`strlcpy`]] in glibc 2.38 (2023+). ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [strlcpy (C)](concepts/Strlcpy.md) — The modern bounded [[CString|C-string]] copy from [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]] — like [[Strncpy|`strncpy`]] but **always null-terminates** the destination, returning the would-have-been-copied length for truncation detection. Per [[dis-2-6-strings|Ch 2.6]] *"similar to `strncpy`, except it always adds the `'\0'` character to the end of the destination string"* — removes the post-call `dst[size-1] = '\0';` line. Long-present in BSD libcs; landed in GNU libc 2.38 (mid-2023); not yet portable. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [strcmp (C)](concepts/Strcmp.md) — The tri-valued byte-by-byte [[CString|C-string]] comparison from [[StringLibrary|`<string.h>`]]: returns 0 if equal, negative if `s1 < s2`, positive if `s1 > s2`. Per [[dis-2-6-strings|Ch 2.6]] *"compares strings character by character based on their ASCII representation."* The answer to *"why doesn't `s1 == s2` work?"* — `==` on `char *` compares **base addresses**, not contents. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [strncmp (C)](concepts/Strncmp.md) — The bounded variant of [[Strcmp|`strcmp`]] — compares at most `n` bytes. Same tri-valued return. Useful for prefix matching and fixed-width header comparisons. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [strcat (C)](concepts/Strcat.md) — Appends `src` to the end of `dst` per [[dis-2-6-strings|Ch 2.6]]. Shares [[Strcpy|`strcpy`]]'s **destination-size-assumed** unsafe contract — `dst` must hold the original contents *plus* the appended bytes *plus* the new [[NullTerminator|`'\0'`]]. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [strncat (C)](concepts/Strncat.md) — The bounded variant of [[Strcat|`strcat`]] — appends at most `n` bytes, always null-terminates (subtle asymmetry with [[Strncpy|`strncpy`]] which does not). ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [strchr (C)](concepts/Strchr.md) — Searches a [[CString|C-string]] for the first occurrence of a character; returns a [[Pointer|pointer]] **into the original buffer** (aliases the input) or [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] if absent. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [strstr (C)](concepts/Strstr.md) — Substring search: returns a [[Pointer|pointer]] to the first occurrence of the needle within the haystack or [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] if absent. Like [[Strchr|`strchr`]], the return value **aliases the input** — it's an address inside the original buffer, not a copy. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [strtok_r (C)](concepts/StrtokR.md) — The **reentrant** + thread-safe replacement for [[Strtok|`strtok`]]: `char *strtok_r(char *str, const char *delim, char **saveptr)`. The previously-hidden saved-position pointer is now the explicit third parameter — each thread owns its own `saveptr` on its private [[Stack|stack]]. The `_r` suffix is the [[POSIX]] **reentrant-variant** naming convention ([[dis-14-6-thread-safety|DIS Ch 14.6]]).
- [strtok (C)](concepts/Strtok.md) — Tokenizes a [[CString|C-string]] on a delimiter set. Per [[dis-2-6-strings|Ch 2.6]] *"a token refers to a subsequence of characters in a string separated by any number of delimiter characters of the programmer's choosing."* **Destructive** — writes [[NullTerminator|`'\0'`]] over delimiter bytes; **stateful** — keeps internal static state between calls (subsequent calls pass [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] as first argument); **not thread-safe** — `strtok_r` is the reentrant variant. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [ctype.h (C)](concepts/CtypeLibrary.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] standard library's character-class predicate + conversion functions — `isalpha` / `isdigit` / `isalnum` / `isspace` / `islower` / `isupper` / `ispunct` (predicates returning *nonzero* for true, not necessarily `1`) and `tolower` / `toupper` (returning the converted ASCII value). The portable replacement for ASCII-range comparisons. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [atoi (C)](concepts/Atoi.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] standard library's [[CString|C-string]] → `int` conversion in `<stdlib.h>`. Parses a leading numeric prefix, returns 0 on parse failure (the **silent-failure footgun** — indistinguishable from a successful parse of `"0"`). Modern code prefers `strtol` for its error-reporting capability. `atof` is the float/double sibling. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).
- [man (Unix manual pages)](concepts/ManPages.md) — The Unix manual-pages system — *"the canonical reference for [[CLanguage|C]] library functions, system calls, and command-line tools"* per [[dis-2-6-strings|Ch 2.6]] (introduced as the textbook's recommended discovery surface: `$ man strcpy`). Section 1 = commands, Section 2 = system calls, Section 3 = library functions, Section 5 = file formats. ([[dis-2-6-strings]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-7-structs]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.7 Structs)

- [Pointer to Struct (C)](concepts/PointerToStruct.md) — A [[Pointer|pointer]]-typed variable whose pointed-at type is a [[CStruct|struct]]. Per [[dis-2-7-structs|Ch 2.7]] §2.7.2 the construct that finally delivers the [[ArrowOperator|`->`]] operator [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]] named-and-deferred, and that admits [[Malloc|heap-allocated]] structs alongside [[StackSection|stack-allocated]] ones. Two equivalent field-access forms — `sptr->grad_yr` (idiomatic) and `(*sptr).grad_yr` (*"cumbersome"*). Canonical use cases: heap-allocated structs that outlive their creating [[StackFrame|stack frame]], and the **mutation channel** for callers (pass `&student`, callee writes through `s->field`). ([[dis-2-7-structs]]).
- [Struct Pointer Field (C)](concepts/StructPointerField.md) — A [[StructMember|struct field]] whose declared type is a [[Pointer|pointer]] (e.g., `char *name` inside `struct personT`). Per [[dis-2-7-structs|Ch 2.7]] §2.7.3 requires the **two-step `malloc` discipline** — one allocation for the struct, separate allocations for each pointer field — beyond the struct allocation itself. The chapter's headline **compositional field-access rule** *"start from the outermost variable type and use its type syntax to access individual parts"* generates the per-pattern access syntax (`p1.age` `.`, `p2->age` `->`, `p1.name[2]` `.` then `[]`, `p2->name[2]` `->` then `[]`). Cleanup is inner-first then outer — reversing order is a [[UseAfterFree|use-after-free]]. The flexibility (runtime-sized fields) vs. embedded-array-field (`char name[64];`) simplicity tradeoff. ([[dis-2-7-structs]]).
- [Self-Referential Struct (C)](concepts/SelfReferentialStruct.md) — A [[CStruct|struct]] type containing a [[StructPointerField|pointer field]] whose pointed-at type is the *same* struct type. Per [[dis-2-7-structs|Ch 2.7]] §2.7.5 the construct that enables *"building linked data structures (linked lists, trees, graphs) without contiguous memory requirements"* — the load-bearing primitive for [[LinkedDataStructure|linked dynamic data structures]] [[dis-2-2-pointers|Ch 2.2]] named-and-deferred. The pointer indirection (not a direct `struct node next;` field) is essential — a non-pointer self-reference would require infinite size. Multi-pointer variants generalize to doubly-linked lists (`prev` + `next`), binary trees (`left` + `right`), and graph nodes (`neighbors[K]`). [[NullPointer|`NULL`]]-terminated by convention — the same sentinel discipline as [[CString|C-strings]]' [[NullTerminator|`'\0'`]] generalized to pointer fields. ([[dis-2-7-structs]]).
- [Linked List (C)](concepts/LinkedList.md) — The simplest [[LinkedDataStructure|linked dynamic data structure]] — a chain of [[SelfReferentialStruct|self-referential struct]] nodes (`struct node { int data; struct node *next; }`), each [[Malloc|heap-allocated]] independently, [[NullPointer|`NULL`]]-terminated, anchored by a stack-allocated **head pointer**. Per [[dis-2-7-structs|Ch 2.7]] §2.7.5 the chapter's worked example uses **prepend-to-head** O(1) construction (`temp->next = head; head = temp;`) which produces an order-reversed list. Traversal walks the `next` field until [[NullPointer|`NULL`]]; cleanup must save `curr->next` before `free(curr)` to avoid [[UseAfterFree|use-after-free]]. **The tradeoff vs. [[CArray|arrays]]**: O(1) head insert vs. O(N) random access; poor cache locality vs. excellent; one [[Malloc|`malloc`]] per node + [[HeapMetadata|heap header]] overhead vs. one contiguous block. ([[dis-2-7-structs]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-8-io]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.8 Input / Output)

- [FILE * (File Pointer, C)](concepts/FilePointer.md) — The opaque [[Pointer|pointer]]-typed handle exposed by [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] for *all* stream I/O — both open files ([[Fopen|`fopen`]] return value) and the three default streams ([[StandardInput|`stdin`]] / [[StandardOutput|`stdout`]] / [[StandardError|`stderr`]] are pre-opened `FILE *` values). Carries position state (settable via [[Fseek|`fseek`]] / [[Rewind|`rewind`]]), buffering state (flushed on [[Fclose|`fclose`]] / `fflush` / newline-on-terminal), and EOF/error flags ([[Feof|`feof`]] / `ferror`). The unifying primitive that makes [[Printf|`printf`]] = `fprintf(stdout, ...)`. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [fopen (C)](concepts/Fopen.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] function that opens a file and returns a [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]] or [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] on failure. Two args — `const char *path`, `const char *mode` ([[FileMode|`"r"` / `"w"` / `"a"`]]). The canonical *check-or-[[Exit|`exit(1)`]]* recipe is *"if `fp == NULL`, error message, exit"* per [[dis-2-8-io|Ch 2.8]] §2.8.3. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [fclose (C)](concepts/Fclose.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] function that releases a [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]] — flushes buffered writes, closes the OS file descriptor, frees the library-side struct. Pairs 1-to-1 with [[Fopen|`fopen`]]; skipping it leaks the handle and risks losing the tail of buffered output. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [File Mode (fopen mode string)](concepts/FileMode.md) — The second-arg [[CString|C-string]] to [[Fopen|`fopen`]] selecting **read** (`"r"` — fails if missing), **write** (`"w"` — **truncates** existing file), or **append** (`"a"` — creates if missing, writes at end). Footgun: `"w"` silently destroys any existing file at the path. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [fgetc / getc (C)](concepts/Fgetc.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] per-byte file reader. Returns [[CPrimitiveType|`int`]] (not `char`) so [[EOF|`EOF`]] can be distinct from any of 256 byte values — the *"[[CPrimitiveType|`int ch`]] not `char ch`"* discipline is the chapter's load-bearing safety rule. [[Getchar|`getchar()`]] = `fgetc(stdin)`. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [fputc / putc (C)](concepts/Fputc.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] per-byte file writer. Takes and returns [[CPrimitiveType|`int`]] for the same [[EOF|`EOF`]]-sentinel reason as [[Fgetc|`fgetc`]]. [[Putchar|`putchar(c)`]] = `fputc(c, stdout)`. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [fgets (C)](concepts/Fgets.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] **bounded line reader**: `fgets(s, n, fp)` reads at most `n-1` chars, stops at newline (included in buffer) or EOF, **always [[NullTerminator|null-terminates]]** on success. The *robust* counterweight to [[Scanf|`scanf("%s")`]]'s unbounded write. The production-grade input recipe is `fgets` + `sscanf`. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [fputs (C)](concepts/Fputs.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] string-level writer. `fputs(s, fp)` writes a [[CString|C string]] without auto-appending a newline (caller controls `\n`, like [[Printf|`printf`]]). ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [fprintf (C)](concepts/Fprintf.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] file-I/O sibling of [[Printf|`printf`]] — first arg is a [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]], otherwise identical. `printf(fmt, ...)` ≡ `fprintf(stdout, fmt, ...)`. The canonical error-reporting form: `fprintf(stderr, "Error: %d\n", ret)`. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [fscanf (C)](concepts/Fscanf.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] file-I/O sibling of [[Scanf|`scanf`]] — first arg is a [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]], otherwise identical (`&`-prefixed receivers, [[FormatSpecifier|format-specifier]] vocabulary). The [[ScanfCharClass|`%[...]` / `%Ns`]] specifier extensions are the **robustness fix** for [[Scanf|`scanf`]]'s [[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]]-flagged fragility. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [EOF (End-of-File Sentinel, C)](concepts/EOF.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] macro (typically `-1`) returned by character-I/O functions on end-of-file or error. **The reason [[Fgetc|`fgetc`]] / [[Getchar|`getchar`]] return [[CPrimitiveType|`int`]] not `char`**: a `char` only has 256 values; `EOF` must be a 257th value distinct from any real byte. Storing the return in `char ch` is a corpus-wide bug. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [feof (C)](concepts/Feof.md) — The [[StandardIOLibrary|`<stdio.h>`]] predicate that returns nonzero **after** a read hit end-of-file. **Not** a pre-read EOF test — `while (!feof(fp))` is a textbook footgun (one extra iteration). Used **after** a failed read to disambiguate EOF from a hard read error (`ferror`). ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [Standard Error (stderr)](concepts/StandardError.md) — The **third** default I/O stream (FD 2) for diagnostic output that should survive `> file` redirection of `stdout`. **Unbuffered by default** — error output appears immediately even if the program crashes right after the call. Idiomatic writer: `fprintf(stderr, "Error: ...\n", ...)`. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [getchar (C)](concepts/Getchar.md) — The [[StandardInput|`stdin`]]-specialized form of [[Fgetc|`fgetc`]]: `getchar()` ≡ `fgetc(stdin)`. Returns [[CPrimitiveType|`int`]] for [[EOF|`EOF`]] support. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [putchar (C)](concepts/Putchar.md) — The [[StandardOutput|`stdout`]]-specialized form of [[Fputc|`fputc`]]: `putchar(c)` ≡ `fputc(c, stdout)`. Bypasses [[Printf|`printf`]]'s format-string overhead for the no-formatting case. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [ungetc (C)](concepts/Ungetc.md) — Pushes one byte back onto a [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]] so the next read returns it. The standard guarantees at least one byte of pushback. Useful for **one-token lookahead** in hand-rolled parsers. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [fseek (C)](concepts/Fseek.md) — Repositions a [[FilePointer|`FILE *`]]'s current position. Three whence anchors: `SEEK_SET` (absolute from start), `SEEK_CUR` (relative to current), `SEEK_END` (relative to end). Sibling `ftell(fp)` returns the position; text-mode offsets are implementation-defined. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [rewind (C)](concepts/Rewind.md) — Shortcut for `fseek(fp, 0, SEEK_SET)` *plus* clearing the error and EOF flags. Used for two-pass file scanning. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [Stream Redirection (Shell)](concepts/StreamRedirection.md) — The shell-level `<` / `>` / `>>` / `2>` / `&>` / `2>&1` / `|` mechanism that rebinds [[StandardInput|`stdin`]] / [[StandardOutput|`stdout`]] / [[StandardError|`stderr`]] *before* the process starts — no code change. The architectural reason [[StandardError|`stderr`]] exists separately from [[StandardOutput|`stdout`]] (so `./prog > out.txt` captures data without swallowing errors). ([[dis-2-8-io]]).
- [scanf Character Class (%[...] / %Ns, C)](concepts/ScanfCharClass.md) — The [[Scanf|`scanf`]] / [[Fscanf|`fscanf`]] specifier extensions that fix [[dis-1-2-input-output|Ch 1.2]]'s flagged fragility: `%[abc]` (chars in set), `%[^abc]` (chars not in set), `%[^\n]` (rest of line), `%20s` (max-width capped read — the [[BufferOverflow|buffer-overflow]] fix, the [[Scanf|`scanf`]] analog of [[Strlcpy|`strlcpy`]]). Residual footgun: `%[^\n]` leaves the `\n` on the stream — use `%[^\n]%*c` to consume it. ([[dis-2-8-io]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-9-1-advanced-switch]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.1 Constants, switch, enum, and typedef)

- [C Constant (#define)](concepts/CConstant.md) — Preprocessor-managed symbolic alias `#define const_name (literal_value)` for a literal, declared outside any function. Per [[dis-2-9-1-advanced-switch|Ch 2.9.1]] *"constants are not lvalues and cannot be reassigned at runtime"* — `N = 50;` is a compile error after substitution. The wrapping parentheses are the convention that prevents operator-precedence surprises in expression substitution (`#define HALF (1/2)`). The headline benefit is **single-point-of-change maintainability** — one `#define` line updates every usage. Contrast: [[ConstQualifier|`const int N = 20;`]] gives type-checking and debugger visibility at the cost of variable allocation; [[CEnum|`enum { N = 20 };`]] gives type-safe **integer**-only constants with sequential auto-numbering. ([[dis-2-9-1-advanced-switch]]).
- [Enumerated Type (enum, C)](concepts/CEnum.md) — `enum type_name { CONST_1, CONST_2, ... };` groups related integer constants under a named type with **default sequential numbering from 0** (`enum days_of_week { MON, TUES, WED, THURS, FRI }` → MON=0, TUES=1, ...). Custom assignment continues from there: `enum { SUN = 1, MON, TUES }` makes MON=2, TUES=3. **Four advantages over [[CConstant|`#define`]]**: logical grouping / type safety on parameters / implicit sequential values / easy insertion-removal without renumbering neighbors. **Runtime reality check** per [[dis-2-9-1-advanced-switch|Ch 2.9.1]]: *"enumerated types print their integer values, not constant names"* — `printf("%d\n", TUES)` outputs `2`, not `"TUES"`. At runtime an `enum` *is* an [[CPrimitiveType|`int`]] with no string metadata (contrast Python `Enum` / Rust `enum`). **Natural pairing with [[SwitchStatement|`switch`]]** — the chapter's worked example dispatches on an `enum days_of_week` value with stacked labels and intentional fall-through (`case FRI:` flows into `case MON: case WED:`). ([[dis-2-9-1-advanced-switch]]).
