- [const Type Qualifier (C)](concepts/ConstQualifier.md) — The typed-variable alternative to [[CConstant|`#define`]] — `const int N = 20;` creates a real read-only variable the [[CCompiler|compiler]] type-checks and the linker can place in a read-only segment. Attempting `N = 50;` after declaration triggers *"assignment of read-only variable 'N'"*. Three-axis split vs `#define`: (a) **mechanism** — preprocessor substitution vs compiler-allocated variable; (b) **type** — none vs type-checked; (c) **scope** — file-global from definition line vs normal C scoping (block / file / function). Pointer-related forms `const int *p` (mutable pointer to const data) / `int *const p` (const pointer to mutable data) — read right-to-left; `const int *` is the canonical read-only parameter signature. **When `#define` still wins**: [[CaseLabel|`switch` case labels]] need true compile-time constants, function-like macros, file-scope array-size declarations. ([[dis-2-9-1-advanced-switch]]).
- [typedef — Three Canonical Patterns (C)](concepts/TypedefExpansion.md) — [[dis-2-9-1-advanced-switch|Ch 2.9.1]]'s formal codification of [[Typedef|`typedef`]] after [[dis-1-6-structs|Ch 1.6]] named-and-deferred and [[dis-2-7-structs|Ch 2.7]] used sparingly. **Three canonical patterns**: (1) [[CEnum|enum]] alias `typedef enum class_year classYr;` → `classYr yr;`; (2) [[CStruct|struct]] alias `typedef struct studentT studentT;` → `studentT s;`; (3) primitive-width alias `typedef unsigned long long ull;` → `ull num;` (the pattern powering `<stdint.h>`). **The idiomatic combined one-liner** `typedef struct studentT { char name[30]; int age; } studentT;` defines struct and alias in one declaration — struct tag and typedef alias can share a name because they live in different identifier namespaces. The tag-less variant `typedef struct { ... } Person;` is even more compact but blocks [[SelfReferentialStruct|self-referential]] use (linked lists / trees keep the tag form: `typedef struct node { int data; struct node *next; } Node;`). ([[dis-2-9-1-advanced-switch]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-9-2-cmd-line-args]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.2 Command Line Arguments)

- [Command Line Arguments (argc/argv)](concepts/CommandLineArguments.md) — The shell-to-program string-passing mechanism that [[dis-2-9-2-cmd-line-args|Ch 2.9.2]] exposes through the full [[MainFunction|`main`]] signature `int main(int argc, char *argv[])`. `argc` is the [[CPrimitiveType|`int`]] count of arguments **including the program name** (`./a.out 10 11 200` → `argc == 4`); `argv` is a length-`argc+1` [[CArray|`char *` array]] with `argv[0]` = program name, `argv[1]..argv[argc-1]` = user arguments, `argv[argc]` = [[NullPointer|`NULL`]] sentinel enabling `while (argv[i] != NULL)` iteration. **All arguments arrive as [[CString|C strings]]** — `./a.out 10` makes `argv[1]` point at `'1' '0' '\0'`, not the integer `10`; conversion via [[Atoi|`atoi`]] / [[Strtol|`strtol`]] (`<stdlib.h>`) is mandatory for numeric input. ([[dis-2-9-2-cmd-line-args]]).
- [main(int argc, char *argv[]) (C)](concepts/MainArgcArgv.md) — The **full form** of the [[MainFunction|`main`]] entry point that accepts [[CommandLineArguments|command-line arguments]] — the variant [[dis-2-9-2-cmd-line-args|Ch 2.9.2]] introduces to fulfill [[dis-1-1-getting-started|Ch 1.1]]'s *"full form appears later in the book"* promise. Equivalent to `int main(int argc, char **argv)` via [[ArrayDecay|array decay]]. Coexists with `int main(void)` — programs that ignore arguments may keep the simpler form, programs that read any argument must declare the `argc`/`argv` form so the runtime hands the vector to them. ([[dis-2-9-2-cmd-line-args]]).
- [strtol (C)](concepts/Strtol.md) — `long strtol(const char *str, char **endptr, int base);` — the production-grade replacement for [[Atoi|`atoi`]] that fixes all three silent failure modes: empty / non-numeric input (caller checks `*endptr == str`), trailing garbage (caller inspects `*endptr` for unparsed bytes), and [[IntegerOverflow|overflow]] (sets [[Errno|`errno`]] = `ERANGE` and returns `LONG_MAX` / `LONG_MIN`). Declared in `<stdlib.h>`. The `base` parameter accepts `2..36` literally or `0` for auto-detect (`0x` → hex, `0` → octal, else decimal). Siblings: `strtoul`, `strtoll`, `strtoull`, `strtod` / `strtof` / `strtold` (floating-point replacements for `atof`). The four-branch result check is the price honest parsing charges — exactly why production code prefers `strtol` over [[Atoi|`atoi`]]'s silence. ([[dis-2-9-2-cmd-line-args]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-9-3-voidstar]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.3 The void* Type)

- [void * (Generic Pointer, C)](concepts/VoidPointer.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] *type-erased pointer* — a [[Pointer|pointer]] that points to any data type. Per [[dis-2-9-3-voidstar|Ch 2.9.3]]: *"the `void *` type in C represents a generic pointer — a pointer to any data type."* Works because **all pointer variables have the same width on a given platform** (4 bytes on 32-bit, 8 on 64-bit) — the compiler can allocate `void *` storage without knowing the pointee type. **Cannot be directly [[DereferenceOperator|dereferenced]]** (no pointee type → no `sizeof(*p)`); programmer must [[TypeCast|recast]] via `(type *)vp` first, idiomatically `*((int *)args)`. Two canonical use cases per Ch 2.9.3: [[Malloc|`malloc`]]'s [[GenericPointer|generic-return-type]] pattern (`void *malloc(size_t)`) and [[Pthreads|pthread]] thread-main parameters (`int my_thr_main(void *args)`). Distinct from [[VoidType|`void`]] (no-value type): adding `*` produces a real, type-erased pointer type. ([[dis-2-9-3-voidstar]]).
- [Type Cast (C)](concepts/TypeCast.md) — The explicit type-conversion syntax `(target_type)expression` — the mechanism that re-specializes a generic pointer per [[dis-2-9-3-voidstar|Ch 2.9.3]]'s *"programmers must recast the parameter to access its actual type"* rule. Headline use case: `(int *)args` recovers a typed view of a [[VoidPointer|`void *`]] for [[DereferenceOperator|dereference]] / pointer-arithmetic / member access. Recast-then-dereference idiom uses **double parens**: `*((T *)vp)` — the inner pair binds the cast, the outer `*` dereferences. Other uses: numeric narrowing/widening, stripping [[ConstQualifier|`const`]] (dangerous). What casts cannot do: convert struct ↔ struct, validate type-system lies — wrong casts compile silently and crash at runtime. In modern [[CLanguage|C]] the `(T *)malloc(...)` cast is **implicit** ([[VoidPointer|`void *`]] assigns to any pointer type); explicit cast survives in legacy code and is required by [[CPlusPlus|C++]]. ([[dis-2-9-3-voidstar]]).
- [Generic Pointer (Design Pattern)](concepts/GenericPointer.md) — The design pattern of a pointer that refers to *any* data type — [[CLanguage|C]] implements it via [[VoidPointer|`void *`]]. The language's escape hatch for **type-erased programming** (no templates, no generics, no dynamic typing — `void *` is how one function or one storage cell works across all pointer-bearing types). **Three canonical uses**: (1) **generic return type** — [[Malloc|`malloc`]] returns `void *` so one signature serves all callers; (2) **generic parameter** — [[Pthreads|pthread]] thread mains, [[Qsort|`qsort`]] comparators, generic iterators take `void *` to support any payload type; (3) **generic storage** — linked lists / hash tables holding `void *data` fields carry heterogeneous payloads. **The bargain**: trade compile-time type-checking for runtime flexibility; the programmer enforces the discipline the compiler no longer can. Most primitive form of type erasure across languages — bare address, no retained type metadata (contrast Java `Object` / Rust `&dyn` / Python `PyObject *`). ([[dis-2-9-3-voidstar]]).
- [memcpy (C)](concepts/Memcpy.md) — `void *memcpy(void *dest, const void *src, size_t n);` — the [[CStandardLibrary|`<string.h>`]] byte-level copy primitive named in [[dis-2-9-3-voidstar|Ch 2.9.3]] as a canonical [[VoidPointer|`void *`]]-bearing routine. Works on bytes, not typed objects — accepts any pointer type via [[VoidPointer|`void *`]] parameters; the [[GenericPointer|generic-pointer]] mechanism is what makes one routine serve all types. **Three rules**: (1) **no overlap** — undefined behavior if `src` and `dest` regions overlap, use `memmove` for overlap-safe copy; (2) **caller owns destination size** — same [[BufferOverflow|buffer-overflow]] footgun as [[Strcpy|`strcpy`]] / [[Strncpy|`strncpy`]]; (3) **byte-level, no type interpretation** — copies verbatim, making it the right tool for serialization, type-punning (the [[StrictAliasing|strict-aliasing]]-safe alternative to pointer casting), and generic-container payload copy. For named typed variables `=` does the same job (compiler emits `memcpy`-equivalent inline); `memcpy` is needed when types are reached through [[VoidPointer|`void *`]] parameters or byte counts are dynamic. ([[dis-2-9-3-voidstar]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-9-4-pointer-arithmetic]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.4 Pointer Arithmetic)

- [Pointer Arithmetic (C)](concepts/PointerArithmetic.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] rule that adding an integer to a [[Pointer|pointer]] advances it by that many **elements of the pointed-to type**, not by that many **bytes**. Per [[dis-2-9-4-pointer-arithmetic|Ch 2.9.4]]: *"`ptr + N` makes the pointer point `N` storage locations beyond its current value (or makes it point to `N` elements beyond the current element)."* The compiler — not the programmer — multiplies `N` by [[SizeOf|`sizeof(T)`]]. Grounds the [[ArrayIndexing|`arr[i] == *(arr + i)`]] identity and the [[ArrayDecay|array-decay]]→pointer pipeline that unifies static and [[DynamicallyAllocatedArray|dynamic arrays]] at `arr[i]`. **Cannot operate on [[VoidPointer|`void *`]]** (no `sizeof(*p)` available). Chapter's closing stance: *"we recommend against using pointer arithmetic to access array elements: it's easy to make errors and more difficult to debug when you do."* ([[dis-2-9-4-pointer-arithmetic]]).
- [Pointer Increment (C)](concepts/PointerIncrement.md) — The specialized [[PointerArithmetic|pointer-arithmetic]] form `ptr++` / `++ptr` / `ptr--` / `--ptr` / `ptr += N` that advances a [[Pointer|pointer]] by one (or N) elements of its pointed-to type. Per [[dis-2-9-4-pointer-arithmetic|Ch 2.9.4]]: *"when incremented, a pointer points to the next storage location of the type it points to."* Byte stride is `sizeof(*ptr)` — 1 for `char *`, 4 for `int *`, 8 for `double *` — *"the compiler generates code to add the appropriate number of bytes."* Powers the canonical [[CString|C-string]] copy idiom `while ((*dst++ = *src++) != '\0');`. Precedence footgun: `*ptr++` reads element then advances; `(*ptr)++` increments the **pointee** value. One-past-the-end is legal to **compute** as a loop sentinel but undefined to dereference. ([[dis-2-9-4-pointer-arithmetic]]).
- [Pointer Difference (C)](concepts/PointerDifference.md) — The subtractive companion: given two same-type pointers into the same array, `p1 - p2` yields the **element-count distance** between them as a `ptrdiff_t` (signed, `<stddef.h>`). The compiler divides the raw byte distance by [[SizeOf|`sizeof(T)`]] to return elements. Canonical use cases: substring offset `strstr(haystack, needle) - haystack`, two-cursor iteration distance, slice length from `(begin, end)` boundary pointers. Subtracting pointers into **different** arrays is [[UndefinedBehavior|undefined behavior]]. Not directly treated by [[dis-2-9-4-pointer-arithmetic|Ch 2.9.4]] but is the natural completion of its element-count model — included for symmetry with [[PointerIncrement|increment]]. ([[dis-2-9-4-pointer-arithmetic]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.6 Writing and Using Your Own C Libraries)

- [Header Guard](concepts/HeaderGuard.md) — The canonical [[CLanguage|C]] idiom `#ifndef _MYLIB_H_ / #define _MYLIB_H_ / ... / #endif` wrapping every [[HeaderFile|`.h` file]] to prevent multi-inclusion in one translation unit. First `#include` defines the macro and exposes the body; subsequent `#include`s of the same header see the macro defined and the [[PreprocessorDirective|preprocessor]] elides the body. Solves the **diamond-include** pattern that otherwise duplicates [[CStruct|struct]] / [[CEnum|enum]] / [[Typedef|typedef]] definitions and breaks stage-2 compilation. Macro-name convention `_MYLIB_H_` is stylistic — alternates include `MYLIB_H` and the non-standard `#pragma once`. ([[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries]]).
- [Include Guard](concepts/IncludeGuard.md) — Industry-standard synonym for [[HeaderGuard|header guard]] — the `#ifndef`/`#define`/`#endif` wrapper around a [[HeaderFile|header file]]. *Header guard* names what is guarded; *include guard* names what is prevented. Same mechanism; see [[HeaderGuard]] for the full treatment. ([[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries]]).
- [ar (Archive Utility)](concepts/ArCommand.md) — The [[Unix|Unix]] archiver that bundles [[ObjectFile|`.o` files]] into a [[StaticLibrary|`lib<name>.a` static archive]]. Canonical invocation per [[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries|Ch 2.9.6]]: `ar -rcs libmylib.a mylib.o`, where `r` inserts with replacement, `c` creates if absent, `s` writes the symbol index (same job as the now-historical [[Ranlib|`ranlib`]]). `ar` doesn't modify the `.o` files — concatenates them with a header and symbol index; at [[LinkingStage|stage-4]] [[Linker|`ld`]] uses the index to pull only the archive members satisfying unresolved references. Predates `tar`; survives almost exclusively for `.a` libraries and Debian `.deb` packages. ([[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries]]).
- [Position-Independent Code (-fPIC)](concepts/PositionIndependentCode.md) — [[GCC|`gcc`]]'s `-fPIC` flag generates machine code with **no absolute addresses** — all internal references via PC-relative offsets or [[GOT|GOT]] indirection. Required for [[DynamicLibrary|shared objects]] because the [[DynamicLinker|dynamic linker]] maps each `.so` at a runtime-chosen [[AddressSpace|address]] that varies per process (and per launch under [[ASLR|ASLR]]). Per [[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries|Ch 2.9.6]]'s two-step recipe: `gcc -fPIC -c mylib.c` → `gcc -shared -o libmylib.so mylib.o`. Skipping `-fPIC` defeats memory sharing across processes, breaks SELinux text-relocation policy, and fails outright on x86-64 / ARM64. Not needed for [[StaticLibrary|`.a` archives]] (linked into one fixed-address executable). ([[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries]]).
- [static (File-Scope Linkage)](concepts/StaticFunction.md) — The [[CLanguage|C]] keyword that, when applied to a function or global at **file scope**, gives the symbol [[InternalLinkage|internal linkage]] — invisible to the [[Linker|linker]] when resolving cross-`.o` references. Per [[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries|Ch 2.9.6]] the library-author's tool for **hiding internal helpers**: `static int internal_helper(int x)` does not appear in `mylib.o`'s exported symbol table. C's **only** access-control mechanism (no `private`/`public` keywords). Unrelated coincident meaning *inside* a function: `static int n = 0;` upgrades a [[LocalVariable|local]] from [[StackSection|stack]] to [[DataSection|data segment]] with cross-call persistence. ([[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries]]).
- [Quoted Include (#include "...")](concepts/QuotedInclude.md) — The `#include "myheader.h"` form that tells the [[PreprocessorDirective|preprocessor]] to **search the current directory first**, then fall through to system paths. Per [[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries|Ch 2.9.6]] *"use quotes for local headers and angle brackets for standard library files."* Encodes author intent — *"this header lives next to my source; I control it."* [[GCC|GCC]] search order: source's directory → `-iquote` dirs → `-I` dirs → system paths. Mismatched quote-style (`<myheader.h>` for a local file) silently works only if a system install puts the header in a system path — a project-portability footgun. ([[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries]]).
- [Angle Include (#include <...>)](concepts/AngleInclude.md) — The `#include <stdio.h>` form that tells the [[PreprocessorDirective|preprocessor]] to **skip the current directory** and search only system header paths and `-I<dir>` additions. Per [[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries|Ch 2.9.6]] reserved for *"standard library files"* — [[CStandardLibrary|`<stdio.h>` / `<stdlib.h>` / `<math.h>`]] / [[PThreads|`<pthread.h>`]] / system-installed third-party headers. The C standard doesn't require system headers to be files — `<stdio.h>` may be a compiler intrinsic; angle brackets signal *"library header, resolve however you do that."* Sibling of [[QuotedInclude]]. ([[dis-2-9-6-writing-libraries]]).

### Added with [[dis-2-9-5-libraries]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 2.9.5 C Libraries: Using, Compiling and Linking)

- [C Library](concepts/CLibrary.md) — A reusable, precompiled [[CLanguage|C]] bundle in **two halves** per [[dis-2-9-5-libraries|Ch 2.9.5]]: an **API** delivered as one or more [[HeaderFile|`.h`]] files (consumed at preprocess time via [[PreprocessorDirective|`#include`]]) and an **implementation** delivered as either a [[StaticLibrary|`.a` archive]] or a [[DynamicLibrary|`.so` shared object]]. Consumed via the `-l<name>` abstraction over the literal `lib<name>.{so,a}` filename — *"this level of abstraction enables programmers to be flexible about the desired linking type."* Canonical examples: `libc` (implicit), `libm` (`-lm`), `libpthread` (`-pthread`). ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Static Library (.a archive)](concepts/StaticLibrary.md) — A [[CLibrary|C-library]] implementation packaged as a `lib<name>.a` **archive** of [[ObjectFile|`.o`]] files. At [[StaticLinking|static-link]] time the [[Linker|linker]] **copies only the archive members containing needed symbols** into the executable, producing a **self-contained binary** with no `.so` dependency at launch. Built by the author with `ar rcs libfoo.a foo*.o`; consumed via `-lfoo --static`. Larger binaries, no runtime dependencies, frozen behavior — the right choice for [[BareMetalProgramming|bare-metal]] firmware, single-file distributions, and security-frozen builds. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Dynamic Library (.so shared object)](concepts/DynamicLibrary.md) — A [[CLibrary|C-library]] implementation packaged as a `lib<name>.so` **shared object** loaded by the [[DynamicLinker|dynamic linker]] (`ld.so` / `ld-linux.so`) at **process launch**. At [[DynamicLinking|dynamic-link]] time the build-time [[Linker|linker]] only **records the symbol references**; the actual addresses resolve at [[RuntimeLinking|stage 5]]. Built with `gcc -shared -fPIC`; versioned via `libfoo.so.MAJOR` symlinks. **The default** when both `.so` and `.a` exist — wins on memory sharing (one resident `libc.so` across all processes), centralized patching, smaller binaries. Failure mode: *"cannot open shared object file"* at launch — fix via [[LDLibraryPath|`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`]]. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Linker (ld)](concepts/Linker.md) — The toolchain stage 4 ([[LinkingStage|link-edit]]) program that **resolves symbol references across [[ObjectFile|`.o`]] files and [[CLibrary|libraries]]** to produce an executable. [[GCC|`gcc`]] invokes it implicitly. Distinct from the runtime [[DynamicLinker|dynamic linker]] (`ld.so`): build-time `ld` vs. launch-time `ld.so`, different programs, complementary roles. Searches `-l<name>` against `lib<name>.so` *then* `lib<name>.a` in the search path; **prefers shared objects** when both exist per [[dis-2-9-5-libraries|Ch 2.9.5]]. Emits [[UndefinedReferenceError|*"undefined reference"*]] when a symbol cannot be matched. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Static Linking](concepts/StaticLinking.md) — The [[Linker|linker]] mode where every referenced symbol's machine code is **copied from a [[StaticLibrary|`.a` archive]] directly into the [[BinaryExecutable|executable]]** at stage 4. Forced via `--static`. The linker pulls **only the archive members containing needed symbols**, not the whole archive. Right choice when no dynamic loader exists ([[BareMetalProgramming|bare-metal]]), when frozen-behavior matters, or when single-file distribution simplifies deployment. Wrong choice when library memory sharing or centralized patching matters. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Dynamic Linking](concepts/DynamicLinking.md) — The [[Linker|linker]] mode (default on Linux) where library symbols are **referenced but not copied** at build time, with resolution deferred to [[DynamicLinker|`ld.so`]] at process launch ([[RuntimeLinking|stage 5]]). Wins: memory sharing (one `libc.so` across hundreds of processes), centralized patching, smaller binaries. Costs: ABI fragility ([[DynamicLibrary|`.so`]] version skew can break every consumer), per-launch resolution cost, runtime failure mode (*"cannot open shared object file"*). Per [[dis-2-9-5-libraries|Ch 2.9.5]]: *"the compiler can choose to dynamically link when both a shared object (`.so`) and an archive (`.a`) version of a library are available."* ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Object File (.o)](concepts/ObjectFile.md) — The binary output of stage 3 ([[AssemblyStage|assemble]]) — machine code for one translation unit with **unresolved external symbol references**. Linux uses [[ELF|ELF]] format; sections: `.text` (code), `.data` (init globals), `.bss` (zero globals), `.rodata` (constants), symbol table, relocation entries. Distinct from a complete [[BinaryExecutable|executable]] (no `.dynamic`, no entry-point, no program-header table) and from a [[StaticLibrary|`.a` archive]] (which **bundles** `.o` files). [[GCC|`gcc -c foo.c`]] stops here. Enables incremental builds and cross-language linking (Rust `.o` + C `.o`). ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Preprocessing Stage](concepts/PreprocessingStage.md) — Stage 1 of the five-stage [[CompilationProcess|compile pipeline]]. A **textual** pass that doesn't understand C syntax — interprets [[PreprocessorDirective|`#`-prefixed directives]] (`#include`, `#define`, `#if`) and produces an expanded translation unit. [[GCC|`gcc -E`]] stops here; `-I<path>` extends the header search path. Failure mode at this stage: *"foo.h: No such file or directory"* (header not on disk) — distinct from the stage-2 *"implicit declaration"* (header not `#include`d). ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Compilation Stage](concepts/CompilationStage.md) — Stage 2 of the five-stage [[CompilationProcess|compile pipeline]]. Translates the preprocessed translation unit to **target-architecture [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]]** — performs type checking, name resolution, optimization, instruction selection, register allocation. [[GCC|`gcc -S`]] stops here, emits `.s`. **Owns language-level errors**: *"implicit declaration"*, *"undeclared identifier"*, type mismatches, syntax errors. Distinct from stage 4 ([[LinkingStage|link]]) which owns symbol-resolution errors like [[UndefinedReferenceError|*"undefined reference"*]] — the [[CompilerVsLinker|stage taxonomy]]. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Assembly Stage](concepts/AssemblyStage.md) — Stage 3 of the five-stage [[CompilationProcess|compile pipeline]]. Translates `.s` [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] to machine-code [[ObjectFile|`.o` object file]] — mnemonic-to-opcode translation, symbol-table emission, relocation entries for external references, section layout into `.text` / `.data` / `.bss` / `.rodata`. [[GCC|`gcc -c`]] stops here. Almost never produces errors in normal compile-from-C workflows — purely mechanical translation; lets the toolchain also accept hand-written `.s` files via the same path. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Assembly Language](concepts/AssemblyLanguage.md) — The **human-readable text form of a machine's native instruction set** — mnemonics (`mov`, `add`, `imull`, `jmp`) and operand syntax mapping one-to-one onto [[BinaryExecutable|binary]] opcodes. Output of [[CompilationStage|stage 2 (compile)]] / input of [[AssemblyStage|stage 3 (assemble)]] in the [[CompilationProcess|compile pipeline]]. [[dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly|Ch 2.9.7]] promotes it from a forward-ref stub to a first-class artifact by showing how to emit it ([[GCC|`gcc -S`]]), read it, hand-write it, and re-feed it (`gcc -c`). Architecture-specific by definition ([[IA32]] / [[X86_64]] / [[ARM]] / [[RISCV]] each have distinct dialects) but the workflow is universal. AT&T (`mov src, dst`, `%`/`$` prefixes) vs. Intel syntax. ([[dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly]], [[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [IA32 (32-bit x86)](concepts/IA32.md) — Intel's **32-bit x86 [[ISA|ISA]]** — the dominant desktop ISA from 1985 through the mid-2000s, used by [[dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly|DIS Ch 2.9.7]]'s worked examples via the `-m32` flag. Eight 32-bit GP registers (`%eax`–`%edi`, `%esp`, `%ebp`), stack-based parameter passing, `%ebp`-relative addressing for [[LocalVariable|locals]] (`-8(%ebp)` is the first local). Superseded by [[X86_64|x86-64]] but remains the canonical pedagogical target — shorter instructions, simpler addressing, more explicit calling convention. ([[dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly]]).
- [Instruction Set Architecture (ISA)](concepts/ISA.md) — The **hardware-software contract**: the set of instructions a [[CPU]] understands, its registers, memory model, addressing modes, and binary encodings. [[CCompiler|Compilers]] target an ISA; [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly languages]] are the text form. [[dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly|Ch 2.9.7]]'s key claim: the `.c → .s → .o → executable` workflow is ISA-agnostic, the `.s` artifact is ISA-specific — *"this functionality is supported by any C compiler, and most compilers support compiling to a number of different assembly languages."* CISC ([[IA32]], [[X86_64]]) vs. RISC ([[ARM]], [[RISCV]]). The reason OS code is written in [[CLanguage|C]]: one codebase, recompile per ISA. ([[dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly]]).
- [objdump](concepts/Objdump.md) — The GNU binutils **disassembler** — the inverse of the [[AssemblyStage|assemble stage]]. `objdump -d simpleops.o` reads machine-code bytes and emits [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] mnemonics with byte offsets. [[dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly|Ch 2.9.7]] introduces it as the inspection tool for `.o` files: *"systems provide utilities that allow users to view binary files. For example, `objdump` displays the machine code and assembly code mappings in `.o` files."* Closes the loop with [[GCC|`gcc -S`]] — same assembly text, recovered from binary instead of emitted by the compiler. Useful for verifying optimizer output, inspecting libraries without source, and pairing with [[GDB|gdb]] for instruction-level debugging. ([[dis-2-9-7-c-to-assembly]]).
- [Linking Stage (Link-Editing)](concepts/LinkingStage.md) — Stage 4 of the five-stage [[CompilationProcess|compile pipeline]]. The [[Linker|`ld`]] consumes [[ObjectFile|`.o`]] files plus `-l<name>` [[CLibrary|libraries]], **matches every undefined reference to a defined symbol**, applies relocations, and emits a final [[BinaryExecutable|executable]] or [[DynamicLibrary|`.so`]]. The classical name *link-editing* distinguishes it from stage 5 ([[RuntimeLinking|runtime linking]]): build-time vs. launch-time. Selectively pulls in only the `.a` archive members needed. Signature error: [[UndefinedReferenceError|*"undefined reference to `foo`"*]] — the link-stage failure mode per [[dis-2-9-5-libraries|Ch 2.9.5]]. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Runtime Linking](concepts/RuntimeLinking.md) — Stage 5 of the five-stage [[CompilationProcess|compile pipeline]] — the **only stage that runs at process launch, not at build time**. The [[DynamicLinker|dynamic linker]] (`ld.so` / `ld-linux.so`) maps required [[DynamicLibrary|`.so`]] files into the process [[AddressSpace|address space]] and resolves deferred symbol references. Triggered by the executable's ELF `INTERP` field. Search path includes [[LDLibraryPath|`LD_LIBRARY_PATH`]] before `/etc/ld.so.cache`. Default uses lazy PLT binding; `LD_BIND_NOW=1` forces eager. The split between build-time stage 4 and launch-time stage 5 is what makes [[DynamicLinking|dynamic linking]] possible. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Dynamic Linker (ld.so / ld-linux.so)](concepts/DynamicLinker.md) — The userspace program that performs stage 5 ([[RuntimeLinking|runtime linking]]). Triggered by the Linux kernel via the ELF `INTERP` field, it loads [[DynamicLibrary|`.so`]] files, resolves [[GOT|GOT]] / [[PLT|PLT]] references, calls each library's `_init` constructors, then jumps to `_start`. **Distinct program from build-time [[Linker|`ld`]]**: similar name, complementary role. Diagnostic tools: `ldd`, `LD_DEBUG=files`, `LD_PRELOAD`, `LD_BIND_NOW`. Failure mode at launch: *"cannot open shared object file"* (the process never reaches `main`). Userspace lives so the kernel stays small and the linking protocol stays upgradable. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [LD_LIBRARY_PATH](concepts/LDLibraryPath.md) — Colon-separated env var the [[DynamicLinker|dynamic linker]] consults at process launch — the **runtime equivalent of `-L<path>`**. `-L<path>` adds to the **build-time** library search path consulted by [[Linker|`ld`]]; `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` adds to the **launch-time** search path consulted by [[DynamicLinker|`ld.so`]]. Asymmetry surprise: program **builds** fine but **won't launch** if [[DynamicLibrary|`.so`]] is in a non-standard location. Consulted **before** system caches (can override system libs — security tool and footgun). Setuid binaries **ignore** it for obvious reasons. Alternative: bake-in via `-Wl,-rpath,/some/path`. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Undefined Reference Error](concepts/UndefinedReferenceError.md) — The signature [[Linker|`ld`]] error at stage 4 ([[LinkingStage|link-edit]]): *"undefined reference to `foo`"*. Means the [[CCompiler|compiler]] **saw the prototype** (source typechecks) but the [[Linker|linker]] **could not find a binary symbol** in any `.o` / `.a` / `.so` input. Canonical cause: missing `-l<name>` — `#include <math.h>` brings the prototype, `-lm` brings the implementation. Per [[dis-2-9-5-libraries|Ch 2.9.5]]: *"missing the library gives an 'undefined reference' error from the linker `ld`; missing the header gives an 'implicit declaration' warning."* Other causes: wrong library order (single-pass `ld`), C++/Rust symbol mangling ([[ExternC]] / [[NoMangle]] fixes), architecture mismatch. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [Compiler vs Linker (Error-Stage Taxonomy)](concepts/CompilerVsLinker.md) — [[dis-2-9-5-libraries|Ch 2.9.5]]'s headline diagnostic insight: **build errors come from one of four tools at four distinct stages**, and the message identifies which to blame. Preprocessor → *"No such file or directory"* (header on disk); [[CCompiler|compiler]] → *"implicit declaration"* (header not `#include`d); [[Linker|`ld`]] → [[UndefinedReferenceError|*"undefined reference"*]] (library not linked); [[DynamicLinker|`ld.so`]] → *"cannot open shared object file"* (`.so` not findable at launch). Same `pow` call, two distinct errors (*"implicit declaration"* vs *"undefined reference"*), two distinct fixes (`#include <math.h>` vs `-lm`) — the **stage-taxonomy is the lookup key**. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).
- [C Source File (.c)](concepts/CSourceFile.md) — The **implementation half** of a [[CLanguage|C]] program or library — function bodies, global definitions, and `#include` directives for the [[HeaderFile|`.h` files]] declaring the API surface. Each `.c` is one **translation unit** — the compiler's atomic processing chunk; one `.c` → one [[ObjectFile|`.o`]] → linked. The `.c`/`.h` split is the library-author discipline: header is the API the user `#include`s, `.c` is what the author compiles into a [[StaticLibrary|`.a`]] or [[DynamicLibrary|`.so`]]. Users of a library never see the `.c`. Extension is convention, not syntax — [[GCC|`gcc`]] dispatches by extension. Library-author side deferred to [[dis-2-9-6-creating-libraries|Ch 2.9.6]]. ([[dis-2-9-5-libraries]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-1-bases]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.1 Number Bases and Unsigned Integers)

- [Number Base](concepts/NumberBase.md) — A **positional number system** with radix $B$ — an $N$-digit number $d_{N-1}\cdots d_0$ denotes $\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} d_i \cdot B^i$, with digits $\in\{0,\ldots,B-1\}$. The unifying framework [[dis-4-1-bases|Ch 4.1]] uses to instantiate decimal ($B=10$) / [[BinaryNumber|binary]] ($B=2$) / [[OctalNumber|octal]] ($B=8$) / [[HexadecimalNumber|hexadecimal]] ($B=16$) — *"the position of each digit in the number determines how important that digit is to the overall value."* ([[dis-4-1-bases]]).
- [Binary Number (Base 2)](concepts/BinaryNumber.md) — A number expressed in [[NumberBase|base]] $B=2$ using digits $\{0,1\}$ (each a **bit**); $N$-bit value is $\sum b_i \cdot 2^i$. The **native form of data inside [[ComputerHardware|hardware]]**; every other base is a human-readable proxy. Ch 4.1's worked examples: `0b1000 = 8`, `0b10110100 = 180`. ([[dis-4-1-bases]]).
- [Hexadecimal Number (Base 16)](concepts/HexadecimalNumber.md) — A number in [[NumberBase|base]] $B=16$ using digits $\{0\text{–}9, A\text{–}F\}$ ($A=10,\ldots,F=15$). Because $16=2^4$, **one hex digit packs exactly four bits** — the reason hex dominates as the compact display form for [[BinaryRepresentation|binary data]] (memory dumps, machine code, pointer addresses, [[GdbExamineMemory|`x/nfu`]] output). Ch 4.1's worked example: `0x23C8 = 2·4096 + 3·256 + 12·16 + 8 = 9160`. ([[dis-4-1-bases]]).
- [Octal Number (Base 8)](concepts/OctalNumber.md) — A number in [[NumberBase|base]] $B=8$ using digits $\{0\text{–}7\}$. Because $8=2^3$, **one octal digit packs exactly three bits**. Historically dominant on PDP-era 3-bit-aligned word widths, mostly displaced by [[HexadecimalNumber|hex]] on modern 4/8/16/32/64-bit machines; survives in Unix `chmod 755` permissions and as the notorious leading-`0` numeric-literal footgun in [[CLanguage|C]]. ([[dis-4-1-bases]]).
- [Unsigned Integer](concepts/UnsignedInteger.md) — A non-negative integer stored as a plain [[BinaryNumber|binary]] place-value pattern with no bit reserved for sign. An $N$-bit unsigned cell stores **$2^N$ distinct values**, the range $[0,\,2^N-1]$. Canonical: 8-bit `unsigned char` holds `0`–`255`; 32-bit `unsigned int` holds `0`–`4 294 967 295`. In [[CLanguage|C]] selected via the `unsigned` qualifier on [[CPrimitiveType|primitive types]]. Signed encodings deferred to subsequent Ch 4 sections. ([[dis-4-1-bases]]).
- [Base Prefix (0b / 0 / 0o / 0x)](concepts/BasePrefix.md) — Leading-character convention on a [[CLanguage|C]]-source numeric literal that disambiguates its [[NumberBase|base]]: `0b` → [[BinaryNumber|binary]], `0` (or modern `0o`) → [[OctalNumber|octal]], `0x` → [[HexadecimalNumber|hexadecimal]], no prefix → decimal. **Source-syntax convenience only** — `0xFF`, `0b11111111`, `0377`, and `255` all compile to the identical 8-bit byte. The bare-`0` octal form is a notorious footgun: `0755` is octal `493`, not decimal `755`. ([[dis-4-1-bases]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-2-conversion]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.2 Converting Between Bases)

- [Base Conversion](concepts/BaseConversion.md) — The umbrella algorithm-family for re-expressing an integer in a different [[NumberBase|positional system]]. [[dis-4-2-conversion|Ch 4.2]] codifies **four routes**: (1) base-$B$ → decimal via the place-value sum $\sum d_i \cdot B^i$; (2) decimal → base-$B$ via powers-of-target-base subtraction; (3) decimal → base-$B$ via [[RepeatedDivisionMethod|repeated division]] with bottom-up remainders; (4) base-$2^k$ ↔ base-$2^j$ via [[BinaryHexConversion|per-group table lookup]]. Methods 2 and 3 are interchangeable — powers-of-$B$ wins with memorized powers, repeated division wins otherwise. ([[dis-4-2-conversion]]).
- [Binary ↔ Hexadecimal Conversion](concepts/BinaryHexConversion.md) — The **arithmetic-free** [[BaseConversion|base-conversion]] shortcut between [[BinaryNumber|binary]] and [[HexadecimalNumber|hex]] derived from $16 = 2^4$: every hex digit corresponds to exactly four bits, so conversion in either direction is **per-digit table lookup with no arithmetic**. Binary → hex: partition bits into groups of four **from the right**, pad leftmost with leading zeros, look up each nibble. Worked example: `0xB491 ↔ 1011 0100 1001 0001`. Octal analog uses 3-bit groups ($8 = 2^3$); hex dominates on modern byte-aligned (8/16/32/64-bit) machines. ([[dis-4-2-conversion]]).
- [Repeated Division Method](concepts/RepeatedDivisionMethod.md) — Algorithm for **decimal → base-$B$** [[BaseConversion|conversion]]: divide by $B$ repeatedly, record each remainder as the next digit, read remainders **bottom-up**. For $B = 2$ simplifies to parity-checking — *"if the decimal value is even, the next bit should be a zero; if it's odd, the next bit should be a one"*. Worked example: $422 \to 211 \to 105 \to 52 \to 26 \to 13 \to 6 \to 3 \to 1 \to 0$ yields bits `1 1 0 1 0 0 1 1 0` → `0b110100110`. Trades memorized powers of $B$ for many small division steps — the right choice for unfamiliar bases or programmatic implementation. ([[dis-4-2-conversion]]).
- [Positional Notation](concepts/PositionalNotation.md) — The numerical-representation principle that **a digit's contribution depends on its position** within the numeral — formalized as $\sum_{i=0}^{N-1} d_i \cdot B^i$ with the rightmost digit at position 0 (least significant). Universal across [[BinaryNumber|binary]] / [[OctalNumber|octal]] / decimal / [[HexadecimalNumber|hex]] — only $B$ and the digit alphabet change. The compactness advantage: $N$ digits in base $B$ encode up to $B^N$ values, growing exponentially with width (vs. tally / sign-value systems' linear growth). Powers [[BaseConversion|base conversion]] route 1 (direct place-value sum evaluation). ([[dis-4-2-conversion]]).

### Added with [[dis-4-3-signed]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 4.3 Signed Binary Integers)

- [Signed Integer](concepts/SignedInteger.md) — A fixed-width binary encoding that represents both non-negative and negative integers — the foil to [[UnsignedInteger|unsigned integers]]. Per [[dis-4-3-signed|Ch 4.3]], signed integers are an **interpretation layer** over plain [[BinaryNumber|binary]] bit patterns. Two historical schemes: [[SignMagnitude|sign-magnitude]] (obsolete, dual-zero pathology) and [[TwosComplement|two's complement]] (universal modern standard, unique zero, asymmetric range $[-2^{N-1},\,2^{N-1}-1]$). [[OnesComplement|One's complement]] not covered by Ch 4.3. ([[dis-4-3-signed]]).
- [Two's Complement](concepts/TwosComplement.md) — The universal modern [[SignedInteger|signed-integer]] encoding: the [[MostSignificantBit|MSB]] is reinterpreted as a place-value digit with **negative weight** $-2^{N-1}$, giving the value formula $-(d_{N-1} \cdot 2^{N-1}) + \sum_{i<N-1} d_i \cdot 2^i$. **Unique zero** (eliminating [[SignMagnitude|sign-magnitude]]'s dual-zero pathology), **asymmetric range** $[-2^{N-1},\,2^{N-1}-1]$ (one more negative than positive — 4-bit range `-8`–`+7`). Negation recipe: *"flip all the bits and add one"* — worked example $13 \to$ `0b00001101` → `0b11110010` → `0b11110011 = −13`. The reason modern hardware adopts it: ordinary unsigned-binary adder hardware produces the correct signed-result bit pattern without sign-special-case logic. ([[dis-4-3-signed]]).
- [Sign Bit](concepts/SignBit.md) — The [[MostSignificantBit|most-significant bit]] of a [[SignedInteger|signed-integer]] bit pattern; signals non-negative (0) vs negative (1). In [[SignMagnitude|sign-magnitude]] it's a **pure flag** (the other bits hold the absolute magnitude, negation flips just this bit). In [[TwosComplement|two's complement]] it plays a **dual role** — both sign indicator **and** a place-value digit with negative weight $-2^{N-1}$ in the value formula; negation requires flipping all bits plus adding 1, not just the sign bit. The sign-direction convention is shared across both schemes — `0b0xxx…` is non-negative, `0b1xxx…` is negative — exposed at the [[CpuRegister|CPU level]] as x86's SF flag and tested by `JS`/`JNS` branches. ([[dis-4-3-signed]]).
- [Sign-Magnitude Representation](concepts/SignMagnitude.md) — A historical [[SignedInteger|signed-integer]] encoding where the [[MostSignificantBit|MSB]] is a pure [[SignBit|sign flag]] (0 = +, 1 = −) and the remaining $N-1$ bits encode the absolute magnitude as plain unsigned binary. Value formula: $(-1)^s \cdot \sum d_i \cdot 2^i$. **Fatal flaw**: two zero representations (`0b0000 = +0`, `0b1000 = −0`) — *"no modern systems use signed magnitude"* (Ch 4.3). Displaced by [[TwosComplement|two's complement]] for integers, but **survives** as the sign convention in [[FloatingPointNumber|IEEE 754 floating-point]] mantissas — the same dual-zero property becomes a defined feature there (`+0.0` vs `−0.0` with `1.0 / +0.0 = +∞` and `1.0 / −0.0 = −∞`). ([[dis-4-3-signed]]).
- [Sign Extension](concepts/SignExtension.md) — The operation that widens a [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] value from $N$ bits to $M > N$ bits while preserving its sign and value: **replicate the [[MostSignificantBit|high-order bit]]** into the new positions — *"non-negative numbers prepend zeros; negative numbers prepend ones"* (Ch 4.3). The unsigned dual is **zero extension** (always prepend zeros) — applying it to a signed value silently turns `-1` (`0b11111111`) into `255` (`0b0000_0000_1111_1111`). Hardware manifestations: x86 `movsx` / `movsxd` / `sar`; ARM `SXTB` / `SXTH`. In [[CLanguage|C]] it's implicit at signed-type widening (`(int)(signed char)0xFF == -1`) and at arithmetic shift right of signed types. ([[dis-4-3-signed]]).

### Added with [[dis-9-5-arm64-functions]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 9.5 Functions in Assembly (ARM64))

- [AAPCS64 (ARM64 Calling Convention)](concepts/ARM64CallingConvention.md) — The **[[ARM64|AArch64]] calling convention** per [[dis-9-5-arm64-functions|Ch 9.5]] — ABI contract every function-call boundary follows. **Argument-passing**: first **eight** parameters in `x0`–`x7` (doubles [[SystemVCallingConvention|System V AMD64]]'s 6-register fast path; fully eliminates [[CdeclCallingConvention|cdecl]]'s stack-only); 9+ on stack. Floating-point args in `s0`–`s7` / `d0`–`d7`. **Return value** in `x0` (or `w0` for 32-bit). **[[LinkRegister|`x30`]]** = link register (return address); **[[FramePointer|`x29`]]** = frame pointer; **[[StackPointer|`sp`]]** = stack pointer (16-byte aligned at every call boundary). **Caller-saved**: `x0`–`x18`; **callee-saved**: `x19`–`x28`. Cross-ISA: AAPCS64 8 regs > [[SystemVCallingConvention|System V]] 6 > [[CdeclCallingConvention|cdecl]] 0 — the [[RISC]] design tradeoff for the larger [[AArch64Registers|31-GPR]] register file. ([[dis-9-5-arm64-functions]]).
- [ARM64 Function Prologue / Epilogue](concepts/ARM64FunctionPrologue.md) — The **canonical [[ARM64]] function-entry/exit idiom** per [[dis-9-5-arm64-functions|Ch 9.5]] / [[dis-9-6-arm64-recursion|Ch 9.6]]. **Prologue**: `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-N]!` (pre-indexed — decrement `sp` by `N`, store fp+lr at new top, one instruction). **Epilogue**: `ldp x29, x30, [sp], #N` (post-indexed — load fp+lr from top, then increment `sp`) + [[ARM64Ret|`ret`]]. **No `push`/`pop` instructions on [[ARM64]]** — replaced by [[ARM64AddressingMode|pre-/post-indexed `stp` / `ldp`]] from [[dis-9-2-arm64-common|Ch 9.2]]. Collapses what [[X86_64|x86-64]] expresses as three instructions (`sub` + two `mov`s) into one. Frame size `N` must be a multiple of **16** (AAPCS64 alignment); typical sizes 16 (fp+lr only), 32 (+16B locals), more for larger frames. Pre-indexed vs post-indexed asymmetry is structural — allocate before write, free after read. Leaf functions may skip the `x30` save entirely. ([[dis-9-5-arm64-functions]], [[dis-9-6-arm64-recursion]]).
- [Link Register (`x30`)](concepts/LinkRegister.md) — The **dedicated GPR holding the return address** during an active [[ARM64]] function call per [[dis-9-5-arm64-functions|Ch 9.5]]. [[ARM64BranchAndLink|`bl addr`]] *"sets `x30 = pc + 4` and sets `pc = addr`"*; [[ARM64Ret|`ret`]] *"sets `pc = x30`"* — pure register-to-register, no memory access. **[[RISC]] family invariant**: [[ARM64]] / [[RISCV]] / MIPS all use a register; [[CISC]] [[X86_64]] / [[IA32]] push to stack via [[CallInstruction|`callq` / `call`]]. **Single register ⇒ non-leaf functions must spill `x30` to the stack** in the [[ARM64FunctionPrologue|prologue]] via `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-N]!` — otherwise nested `bl` overwrites the outer return address. **Leaf functions structurally immune** to [[ReturnAddressOverwrite|return-address overwrite]] buffer-overflow attacks (no stack-resident return address) — a partial structural defense [[X86_64|x86]] / [[IA32]] cannot offer; non-leaf functions equivalent post-spill ([[dis-9-10-arm64-buffer-overflow|Ch 9.10]]). ([[dis-9-5-arm64-functions]], [[dis-9-6-arm64-recursion]], [[dis-9-10-arm64-buffer-overflow]]).
- [ARM64 `bl` (Branch and Link)](concepts/ARM64BranchAndLink.md) — The **[[ARM64]] structured-call instruction** per [[dis-9-5-arm64-functions|Ch 9.5]] — [[RISC]] analog of [[X86_64|x86]]'s [[CallInstruction|`callq`]]. Single atomic semantics: `x30 = pc + 4; pc = addr` — save return address into [[LinkRegister|`x30`]] then jump. **No stack manipulation** (`sp` unchanged) — contrast [[X86_64|x86]] [[CallInstruction|`callq`]] which **pushes** return address to stack. PC-relative immediate has **±128 MB range** (26-bit signed). Family: `bl addr` (PC-relative), `blr xN` (indirect, no range limit), peer `b addr` / `br xN` for branch-without-link (tail call / goto). The unlinked `b` / `br` do **not** write `x30` — preserves the caller's return address. ([[dis-9-5-arm64-functions]]).
- [ARM64 `ret` Instruction](concepts/ARM64Ret.md) — The **[[ARM64]] function-return instruction** per [[dis-9-5-arm64-functions|Ch 9.5]] — [[RISC]] analog of [[X86_64|x86]]'s [[RetInstruction|`retq`]]. Semantics: `pc = x30` (or `pc = xN` for explicit `ret xN` form). **No stack manipulation** — `sp` unchanged; the load of `x30` from the spilled stack slot happens **separately** in the [[ARM64FunctionPrologue|epilogue]] via `ldp x29, x30, [sp], #N` (contrast [[X86_64|x86]] [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] which combines pop + jump). Leaf functions omit the `ldp` entirely — `x30` still holds the value [[ARM64BranchAndLink|`bl`]] wrote at entry. Encoded as a hint-form alias of `br x30` to feed the branch predictor's return-address-prediction stack. Return value in `x0` / `w0` at the moment `ret` executes ([[ARM64CallingConvention|AAPCS64]] contract). ([[dis-9-5-arm64-functions]]).

### Added with [[dis-9-4-1-arm64-preliminaries]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 9.4.1 Preliminaries (ARM64 Conditional Control))

- [ARM64 NZCV Flag Register](concepts/ARM64FlagsRegister.md) — The **[[ARM64]] condition-flag register** per [[dis-9-4-1-arm64-preliminaries|Ch 9.4.1]] — four single-bit flags inside `PSTATE` (the [[ARM64]] processor-state register): **N** (negative — MSB of result = 1 under [[TwosComplement|two's complement]]), **Z** (zero — result == 0), **C** (carry / borrow — *inverted polarity from [[X86FlagsRegister|x86 CF]]*: `cmp` sets C=1 when subtraction does **not** borrow), **V** (signed overflow). Structural analog of [[X86FlagsRegister|x86 FLAGS]]'s ZF/SF/OF/CF with **three structural deltas**: (1) flag-setting is **opt-in via `s` suffix** on the producer (`adds`, `subs`, `ands`) rather than default-on; (2) inverted borrow polarity; (3) lives inside `PSTATE` as an aggregate, not a dedicated `%eflags`-style register. The signed/unsigned interpretation split is encoded in the **consumer suffix** (`lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` consume N+V; `lo`/`ls`/`hi`/`hs` consume C), not in the producer. Consumed by [[ARM64ConditionalBranch|`b.cond`]] and [[ARM64ConditionalSelect|`csel`]]. ([[dis-9-4-1-arm64-preliminaries]], [[dis-9-3-arm64-arithmetic]]).
- [ARM64 cmp / cmn / tst](concepts/ARM64Cmp.md) — The **flag-only comparison family** on [[ARM64]] per [[dis-9-4-1-arm64-preliminaries|Ch 9.4.1]] — three instructions whose entire purpose is to set [[ARM64FlagsRegister|NZCV]] and discard the arithmetic result. `cmp O1, O2` = `subs xzr, O1, O2` (subtract-and-discard); **`cmn O1, O2`** = `adds xzr, O1, O2` (add-and-discard — **compare negative**, no direct [[X86_64|x86]] equivalent, useful for comparing against negative immediates like `cmn x0, #1` testing `x0 == -1`); `tst R1, R2` = `ands xzr, R1, R2` (bitwise-AND-and-discard). Canonical zero-test idiom **`tst x0, x0`** (analog of [[X86_64|x86]]'s `test %rax, %rax`). The destination-first operand order from [[dis-9-1-arm64-basics|Ch 9.1]] reads naturally left-to-right here because the discard slot is implicit `xzr` — `cmp x0, x1` evaluates `x0 - x1` (cf. [[CmpInstruction|x86 AT&T `cmp`]] which evaluates `src2 - src1` due to the [[AtAndTSyntax|AT&T source-first quirk]]). After `cmp O1, O2`: **Z=1** ⇒ equal; **N=1** + interpret via V ⇒ signed less; **C=1** ⇒ unsigned `O1 >= O2`. ([[dis-9-4-1-arm64-preliminaries]]).
- [ARM64 Conditional Branch (b.cond family)](concepts/ARM64ConditionalBranch.md) — The **[[ARM64]] conditional-branch family** per [[dis-9-4-1-arm64-preliminaries|Ch 9.4.1]] — analog of [[X86JumpInstructions|x86 `jXX`]]. Mnemonic shape `b.<cond> <label>` with the **condition suffix dot-separated**: `b.eq` / `b.ne` / `b.lt` / `b.le` / `b.gt` / `b.ge` / `b.lo` / `b.ls` / `b.hi` / `b.hs` / `b.mi` / `b.pl` / `b.vs` / `b.vc` / `b.al`. The signed/unsigned split is **encoded in the mnemonic**: `lt`/`le`/`gt`/`ge` consume N + V (signed); `lo`/`ls`/`hi`/`hs` consume C (unsigned). **Range limit**: *"conditional branch instructions have a much more limited range (1 MB) than the `b` instruction"* — 19-bit signed offset (±1 MB) vs unconditional `b`'s 26-bit (±128 MB); long conditional jumps use a chained-branch idiom (`b.eq 1f; b far_label; 1:`). **Forward-branch shape** used for [[dis-9-4-2-arm64-if-statements|Ch 9.4.2]] [[IfStatement|`if`]]-compilation; **backward-branch shape** used for [[dis-9-4-3-arm64-loops|Ch 9.4.3]] loop-compilation. Companion zero/bit-test branches `cbz` / `cbnz` / `tbz` / `tbnz` bypass [[ARM64Cmp|`cmp`]] entirely (±32 KB range). ([[dis-9-4-1-arm64-preliminaries]], [[dis-9-4-2-arm64-if-statements]], [[dis-9-4-3-arm64-loops]]).
- [ARM64 csel (Conditional Select)](concepts/ARM64ConditionalSelect.md) — The **branch-free conditional-data-transfer** instruction on [[ARM64]] per [[dis-9-4-2-arm64-if-statements|Ch 9.4.2]] — analog of [[X86ConditionalMove|x86 `cmov`]] but **3-operand** (more expressive — destination is independent of both sources). Shape `csel D, R1, R2, cond` ⇒ `if (cond) D = R1 else D = R2`. **Both source registers are read unconditionally**; only the writeback is gated by [[ARM64FlagsRegister|NZCV]] — *"no branch instruction emitted"*, no [[ControlHazard|control hazard]] / [[BranchPrediction|branch-prediction]] cost. **Family members** (assembler aliases of `csel` encodings): `csinc` (increment second source), `csinv` (invert), `csneg` (negate), plus **`cset D, cond`** (= `D = cond ? 1 : 0`, the [[ARM64]] analog of [[X86_64|x86]] `setCC`) and **`csetm`** (= `D = cond ? -1 : 0`). **Compiler caution caveat**: *"the compiler is very cautious about optimizing branch instructions into `csel` instructions, especially in cases where side effects and pointer values are involved"* — both arms must be safely pre-evaluable (no possibly-[[NullPointerSafety|null]] pointer dereference, no side-effecting calls, no trapping division on the not-taken arm) or the compiler falls back to the [[ARM64ConditionalBranch|`b.cond`]]-based form. Same caveat as [[X86ConditionalMove|x86 `cmov`]]. ([[dis-9-4-1-arm64-preliminaries]], [[dis-9-4-2-arm64-if-statements]]).

### Added with [[dis-9-3-arm64-arithmetic]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 9.3 Arithmetic Instructions (ARMv8))

- [ARM64 Arithmetic Instructions](concepts/ARM64ArithmeticInstructions.md) — The **register-only arithmetic family** on [[ARM64]] per [[dis-9-3-arm64-arithmetic|Ch 9.3]]. Three sub-families: **basic** (`add D, O1, O2` / `sub D, O1, O2` / `neg D, O1`); **carry-variant** for extended precision (`adc` / `sbc` / `ngc` — note `~C` complement appears because [[ARM64]] sets `C` as *borrow == 0*); **multiplication / division** with **fully explicit operands** (`mul` / `udiv` / `sdiv` — **no hidden `%rax`/`%rdx`** as in [[X86MulInstruction|x86 `imul`]] / [[X86DivInstruction|x86 `idiv`]]) plus the **four-operand fused multiply-accumulate composites** (`madd D, O1, O2, O3` = `O3 + O1×O2`; `msub` = `O3 - O1×O2`; `mneg` = `-(O1×O2)`) which have **no [[CISC]] equivalent**. **Headline ISA-distinctive feature**: the **`s` suffix** (`adds` / `subs` / `ands`) toggles flag-setting at the instruction level — inlining what [[X86_64|x86]] requires as a separate [[CmpInstruction|`cmp`]] / [[TestInstruction|`test`]] instruction. ([[dis-9-3-arm64-arithmetic]]).
- [ARM64 Shift Instructions](concepts/ARM64ShiftInstructions.md) — The **four bit-shift instructions** on [[ARM64]] per [[dis-9-3-arm64-arithmetic|Ch 9.3]]: `lsl` (logical/arithmetic left shift — same for both directions), `lsr` (logical right — zero-fill upper), `asr` (arithmetic right — sign-fill upper; preserves signedness of [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]] values), `ror` (rotate right — wrap low to high). Shift amount is a **6-bit constant** (`0`–`63` for 64-bit `x`-register ops). **One left shift, two right shifts** because the fill choice splits unsigned (`lsr`) from signed (`asr`). Compilers automatically substitute `lsl D, x, #k` for `x * 2^k` and `lsr` / `asr` for `x / 2^k` — the canonical anti-premature-optimization caveat applies. **No `rol` mnemonic** — left rotate is `ror D, R, #(N - k)`. ([[dis-9-3-arm64-arithmetic]]).
- [ARM64 Bitwise Instructions](concepts/ARM64BitwiseInstructions.md) — The **bitwise instruction family** on [[ARM64]] per [[dis-9-3-arm64-arithmetic|Ch 9.3]]: four basic (`and` / `orr` / `eor` / `mvn` — note **doubled `r`** in `orr` and *exclusive-or* spelling `eor` vs [[X86BitwiseInstructions|x86 `xor`]]) plus **three [[ARM64]]-specific inverted-operand composites** (`bic D, O1, O2` = `O1 & ~O2` for *bit clear*; `orn` = `O1 | ~O2`; `eon` = `O1 ^ ~O2`) which have **no [[CISC]] equivalent** — they compress the common `mask & ~clear_bits` pattern into one instruction. **`mvn` ≠ `neg`**: `mvn` is **bitwise NOT** (flips bits, no add-1); the [[ARM64ArithmeticInstructions|`neg`]] arithmetic negation adds 1 per [[TwosComplement|two's-complement]]. **`ands`** flag-set variant inlines the [[TestInstruction|`test`]] instruction. ([[dis-9-3-arm64-arithmetic]]).

### Added with [[dis-9-2-arm64-common]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 9.2 Common ARMv8 Instructions)

- [ARM64 Data Movement Instructions](concepts/ARM64DataMovement.md) — The **only [[ARM64]] instruction family that touches memory** under the [[LoadStoreArchitecture|load/store rule]] per [[dis-9-2-arm64-common|Ch 9.2]]. **Five instructions**: `mov D, S` (**register-only** — no memory operand), `ldr D, [addr]` (load: memory → register), `str S, [addr]` (store: register → memory — note `str` puts source register first, memory second), and the **pair extensions** `ldp D1, D2, [addr]` / `stp S1, S2, [addr]` which move **two consecutive 64-bit values** in one instruction (no [[CISC]] equivalent). **Three indexing variants** on the bracketed operand: plain `[xN, #imm]` (base unchanged), pre-indexed `[xN, #imm]!` (base updated **before** access), post-indexed `[xN], #imm` (base updated **after** access). **Canonical prologue idiom**: `stp x29, x30, [sp, #-16]!` saves frame pointer + link register **and** advances `sp` in one instruction — collapsing what [[X86_64|x86-64]] expresses as three instructions (`sub` + two `mov`s). Distinct from [[X86MovInstruction|x86 `mov`]] which collapses [[ARM64]]'s three-way `mov` / `ldr` / `str` split into one mnemonic. ([[dis-9-2-arm64-common]]).

### Added with [[dis-9-1-arm64-basics]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 9.1 ARMv8 Assembly Basics)

- [ARM64 (ARMv8-A AArch64)](concepts/ARM64.md) — The **64-bit [[RISC]] [[ISA]]** developed by Arm Holdings (Apple Silicon, modern Android, AWS Graviton, [[RaspberryPi|Raspberry Pi]] 3+) — also called **AArch64**, the 64-bit execution state of [[ARMv8]]. Per [[dis-9-1-arm64-basics|Ch 9.1]]: **fixed-width 4-byte instructions**, **[[LoadStoreArchitecture|load/store architecture]]** (memory operands restricted to `ldr` / `str`), **31 general-purpose 64-bit registers** `x0`–`x30` with 32-bit `w0`–`w30` component aliases (low-32 with upper-32-zeroed-on-`wN`-write), three architectural special-purpose registers ([[StackPointer|`sp`]] / `pc` / `zr`), **destination-first** `opcode D, O1, O2` operand order (Intel-direction, **not** [[AtAndTSyntax|AT&T]]), no `%`/`$`/suffix decoration, `#`-prefixed immediates, bracketed memory. Worked example `adder2(int a)` compiles to three instructions (`str` → `ldr` → `add`) — the load/store discipline operationalized. **Not** a structural twin of [[X86_64|x86-64]] / [[IA32]] — a distinct ISA with its own register file, addressing-mode family, and operand-policy regime. ([[dis-9-1-arm64-basics]]).
- [AArch64 Register Set](concepts/AArch64Registers.md) — The **[[ARM64|AArch64]]** register file per [[dis-9-1-arm64-basics|Ch 9.1]]: **31 general-purpose 64-bit registers** `x0`–`x30` plus 32-bit component aliases `w0`–`w30` (low 32 bits; *"the upper 32 bits of the register become inaccessible, and are zeroed out"* on `wN` write — structurally analogous to [[X86_64|x86-64]]'s 32-bit-write-zeros-upper-32 rule). Only **two visible register widths** (`xN` and `wN`) — no 16-bit / 8-bit subregister hierarchy at the chapter's surface. Three architectural special-purpose registers: [[StackPointer|`sp`]] (stack pointer), `pc` (program counter — read-only at user mode), `zr` (zero register — permanently 0; the structural reason the GPR count is **31** rather than 32). Compiler picks `xN` for `long` / pointer values, `wN` for `int` values — operand width selected at the **register-name** layer, not via a mnemonic suffix as in [[X86_64]] / [[IA32]]. Cross-ISA GPR-count comparison: [[IA32]] 8 / [[X86_64]] 16 / [[ARM64]] **31** / [[RISCV]] 32 — the [[RISC]] families roughly double the [[CISC]] ones, compensating for the [[LoadStoreArchitecture|load/store]] rule's higher register pressure. ([[dis-9-1-arm64-basics]]).
- [Load/Store Architecture](concepts/LoadStoreArchitecture.md) — [[ISA]]-design discipline that **confines memory operands to two dedicated instruction classes** — `load` (memory → register) and `store` (register → memory). Every other instruction class (arithmetic, logic, shift, comparison, branch) operates **exclusively on registers and immediate constants** — memory is **never** the destination of computation. Per [[dis-9-1-arm64-basics|Ch 9.1]]: *"Data cannot be read or written to memory directly; instead, ARM follows a load/store model, which requires data to be operated on in registers."* The defining feature of [[RISC]] [[ISA|ISAs]] ([[ARM64]] / [[RISCV]] / MIPS / PowerPC); contrasts with [[CISC]]'s **register-memory** regime ([[X86_64]] / [[IA32]]) where any memory-operand instruction can take a memory source or destination. Consequences: more instructions per C operation (visible in the unoptimized `adder2`'s store-then-reload), simpler pipeline + more uniform timing, larger register file needed to absorb intermediate values ([[AArch64Registers|31 GPRs]] / [[RISCV]] 32 vs [[X86_64]] 16 / [[IA32]] 8), fixed-width 4-byte instruction encoding becomes feasible. **Not** a capability restriction — every computation expressible on [[X86_64]] is expressible on [[ARM64]]; the difference is instruction count, not power. ([[dis-9-1-arm64-basics]]).
- [ARM64 Addressing Modes](concepts/ARM64AddressingMode.md) — The **memory-operand forms** permitted on [[ARM64|AArch64]] `ldr` / `str` instructions per [[dis-9-1-arm64-basics|Ch 9.1]]. **Four bracketed forms**: `[xN]` (plain dereference — `*p`), `[xN, #imm]` (base + signed immediate offset — struct field / stack slot like `[sp, #12]`), `[xN, xM]` (base + register index), `[xN, xM, LSL, #s]` (scaled-index — base + register-index shifted left by `s` bits). The fourth form is [[ARM64]]'s analog of [[ScaledIndexAddressing|x86-64 scaled-index addressing]] with **two structural differences**: (1) **explicit shift mnemonic** (`LSL` = logical shift left) rather than a numeric scale field; (2) shift amount is a **bit count, not a byte count** — `LSL, #2` = ×4 (for `int` arrays), `LSL, #3` = ×8 (for `long` / pointer arrays). Forms appear **only** on `ldr` / `str` — no other instruction class accepts a bracketed memory operand, the [[LoadStoreArchitecture|load/store rule]] expressed at the addressing-mode-availability surface. Same effective-address space as [[X86AddressingMode|`disp(base, index, scale)`]], different surface syntax + scale-encoding convention. ([[dis-9-1-arm64-basics]]).

### Added with [[dis-8-1-ia32-basics]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 8.1 IA32 Assembly Basics)

- [cdecl Calling Convention (IA32)](concepts/CdeclCallingConvention.md) — Standard [[CallingConvention|calling convention]] for [[IA32|32-bit x86]] [[CLanguage|C]] code on Linux / macOS / BSD — **the headline ABI delta from [[X86_64|x86-64]]** per [[dis-8-1-ia32-basics|Ch 8.1]]. **All function arguments pushed on the stack** (no register-based argument passing à la [[SystemVCallingConvention|System V AMD64]]'s `%rdi`/`%rsi`/`%rdx`/`%rcx`/`%r8`/`%r9`); inside the callee, parameters at `8(%ebp)`, `12(%ebp)`, `16(%ebp)`, ... after the standard `push %ebp; mov %esp, %ebp` prologue. Return value in `%eax` (or `%edx:%eax` for 64-bit). **Caller cleanup** (vs Windows stdcall's callee cleanup) — naturally compatible with variadic functions ([[Printf|`printf`]], [[Scanf|`scanf`]]). Caller-saved: `%eax`, `%ecx`, `%edx`; callee-saved: `%ebx`, `%esi`, `%edi`, `%ebp`. ([[dis-8-1-ia32-basics]]).

### Added with [[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 7.10 Buffer Overflows (x86-64))

- [Stack Smashing](concepts/StackSmashing.md) — The [[BufferOverflow|buffer-overflow]] exploit technique that corrupts a function's [[StackFrame|stack frame]] — overwriting the saved return address — to redirect [[InstructionPointer|`%rip`]] on [[RetInstruction|`retq`]]. Canonical exploitation pattern: unbounded write → adjacent stack corruption → return-address overwrite → `retq` jumps to attacker-chosen code. Per [[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow|Ch 7.10]]'s `secret` worked example: 40-byte padding + 8-byte little-endian address (`\xda\x06\x40\x00\x00\x00\x00\x00`) redirects control to a never-normally-called `endGame()` function at `0x4006da`. ([[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow]]).
- [Return Address Overwrite](concepts/ReturnAddressOverwrite.md) — The [[StackSmashing|stack-smashing]] exploit *primitive*: the moment a [[BufferOverflow|buffer overflow]] replaces the saved return address at **`8(%rbp)`** in the current [[StackFrame|stack frame]] with attacker-controlled bytes — when the function returns via [[RetInstruction|`retq`]], [[InstructionPointer|`%rip`]] takes those bytes. The [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[CallingConvention|System V calling convention]] makes `8(%rbp)` the only stack location `retq` reads, so it is the only target an attacker needs to corrupt. Target classes: existing program functions, injected shellcode (pre-[[ExecutableSpaceProtection|NX]]), libc functions (return-to-libc), [[ReturnOrientedProgramming|ROP gadget chains]] (post-NX). ([[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow]]).
- [Stack Canary](concepts/StackCanary.md) — [[CCompiler|Compiler]]-inserted **guard value** placed between locals and the saved return address in a [[StackFrame|stack frame]]; checked at function epilogue against a known-good copy. A [[StackSmashing|linear stack-smashing]] overflow must cross the canary — mismatch → `__stack_chk_fail` aborts before `retq`. Per [[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow|Ch 7.10]]: *"a guard value in nonwriteable memory detecting stack corruption."* GCC: `-fstack-protector` / `-fstack-protector-strong`. Bypasses: value leak + replay, byte-by-byte brute force on forking servers, non-contiguous writes. ([[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow]]).
- [Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR)](concepts/AddressSpaceLayoutRandomization.md) — [[OperatingSystem|OS]]-level mitigation that **randomizes the base addresses** of process memory regions ([[StackSection|stack]], [[HeapSection|heap]], shared libraries, [[PositionIndependentCode|PIE]] executable) at process start. Defeats hardcoded-address [[StackSmashing|stack-smashing]] payloads; converts most one-shot exploits into two-stage (leak + execute) exploits. Per [[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow|Ch 7.10]]: the OS *"allocates random stack starting addresses."* Bypasses: brute force on low-entropy systems, NOP sleds, info leaks, non-PIE binaries (`.text` at fixed address). ([[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow]]).
- [Executable Space Protection (NX / DEP / W^X)](concepts/ExecutableSpaceProtection.md) — Hardware-assisted mitigation that marks [[PageTable|page-table]] entries as either **writable** *or* **executable**, never both. [[X86_64|x86-64]]'s NX bit (bit 63 of PTE) faults on instruction fetch from a non-executable page; [[ARM|ARMv8]]'s equivalent is the XN bit. Defeats classical injected-shellcode [[StackSmashing|stack smashing]] entirely. Per [[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow|Ch 7.10]]: *"restricts code execution to specific memory regions."* Bypassed by [[ReturnOrientedProgramming|ROP]] — gadget addresses point to already-executable memory, so NX has nothing to enforce. ([[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow]]).
- [Return-Oriented Programming (ROP)](concepts/ReturnOrientedProgramming.md) — The post-[[ExecutableSpaceProtection|NX]] [[StackSmashing|stack-smashing]] technique: chain pre-existing executable instruction sequences (*gadgets*) each ending in [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] to build arbitrary computation **without injecting any new code**. The stack becomes a list of gadget addresses; each `retq` advances to the next. Per [[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow|Ch 7.10]]: *"a technique cherry-picking instructions across executable regions."* Turing-complete on any moderately large code base (libc alone suffices, per Shacham 2007). Defeated by [[AddressSpaceLayoutRandomization|ASLR]] + info-leak prevention, [[ControlFlowIntegrity|CFI]], shadow stacks (Intel CET), [[ARM|ARMv8.3-A PAC]]. ([[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow]]).
- [Daemon (UNIX)](concepts/Daemon.md) — A [[UNIX]] / [[Linux]] **background process** running detached from any controlling terminal — `sshd`, `httpd`, `cron`, historically `fingerd`. Per [[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow|Ch 7.10]]: *"background process performing monitoring and cleanup tasks in UNIX systems."* Naming convention: `d` suffix. Daemons matter for security because they typically listen on network sockets, run with elevated privileges, and process untrusted input — a [[BufferOverflow|buffer overflow]] in a daemon is remote, often root, often unauthenticated. The **Morris Worm (1988)** exploited a buffer overrun in `fingerd` to propagate across UNIX hosts on the early internet — the first internet-scale security incident. ([[dis-7-10-x86-64-buffer-overflow]]).

### Added with [[dis-7-9-x86-64-structs]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 7.9 Structs in Assembly (x86-64))

- [Struct Layout](concepts/StructLayout.md) — Contiguous declaration-order arrangement of a [[CStruct|C struct]]'s [[StructMember|fields]] in memory; each field has a fixed compile-time offset the [[CCompiler|compiler]] uses to emit `disp(%base)` [[X86AddressingMode|addressing-mode]] [[X86_64|x86-64]] accesses (`mov %edx, 0x44(%rax)` ⇒ `struct.grad_yr = edx`). Declaration order is load-bearing — reordering fields can change total [[SizeOf|`sizeof`]] via differing [[StructPadding|padding]] insertion. ([[dis-7-9-x86-64-structs]]).
- [Struct Padding](concepts/StructPadding.md) — [[CCompiler|Compiler]]-inserted empty bytes between [[StructMember|struct fields]] (and trailing the struct) to satisfy the [[AlignmentRule|alignment rule]] — *"the compiler adds empty bytes as padding between fields to ensure that each field satisfies its alignment requirements"* ([[dis-7-9-x86-64-structs|Ch 7.9]]). A `char[63]` followed by an `int` forces one padding byte to push the `int` to a 4-byte boundary. Reorder largest-to-smallest to minimize total padding — the standard C-systems optimization. ([[dis-7-9-x86-64-structs]]).
- [Alignment Rule (x86-64)](concepts/AlignmentRule.md) — The [[X86_64|x86-64]] platform-level policy that **size = alignment** for every primitive type — *"x64's alignment policy requires that two-byte data types (i.e., `short`) reside at a two-byte-aligned address, four-byte data types (i.e., `int`, `float`, and `unsigned`) reside at four-byte-aligned addresses, and larger data types (`long`, `double`, and pointer data) reside at eight-byte-aligned addresses"* ([[dis-7-9-x86-64-structs|Ch 7.9]]). Drives [[StructPadding|struct padding]]; companion to the [[CallingConvention|System V AMD64]] **16-byte stack alignment** rule at `callq` boundaries. ([[dis-7-9-x86-64-structs]]).
- [Memory Alignment](concepts/MemoryAlignment.md) — General hardware principle that data items should reside at addresses that are multiples of their size (or word/cache-line size). Motivated by **single-transaction memory access**, **atomicity** of word-sized reads/writes, **single-cache-line non-straddling**, and stricter ISAs ([[ARM]]) faulting on misaligned access via [[SIGBUS]]. The [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AlignmentRule|alignment rule]] is the specific instantiation [[dis-7-9-x86-64-structs|Ch 7.9]] codifies; [[Malloc|`malloc`]] returns pointers aligned to `alignof(max_align_t)`. ([[dis-7-9-x86-64-structs]]).

### Added with [[dis-7-8-x86-64-matrices]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 7.8 Matrices in Assembly (x86-64))

- *No new concept pages.* Ch 7.8 reuses the existing [[MultidimensionalArray]] / [[RowMajorOrder]] / [[ArrayOfArrays]] / [[AsmArrayAccess]] / [[ScaledIndexAddressing]] / [[LeaInstruction]] / [[X86MulInstruction]] machinery — the chapter's novelty is the **compilation pattern** that maps the [[dis-2-5-arrays|Ch 2.5]] source-level 2-D-array layout choice (contiguous vs array-of-arrays) onto the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] surface as **single linear offset** vs **two-stage pointer chase**. ([[dis-7-8-x86-64-matrices]]).

### Added with [[dis-7-7-x86-64-arrays]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 7.7 Arrays in Assembly (x86-64))

- [Array Access Compilation Pattern (x86-64 Assembly)](concepts/AsmArrayAccess.md) — The canonical [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] pattern for compiling [[CLanguage|C]] [[CArray|array]] access — `arr[i]` → `mov (%rdx, %rcx, 4), %eax` (one instruction via [[ScaledIndexAddressing|scaled-index addressing]] with `scale = sizeof(T)`), `&arr[3]` → `lea 0xc(%rdx), %rax` (constant-index degenerate form, scale folded into displacement), `*(arr+5)` → identical to `arr[5]` ([[ArrayDecay|array decay]] equivalence). Walked example: `sumArray` using `cltq` to widen 32-bit `int` index to 64-bit, then [[LeaInstruction|`lea 0x0(,%rax,4),%rdx`]] to materialize `i*4` without memory access. Scale-factor selection is automatic per element type. ([[dis-7-7-x86-64-arrays]]).
- [Scaled-Index Addressing Mode (x86-64)](concepts/ScaledIndexAddressing.md) — The full form of the [[X86_64|x86-64]] memory operand `disp(base, index, scale)` per [[dis-7-7-x86-64-arrays|Ch 7.7]] — computes `base + index*scale + displacement` in hardware as part of a single instruction. **`scale` ∈ `{1, 2, 4, 8}`** — hardware-encoded restriction matching exactly the [[CLanguage|C]] primitive-type size set (`char`/`short`/`int`/`long`/pointer). Collapses three instructions (`imul` + `add` + `mov`) into one. Degenerate forms when operands are missing — constant-index `arr[3]` folds `3*4 = 12` into `disp`. Reused by [[LeaInstruction|`lea`]] for non-memory arithmetic. **Promoted from named-only reference** in [[dis-7-1-x86-64-basics|Ch 7.1]]'s [[X86AddressingMode|addressing-mode table]]. ([[dis-7-7-x86-64-arrays]], [[dis-7-1-x86-64-basics]]).

### Added with [[dis-7-6-x86-64-recursion]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 7.6 Recursion (x86-64))

- [Recursion](concepts/Recursion.md) — The [[ComputerScience|CS]] pattern in which a [[Function|function]] **invokes itself** as part of computing its result. **Promoted from forward-reference** by [[dis-7-6-x86-64-recursion|Ch 7.6]] — operationalized at the [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] level via the `sumr` worked example. Two-case structure (base case: input(s) returning directly without further calls; recursive case: input(s) calling self on a strictly smaller sub-problem); each invocation gets its own [[StackFrame|stack frame]]; recursion depth $d$ ⇒ $d + 1$ live frames stacked along the [[CallStack|call stack]]; the recursive [[CallInstruction|`callq`]] is structurally identical to any other call — recursion requires **no new instructions** beyond the [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]] apparatus. The `sumr` example is **not** tail-recursive (the `add` happens *after* the recursive call returns) — [[TailRecursion|tail-call optimization]] flagged as forward-reference. ([[dis-7-6-x86-64-recursion]]).
- [Call Stack](concepts/CallStack.md) — The LIFO sequence of [[StackFrame|stack frames]] representing every currently-active [[Function|function]] invocation along a single thread of execution. **Promoted from forward reference** (used since [[dis-7-2-x86-64-common|Ch 7.2]]'s `adder2` trace tracked call-stack state at each step, by [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]]'s [[CallInstruction|`callq`]] / [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] / [[LeaveInstruction|`leaveq`]] treatment, and by [[StackPointer]] / [[X86StackInstructions]] / [[CallInstruction]] concept pages) to first-class page. Synonym for [[ExecutionStack]] (the source-level term [[dis-1-4-functions|Ch 1.4]] uses). [[X86_64|x86-64]] realization: grows downward; frames bracketed by [[StackPointer|`%rsp`]] (top) and [[FramePointer|`%rbp`]] (base); saved-`%rbp` values form a backward-linked frame chain (basis for [[GDB|debugger]] `backtrace`); return addresses interleaved with frame data. [[Recursion|Recursive]] call chains stack the same function multiple times — the call-stack realization of recursion's linear stack-depth cost. ([[dis-7-6-x86-64-recursion]]).

### Added with [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 7.5 Functions in Assembly (x86-64))

- [x86-64 `callq` Instruction](concepts/CallInstruction.md) — [[X86_64|x86-64]]'s **function-call primitive** per [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]] — *"pushes the current value of [[InstructionPointer|`%rip`]] onto the stack and jumps to the function address"*. Atomic save-return-address-then-jump pair; equivalent to `sub $0x8, %rsp; mov %rip, (%rsp); jmp addr`. Every `callq` must be matched by exactly one [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] on every callee control path — the stack-discipline invariant whose violation is the foundation of [[BufferOverflow|stack-buffer-overflow]] exploits. ([[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions]]).
- [x86-64 `retq` Instruction](concepts/RetInstruction.md) — [[X86_64|x86-64]]'s **function-return primitive** per [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]] — *"pops the saved return address from the stack back into [[InstructionPointer|`%rip`]]"*. Operand-free: source is always `(%rsp)`, destination is always `%rip`. Preconditions: `%rsp` must point to the saved return address ([[LeaveInstruction|`leaveq`]] ensures this) and the pushed address must not be tampered with (else attacker-controlled control flow). ([[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions]]).
- [x86-64 `leaveq` Instruction](concepts/LeaveInstruction.md) — [[X86_64|x86-64]]'s **function-epilogue helper** per [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]] — *"equivalent to `mov %rbp, %rsp` then `pop %rbp`"*. Bundles the standard stack-frame teardown into one instruction; sets `%rsp` to the saved-return-address slot (the precondition [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] requires). Omitted when the function omits its frame pointer (`-fomit-frame-pointer`). ([[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions]]).
- [Calling Convention](concepts/CallingConvention.md) — The **ABI contract** between caller and callee at a function-call boundary — which registers hold which arguments, who preserves which registers, how the stack is laid out. Ch 7.5 covers **System V AMD64** (Linux / macOS / BSD x86-64): first 6 args in `%rdi`/`%rsi`/`%rdx`/`%rcx`/`%r8`/`%r9`, 7+ on stack, return in `%rax`, [[CallerSavedRegister|caller-saved]] (`%rax`/`%rcx`/`%rdx`/`%rsi`/`%rdi`/`%r8`–`%r11`) vs [[CalleeSavedRegister|callee-saved]] (`%rbx`/`%rbp`/`%r12`–`%r15`) split. Different from Microsoft x64 (Windows) and IA32 cdecl. ([[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions]]).
- [Caller-Saved Register](concepts/CallerSavedRegister.md) — Register the **caller** must preserve across a [[CallInstruction|`callq`]] boundary; callee may freely clobber. System V x86-64 set: `%rax`, `%rcx`, `%rdx`, `%rsi`, `%rdi`, `%r8`, `%r9`, `%r10`, `%r11`. Overlaps with argument-passing registers (the caller is already writing them at the call site). Allocator's home for short-lived temporaries whose live range doesn't cross calls. ([[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions]]).
- [Callee-Saved Register](concepts/CalleeSavedRegister.md) — Register the **callee** must preserve across a [[CallInstruction|`callq`]] boundary; saved+restored via push/pop in prologue/epilogue. System V x86-64 set: `%rbx`, `%rbp`, `%r12`–`%r15` (plus `%rsp` implicitly via [[LeaveInstruction|`leaveq`]]). Allocator's home for long-lived variables whose live range crosses calls. ([[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions]]).
- [Stack Pointer (`%rsp`)](concepts/StackPointer.md) — [[X86_64|x86-64]] special-purpose register that **always points to the top of the [[CallStack|call stack]]** per [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]]. **Promoted from forward reference** (first flagged in [[dis-7-2-x86-64-common|Ch 7.2]]) to first-class page. Adjusted by every [[X86StackInstructions|`push` / `pop`]] / [[CallInstruction|`callq`]] / [[RetInstruction|`retq`]] / [[LeaveInstruction|`leaveq`]]. Stack-grows-down: push decrements, pop increments. System V ABI requires 16-byte alignment at call sites. ([[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions]]).
- [Frame Pointer (`%rbp`)](concepts/FramePointer.md) — [[X86_64|x86-64]] special-purpose register that **points to the base of the current [[StackFrame|stack frame]]** per [[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions|Ch 7.5]]. **Promoted from forward reference** (first flagged in [[dis-7-2-x86-64-common|Ch 7.2]]) to first-class page. Established in prologue (`push %rbp; mov %rsp, %rbp`), held constant for function lifetime as stable anchor for `[disp](%rbp)` local/arg access, restored in epilogue via [[LeaveInstruction|`leaveq`]]. Saved-`%rbp` values form a backward chain through frames — basis for [[GDB|debugger]] `backtrace`. Callee-saved under System V. ([[dis-7-5-x86-64-functions]]).

### Added with [[dis-7-4-3-x86-64-loops]] (Dive into Systems — Ch 7.4.3 Loops in Assembly, x86-64)

- [Loop Compilation Pattern (x86-64 Assembly)](concepts/AsmLoopPattern.md) — The **canonical [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[AssemblyLanguage|assembly]] compilation pattern** for [[CLanguage|C]]'s three loop constructs — [[WhileLoop|`while`]], [[ForLoop|`for`]], [[DoWhileLoop|`do`–`while`]] — per [[dis-7-4-3-x86-64-loops|Ch 7.4.3]]. The [[X86_64|x86-64]] [[InstructionSet|ISA]] has **no dedicated loop instruction**; the compiler synthesizes loop semantics out of the [[dis-7-4-1-x86-64-preliminaries|Ch 7.4.1]] primitives — [[CmpInstruction|`cmp`]] + the [[X86JumpInstructions|jump-instruction family]] reading [[X86FlagsRegister|FLAGS]] — in **two structural forms**: **Form 1** (test-first, `while`/`for`) — leading unconditional [[X86JumpInstructions|`jmp`]] to the condition check, then body, then `cmp` + **backward conditional jump on the un-negated condition** (`jle body` for `i <= n`); **Form 2** (test-last, `do`–`while`) — **drops the leading `jmp`** because the body executes unconditionally on first entry, so the pattern collapses to body → `cmp` → backward conditional jump.
